stem: A development team uses AWS CodePipeline to deploy a microservices application to Amazon ECS. The team wants to implement a blue/green deployment strategy that automatically rolls back if the new version's error rate exceeds 5% during a 10-minute evaluation period. Which configuration achieves this requirement?

options.text: Configure CodePipeline to deploy a new ECS service behind a separate target group. Use an Application Load Balancer listener rule with weighted routing and a Step Functions workflow that monitors CloudWatch error metrics and shifts DNS weights.

Configure CodePipeline with an ECS rolling update deployment action. Create a CloudWatch composite alarm combining 5xx error rate and latency metrics, then use an EventBridge rule to trigger a Lambda function that calls the ECS UpdateService API to revert.

Configure CodePipeline with a CodeDeploy EC2 in-place deployment action. Attach a CloudWatch alarm on the Application Load Balancer TargetResponseTime metric and enable CodeDeploy automatic rollback on alarm state to revert to the previous task definition.

Configure CodePipeline with a CodeDeploy ECS blue/green deployment action. Set up a CloudWatch alarm monitoring HTTP 5xx error rate with a 5% threshold and attach the alarm to CodeDeploy's automatic rollback configuration for deployment monitoring.

explanation: D is correct: the CodeDeploy ECS compute platform performs a true blue/green deployment by creating a replacement task set behind a second target group, shifting the ALB production listener to it, and then holding the original task set for a bake period. CodeDeploy's automatic rollback configuration accepts CloudWatch alarms, so an alarm on the ALB/target-group HTTP 5xx error rate at a 5% threshold that breaches during the 10-minute monitoring window makes CodeDeploy shift the listener straight back to the original task set. A is incorrect because it hand-builds blue/green with Step Functions and weighted DNS: it is all custom orchestration, and DNS weight changes are subject to resolver and client caching, so rollback is not immediate. B is incorrect because an ECS rolling update replaces tasks in place, so there is no preserved previous environment to fail back to; reverting via UpdateService triggers another slow rolling replacement. C is incorrect because the CodeDeploy EC2/On-Premises in-place deployment type cannot deploy ECS task definitions, and TargetResponseTime measures latency, not error rate.

stem: A company manages infrastructure across 15 AWS accounts using AWS CloudFormation. Engineers occasionally make manual console changes that cause stack drift. The company wants to detect drift automatically and alert the team, while still allowing emergency changes with proper documentation. Which approach BEST addresses this?

options.text: Use CloudTrail to log all API calls and create EventBridge rules that match resource modification events. Compare events against CloudFormation change sets using a Lambda function and notify via SNS when unmanaged changes occur.

Enable AWS Config rules to detect CloudFormation stack drift on a schedule. Use an SNS topic to notify the team when drift is detected, and require engineers to tag emergency changes with a change request ID for audit tracking.

Schedule a Lambda function to call the CloudFormation DetectStackDrift API for all stacks hourly. Publish drift results to an SNS topic, and implement an SCP that denies all resource modifications except through CloudFormation service principal.

Deploy AWS Config with the cloudformation-stack-drift-detection-check managed rule across all accounts via AWS Organizations. Send non-compliant findings to a centralized SNS topic and use SCP exemption with a condition key for emergency roles.

explanation: D is correct: the AWS Config managed rule cloudformation-stack-drift-detection-check invokes drift detection on each stack and reports NON_COMPLIANT when a stack or any of its resources has drifted. Deploying it as an organization Config rule or conformance pack from the delegated administrator covers all 15 accounts from one definition, with findings routed to a central SNS topic. SCPs that exempt a documented break-glass role (via an aws:PrincipalARN condition) keep emergency changes possible while still recorded. A is incorrect because correlating raw CloudTrail events against change sets is bespoke code reporting API activity rather than actual divergence from the template, with no organization-wide deployment. B is incorrect because it stops at scheduled detection plus a manual tagging convention: there is no multi-account rollout through Organizations and tags do not control who may make the emergency change. C is incorrect because its SCP denies every modification not made by CloudFormation, which blocks the emergency changes the company explicitly wants to allow, and hourly DetectStackDrift polling from Lambda reimplements a managed rule.

stem: A company runs a critical application on Amazon EC2 instances behind an Application Load Balancer across two Availability Zones. The application connects to an Amazon Aurora MySQL cluster. During a recent AZ failure, the application experienced 15 minutes of downtime because unhealthy instances were not replaced quickly enough. Which solution minimizes downtime during an AZ failure?

options.text: Configure the Auto Scaling group with a shorter health check grace period of 60 seconds and set the default instance warmup to 120 seconds. Enable capacity rebalancing and set the minimum healthy percentage to 100% in the deployment configuration.

Create a cross-Region read replica of the Aurora cluster in a secondary Region. Configure Route 53 health checks on the ALB endpoint and set up an active-passive failover routing policy with a TTL of 60 seconds for the DNS record.

Configure the Auto Scaling group to use three Availability Zones with capacity distributed evenly. Enable ELB health checks with a 30-second interval and set the unhealthy threshold to 2, so failed instances are replaced within approximately 90 seconds.

Deploy the application using an ECS Fargate service across two Availability Zones with a minimum healthy percent of 100. Configure the ALB health check with a 10-second interval and deregistration delay of 30 seconds on the target group.

explanation: C is correct: the 15-minute outage happened because losing one of two AZs removed 50% of capacity at once. Spreading the Auto Scaling group evenly over three AZs means an AZ loss costs only about one third of capacity, so the surviving instances can carry traffic while replacements launch. Switching the ASG to ELB health checks with a 30-second interval and an unhealthy threshold of 2 lets the ALB mark targets unhealthy in roughly 60 seconds, after which Auto Scaling terminates and replaces them. A is incorrect because shortening the grace period and warmup only tunes how quickly a replacement counts as in service; it does not change the fact that half of the fleet disappears with one AZ. Capacity rebalancing responds to Spot rebalance recommendations, which is unrelated to an AZ failure of On-Demand instances. B is incorrect because cross-Region replicas and Route 53 failover address a Region-level event; during an AZ failure the ALB endpoint stays reachable and healthy, so the failover record would never flip. D is incorrect because re-platforming to Fargate leaves the workload spread across the same two AZs, so the identical 50% capacity loss recurs.

stem: A company needs to aggregate logs from 200 microservices running on Amazon ECS Fargate across three AWS Regions into a centralized logging solution. The solution must support near-real-time search, retain logs for 90 days, and archive logs older than 90 days to reduce costs. Which architecture meets these requirements?

options.text: Configure each ECS task with the awslogs log driver to send logs to CloudWatch Logs. Create Kinesis Data Firehose delivery streams with a Lambda transformation to forward logs to an S3 bucket, then use Amazon Athena for ad-hoc querying.

Configure each ECS task with a FireLens log driver using a Fluent Bit sidecar to send logs to Amazon CloudWatch Logs in each Region. Create cross-account CloudWatch subscriptions to stream all logs to a central account's CloudWatch log group.

Configure each ECS task with a FireLens log driver to send logs directly to a centralized Amazon OpenSearch Service domain. Set up an Index State Management policy to transition indices older than 90 days to UltraWarm storage and delete after 365 days.

Configure each ECS task with a FireLens log driver to send logs to Amazon Kinesis Data Streams in each Region. Use Kinesis Data Firehose to deliver logs to a centralized S3 bucket and query using Amazon Redshift Spectrum with materialized views.

explanation: C is correct: FireLens with Fluent Bit lets each Fargate task ship its stdout/stderr straight to one Amazon OpenSearch Service domain from all three Regions, giving near-real-time indexed full-text search across the 200 services. An Index State Management policy then satisfies retention natively: indices stay hot for 90 days, roll to UltraWarm (S3-backed and far cheaper per GB) as the archive tier, and are deleted later. A is incorrect because Firehose buffers to S3 and Athena scans objects per query, so it is a batch analytics path with seconds-to-minutes latency, not near-real-time search. B is incorrect because CloudWatch Logs subscription filters deliver to Kinesis, Firehose or Lambda destinations, not into another account's log group, so the described central log group does not exist as a subscription target, and Logs Insights is not a cross-Region full-text search tier with automatic archival. D is incorrect because Redshift Spectrum is a structured analytics engine over S3; it adds a Redshift cluster and materialized-view maintenance while still not offering near-real-time log search.

stem: A company's production Amazon RDS Multi-AZ PostgreSQL database experienced a failover event that caused a brief application outage. The operations team was not notified until users reported the issue 30 minutes later. The team needs an automated notification system that alerts on-call engineers within 1 minute of any RDS failover event. Which solution meets this requirement?

options.text: Enable Amazon RDS Enhanced Monitoring with a 1-second granularity. Create a CloudWatch alarm on the CPUUtilization metric with a 60-second evaluation period and configure the alarm to send notifications to an SNS topic subscribed by the on-call team.

Create a CloudWatch Logs metric filter on the RDS PostgreSQL error log for failover-related keywords. Configure a CloudWatch alarm on the custom metric with a 1-minute evaluation period and send alarm state changes to an SNS topic.

Enable RDS Performance Insights for the database instance. Create a CloudWatch alarm on the db.SessionsActive performance counter and set a threshold anomaly detection band to trigger an SNS notification when connection patterns change.

Configure an Amazon EventBridge rule to match RDS DB instance events with the detail-type of 'RDS DB Instance Event' and event ID for multi-AZ failover. Set the target as an SNS topic with the on-call team's email and SMS subscriptions.

explanation: D is correct: RDS publishes DB instance event notifications to Amazon EventBridge under the detail-type 'RDS DB Instance Event', including the failover-category events emitted when a Multi-AZ instance fails over. A rule matching those event IDs fires within seconds of the failover and can target an SNS topic with the on-call team's email and SMS subscriptions, so notification happens well inside one minute with no polling, parsing or thresholds. A is incorrect because Enhanced Monitoring only adds OS-level metrics at finer granularity; CPUUtilization is not a failover signal and can look entirely normal across the event. B is incorrect because PostgreSQL error logs are published to CloudWatch Logs on a delay, a metric-filter alarm must wait a full evaluation period before it can change state, and detection depends on brittle keyword matching that a log-format change would silently break. C is incorrect because Performance Insights counters such as db.SessionsActive only reveal a side effect (connections dropping and reconnecting), and anomaly-detection bands add both evaluation latency and false positives.

stem: A company must ensure that all Amazon S3 buckets across 50 AWS accounts enforce encryption at rest using AWS KMS customer-managed keys and block public access. Non-compliant buckets must be automatically remediated within 1 hour. Which solution provides continuous compliance enforcement?

options.text: Configure AWS CloudTrail to log all S3 API calls across all accounts. Create EventBridge rules in each account to match CreateBucket and PutBucketEncryption events and trigger a Lambda function that applies the required encryption and access settings.

Deploy Amazon Macie across all accounts using AWS Organizations delegated administrator. Configure Macie to scan buckets for encryption settings and use EventBridge rules to trigger Lambda remediation functions for non-compliant buckets.

Deploy AWS Config rules s3-bucket-server-side-encryption-enabled and s3-bucket-public-read-prohibited across all accounts using AWS Organizations. Attach auto-remediation actions using Systems Manager Automation documents to enforce encryption and block public access.

Create an SCP in AWS Organizations that denies s3:CreateBucket unless the request includes SSE-KMS encryption and BlockPublicAccess parameters. Deploy a Lambda function on a 1-hour schedule to scan existing buckets and apply missing configurations.

explanation: C is correct: AWS Config managed rules re-evaluate on every configuration change as well as periodically, so a bucket created or modified without SSE-KMS or with public access is flagged within minutes; deploying the rules as organization Config rules from the delegated administrator covers all 50 accounts from one definition. Attaching Config remediation actions backed by SSM Automation documents applies the encryption and public-access-block settings automatically, easily inside the one-hour window, and it fixes pre-existing buckets rather than only new ones. A is incorrect because event-driven remediation only sees the specific API calls you enumerate, so buckets made non-compliant by other actions slip through, and you must build and maintain the rule plus Lambda in all 50 accounts. B is incorrect because Amazon Macie discovers and classifies sensitive data in S3; it is not a configuration-compliance engine for bucket encryption keys or Block Public Access settings. D is incorrect because an SCP on s3:CreateBucket is purely preventive: it cannot remediate buckets that already exist or that drift after creation, and it leans on a hand-built hourly scanner instead of managed continuous evaluation.

stem: A team uses AWS CodeBuild to run unit tests and build Docker images for 30 microservices. Build times average 12 minutes, and the team wants to reduce them to under 5 minutes. Each microservice has its own buildspec.yml and Dockerfile. The Docker images range from 500MB to 2GB. Which optimization strategy is MOST effective?

options.text: Migrate from CodeBuild to Amazon ECS tasks with Kaniko for building Docker images. Store base images in Amazon ECR with immutable tags and configure ECS tasks to pull base images from a VPC endpoint to reduce network transfer time.

Create a single monorepo CodeBuild project that builds all 30 microservices in sequence. Use CodeBuild batch builds with the build graph strategy to identify dependencies between services and skip unchanged services using git diff checks.

Enable CodeBuild local caching with Docker layer cache mode and configure a custom cache S3 bucket. Refactor each Dockerfile to use multi-stage builds with dependency installation layers ordered before source code copy for optimal layer reuse.

Upgrade all CodeBuild projects to use compute type BUILD_GENERAL1_2XLARGE with 145 GB memory and 72 vCPUs. Enable privileged mode for Docker builds and configure concurrent build limits to allow all 30 services to build simultaneously.

explanation: C is correct: for images of 500 MB to 2 GB the dominant cost in a 12-minute build is rebuilding image layers and reinstalling dependencies on every run. CodeBuild local caching in DOCKER_LAYER mode preserves layers between builds, and restructuring each Dockerfile as a multi-stage build that installs dependencies before COPYing source means a source-only change invalidates just the final layers. Combined, these eliminate most of the repeated work and cut typical builds to a few minutes. A is incorrect because migrating to self-managed ECS tasks with Kaniko is a large change that still rebuilds the same layers; immutable ECR tags and a VPC endpoint only shave base-image pull time. B is incorrect because a monorepo project building 30 services in sequence increases wall-clock time, and batch build graphs express dependency ordering rather than removing the layer-rebuild cost that is the actual bottleneck. D is incorrect because a larger compute type speeds up CPU-bound steps but cannot avoid re-downloading and re-installing dependencies each run, privileged mode is already required for Docker builds at any size, and concurrency limits affect fleet throughput rather than the 12-minute duration of a single build.

stem: A company is migrating from manually provisioned infrastructure to AWS CloudFormation. The team needs to import 50 existing EC2 instances, their associated security groups, and EBS volumes into CloudFormation management without downtime. Which TWO steps are required to accomplish this?

options.text: After importing resources, run a CloudFormation drift detection operation on the stack to identify any configuration differences between the template definitions and the actual resource configurations, then update the template to match actual state.

Write a CloudFormation template that defines each existing resource with a DeletionPolicy of Retain and matching configuration. Use the CloudFormation import operation to associate each existing resource with its template definition by providing resource identifiers.

Run CloudFormation drift detection on the existing resources to generate a baseline template. Export the drift results as a CloudFormation template using the console's export feature and create a new stack from the exported template.

Use the AWS CloudFormation CLI create-stack command with the --import-resources flag and provide a JSON mapping file that lists each existing resource's physical ID alongside its desired logical ID in the new stack template.

explanation: B and A are correct. B is the import prerequisite: you author a template that describes each existing instance, security group and volume exactly, mark the imported resources with DeletionPolicy: Retain (required for import), and run the import operation supplying each resource's physical identifier so CloudFormation adopts the resource in place rather than creating a new one, which is why there is no downtime. A is the necessary follow-up: import validates only the identifying properties, so running drift detection on the resulting stack shows where the template does not match the live configuration, and you update the template to match actual state before making any real changes. C is incorrect because CloudFormation has no feature that exports drift results as a template; drift detection reports differences only for resources already managed by a stack, so it cannot generate a baseline for unmanaged resources. D is incorrect because create-stack has no --import-resources flag; import is performed with a change set of type IMPORT (create-change-set --change-set-type IMPORT --resources-to-import) or the equivalent console workflow.

stem: A company operates a stateful application on EC2 instances that process financial transactions. Each transaction takes up to 30 seconds to complete and must not be interrupted. The Auto Scaling group needs to scale in during off-peak hours. How should the team configure the Auto Scaling group to prevent transaction loss during scale-in events?

options.text: Configure the Auto Scaling group with a default cooldown period of 300 seconds between scaling activities. Set the health check grace period to 120 seconds and enable instance protection on all instances that are actively processing transactions.

Enable Auto Scaling lifecycle hooks for the autoscaling:EC2_INSTANCE_TERMINATING event. Configure the application to complete in-flight transactions when it receives the lifecycle notification and send a CONTINUE signal via the CompleteLifecycleAction API.

Set the Auto Scaling group's termination policy to OldestInstance and configure a deregistration delay of 120 seconds on the target group. Enable connection draining on the Application Load Balancer with a timeout matching the longest transaction duration.

Configure the Auto Scaling group to use a scheduled scaling policy that reduces capacity only during a maintenance window. Send an SNS notification 5 minutes before the scheduled action and have engineers manually verify no transactions are in progress.

explanation: B is correct: an autoscaling:EC2_INSTANCE_TERMINATING lifecycle hook holds the instance in the Terminating:Wait state (default 1 hour, configurable up to 48) instead of terminating it immediately. The application receives the hook notification through EventBridge, SNS or instance metadata, stops accepting new transactions, finishes the in-flight ones (up to 30 seconds each), and then calls CompleteLifecycleAction with CONTINUE so termination proceeds at once rather than waiting out the heartbeat timeout. That is the only option that both pauses termination and gives the application an explicit completion signal. A is incorrect because cooldown merely spaces successive scaling activities apart, and instance protection must be set and cleared per instance by code you write; neither creates a drain window nor tells the application anything. C is incorrect because deregistration delay and connection draining stop new load-balancer requests and wait a fixed timer for open connections; the application is never notified to finish work, and background or non-HTTP transaction state is not covered. D is incorrect because it depends on engineers manually verifying quiescence, which is neither automated nor reliable, and scheduled scaling still terminates instances mid-transaction.

stem: A company's application generates custom business metrics that must be monitored with sub-second granularity. The operations team needs to create dashboards showing the 99th percentile of order processing latency and trigger alarms when the p99 exceeds 500ms for 3 consecutive 10-second periods. Which approach supports this requirement?

options.text: Use the CloudWatch PutMetricData API to publish individual metric values with StorageResolution set to 1 (high resolution). Create a CloudWatch alarm using the ExtendedStatistic p99 with a 10-second period and set datapoints to alarm at 3 out of 3.

Use the CloudWatch embedded metric format in application logs sent via the CloudWatch Logs agent. Configure the metric filter to extract latency values and create a dashboard widget displaying the p99 statistic with a 1-minute refresh interval.

Use Amazon Managed Service for Prometheus to ingest custom metrics via the remote write endpoint. Create recording rules to compute the 99th percentile histogram over 10-second windows and configure Alertmanager rules for threshold-based alerting.

Use the CloudWatch PutMetricData API with the StatisticValues parameter to publish aggregated statistics every 10 seconds. Create a CloudWatch alarm on the Average statistic with a 10-second period and 3 evaluation periods with a 500ms threshold.

explanation: A is correct: publishing each observation with PutMetricData and StorageResolution=1 creates a high-resolution metric, which is the only way to store CloudWatch data at sub-minute granularity. Because individual values are stored rather than pre-aggregated summaries, CloudWatch can compute percentile statistics, so an alarm using ExtendedStatistic p99 fires correctly; high-resolution metrics are also what permit the 10-second alarm period, and 3 out of 3 datapoints to alarm implements the three consecutive 10-second breaches. B is incorrect because embedded metric format metrics extracted from logs are standard resolution (1-minute) unless explicitly marked high resolution, and a dashboard widget refresh interval is not an alarm, so the 10-second alarming requirement is unmet. C is incorrect because Amazon Managed Service for Prometheus could compute the percentile but requires remote-write plumbing, recording rules and Alertmanager, adding a whole monitoring stack for something CloudWatch supports natively. D is incorrect because StatisticValues publishes only SampleCount, Sum, Minimum and Maximum, from which CloudWatch cannot derive percentiles, and alarming on Average hides exactly the tail latency the team must catch.

stem: An e-commerce application experiences intermittent 504 Gateway Timeout errors during peak traffic periods. The application runs on ECS Fargate behind an Application Load Balancer, with an Aurora PostgreSQL database backend. CloudWatch metrics show normal CPU and memory utilization on ECS tasks. Which investigation approach will MOST likely identify the root cause?

options.text: Enable ALB access logs and analyze the target_processing_time field to determine if backend tasks are slow to respond. Check the Aurora DatabaseConnections metric and compare against the max_connections parameter to identify connection pool exhaustion.

Configure CloudWatch Container Insights for the ECS cluster to collect per-task CPU and memory metrics at 1-minute granularity. Create a CloudWatch dashboard correlating task-level resource utilization with the ALB HTTP 504 count metric over time.

Enable AWS X-Ray tracing on the ECS tasks and ALB to generate a service map showing latency distribution across components. Review the X-Ray analytics console to identify latency outliers correlated with specific API endpoints or downstream dependencies.

Enable VPC Flow Logs for the subnets hosting the ECS tasks and Aurora cluster. Analyze flow logs in CloudWatch Logs Insights to identify dropped packets or connection resets between the application tasks and the database endpoints.

explanation: A is correct: an ALB returns HTTP 504 when a target does not respond within the load balancer's timeout. ALB access logs record target_processing_time per request, which immediately distinguishes a slow backend from a target the ALB could not reach, and identifies which requests, targets and time windows are involved. Because the scenario states task CPU and memory are normal, the classic remaining cause is threads blocking on the database, so comparing Aurora's DatabaseConnections against the cluster's max_connections directly tests the connection-exhaustion hypothesis. B is incorrect because the scenario already reports normal task CPU and memory; Container Insights just re-collects those same dimensions at finer granularity and adds no new signal. C is incorrect because X-Ray, while useful, requires instrumenting and redeploying every service first, and default sampling means the intermittent slow requests may never be captured, so it is a slower and less certain route to the answer the access logs already contain. D is incorrect because VPC Flow Logs record 5-tuple flow summaries and ACCEPT/REJECT decisions; they show no application response time and will look entirely normal when requests are simply queued waiting on a saturated database.

stem: A company needs to rotate database credentials for 50 Amazon RDS instances automatically every 30 days. Applications retrieve credentials at startup and cache them in memory. The solution must ensure applications can still connect during and immediately after rotation without restarts. Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Store credentials in AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store SecureString parameters with a Lambda function on a 30-day EventBridge schedule. Update each parameter with new credentials and configure applications to poll Parameter Store every 5 minutes for changes.

Store credentials in AWS Secrets Manager with automatic rotation enabled using a Lambda rotation function. Configure the rotation to use the alternating users strategy with a 30-day rotation schedule and update applications to call GetSecretValue before each connection.

Store credentials in AWS Secrets Manager with automatic rotation enabled using a single-user rotation strategy. Configure the rotation Lambda in the same VPC as the RDS instances and update applications to retrieve credentials once at startup with a 30-day TTL cache.

Store credentials in HashiCorp Vault running on ECS Fargate with a dynamic secrets engine for RDS PostgreSQL. Configure Vault to generate short-lived credentials with a 30-day maximum TTL and integrate applications using the Vault Agent sidecar pattern.

explanation: B is correct: Secrets Manager's alternating-users rotation maintains two database users and rotates them in turn. During rotation the second user is created or updated and tested before the secret's AWSCURRENT stage moves, so the credentials that were valid before rotation remain valid throughout and immediately after it. Having applications call GetSecretValue before each connection (rather than caching for process lifetime) means they always receive the current version and never need a restart. A is incorrect because Parameter Store has no built-in rotation: you would build the rotation Lambda, the ALTER USER logic and the polling yourself, and a 5-minute poll still leaves a window in which cached credentials are wrong. C is incorrect because single-user rotation changes the password of the one user in place, instantly invalidating anything cached, and the option compounds that by caching credentials for a 30-day TTL - precisely the failure the requirement forbids. D is incorrect because running HashiCorp Vault on Fargate means owning unsealing, HA, upgrades and backups for 50 databases when Secrets Manager already provides managed rotation with native RDS integration.

stem: A team manages 20 AWS Lambda functions deployed via AWS SAM. Each function requires environment-specific configuration for dev, staging, and production stages. The team wants to use a single SAM template across all environments and promote the exact same artifact through stages without rebuilding. Which deployment strategy achieves this?

options.text: Use SAM template parameters with environment-specific parameter override files stored in S3. Configure CodePipeline to build once in the source stage and use CloudFormation deploy actions with ParameterOverrides referencing environment-specific JSON files from S3.

Create separate SAM template files for each environment with hardcoded configuration values. Use CodePipeline with separate source actions for each template and deploy each environment using its own CloudFormation deploy action with the respective template.

Store environment configurations in AWS AppConfig feature flags for each Lambda function. Deploy the same SAM template to all stages and configure each Lambda function to retrieve its configuration from AppConfig at invocation time using the AppConfig Lambda extension.

Use SAM nested stacks with a parent template that accepts an Environment parameter. Create child stacks for each Lambda function group and use CloudFormation Mappings to select the correct configuration values based on the Environment parameter value.

explanation: A is correct: parameterizing the single SAM template and supplying per-stage values through CloudFormation ParameterOverrides preserves one template and, crucially, one build artifact. CodePipeline builds and packages once, and each environment's CloudFormation deploy action consumes that same output artifact while pointing at a different parameter file, which is the build-once/deploy-many pattern the team asked for. B is incorrect because maintaining a separate hardcoded template per environment directly violates the single-template requirement and guarantees the environments drift apart. C is incorrect because AppConfig externalizes runtime configuration but says nothing about promoting the same packaged artifact through pipeline stages, and it adds per-invocation configuration retrieval for values that are static within an environment. D is incorrect because nested stacks with Mappings still require editing the mapping table inside the template whenever an environment value changes, and the extra stack nesting adds change-set and rollback complexity without improving on parameter overrides for artifact promotion.

stem: A company uses AWS CDK with TypeScript to define infrastructure. The team wants to enforce that all S3 buckets created through CDK have versioning enabled, encryption with KMS CMKs, and access logging configured. The enforcement must happen before deployment and prevent non-compliant stacks from being synthesized. Which approach provides this pre-deployment enforcement?

options.text: Create a custom CDK L3 construct called SecureBucket that wraps the S3 Bucket construct with mandatory versioning, KMS encryption, and access logging. Publish the construct to an internal CodeArtifact repository and prohibit direct S3 Bucket usage.

Write custom AWS Config rules using Lambda functions that evaluate S3 bucket configurations. Deploy the Config rules before the CDK stack and configure CloudFormation stack policies to prevent updates that would create non-compliant S3 resources.

Implement a custom CloudFormation Guard rule set that validates the synthesized CloudFormation template. Integrate cfn-guard as a CodeBuild step in the CI/CD pipeline to validate templates and fail the build if S3 bucket rules are violated.

Create CDK Aspects that visit all S3 Bucket constructs in the construct tree during synthesis. Check for versioning, KMS encryption, and access logging properties, and call Annotations.of(node).addError() for non-compliant buckets to fail synthesis.

explanation: D is correct: a CDK Aspect is applied to a scope and its visit() method is invoked for every node in the construct tree during synthesis, so it can inspect each S3 Bucket (or the underlying CfnBucket properties) for versioning, a KMS key and a logging configuration. Calling Annotations.of(node).addError() records a synthesis-time error, and cdk synth or cdk deploy then fails before a template is produced - exactly the pre-deployment enforcement required. A is incorrect because a SecureBucket L3 construct is opt-in: nothing in the toolchain prevents an engineer from instantiating s3.Bucket directly, so it is a convention rather than an enforced control. B is incorrect because AWS Config evaluates resources only after they exist, and CloudFormation stack policies restrict which existing resources an update may modify - neither validates properties before deployment. C is incorrect because cfn-guard against the synthesized template is real enforcement but happens after synthesis has already succeeded, only for code pushed through that pipeline, whereas the requirement is to prevent non-compliant stacks from being synthesized at all.

stem: A company operates a multi-Region active-active application using Amazon DynamoDB global tables. During a simulated Region failover test, the team discovered that some writes were lost because both Regions accepted conflicting updates to the same item simultaneously. The business requires that the active-active topology be retained and that no accepted order update be silently discarded. Which strategy prevents data loss from conflicting writes in this configuration?

options.text: Switch from active-active to active-passive configuration using Route 53 health checks for Region failover. Configure DynamoDB global tables to replicate from the primary Region only, and use a Lambda function behind a Route 53 failover record to redirect all writes to whichever Region is currently active, so that only one Region ever accepts a write for a given item.

Implement application-level conflict resolution by adding a vector clock attribute to each item. Use DynamoDB conditional expressions with attribute_exists and version checks to detect conflicts and route resolution to a designated primary Region for arbitration.

Enable DynamoDB Streams on the global table and configure a Lambda function to detect conflicting writes by comparing version attributes. Implement a custom conflict-resolution strategy that reconciles the divergent item states and persists the merged result using conditional writes guarded by a monotonically increasing version number.

Configure DynamoDB global tables with the last-writer-wins reconciliation default behavior and add a timestamp attribute updated by the application. Accept DynamoDB's built-in conflict resolution and design the application to tolerate eventual consistency across Regions.

explanation: Option C is correct because DynamoDB global tables reconcile concurrent writes internally with last-writer-wins, and the only way to avoid silently discarding an update is to detect the divergence yourself and merge it. Enabling DynamoDB Streams on each replica gives the application a durable, ordered record of every accepted item change, so a Lambda consumer can compare the version attribute it sees against the version currently stored, recognize that two Regions advanced the same item independently, and write back a reconciled item. Guarding that write with a conditional expression on a monotonically increasing version number makes the reconciliation itself idempotent and safe against races, so no accepted update is lost while the active-active topology is preserved. Option A fails because it abandons the required active-active architecture, and a global table is bidirectional by definition - you cannot configure a global table to replicate from one Region only, so the described configuration is not possible. Option B fails because DynamoDB conditional expressions evaluate simple comparisons on attributes; they cannot compare vector clocks, which encode a partial order, and attribute_exists only tests presence. Routing every conflict to a designated arbitration Region also reintroduces a single point of coordination on the write path, and it still does not stop the losing write from being overwritten by the global table's own replication. Option D fails outright against the stem: it explicitly accepts DynamoDB's last-writer-wins outcome and tells the team to tolerate the loss, which is the problem being solved. An application-supplied timestamp attribute also has no influence on global tables' internal reconciliation, which uses its own replication metadata rather than any attribute you write.

stem: A company wants to implement centralized logging for applications running across 10 AWS accounts. CloudWatch Logs data from every source account must land in a central account's S3 bucket, and the archived logs must be retained and protected from deletion for 7 years to satisfy an audit requirement. Which configurations are required? (Choose two.)

options.text: Create a KMS key in the central account with a key policy that grants kms:GenerateDataKey and kms:Decrypt permissions to the CloudWatch Logs service principal from each source account, enabling cross-account log encryption at the destination.

Configure S3 Object Lock in Governance mode on the central logging bucket with a retention period of 7 years. Enable S3 Versioning and create lifecycle rules to transition logs to S3 Glacier Deep Archive after 90 days for cost optimization.

Configure CloudWatch Logs subscription filters in each source account to stream log events directly to a Kinesis Data Firehose delivery stream in the central account. Set the Firehose destination to the central logging S3 bucket with SSE-KMS encryption using the central account's customer managed KMS key and a 5-minute buffering hint.

Deploy a CloudWatch Logs destination in the central account with a resource policy allowing source accounts to put subscription filters. Configure the destination to forward logs to a Kinesis Data Stream that feeds into a Firehose delivery stream writing to S3.

explanation: Option B is correct because it is the only configuration that delivers the 7-year protected retention the audit requires. S3 Object Lock places a retention date on each object version so it cannot be deleted or overwritten before that date, Versioning is a prerequisite for Object Lock, and lifecycle transitions to Glacier Deep Archive keep the seven-year archive affordable. Option D is correct because it is the supported cross-account delivery pattern. PutSubscriptionFilter in a source account cannot name an arbitrary resource in another account; it accepts a logical CloudWatch Logs destination ARN, and that destination must be created in the recipient account with a destination resource policy that names the source account principals. The destination then fans out to a Kinesis Data Stream, which a Firehose delivery stream consumes and writes to S3. Option A fails because it grants the wrong principal. The encryption of the objects landing in the central bucket is performed by the Firehose delivery role and S3, not by the CloudWatch Logs service principal in each source account, so this key policy grants permissions to an identity that never touches the KMS key in this flow, and the delivery role is left without kms:GenerateDataKey. Option C fails because it is not configurable as described: a subscription filter cannot target a Firehose delivery stream that lives in a different account. Only the CloudWatch Logs destination abstraction in option D makes the cross-account hop, so the source-account filters in option C would be rejected.

stem: A company's Auto Scaling group launches EC2 instances that take 5 minutes to fully bootstrap using a UserData script. During a traffic spike, new instances were added to the load balancer before bootstrapping completed, causing HTTP 503 errors. How should the team prevent instances from receiving traffic before they are ready?

options.text: Set the Auto Scaling group health check type to ELB and increase the health check grace period to 600 seconds. Configure the ALB deregistration delay to 300 seconds and enable slow start mode on the target group with a 300-second duration.

Add an Auto Scaling lifecycle hook for EC2_INSTANCE_LAUNCHING that pauses the instance in Pending:Wait state. Have the UserData script send a CONTINUE signal via the CompleteLifecycleAction API only after bootstrapping finishes successfully.

Create a CloudWatch alarm that monitors the custom health check metric published by each instance during bootstrapping. Configure the Auto Scaling group to use the alarm as a scaling trigger and only register instances with the target group when the alarm is in OK state.

Configure the ALB target group health check to use the /status path served by the nginx front-end process, which starts and begins returning HTTP 200 roughly 20 seconds after boot, well before the UserData bootstrap script finishes. Set the health check interval to 10 seconds and the healthy threshold to 3.

explanation: Option B is correct because an EC2_INSTANCE_LAUNCHING lifecycle hook holds the instance in Pending:Wait, and Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling does not attach an instance to the target group until it leaves Pending:Wait and reaches InService. The UserData script therefore controls the gate: it calls CompleteLifecycleAction with CONTINUE only once bootstrapping has actually succeeded, so the instance is never registered with the load balancer in a half-initialized state and no request can hit it early. Option A fails because neither setting keeps traffic away. The health check grace period only suppresses Auto Scaling from marking and replacing an instance as unhealthy; the instance is still registered with the target group during the grace period, and slow start merely ramps the share of requests it receives rather than withholding them, so the first requests still return 503. Deregistration delay applies to instances leaving service and is irrelevant here. Option C fails because a CloudWatch alarm cannot gate target group registration. Auto Scaling registers instances with attached target groups automatically as part of the launch flow, and alarms can only drive scaling policies, so there is no mechanism to hold registration until the alarm reaches OK. Option D fails for one precise reason: the health check path is served by the nginx front end, which returns HTTP 200 about 20 seconds after boot, long before the 5-minute bootstrap finishes. The target therefore passes three checks and is declared healthy while the application behind it is still initializing, which reproduces exactly the 503 errors described in the scenario.

stem: A company deploys containerized applications on Amazon EKS and needs to prevent pods from running as root, ensure all container images come from a trusted ECR registry, and enforce resource limits on every pod. Which solution provides automated enforcement of these policies at admission time?

options.text: Enable Pod Security Standards in the EKS cluster at the Restricted level. Configure namespace labels to enforce the restricted profile and create custom ValidatingWebhookConfigurations to check for ECR registry sources and resource limit requirements.

Configure Amazon Inspector to scan EKS workloads continuously for security findings. Create EventBridge rules that trigger a Lambda function to delete non-compliant pods and send notifications to the security team via SNS when policy violations are detected.

Deploy AWS Config rules for EKS clusters that evaluate pod security configurations against CIS benchmarks. Configure auto-remediation using SSM Automation documents that patch non-compliant pod specifications and restart affected deployments automatically.

Install OPA Gatekeeper on the EKS cluster and define ConstraintTemplates that enforce non-root security context, restrict image sources to the trusted ECR registry, and require resource limits. Apply Constraints to target all namespaces except kube-system.

explanation: D is correct: OPA Gatekeeper installs a validating admission webhook, so every pod create and update is evaluated against Rego policy before the object is persisted to etcd. ConstraintTemplates plus Constraints can require securityContext.runAsNonRoot, restrict image references to the trusted ECR registry prefix, and require resources.limits on every container - all three requirements enforced at admission time by one mechanism, with kube-system excluded so cluster components are not broken. A is incorrect because the restricted Pod Security Standard covers only the security context (non-root, capabilities, seccomp, volume types); it has no concept of image provenance or resource limits, so the answer still depends on custom admission webhooks you must write, deploy and operate. B is incorrect because Amazon Inspector scans images and workloads for vulnerabilities after they exist; deleting an already-running pod is detect-and-respond, not admission control, and the non-compliant workload runs in the meantime. C is incorrect because AWS Config evaluates AWS resource configurations such as the EKS cluster itself, not individual Kubernetes pod specs, and any remediation would occur after admission.

stem: A company has a monorepo containing 10 microservices in a single AWS CodeCommit repository. Each microservice has its own directory with source code and buildspec.yml. The team wants CodePipeline to build and deploy only the microservices that have changed in each commit, not all 10 every time. Which solution achieves selective builds?

options.text: Configure an EventBridge rule to trigger a Lambda function on CodeCommit repository state change events. Have the Lambda function parse the commit diff and start individual CodePipeline executions by calling the StartPipelineExecution API for affected services.

Create a single CodePipeline with a CodeBuild batch build using the build-matrix strategy. Define each microservice as a separate build environment in the batch configuration and use the buildspec to check for changes before executing each build.

Create a single CodePipeline with a CodeCommit source action. Add a CodeBuild project that runs a git diff script to identify changed directories, then dynamically triggers individual CodeBuild projects for each changed microservice using the AWS SDK.

Create 10 separate CodePipeline pipelines, each with a CodeCommit source action filtered by file path using the CloudWatch Events trigger configuration. Set each pipeline's event filter to match only the object paths beneath its corresponding microservice directory, so that a commit touching unrelated directories never starts it.

explanation: Option A is correct because CodeCommit cannot filter on changed files by itself, so the file-path decision has to be made by code you run. The EventBridge rule fires on the repository state change, and the Lambda function calls GetDifferences against the before and after commit IDs to learn which directories actually changed. It then calls StartPipelineExecution only for the pipelines belonging to those microservices, which gives exactly the selective behaviour requested while leaving each service's normal build, test and deploy stages intact. Option B fails because a CodeBuild batch build with a build-matrix strategy expands to every combination in the matrix: all 10 build environments are provisioned and billed on every commit, and a buildspec that exits early merely makes the unnecessary builds short rather than preventing them, so nothing is genuinely skipped. Option C fails on two counts. The CodeCommit source action delivers a zipped snapshot of the repository by default, with no git history, so git diff has nothing to compare against unless the action is reconfigured for full clone. More importantly, calling StartBuild from inside a build step bypasses CodePipeline entirely, so the downstream deploy stages, approvals and artifact tracking never run for the services that changed. Option D fails because the trigger it describes does not exist for CodeCommit. CodeCommit Repository State Change events carry references and commit IDs but no changed-file paths, so an EventBridge event pattern cannot match on a directory, and CodePipeline V2 filePaths trigger filters are supported only for CodeConnections sources such as GitHub, GitLab and Bitbucket.

stem: A company uses Terraform to manage AWS infrastructure across multiple teams. They need to ensure that the Terraform state file is stored securely with encryption, supports locking to prevent concurrent modifications, and maintains a history of state changes for audit purposes. Which configuration meets ALL requirements?

options.text: Store the Terraform state in AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store as a SecureString parameter with KMS encryption. Implement locking using a DynamoDB table with conditional writes and version the state by creating timestamped parameter copies before each update.

Configure the Terraform backend to use an S3 bucket with SSE-S3 encryption and MFA Delete enabled for state protection. Use an SQS FIFO queue as a custom locking mechanism via a wrapper script and enable CloudTrail S3 data events for state change auditing.

Configure the Terraform backend to use Terraform Cloud with remote state storage and built-in locking. Enable state versioning in Terraform Cloud's workspace settings and configure SAML SSO integration with the company's identity provider for access control.

Configure the Terraform backend to use an S3 bucket with SSE-KMS encryption and versioning enabled for state history. Add a DynamoDB table for state locking with a LockID partition key and enable S3 access logging to an audit bucket for access tracking.

explanation: D is correct: the S3 backend with SSE-KMS encrypts the state under a customer-managed key, S3 bucket versioning retains every previous state file for audit history and rollback, and the backend's DynamoDB table (with a LockID partition key) provides state locking through conditional writes so two engineers cannot apply concurrently. This is the standard, fully supported AWS backend configuration and it satisfies all three requirements natively. A is incorrect because Parameter Store is not a Terraform backend at all, and its 4 KB standard / 8 KB advanced value limit cannot hold a real state file; timestamped parameter copies are a hand-rolled substitute for versioning. B is incorrect on two counts: SSE-S3 uses S3-managed keys rather than a customer-managed KMS key, and Terraform has no SQS locking integration, so the wrapper script is an unsupported custom mechanism; MFA Delete protects against deletion but is not state history. C is incorrect because Terraform Cloud does meet the functional requirements but stores state outside the company's AWS accounts and outside its KMS control, which is what the encryption and audit requirements are asking to keep in-house.

stem: A company runs a batch processing system on Amazon EC2 Spot Instances that processes jobs from an SQS queue. Each job takes between 10 and 45 minutes to complete. When Spot Instances are interrupted, in-progress jobs are lost and must be reprocessed. Which solution ensures jobs are not lost during Spot interruptions?

options.text: Configure the application to check the EC2 instance metadata endpoint for Spot interruption notices every 5 seconds. When a notice is received, save the job's progress to an S3 checkpoint file and return the message to the SQS queue by resetting its visibility timeout.

Deploy the batch processing on AWS Fargate Spot tasks instead of EC2 Spot Instances. Configure the ECS service to automatically restart interrupted tasks and set the SQS queue visibility timeout to match the maximum job processing duration of 45 minutes.

Use an Auto Scaling group with mixed instance types and a capacity-optimized Spot allocation strategy. Configure the SQS queue visibility timeout to 60 minutes and enable dead-letter queue redrive with a maximum receive count of 3 for failed jobs.

Switch from Spot Instances to On-Demand Instances in a Reserved capacity pool to eliminate interruptions entirely. Configure Auto Scaling scheduled actions to scale capacity based on the expected queue depth during peak processing hours.

explanation: A is correct: EC2 publishes a Spot interruption notice to the instance metadata endpoint (and to EventBridge) approximately two minutes before reclamation. Polling metadata every few seconds gives the worker time to checkpoint the partially completed job to S3 and to make the SQS message immediately available again by calling ChangeMessageVisibility with a timeout of 0, so a surviving worker picks it up and resumes from the checkpoint instead of waiting for the full visibility timeout and reprocessing from the start. B is incorrect because Fargate Spot tasks are also reclaimed (with a SIGTERM and a stopTimeout grace window), so changing platforms does not stop in-flight jobs being lost unless the application still checkpoints. C is incorrect because capacity-optimized allocation and instance diversification reduce how often interruptions occur but do nothing when one happens, and a 60-minute visibility timeout actually delays redelivery of the abandoned message by up to an hour. D is incorrect because abandoning Spot removes the cost advantage that motivates using Spot for batch processing, and it addresses availability rather than the durability of in-progress work.

stem: A company uses AWS X-Ray to trace requests through a distributed microservices architecture. The team notices that some traces are incomplete, missing segments from downstream services. All services are instrumented with the X-Ray SDK and run on ECS Fargate. Which configuration issue is MOST likely causing incomplete traces?

options.text: The downstream services are not propagating the X-Amzn-Trace-Id header in their HTTP responses to upstream callers. Update the application code to extract the trace header from incoming requests and include it in all outbound HTTP client requests.

The X-Ray sampling rules are configured with a low fixed rate that drops segments from high-throughput downstream services. Update the centralized sampling rules in the X-Ray console to increase the reservoir size and fixed rate for downstream services.

The X-Ray daemon sidecar container is not configured in the ECS task definitions for downstream services. Add an aws-xray-daemon container to each task definition and configure the application containers to send trace data to the daemon on UDP port 2000.

The ECS task execution role lacks the xray:PutTraceSegments and xray:PutTelemetryRecords permissions. Update the task execution role's IAM policy to include these X-Ray API actions with a resource scope of the account's trace group ARN.

explanation: C is correct: on Fargate there is no host on which to install the X-Ray daemon, so every task definition needs its own aws-xray-daemon sidecar container; the X-Ray SDK emits segments over UDP to 127.0.0.1:2000 inside the task's shared network namespace. Any service whose task definition omits the sidecar silently discards its segments, which produces exactly the reported symptom - traces exist, but segments from particular downstream services are consistently absent. A is incorrect because the trace context travels in the X-Amzn-Trace-Id header on outbound requests, not in responses back to the caller, and the SDK's instrumented HTTP clients propagate it automatically; a propagation bug would also break parent/child linkage rather than remove whole services. B is incorrect because sampling decisions are made at the entry point for a whole trace, so a low fixed rate yields fewer complete traces rather than complete traces missing specific downstream segments. D is incorrect because xray:PutTraceSegments and xray:PutTelemetryRecords must be granted on the task role used by the application, not the task execution role that pulls images and writes logs, so the described fix targets the wrong role and would not restore the missing segments.

stem: A company detected unauthorized API calls in AWS CloudTrail logs that created IAM users with administrative privileges. The security team needs to immediately contain the incident and determine the scope of the breach. Which sequence of actions should the team take FIRST?

options.text: Isolate the affected account by removing it from the AWS Organization and applying an SCP that denies all actions. Launch a forensic EC2 instance in a separate account to analyze CloudTrail logs stored in the centralized logging S3 bucket for the past 30 days.

Delete the unauthorized IAM users and their access keys immediately. Rotate all IAM user passwords and access keys across the account. Enable MFA on the root account and all IAM users, then review CloudTrail logs for the past 90 days to assess impact.

Enable AWS Security Hub with the Foundational Security Best Practices standard to identify all compromised resources. Run an Amazon Inspector assessment on all EC2 instances in the account and generate an automated remediation plan using Systems Manager OpsCenter.

Attach a deny-all IAM policy to the unauthorized IAM users to disable their access without deleting evidence. Revoke all active sessions for the compromised principal using an inline policy with a NotBefore condition, then analyze CloudTrail logs for full scope.

explanation: D is correct: the first objective is containment without destroying evidence. An explicit Deny-all policy on the unauthorized IAM users strips their effective permissions instantly while leaving the principals, keys and metadata intact for forensics, and an inline policy denying all actions for credentials issued before now (the AWSRevokeOlderSessions pattern using an aws:TokenIssueTime DateLessThan condition) kills temporary sessions already in circulation. With access frozen, CloudTrail establishes scope. A is incorrect because removing an account from AWS Organizations is drastic and counterproductive: it drops SCP coverage, consolidated billing and centralized logging exactly when they are needed, and it does not revoke the attacker's credentials. B is incorrect because deleting the IAM users and keys destroys the primary artifacts (attached policies, key IDs, creation timestamps) required to attribute activity in CloudTrail, and a fleet-wide credential rotation is a recovery step rather than the first containment action. C is incorrect because Security Hub and Inspector are posture-assessment and vulnerability tools; enabling them provides no immediate containment, and Inspector's software findings are unrelated to compromised IAM credentials.

stem: A company is implementing a CI/CD pipeline for container deployments to Amazon ECS. The security team requires that container images are scanned for vulnerabilities before deployment and that images with critical or high severity vulnerabilities are blocked from being deployed. Which actions should be implemented? (Choose two.)

options.text: Create an EventBridge rule that matches ECR image scan completion events with findings of CRITICAL or HIGH severity. Configure the rule target as a Lambda function that updates the ECR repository policy to deny pulls for the specific image tag.

Configure an ECR lifecycle policy that automatically deletes images older than 30 days. Enable ECR image tag immutability to prevent overwriting scanned images, configure the ECS task definition to always pull the latest tagged image version, and restrict the ecr:PutImage action to the pipeline's build role.

Add a CodeBuild stage after the image push that calls the ECR DescribeImageScanFindings API for the pushed image digest, waits until the scan status is COMPLETE, and exits with a non-zero code to fail the pipeline stage if the findings include any CRITICAL or HIGH severity vulnerabilities.

Enable Amazon ECR image scanning with enhanced scanning powered by Amazon Inspector. Configure scan-on-push to automatically scan images when they are pushed to the repository and generate findings with severity classifications for each vulnerability.

explanation: Options D and C together satisfy the two halves of the requirement. Option D supplies the detection: ECR enhanced scanning, backed by Amazon Inspector, scans operating system and programming language packages and assigns a severity to each finding, and scan-on-push guarantees that every image built by the pipeline is assessed the moment it lands in the repository rather than on an ad hoc schedule. Option C supplies the enforcement: a CodeBuild stage that polls DescribeImageScanFindings for the image digest and exits non-zero on any CRITICAL or HIGH finding fails the pipeline stage, so the deploy action to ECS never executes and the vulnerable image is never rolled out. Keying on the digest rather than the tag also ensures the gate evaluates the exact artifact that was just built. Option A fails because it is not implementable. ECR provides no IAM condition key for an image tag - only repository-level keys such as ecr:ResourceTag exist - so a repository policy cannot deny ecr:BatchGetImage for one specific tag. It is also purely reactive: the scan-completion event arrives after the image is already in the registry and potentially already being pulled, so it is not a pre-deployment gate. Option B fails because nothing in it looks for vulnerabilities. Lifecycle policies control retention, and tag immutability prevents a tag from being reassigned, which are hygiene controls rather than security scanning. Configuring the task definition to always pull the latest tagged image actively works against the requirement, because it lets ECS pick up an image that has never been assessed.

stem: A company uses AWS CodeDeploy to perform rolling deployments to a fleet of 100 EC2 instances. During a recent deployment, a bug in the application caused errors that were only detected after 60% of the fleet was updated. The team wants to minimize the blast radius of future faulty deployments. Which deployment configuration achieves this?

options.text: Configure CodeDeploy with AllAtOnce deployment and add a manual approval step in CodePipeline between the staging and production deploy actions. Require two team leads to approve the deployment after reviewing staging test results before proceeding to production.

Create a custom CodeDeploy deployment configuration for the EC2/on-premises platform with MinimumHealthyHosts set to 95 percent, so no more than 5 instances are updated in any batch. Associate the deployment group with a CloudWatch alarm on the HTTP 5xx count and enable automatic rollback on alarm.

Configure CodeDeploy with the CodeDeployDefault.OneAtATime deployment configuration to update a single instance at a time, keeping the number of instances offline at any moment as low as possible. Enable automatic rollback when a deployment fails, so that any instance whose lifecycle event hooks return a non-zero exit code triggers a revert to the previously deployed revision.

Configure a CodeDeploy deployment group with a linear deployment configuration that deploys to 10% of instances every 5 minutes. Add a CloudWatch alarm monitoring the application error rate and configure automatic rollback on alarm to revert all updated instances.

explanation: Option B is correct because it combines the only blast-radius control that the EC2/on-premises compute platform actually offers with the only signal that would have caught this particular bug. A custom deployment configuration with MinimumHealthyHosts at 95 percent forces CodeDeploy to keep 95 of the 100 instances in service, so it updates at most 5 at a time. Attaching a CloudWatch alarm on HTTP 5xx count to the deployment group and enabling rollback on alarm means the deployment stops and reverts as soon as the error metric breaches, which for a bug that only surfaces in production traffic is the difference between 5 affected instances and 60. Option A fails because AllAtOnce updates the entire fleet simultaneously and therefore provides no blast-radius control whatsoever; a human approval gate placed before the deploy cannot detect a defect that staging tests already missed. Option C fails because its rollback trigger is wrong for this failure mode. Rollback on deployment failure fires only when a lifecycle event hook returns non-zero or an instance is marked failed; a bug that manifests as elevated application errors leaves every hook succeeding, so CodeDeploy would work its way through all 100 instances one by one without ever rolling back. Option D fails because linear deployment configurations - like canary configurations - exist only for the Lambda and ECS compute platforms. An EC2/on-premises deployment group supports AllAtOnce, HalfAtATime, OneAtATime or a custom MinimumHealthyHosts configuration, so the linear configuration described cannot be created for this fleet.

stem: A company needs to deploy identical infrastructure stacks across 20 AWS accounts and 4 Regions using AWS CloudFormation. The stacks include VPCs, security groups, and IAM roles. Some resources like IAM roles must only be created once per account regardless of Region. Which approach handles this multi-account, multi-Region deployment efficiently?

options.text: Write a single CloudFormation template with conditions using AWS::Region pseudo-parameter to conditionally create IAM roles only in us-east-1. Deploy the template as a StackSet across all 20 accounts and 4 Regions, relying on conditions to skip IAM creation in other Regions.

Create a CodePipeline that iterates through each account and Region combination. Use CloudFormation deploy actions with separate templates for regional and global resources, and implement a Lambda function to track which accounts have already received global resources.

Use Terraform with a multi-provider configuration referencing all 20 accounts using assumed roles. Define modules for regional and global resources with conditional deployment logic based on the provider's Region, storing state in a centralized S3 backend.

Use AWS CloudFormation StackSets with service-managed permissions through AWS Organizations. Create two StackSets: one for Region-specific resources deployed to all 4 Regions, and one for global IAM resources deployed to only one Region per account using Region filters.

explanation: D is correct: StackSets with service-managed permissions deploy through AWS Organizations to OUs, so no per-account execution roles need to be created, and each StackSet carries its own target Region list. One StackSet holds the regional VPC and security-group resources and targets all four Regions; a second holds the global IAM roles and targets a single Region per account. Each resource class then gets exactly the deployment scope it needs, with no empty stack instances and independent update lifecycles. A is incorrect because a Region-conditioned single template still creates a stack instance in all four Regions of every account; three of them contain nothing, and every change to the global resources still ripples through 80 stack instances. B is incorrect because it hand-builds the account and Region iteration plus a Lambda bookkeeping table for behaviour StackSets performs natively, and that orchestration scales poorly across 80 account-Region pairs. C is incorrect because it swaps toolchains: managing 20 assume-role providers and a single shared state file is far more fragile operationally than StackSets, which exists precisely for multi-account, multi-Region CloudFormation deployment.

stem: A company's web application uses Amazon ElastiCache for Redis as a session store. When the primary Redis node fails, the application loses all user sessions, forcing users to re-authenticate. Which ElastiCache configuration ensures sessions are preserved during a primary node failure?

options.text: Deploy ElastiCache Memcached with a multi-node cluster across multiple Availability Zones. Configure automatic discovery enabled and client-side consistent hashing to distribute session data evenly and survive individual node failures without data loss.

Deploy ElastiCache Redis in cluster mode disabled with Multi-AZ enabled and automatic failover. Configure at least one read replica in a different AZ that automatically promotes to primary during failure, preserving the existing data through asynchronous replication.

Deploy ElastiCache Redis in cluster mode enabled with multiple shards across Availability Zones. Configure each shard with two replicas and enable in-transit encryption with AUTH token authentication to secure session data during inter-node replication.

Deploy ElastiCache Redis with daily automated backups retained for 7 days. Configure a Lambda function triggered by ElastiCache SNS failover notifications to restore the most recent backup to a new Redis cluster and update the application endpoint.

explanation: B is correct: with Redis cluster mode disabled, enabling Multi-AZ with automatic failover keeps one or more read replicas asynchronously replicating the primary's dataset into another AZ. When the primary node fails, ElastiCache promotes a replica and updates the primary endpoint's DNS, so the replicated session data survives and clients reconnect to the new primary without users having to re-authenticate. A is incorrect because Memcached has no replication: each node holds a distinct slice of the keyspace, so losing a node permanently loses every session hashed to it, which is exactly the failure being fixed. C is incorrect because cluster mode with multiple shards is a scaling answer for datasets or throughput too large for one node; it also depends on the same replica-promotion mechanism, and the encryption and AUTH details it emphasizes are security controls that contribute nothing to failover behaviour. D is incorrect because restoring a daily snapshot loses up to 24 hours of sessions and takes many minutes to create a new cluster and repoint the application - a recovery procedure with an outage, not a failover.

stem: A company needs to create a CloudWatch dashboard that displays the total number of API Gateway requests across 50 REST APIs, broken down by HTTP status code categories (2xx, 4xx, 5xx). The dashboard should update every 1 minute and support drill-down into individual APIs. Which approach creates this dashboard efficiently?

options.text: Build a metric math widget that uses SEARCH expressions over the AWS/ApiGateway namespace to pick up the Count, 4XXError and 5XXError metrics for every ApiName automatically. Derive the 2xx series as Count minus 4XXError minus 5XXError, and render the three series in a stacked area widget at a 1-minute period.

Configure API Gateway access logging to CloudWatch Logs for all 50 APIs. Create CloudWatch Logs Insights queries that parse status codes and aggregate by API name, then add the query results as a dashboard widget with a 1-minute auto-refresh interval.

Enable detailed CloudWatch metrics for each API Gateway stage. Create individual CloudWatch metric widgets for each of the 50 APIs showing 4xxError and 5xxError metrics, then use a CloudWatch dashboard text widget to display the calculated totals.

Create a Lambda function on a 1-minute schedule that reads the list of APIs from a DynamoDB table and calls the CloudWatch GetMetricData API for all 50 of them. Aggregate the results into 2xx, 4xx and 5xx totals, publish them as custom metrics using PutMetricData, and build the dashboard widgets from those custom metrics.

explanation: Option A is correct because it works with the dimensions API Gateway actually publishes. There is no StatusCode dimension on AWS/ApiGateway metrics - the dimensions are ApiName, Stage, Method and Resource - and status categories are exposed as the separate 4XXError and 5XXError metrics alongside the total Count. A SEARCH expression over each of those three metrics matches every ApiName without naming any API, so new APIs appear on the dashboard automatically, SUM collapses each search into a fleet total, and simple metric math yields the 2xx series by subtracting the two error metrics from Count. The individual time series returned by each SEARCH remain selectable in the widget, which is what gives the per-API drill-down, and CloudWatch renders the widget at a 1-minute period. Option B fails because a Logs Insights widget re-runs its query against ingested log data on each refresh; that adds ingestion delay and query latency on top of the metric pipeline, requires enabling and paying for access logging on all 50 APIs, and is far slower than reading metrics that already exist. Option C fails because a text widget renders static Markdown - it cannot compute or display a calculated total from other widgets - and 50 hand-built widgets must be edited every time an API is added or removed. Option D fails because it reimplements metric math in application code: it duplicates the data as custom metrics at extra cost, introduces at least a minute of aggregation lag, and adds a scheduled Lambda function that must be maintained and monitored, all to produce what a single SEARCH-based widget already provides.

stem: A company's application on EC2 runs behind a Network Load Balancer and experiences periodic connection timeouts. The operations team suspects the issue is related to EC2 instance networking but cannot reproduce it consistently. Which approach provides the MOST detailed network-level troubleshooting data?

options.text: Enable VPC Flow Logs on the ENIs attached to the affected EC2 instances with maximum aggregation interval of 1 minute. Publish logs to CloudWatch Logs and create a Logs Insights query that filters for REJECT actions and correlates timestamps with timeout reports.

Enable Traffic Mirroring on the ENIs of the affected EC2 instances with a filter for TCP traffic on the application port. Send mirrored traffic to a monitoring EC2 instance running tcpdump to capture full packet headers and analyze TCP retransmissions and resets.

Install the CloudWatch agent on the affected EC2 instances configured to collect netstat and ss output as custom metrics. Publish TCP connection state counts including ESTABLISHED, TIME_WAIT, and CLOSE_WAIT every 10 seconds to identify connection leaks.

Configure CloudWatch network performance metrics for the EC2 instances including NetworkPacketsIn, NetworkPacketsOut, and NetworkPacketsDropped. Create a CloudWatch alarm on the PacketsDropped metric and correlate spikes with the NLB HealthyHostCount metric changes.

explanation: B is correct: VPC Traffic Mirroring copies the actual packets from the instance ENI to a monitoring target, so tcpdump or Wireshark can reveal TCP-level detail that no AWS metric exposes - SYNs with no SYN/ACK, retransmissions and their timing, RSTs, and zero-window conditions. For an intermittent failure that cannot be reproduced on demand, capturing real traffic during the event is the only way to see which side stopped responding and why. A is incorrect because VPC Flow Logs are aggregated flow records (5-tuple, packet and byte counts, ACCEPT/REJECT) with no TCP flags, sequence numbers or retransmission data, and a REJECT appears only when a security group or NACL blocks traffic, which is a different failure mode from a timeout. C is incorrect because netstat/ss connection-state counts show the aftermath - accumulating TIME_WAIT or CLOSE_WAIT sockets - rather than the packet-level events that cause the timeouts. D is incorrect because instance NetworkPacketsIn/Out are coarse aggregates with no per-connection detail, and EC2 does not publish a NetworkPacketsDropped CloudWatch metric; ENA allowance-exceeded counters are surfaced only through the CloudWatch agent or ethtool.

stem: A company needs to enforce that all EC2 instances launched in production accounts use only approved AMIs from a central shared services account. Instances launched from non-approved AMIs must be automatically terminated. Which approach provides this enforcement?

options.text: Configure Amazon Inspector to continuously assess EC2 instances against a custom assessment template. Create an EventBridge rule matching Inspector findings for non-approved AMIs and target a Step Functions state machine that terminates instances after confirmation.

Create an AWS Config rule using the approved-amis-by-id managed rule with the list of approved AMI IDs. Configure auto-remediation with an SSM Automation document that terminates EC2 instances launched from non-approved AMIs and sends an SNS notification.

Deploy a Service Control Policy in AWS Organizations that uses a condition key to restrict ec2:RunInstances to only the approved AMI ARNs. Configure the SCP at the production organizational unit level and exempt the shared services account from the policy.

Create an IAM policy in each production account that denies ec2:RunInstances unless the imageId condition matches the approved AMI list. Attach the policy to all IAM roles and users in the production accounts and update the AMI list monthly in each account.
