explanation: B is correct: the requirement includes terminating instances that are already running from unapproved AMIs, which needs a detective control plus remediation. The AWS Config managed rule approved-amis-by-id evaluates every EC2 instance's imageId against the supplied list of approved AMI IDs and marks non-conforming instances NON_COMPLIANT, and an attached automatic remediation action running an SSM Automation document (such as AWS-TerminateEC2Instance) terminates them and can notify via SNS. A is incorrect because Amazon Inspector assesses software vulnerabilities and network reachability; there is no assessment template that evaluates instances against an approved AMI list. C is incorrect because an SCP with an ec2:RunInstances condition on the AMI is purely preventive - it blocks future launches but never detects or terminates the instances launched before the policy existed - so it satisfies only half the requirement. D is incorrect because per-account IAM policies must be attached to and maintained on every user and role, are bypassed by any principal you miss, and like the SCP they only block launches rather than terminating running instances.

stem: A development team needs to implement database schema migrations as part of their CI/CD pipeline deploying to Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL. The migrations must run automatically during deployment, support rollback on failure, and not block application deployments for more than 30 seconds. Which approach meets these requirements?

options.text: Package Liquibase in a container-image Lambda function deployed into the Aurora VPC subnets and invoke it from a CodePipeline Lambda action before the ECS deploy stage. Set the function timeout to 30 seconds to bound how long the pipeline is blocked, and have the handler roll back to the previous changeset tag if the update fails.

Use an RDS Data API endpoint to execute migration SQL scripts directly from a CodePipeline Lambda invoke action. Store migration scripts in an S3 bucket versioned by deployment and configure the Lambda to execute statements sequentially using the Data API batch endpoint.

Add a CodeBuild stage before the application deployment that connects to Aurora through a VPC-configured build environment and runs Flyway migrations. Configure Flyway with outOfOrder set to false and enable baseline-on-migrate for the initial deployment run.

Configure the application container to run database migrations on startup before accepting traffic. Use an ECS container dependency so that a migration sidecar container running Flyway must reach a SUCCESS state, reported through a health check endpoint, before the main application container is started and registered with the load balancer target group.

explanation: Option A is correct because it is the only choice that satisfies all three stated constraints at once. Running Liquibase inside a Lambda function attached to the Aurora VPC subnets gives network reachability to the cluster, invoking it as a CodePipeline Lambda action makes the migration an automatic pipeline step rather than a manual one, and the 30-second function timeout puts a hard upper bound on how long the pipeline can be blocked - the requirement the stem states explicitly. Liquibase also maintains a changelog table and supports rollback to a prior tag, so the failure path required by the stem is genuinely available. Option B fails because the Data API batch endpoint, batchExecuteStatement, runs one parameterized statement over a set of parameter sets; it cannot execute an arbitrary multi-statement migration script, and nothing in the design tracks which migrations have already been applied, so a re-run reapplies them. There is also no rollback of DDL that has already committed. Option C fails on two of the three requirements: a CodeBuild stage runs to completion with no bound on how long the pipeline waits, so the 30-second constraint is unmet, and Flyway Community Edition has no undo command, so a failed migration cannot be rolled back. Option D fails because it couples schema change to task lifecycle. Every task in the ECS service starts its own migration sidecar, so a scale-out or rolling deployment runs the migration concurrently from many tasks, and a migration failure surfaces as repeated task startup failures during the rolling update rather than as a clean, revertible pipeline step.

stem: A company uses AWS Systems Manager to manage configuration across 500 EC2 instances. The team needs to deploy a new version of a configuration file to all instances in a controlled manner: 10% first, verify for 10 minutes, then the remaining 90%. If any instance reports failure during the rollout, the deployment must stop. Which SSM feature achieves this?

options.text: Create an SSM Distributor package containing the configuration file with an install script. Use SSM State Manager to create an association targeting all instances with the distributor package, setting the schedule to apply the configuration with a rate expression.

Configure AWS AppConfig with a deployment strategy that deploys to 10% of instances with a 10-minute bake time before proceeding to the remaining 90%. Create a configuration profile backed by an S3 object and integrate the application with the AppConfig agent.

Create an SSM State Manager association with a rate control configuration set to 10% concurrency and 1 error threshold. Apply the association to all 500 instances with an AWS-RunDocument command document that deploys the configuration file to each target instance.

Use SSM Run Command with a custom command document that copies the configuration file from S3. Configure the command with MaxConcurrency at 10% and MaxErrors at 0, and use a maintenance window with a two-phase execution schedule for the canary and full rollout.

explanation: B is correct: AWS AppConfig deployment strategies are built for this exact shape - a growth factor that releases the new configuration to 10% of targets, a bake time during which AppConfig monitors the CloudWatch alarms you associate with the environment, and then completion to the remaining hosts. If an alarm enters ALARM during deployment or bake, AppConfig rolls back automatically, which is the required stop-on-failure behaviour. Backing the configuration profile with an S3 object and retrieving it through the AppConfig agent delivers the file without a fleet-wide push. A is incorrect because an SSM Distributor package applied by a State Manager association installs on a schedule with no canary phase, no bake period and no alarm-driven halt. C is incorrect because State Manager rate control (concurrency percentage and error threshold) only throttles how fast the association applies and aborts on errors; it cannot pause for a 10-minute validation window between a 10% wave and the remainder. D is incorrect because Run Command MaxConcurrency and MaxErrors likewise control throttling and abort behaviour, and chaining two maintenance-window executions is a manual approximation of a canary with no automated verification gate between the phases.

stem: A company's application uses Amazon SQS standard queues for asynchronous processing. During a recent incident, a poison message caused the consumer Lambda function to repeatedly fail and retry, blocking other messages in the queue. Which solution prevents a single poison message from blocking queue processing?

options.text: Switch from SQS standard queue to an SQS FIFO queue with content-based deduplication enabled. Configure the FIFO queue's deduplication scope to messageGroup and set the visibility timeout to 30 seconds to ensure messages are reprocessed by other consumer instances.

Implement exponential backoff in the Lambda function code using a try-catch block around message processing. Store the retry count in a DynamoDB table keyed by message ID, and manually delete the message from the queue after the maximum retry count is exceeded.

Configure the Lambda event source mapping with a maximum retry attempts setting of 2 and a maximum batching window of 5 seconds. Enable bisect-on-function-error to split failed batches and send failed records to a configured on-failure destination SQS queue.

Configure the SQS queue with a redrive policy that moves messages to a dead-letter queue after 3 receive attempts. Set the main queue's visibility timeout to 6 times the Lambda function timeout and create a CloudWatch alarm on the DLQ ApproximateNumberOfMessages metric.

explanation: D is correct: a redrive policy with maxReceiveCount 3 makes SQS itself move a message to the dead-letter queue after the third unsuccessful receive, so the poison message stops reappearing and consumers drain the rest of the queue. Setting the source queue's visibility timeout to about six times the Lambda timeout is documented guidance preventing redelivery while a message is still in flight, and an alarm on the DLQ's ApproximateNumberOfMessages surfaces trapped messages. A is incorrect because FIFO makes head-of-line blocking worse: a failing message blocks its entire message group until it succeeds or is removed, and content-based deduplication has nothing to do with repeated processing failures. B is incorrect because tracking retry counts in DynamoDB and deleting messages from application code reimplements the DLQ; any crash before the delete leaves the poison message in the queue, and it adds a table plus state management to maintain. C is incorrect because BisectBatchOnFunctionError and OnFailure destinations are event source mapping features for Kinesis and DynamoDB Streams, not SQS, and SQS event source mappings expose no maximum-retry-attempts setting - retry behaviour is governed by the queue's redrive policy.

stem: A company runs a serverless application using API Gateway, Lambda, and DynamoDB. The operations team needs end-to-end visibility into request latency, error rates by endpoint, and DynamoDB throttling events. Which TWO services should be configured together to provide comprehensive observability?

options.text: Deploy Amazon Managed Grafana with the CloudWatch data source plugin configured for the production account. Create Grafana dashboards displaying API Gateway latency percentiles, Lambda concurrent execution metrics, and DynamoDB ConsumedReadCapacityUnits over time.

Enable AWS X-Ray active tracing on API Gateway and Lambda functions. Instrument the Lambda function code with the X-Ray SDK to create subsegments for DynamoDB calls and enable the X-Ray service map to visualize latency distribution across all components.

Enable Amazon CloudWatch ServiceLens to aggregate metrics, logs, and traces into a unified observability view. Configure ServiceLens resource health monitoring for the Lambda functions and DynamoDB tables to correlate performance anomalies across the application stack.

Configure API Gateway access logging with detailed request and response fields sent to CloudWatch Logs. Create CloudWatch Logs Insights queries to compute p50 and p99 latency by endpoint, error rates by HTTP status code, and correlation with DynamoDB throttle events.

explanation: B and D are correct. B supplies the distributed-trace layer: active tracing on API Gateway plus the X-Ray SDK in the Lambda functions creates subsegments around the DynamoDB calls, so the service map and individual traces attribute end-to-end latency to the gateway, the function, or the table, and DynamoDB throttling appears as ProvisionedThroughputExceededException on the traced subsegment. D supplies the aggregate per-endpoint layer: API Gateway access logging with the full $context fields lets CloudWatch Logs Insights compute p50/p99 latency and error rates grouped by resource path and HTTP status - complete counts that sampled traces cannot provide. A is incorrect because Amazon Managed Grafana is only a visualization front end over CloudWatch; it collects no telemetry itself, so configuring it does not produce the observability data. C is incorrect for the same reason one level up - CloudWatch ServiceLens stitches together metrics, logs and X-Ray traces into one view, so it presupposes that X-Ray tracing and the logging in B and D are already configured.

stem: A company needs to automatically remediate security group rules that allow unrestricted SSH access (0.0.0.0/0 on port 22) within 5 minutes of creation. The remediation must work across all AWS accounts in the organization and log all remediation actions for audit. Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Deploy the AWS Config managed rule restricted-ssh across all accounts using a conformance pack via AWS Organizations. Configure auto-remediation with the AWS-DisablePublicAccessForSecurityGroup SSM Automation document and log remediation actions to a centralized CloudTrail trail.

Enable AWS Security Hub across all accounts with the AWS Foundational Security Best Practices standard. Configure custom actions for non-compliant security group findings and create an EventBridge rule that triggers automated remediation through a cross-account Lambda function.

Deploy Amazon GuardDuty across all accounts using a delegated administrator. Configure GuardDuty to detect unrestricted security group changes as a custom threat intelligence indicator and use a Step Functions workflow to revoke the offending rules and notify the team.

Create an EventBridge rule in each account that matches AuthorizeSecurityGroupIngress API calls from CloudTrail. Target a Lambda function that checks if the rule allows 0.0.0.0/0 on port 22 and calls RevokeSecurityGroupIngress, then publishes audit events to a central SNS topic.

explanation: A is correct: restricted-ssh is a change-triggered AWS Config managed rule, so a security group opening 0.0.0.0/0 on port 22 is evaluated within minutes, inside the 5-minute goal. A conformance pack deployed through AWS Organizations from the delegated administrator gives every account the rule from one artifact; Config's automatic remediation runs AWS-DisablePublicAccessForSecurityGroup to revoke the rule, and both the remediation and the RevokeSecurityGroupIngress call land in the organization CloudTrail for audit. B is incorrect because Security Hub custom actions are operator-initiated console buttons rather than automatic triggers, and the answer still requires building and operating cross-account remediation Lambda functions yourself. C is incorrect because GuardDuty analyzes CloudTrail, DNS and flow-log telemetry for threat activity; it does not evaluate security group configuration, and custom threat intelligence sets accept only IP addresses and domains. D is incorrect because it needs an EventBridge rule and Lambda function deployed and maintained in every account, and matching only AuthorizeSecurityGroupIngress misses other paths to the same state, such as ModifySecurityGroupRules or rules created before the automation existed.

stem: A company needs to implement least-privilege access for its CI/CD pipeline that deploys CloudFormation stacks. The pipeline runs in a tools account and deploys to staging and production accounts using cross-account IAM roles. How should the cross-account deployment roles be configured to follow least privilege?

options.text: Create IAM roles in staging and production accounts with CloudFormation service-linked role permissions. Configure the roles with a permissions boundary that limits the maximum permissions to the specific services used in the CloudFormation templates.

Create IAM roles in staging and production accounts with inline policies that allow only the specific CloudFormation, EC2, S3, and IAM actions required by the stacks. Configure trust policies that allow only the tools account's pipeline role ARN with an external ID condition.

Create a single IAM role in the tools account with cross-account resource policies on each target account's CloudFormation stacks. Grant cloudformation:* and iam:PassRole permissions scoped to the specific stack ARNs in each target account using resource-based conditions.

Create IAM roles in staging and production accounts with the AdministratorAccess managed policy attached. Configure trust policies that allow the tools account's root principal and add an IP address condition restricting access to the tools account's NAT Gateway Elastic IPs.

explanation: B is correct: least privilege has two halves and only B has both. The permissions half is a policy in each target account granting only the CloudFormation, EC2, S3 and IAM actions the stacks need, scoped to the relevant resources, rather than blanket admin. The trust half restricts sts:AssumeRole to the specific pipeline role ARN in the tools account - not the account root - with an ExternalId condition, so only that pipeline can assume the role. A is incorrect because service-linked roles are created and controlled by the service itself and cannot be repurposed as assumable cross-account deployment roles, and a permissions boundary only caps the maximum permissions an identity policy can grant; it never grants anything, so on its own it produces a role that can do nothing. C is incorrect because CloudFormation stacks do not support resource-based policies, so cross-account access cannot be granted the way the option describes, and cloudformation:* with broad iam:PassRole is the opposite of least privilege. D is incorrect because AdministratorAccess plainly violates least privilege, trusting the tools account root principal delegates trust to every principal in that account, and an aws:SourceIp condition does not constrain calls made by AWS-managed CodePipeline and CodeBuild compute.

stem: A team uses AWS CodePipeline with a GitHub source action. They want to require that all pull requests pass automated tests in CodeBuild before merging, and that only merged code from the main branch triggers production deployments. Which configuration implements this workflow?

options.text: Configure a CodePipeline triggered by GitHub webhook events on the main branch for production deployments. Separately, create a CodeBuild project triggered by GitHub pull request webhook events to run tests and report status checks back to the GitHub pull request.

Configure CodePipeline with two source actions: one for pull requests that triggers a CodeBuild test stage, and one for main branch pushes that triggers the full deployment pipeline. Use a CodePipeline manual approval action between the test and deploy stages.

Configure CodePipeline with a GitHub source action on all branches. Add a CodeBuild stage that checks the branch name from the CODEBUILD_WEBHOOK_HEAD_REF environment variable and conditionally executes tests for PRs or deployment for the main branch pushes.

Configure CodePipeline with a GitHub source action using GitHub Actions as the CI provider. Create a GitHub Actions workflow that runs tests on pull requests and triggers the CodePipeline execution via AWS CLI only when tests pass on the main branch.

explanation: Separate CodeBuild projects triggered by PR webhooks handle pre-merge testing, while CodePipeline triggered by main branch changes handles production deployment. This separates concerns cleanly. Option B's dual source actions in a single pipeline don't work as described since CodePipeline triggers on any source change. Option C uses branch checking in CodeBuild which is fragile and doesn't properly integrate with GitHub PR status checks. Option D introduces GitHub Actions as an external dependency when AWS-native services handle the workflow.

stem: A company uses AWS CloudFormation to deploy a VPC with public and private subnets, NAT gateways, and route tables. The template frequently fails during updates because of dependency issues between route table associations and NAT gateway replacements. Which CloudFormation feature resolves the dependency ordering problem?

options.text: Use CloudFormation resource import to manage existing VPC resources instead of updating them in place. Create a change set preview before each update to identify potential dependency conflicts and manually reorder resource operations in the change set execution.

Refactor the template to use CloudFormation nested stacks, separating the VPC, subnet, NAT gateway, and route table resources into individual child stacks. Use stack outputs and cross-stack references with Fn::ImportValue in the consuming stacks to establish an explicit, enforced dependency chain between the layers.

Add UpdateReplacePolicy and DeletionPolicy attributes set to Retain on NAT gateway and route table resources. Use Fn::GetAtt instead of Ref to reference NAT gateway attributes in route table entries, ensuring CloudFormation infers the correct dependency graph.

Add explicit DependsOn attributes to the route and route table association resources so they depend on the NAT gateway resource, and reference the NAT gateway with Ref in the NatGatewayId property of each AWS::EC2::Route so CloudFormation also carries the dependency through a replacement.

explanation: Option D is correct because it addresses the ordering problem with the two mechanisms CloudFormation actually offers. An explicit DependsOn on the route and route table association resources forces CloudFormation to finish creating or replacing the NAT gateway before it touches the routes, and referencing the NAT gateway with Ref inside the AWS::EC2::Route NatGatewayId property adds the same edge to the dependency graph implicitly, so when the NAT gateway is replaced the dependent routes are updated in the correct order rather than racing the replacement. Option A fails because resource import is for bringing existing, unmanaged resources under stack management; it does nothing for ordering during subsequent updates, and change sets are read-only previews - CloudFormation does not let you reorder the operations inside a change set before executing it. Option B fails because splitting the resources into child stacks does not remove the dependency, it only moves it across a stack boundary, and Fn::ImportValue makes matters worse: an exported value cannot be changed or deleted while another stack imports it, so a NAT gateway replacement that changes the exported ID is blocked outright. Option C fails because Retain policies govern what happens to a resource when it is replaced or deleted - they leave orphaned NAT gateways accruing charges rather than fixing sequencing - and swapping Ref for Fn::GetAtt changes nothing about dependency inference, since CloudFormation derives the same edge from either intrinsic function.

stem: A company operates an event-driven ordering system. Amazon API Gateway receives orders and invokes a Lambda function that publishes each order to an Amazon SNS topic, and several SQS queues subscribe to that topic for different processing pipelines. During a flash-sale traffic spike, the ingestion Lambda function exhausted the account's available concurrency and was throttled. API Gateway returned HTTP 500 to the callers, and because the orders were never published to the topic they were lost entirely. Which design change prevents order loss during future traffic spikes?

options.text: Replace the Lambda ingestion step with a direct API Gateway service integration to an Amazon Kinesis Data Streams stream that durably buffers incoming orders. Use on-demand capacity mode and a 7-day retention period, and have a consumer publish from the stream to the SNS topic at a sustainable rate.

Replace the SNS-to-SQS fan-out with Amazon EventBridge as the central event bus. Configure EventBridge rules to route orders to the target SQS queues, enable the EventBridge dead-letter queue for failed target deliveries, and set the target retry policy to retry with exponential backoff for up to 24 hours before an event is dead-lettered.

Increase the SQS queue maximum message retention period to 14 days and enable long polling with a 20-second wait time. Configure the consumer Lambda functions with reserved concurrency matching the expected peak throughput to process messages faster during spikes.

Configure the SNS topic with a delivery retry policy that includes exponential backoff with a maximum of 100 retries over 24 hours. Enable server-side encryption on the SNS topic and SQS queues, and set the SQS queue visibility timeout to 5 minutes.

explanation: Option A is correct because the loss occurs at ingestion, before anything durable has accepted the order, and the only way to stop that is to make the very first hop a durable buffer. An API Gateway direct service integration to Kinesis Data Streams writes each order to the stream synchronously with no Lambda function in the path, so there is no function concurrency to exhaust. On-demand capacity mode scales the stream's shards automatically with the flash-sale traffic, and the 7-day retention means orders survive even if the consumer that publishes to SNS falls badly behind. Decoupling ingestion rate from processing rate is exactly what absorbs the spike. Option B fails because it changes the fan-out downstream of the topic, but the orders in this incident never reached the topic. An EventBridge dead-letter queue captures events the bus failed to deliver to a target; it cannot capture a request that was rejected at the front door. Option C fails for the same reason: longer SQS retention and long polling only affect messages that are already in a queue, and reserved concurrency on the consumers caps rather than guarantees concurrency, doing nothing for the ingestion path that dropped the orders. Option D fails because SNS retry policies govern delivery from the topic to its subscribers, and encryption and visibility timeout are unrelated controls; none of them help when the publish call itself never happened.

stem: A company wants to detect anomalous behavior in its AWS account, such as unusual API call patterns, unexpected resource provisioning, or access from unfamiliar IP addresses. The detection must be automated and require minimal configuration. Which service provides this capability with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Deploy CloudWatch Anomaly Detection on key CloudTrail metrics including API call counts by service, error rates, and unique source IP addresses. Create CloudWatch alarms that trigger when metrics deviate from the anomaly detection band by more than 2 standard deviations.

Create a Kinesis Data Analytics application that processes CloudTrail events in real-time using SQL queries. Implement sliding window aggregations to detect unusual API call volumes and source IP patterns, and send alerts through an SNS topic when anomalies are detected.

Configure Amazon Detective to automatically investigate security findings from CloudTrail and VPC Flow Logs. Use Detective's behavioral graph to identify anomalous patterns and create custom detection rules based on historical baseline analysis of account activity.

Enable Amazon GuardDuty in all accounts and Regions. GuardDuty uses machine learning to analyze CloudTrail management events, VPC Flow Logs, and DNS logs to detect threats and anomalies, providing findings with severity levels and recommended remediation actions.

explanation: D is correct: GuardDuty is a fully managed detector that continuously consumes CloudTrail management events, VPC Flow Logs and Route 53 DNS query logs with no agents or log pipelines, and can be enabled organization-wide from a delegated administrator with auto-enrollment of new accounts. Its ML and threat intelligence already cover the anomaly classes named - unusual API patterns, unexpected provisioning (Recon, CryptoCurrency findings) and access from unfamiliar or anonymizing IPs - emitting severity-scored findings. A is incorrect because CloudWatch anomaly detection requires you to first manufacture a metric for every behaviour of interest (metric filters over CloudTrail logs), then create and tune an anomaly detector and alarm per metric - substantial and ongoing configuration. B is incorrect because a streaming SQL application over CloudTrail is an entire system to build, operate, scale and tune; it is the highest-overhead option here. C is incorrect because Amazon Detective is an investigation tool that visualizes and pivots on findings produced by services like GuardDuty and Security Hub; it does not generate detections and does not support user-authored detection rules.

stem: A company uses AWS Systems Manager Incident Manager to handle production incidents. The team needs to ensure that when a critical CloudWatch alarm triggers, an incident is automatically created, the on-call engineer is paged, a response plan is activated, and all actions are documented in a timeline. Which configuration achieves this?

options.text: Configure the CloudWatch alarm to send notifications to an SNS topic subscribed by PagerDuty. Create a PagerDuty webhook integration that calls the Incident Manager CreateTimelineEvent API to log the alarm trigger and initiate the escalation process.

Configure AWS Chatbot integration with Incident Manager and the team's Slack workspace. Set up a CloudWatch alarm that sends notifications to the Chatbot SNS topic, and configure Chatbot to create incidents when team members react to the alarm notification in Slack.

Create an EventBridge rule matching CloudWatch alarm state changes. Target a Step Functions state machine that creates an Incident Manager incident via the StartIncident API, sends page notifications through SNS, and logs timeline events at each workflow step.

Create an Incident Manager response plan that defines the escalation path, runbook, and engagement contacts. Configure the CloudWatch alarm to trigger the response plan via an EventBridge rule target, automatically creating an incident and paging the on-call rotation.

explanation: D is correct: an Incident Manager response plan is the object that bundles impact level, engagement contacts and the escalation plan, the runbook (an SSM Automation document) and chat channel integration. A CloudWatch alarm entering ALARM can start that response plan directly - as an alarm action or through an EventBridge rule targeting the plan - and Incident Manager then creates the incident record, pages the on-call rotation via the escalation plan, and writes every engagement, runbook step and note into the incident timeline automatically, satisfying all four requirements with configuration rather than code. A is incorrect because paging through PagerDuty and calling CreateTimelineEvent yourself never creates an Incident Manager incident or engages its contacts; you get orphan timeline entries with no incident workflow behind them. B is incorrect because it requires a human to react to a Slack message before an incident exists, so incident creation is not automatic. C is incorrect because calling StartIncident from a Step Functions state machine and hand-rolling SNS paging and timeline writes reimplements what the response plan does natively, adding a state machine to build, test and maintain.

stem: A company needs to ensure that all traffic between microservices running on Amazon ECS Fargate is encrypted in transit using certificates that are issued and rotated automatically by a private certificate authority. The services currently communicate over plain HTTP using service discovery names, and the team wants to avoid modifying application code or managing certificate material inside the containers. Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Enable Amazon ECS Service Connect for the services and configure Service Connect TLS with an AWS Private Certificate Authority. Amazon ECS injects a managed proxy sidecar into each task that terminates and originates TLS, issuing and rotating certificates automatically while the applications keep speaking plain HTTP.

Install and configure Istio service mesh on the ECS cluster using the Istio ECS integration. Enable strict mTLS peer authentication policies across all namespaces and configure Istio's Citadel component to automatically provision and rotate certificates for each service.

Deploy Amazon API Gateway as an internal REST API between each microservice pair. Enable mutual TLS on the API Gateway custom domain name with a truststore in S3 and configure each service to communicate through its dedicated API Gateway endpoint.

Configure an internal Application Load Balancer in front of every microservice with mutual TLS authentication enabled on each HTTPS listener. Import the client certificates into AWS Certificate Manager and configure each ALB to validate presented client certificates against a trust store containing the CA certificate chain for every microservice.

explanation: Option A is correct because ECS Service Connect is the currently supported, fully managed way to get transparent transit encryption between Fargate tasks. When Service Connect TLS is enabled with an AWS Private CA, Amazon ECS requests a certificate per Service Connect service, injects the managed proxy sidecar into each task, and handles issuance and rotation of the certificate material without the container ever seeing it. Because the proxy intercepts traffic addressed to the Service Connect discovery name, the application continues to make ordinary plain-HTTP calls and no code changes are needed - precisely the constraint in the stem. Option B fails because there is no Istio ECS integration: Istio's control plane and sidecar injection depend on the Kubernetes API and CRDs, so it cannot be installed on an ECS cluster, and Citadel is a component that was folded into istiod several releases ago. Option C fails because API Gateway mutual TLS applies to clients connecting to a custom domain name, which makes it a front-door control rather than a service-to-service one; placing a dedicated API Gateway between every pair of microservices multiplies latency, cost and configuration to an impractical degree, and it would require each service to be reconfigured to call gateway endpoints instead of its peers. Option D fails on a concrete detail: ALB mutual TLS validates client certificates against a trust store built from CA certificate bundles uploaded to Amazon S3, not from client certificates imported into ACM, so the configuration as described cannot be created - and routing every east-west call through an ALB adds a hop that the Service Connect proxy avoids.

stem: A company wants to implement trunk-based development where all developers commit to the main branch. Feature flags control the visibility of incomplete features. The team needs a managed service to control feature flags with gradual rollout percentages and instant kill-switch capability. Which AWS service is purpose-built for this use case?

options.text: Use AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store to store feature flag values as JSON StringList parameters. Configure each application to poll Parameter Store every 30 seconds and parse the JSON to determine feature visibility based on user ID hashing.

Use AWS Lambda@Edge functions integrated with CloudFront to evaluate feature flags at the edge. Store flag configurations in an S3 bucket as JSON files and have Lambda@Edge read the flags to modify response headers that control feature visibility in the client application.

Use Amazon DynamoDB with a feature flags table containing flag name, enabled status, and rollout percentage attributes. Implement a DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) cluster for low-latency reads and use DynamoDB Streams to propagate flag changes to application instances.

Use AWS AppConfig with feature flag configuration profiles. Define each feature as a flag with a percentage-based deployment strategy, and configure the AppConfig Lambda extension in each service to retrieve flag values with local caching and instant flag updates.

explanation: D is correct: AWS AppConfig has first-class feature flag configuration profiles - each flag is a typed, validated object, flags are released through deployment strategies that can grow exposure by percentage, and turning a flag off and deploying it takes effect as soon as clients next poll, which is the instant kill switch. The AppConfig agent or Lambda extension caches the configuration locally and polls in the background, so application lookups are local and fast while still converging quickly on changes. A is incorrect because Parameter Store stores values but supplies no flag semantics, no rollout strategy, no validation and no deployment or rollback - the percentage logic and user hashing all become code you write and test. B is incorrect because Lambda@Edge evaluates flags only for requests passing through CloudFront, so backend services making their own decisions are not covered, and JSON in S3 again leaves gradual rollout as custom logic. C is incorrect because a DynamoDB table with DAX and Streams is a feature flag service you build and operate; DynamoDB Streams also cannot push changes to application instances without additional fan-out infrastructure.

stem: A company needs to create a self-service provisioning system where development teams can request pre-approved infrastructure templates through a service catalog. The system must enforce tagging standards, limit instance types, and track costs per team. Which AWS service combination provides this governed self-service capability?

options.text: Deploy AWS Control Tower with Account Factory to provision development team accounts. Use Control Tower guardrails to enforce instance type restrictions and tagging standards, and provide teams with pre-configured account vending machine templates for infrastructure.

Create a custom web portal using API Gateway and Lambda that presents a list of approved CloudFormation templates stored in S3. Implement Lambda functions that deploy stacks with mandatory tags and validate instance types against an approved list before provisioning.

Configure AWS Organizations with SCPs that restrict resource creation to approved instance types only. Create shared CloudFormation templates in a central S3 bucket accessible to all accounts and rely on SCPs to enforce tagging through condition keys in the policies.

Deploy AWS Service Catalog with portfolios containing approved CloudFormation products. Apply launch constraints with IAM roles that enforce tagging through CloudFormation stack policies, and configure TagOptions to require team and cost-center tags on all provisioned resources.

explanation: D is correct: AWS Service Catalog is the governed self-service layer. Administrators publish approved CloudFormation templates as products inside portfolios and grant portfolio access per team; launch constraints let a developer provision through a Service Catalog role they do not otherwise hold, so their own IAM permissions stay minimal; template constraints restrict parameter values such as permitted instance types; and TagOptions enforce mandatory key/value pairs (team, cost-center) on every provisioned resource, which is what makes per-team cost tracking work in Cost Explorer and AWS Budgets. A is incorrect because Control Tower Account Factory vends accounts and applies guardrails at account and OU scope; it is not a catalog of infrastructure products developers launch on demand. B is incorrect because a bespoke API Gateway and Lambda portal recreates Service Catalog's product versioning, access control, constraints and provisioned-product tracking as code the company must build and maintain. C is incorrect because SCPs are preventive guardrails with no self-service interface, and they cannot apply tags - at most they deny an action when a required tag is absent from the request, leaving teams with no catalog to browse and no approved templates to launch.

stem: A company runs a containerized application on Amazon EKS that must maintain 99.99% availability. The application uses persistent volumes backed by Amazon EBS. During an AZ outage, pods with EBS volumes could not be rescheduled to another AZ because EBS volumes are AZ-specific. Which solution ensures pod reschedulability across AZs?

options.text: Enable EBS Multi-Attach on io2 volumes to allow the same volume to be attached to instances in multiple AZs simultaneously. Update the PersistentVolume accessMode to ReadWriteMany and configure the StatefulSet to use a podAntiAffinity rule spreading replicas across AZs.

Configure EBS volume snapshots on a 5-minute schedule using AWS Backup. Deploy a custom Kubernetes operator that detects AZ failures, creates new EBS volumes from the latest snapshot in the healthy AZ, and patches PersistentVolume definitions to reference the new volumes.

Replace EBS-backed PersistentVolumes with Amazon EFS-backed PersistentVolumes using the EFS CSI driver. Configure the EFS file system with mount targets in all cluster AZs and set the StorageClass reclaim policy to Retain for data persistence across pod rescheduling.

Deploy the application using a StatefulSet with volumeClaimTemplates and configure topology-aware volume provisioning. Set the StatefulSet's podManagementPolicy to Parallel and use the EBS CSI driver's topology constraints to create volumes in the same AZ as scheduled pods.

explanation: C is correct: Amazon EFS is a regional file system reachable from every AZ through mount targets, so a PersistentVolume provisioned by the EFS CSI driver has no AZ affinity at all. When an AZ fails, the scheduler can place the pod on a node in a surviving AZ and it mounts the same file system with the same data, which is what a stateful workload needs to meet 99.99% availability; EFS also supports ReadWriteMany so multiple replicas can share the volume. A is incorrect because EBS Multi-Attach is limited to io1/io2 volumes attached to up to 16 Nitro instances within a single Availability Zone - it never spans AZs - and it presents a raw block device that requires a cluster-aware file system rather than providing Kubernetes ReadWriteMany semantics. B is incorrect because snapshot-and-restore loses up to five minutes of writes, takes minutes to create and attach a replacement volume, and requires a custom operator the company must build and maintain. D is incorrect because topology-aware provisioning is precisely what binds each EBS volume to the AZ of its pod; it prevents unschedulable pods at creation time but leaves the volume, and therefore the pod's data, stranded when that AZ fails.

stem: A company's Lambda functions write structured JSON logs to CloudWatch Logs. The operations team wants to create metric filters that extract business metrics like order amounts and processing times from the log entries, and alarm when the average order processing time exceeds 3 seconds over a 5-minute period. Which approach is MOST efficient?

options.text: Create a Kinesis Data Firehose delivery stream subscribed to the CloudWatch log groups. Configure a Lambda transformation function to parse JSON logs, extract metrics, and call the CloudWatch PutMetricData API to publish custom metrics before forwarding logs to S3.

Use CloudWatch Logs Insights to run scheduled queries every 5 minutes that parse the JSON logs and compute average processing times. Configure the scheduled query to publish results as custom metrics and create alarms on the query result metrics.

Modify the Lambda functions to use the CloudWatch Embedded Metric Format (EMF) to publish processingTime and orderAmount as custom metrics directly within log entries. Create CloudWatch alarms on the automatically generated metrics without needing separate metric filters.

Use CloudWatch Logs metric filters with JSON filter pattern syntax to extract the processingTime field from structured log entries. Create a custom CloudWatch metric from the extracted values and configure a CloudWatch alarm on the Average statistic with a 5-minute period.

explanation: CloudWatch Embedded Metric Format (EMF) generates custom metrics directly from structured log output without separate metric filters. Metrics are automatically created with dimensions and appear in CloudWatch Metrics for alarming. Option A works but requires creating and maintaining separate metric filters outside the application code. Option C introduces unnecessary Kinesis infrastructure for metric extraction. Option D uses scheduled queries which have minimum 1-hour evaluation intervals and are not designed for real-time alarming.

stem: A company uses Amazon Route 53 with health checks to route traffic between two Regions. The health check monitors an HTTP endpoint on port 443. During a recent certificate renewal, the health check temporarily failed because the new certificate's Subject Alternative Name didn't match the health check's configured FQDN. How should the team prevent this from recurring?

options.text: Configure the Route 53 health check to use the EnableSNI setting with the FullyQualifiedDomainName matching the certificate's SAN. Use AWS Certificate Manager to manage certificate renewals with automatic renewal enabled, ensuring SANs are preserved during renewal.

Configure the Route 53 health check to use a calculated health check that combines an HTTPS check with a TCP port 443 check. Set the health check routing to failover only when both child checks report unhealthy, preventing certificate-only failures from triggering failover.

Change the Route 53 health check from HTTPS to TCP on port 443 to bypass SSL certificate validation entirely. Configure the health check with a request interval of 10 seconds and a failure threshold of 3 to quickly detect genuine endpoint failures without certificate issues.

Create a CloudWatch alarm that monitors the ACM certificate expiration DaysToExpiry metric. Configure an EventBridge rule to trigger a Lambda function that updates the Route 53 health check FQDN to match the new certificate's SAN before certificate renewal completes.

explanation: A is correct: an HTTPS Route 53 health check completes a TLS handshake, and EnableSNI sends the configured FullyQualifiedDomainName as the SNI server name, requiring that name to appear in the certificate's CN or SAN list. Aligning the FQDN with a name genuinely on the certificate and letting ACM manage renewal (ACM reissues with the same SAN set and auto-deploys eligible renewals) removes the mismatch while keeping full TLS validation. B is incorrect because a calculated health check that only reports unhealthy when both an HTTPS and a TCP child fail permanently masks genuine HTTPS failures: the TCP child stays healthy whenever the listener accepts connections, so a broken application would never trigger failover. C is incorrect because a TCP check on port 443 verifies only that the port accepts connections - it validates neither the certificate nor that the application responds correctly - so it permanently degrades health-check fidelity to work around a one-off misconfiguration. D is incorrect because a DaysToExpiry-driven Lambda races the renewal it is trying to precede, and ACM renewals do not change a certificate's domain names, so the health check FQDN should never need rewriting in the first place.

stem: A financial services company needs to implement network segmentation for its VPC to isolate the web tier, application tier, and database tier. Each tier must only be able to communicate with its adjacent tier, and all inter-tier traffic must be logged. Which architecture implements this network segmentation?

options.text: Place each tier in separate subnets with Network ACLs configured to allow traffic only between adjacent tier subnets. Enable VPC Flow Logs on all subnet ENIs and configure the flow logs to publish to a CloudWatch log group with a 1-minute aggregation interval.

Place each tier in separate subnets with security groups that reference adjacent tier security group IDs as allowed sources. Deploy AWS Network Firewall between tiers with stateful rules logging allowed and denied traffic to a centralized S3 bucket via Firehose.

Deploy each tier in a separate subnet and use AWS PrivateLink to create VPC endpoints between adjacent tiers. Configure endpoint policies to restrict access to specific service actions and enable CloudTrail logging for all VPC endpoint API calls.

Deploy each tier in a separate VPC connected via VPC peering with non-overlapping CIDR blocks. Configure security groups to allow traffic only from the peered VPC's CIDR range and enable VPC Flow Logs on the peering connection ENIs for traffic logging.

explanation: B is correct: putting each tier in its own subnet and writing security group rules that reference the adjacent tier's security group ID rather than a CIDR gives stateful, identity-based segmentation that stays correct as instances scale - the web SG is the only allowed source for the app SG, and the app SG the only allowed source for the database SG. AWS Network Firewall between the tier subnets adds stateful inspection and emits alert and flow logs for allowed and denied traffic, delivered through Firehose to a central S3 bucket. A is incorrect because network ACLs are stateless, so every flow needs matching inbound and outbound rules plus ephemeral port ranges (error-prone at three tiers), and VPC Flow Logs record only 5-tuple summaries rather than inspected inter-tier traffic. C is incorrect because PrivateLink exposes a specific service behind an endpoint service and NLB; it is not a general mechanism for tiers of one application to communicate, and CloudTrail logs API calls rather than data-plane traffic. D is incorrect because splitting tiers into peered VPCs adds routing and CIDR management with no segmentation benefit over subnets plus security groups, and peering connections have no ENIs on which to enable flow logs.

stem: A company needs to implement automated testing in their CI/CD pipeline that validates infrastructure changes before deployment. The tests must verify that a CloudFormation template creates the expected resources with correct configurations, without actually deploying resources to AWS. Which testing approach satisfies this requirement?

options.text: Use TaskCat in a CodeBuild stage to test CloudFormation templates across multiple Regions simultaneously. Configure TaskCat with test parameters for each Region and validate that stacks create successfully and output values match expected results before deletion.

Deploy the CloudFormation template to a dedicated testing account using a CodePipeline stage. Run integration tests against the deployed resources using a CodeBuild project, then delete the test stack and promote the template to production if tests pass.

Use the CloudFormation Linter (cfn-lint) in a CodeBuild stage to validate template syntax and check against the CloudFormation resource specification. Add cfn-nag for security scanning and integrate both tools as build steps that fail the pipeline on errors or warnings.

Write unit tests using the CDK assertions library or cfn-guard policy-as-code rules to validate the synthesized CloudFormation template. Run the tests in a CodeBuild stage to verify resource counts, property values, and security configurations without deploying to AWS.

explanation: D is correct: the CDK assertions module (Template.fromStack with resourceCountIs and hasResourceProperties) and cfn-guard rules both operate on the synthesized CloudFormation template as static data, so a CodeBuild stage can assert that the expected resources exist with the expected property values and fail the build without ever calling CreateStack. Nothing is provisioned, which is exactly the stated constraint, and the tests run in seconds. A is incorrect because TaskCat works by actually creating the stacks in each test Region to observe whether they deploy and what they output, which is the opposite of testing without deploying, and it costs both time and money. B is incorrect for the same reason: deploying to a dedicated testing account provisions real resources, even though they are deleted afterwards. C is incorrect because cfn-lint validates syntax against the CloudFormation resource specification and cfn-nag flags known-risky patterns; neither asserts that the template produces the specific resources and property values the team expects.

stem: A company uses AWS CloudFormation custom resources backed by Lambda functions to configure third-party SaaS integrations during stack creation. The custom resource Lambda function occasionally times out after 15 minutes, causing stack creation to hang for hours until the custom resource times out. Which approach resolves the timeout issue?

options.text: Increase the Lambda function timeout to the maximum of 15 minutes and add retry logic with exponential backoff within the handler. Configure the Lambda to send a FAILED response to CloudFormation's pre-signed S3 URL if the operation exceeds a configured time limit.

Implement the custom resource as an asynchronous workflow using Step Functions. Have the Lambda function start the Step Functions execution and immediately return SUCCESS to CloudFormation, while the state machine handles the SaaS integration with built-in retry logic.

Configure the custom resource with a ServiceTimeout property set to 7200 seconds so CloudFormation stops waiting after two hours. Add a CloudWatch alarm on the Lambda function Duration metric that sends an SNS notification when execution time approaches the 15-minute Lambda limit.

Replace the Lambda-backed custom resource with an AWS CloudFormation macro that transforms the template to include the SaaS integration configuration. Run the macro during template processing to avoid runtime timeouts during stack creation operations.

explanation: Option A is correct because the hang is caused by CloudFormation never receiving a response. A custom resource provider must PUT a SUCCESS or FAILED document to the pre-signed S3 response URL; if the Lambda function is killed by its own timeout before doing so, CloudFormation simply keeps waiting. Adding an internal deadline that fires before the function timeout - a timer, or a check against the remaining execution time from the context object - lets the handler send an explicit FAILED response with a Reason, so the stack fails fast with a diagnostic instead of sitting in CREATE_IN_PROGRESS for hours. The bounded retries with exponential backoff let transient SaaS errors succeed within the window. Option B fails because returning SUCCESS before the work has happened breaks the contract the stack depends on: CloudFormation marks the resource CREATE_COMPLETE and proceeds to dependent resources while the SaaS integration is still in flight, and if the state machine later fails there is no way to fail the stack or roll it back. Option C fails on its own numbers and on its reasoning. ServiceTimeout does exist for custom resources, but it accepts 60 to 3600 seconds, so 7200 is rejected at validation; even set to a legal value it only shortens how long CloudFormation waits before failing the resource, it does not obtain a response or make the integration succeed, and the alarm is a notification rather than a fix. Option D fails because macros execute during template transformation and only return modified template content; they cannot call a third-party SaaS API to provision anything, so the integration would never be performed.

stem: A company runs a message processing application that reads from an Amazon Kinesis Data Stream with 10 shards. During peak hours, the consumer Lambda function falls behind, causing the iterator age to exceed 1 hour. The team needs to increase throughput without modifying the producer application. Which solution addresses the consumer lag?

options.text: Enable enhanced fan-out on the Kinesis stream for the consumer Lambda function. This provides a dedicated 2 MB/s read throughput per shard, eliminating contention with other consumers and significantly improving the read rate for the lagging consumer application.

Replace the Lambda consumer with an ECS Fargate service using the Kinesis Client Library (KCL). Configure the KCL application with a DynamoDB lease table and set the maxRecords per GetRecords call to 10000 for higher per-shard throughput.

Configure the Lambda event source mapping with a batch size of 10000 records and a maximum batching window of 5 seconds. Increase the Lambda function memory to 10240 MB to improve CPU allocation and enable provisioned concurrency matching the shard count.

Increase the number of shards in the Kinesis stream from 10 to 20 using the UpdateShardCount API. Update the Lambda event source mapping to increase the parallelization factor, allowing multiple Lambda invocations to process each shard simultaneously.

explanation: D is correct: with 10 shards the stream caps consumption at 2 MB/s per shard and, by default, one concurrent Lambda invocation per shard. UpdateShardCount to 20 doubles both the throughput ceiling and the number of parallel consumers, and raising the event source mapping's ParallelizationFactor (up to 10) lets Lambda run multiple concurrent batches per shard while preserving order per partition key - all without touching the producer. A is incorrect because enhanced fan-out gives each registered consumer a dedicated 2 MB/s per shard and lower propagation delay, but the Lambda concurrency remains one invocation per shard; if function processing time is the bottleneck, delivering records faster does not drain the backlog. B is incorrect because a KCL application on Fargate still processes one lease (one shard) per worker, so a larger maxRecords fetches bigger batches against the same per-shard limits and the same processing cost, while adding an application and a DynamoDB lease table to operate. C is incorrect because a bigger batch size and batching window change how records are grouped, not how many invocations run per shard, and extra memory or provisioned concurrency cannot lift the one-invocation-per-shard ceiling that is driving iterator age up.

stem: A company needs to monitor the availability and latency of 150 public API endpoints belonging to applications that run in multiple AWS accounts and Regions. Each endpoint must be checked at least every 30 seconds from several geographic locations, and the operations team needs a single consolidated dashboard showing whether each endpoint is up and how long it takes to respond. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Use AWS Distro for OpenTelemetry (ADOT) collectors deployed as ECS Fargate tasks in each Region. Configure HTTP check receivers to probe endpoints every 30 seconds and export metrics to Amazon Managed Service for Prometheus with a centralized Grafana dashboard.

Create Amazon CloudWatch Synthetics canaries for each endpoint using the heartbeat monitoring blueprint. Configure the canary schedules to run every 1 minute from each Region and publish the SuccessPercent and Duration metrics to CloudWatch. Use CloudWatch cross-account observability to aggregate all of the canary metrics into a central monitoring account.

Deploy a fleet of EC2 instances in each Region running a custom health check script that tests each endpoint every 30 seconds. Publish results as CloudWatch custom metrics using the PutMetricData API with dimensions for account, Region, and endpoint name.

Configure Route 53 health checks for each endpoint with a 30-second request interval. Enable CloudWatch metrics on the health checks and build a single CloudWatch dashboard in the us-east-1 Region that graphs HealthCheckStatus, HealthCheckPercentageHealthy, ConnectionTime, and TimeToFirstByte for all of the health checks.

explanation: Option D is correct because Route 53 health checks natively provide everything the stem asks for with no infrastructure to run. A health check can be configured with a 30-second request interval, checkers in multiple AWS Regions probe the endpoint independently regardless of which account or Region hosts it, and the resulting CloudWatch metrics - HealthCheckStatus and HealthCheckPercentageHealthy for availability, ConnectionTime and TimeToFirstByte for latency - are all published in us-east-1, so one dashboard in that Region shows every endpoint. Because the checks are global and account-agnostic, there is no cross-account plumbing to build. Option A fails the operational-overhead comparison: it works technically, but the team would own collector tasks in every Region, an Amazon Managed Service for Prometheus workspace, remote-write configuration, and a Grafana deployment, all to replicate a managed capability. Option B fails on a hard requirement - the minimum frequency for a CloudWatch Synthetics canary schedule is one minute, so canaries cannot check every 30 seconds - and 150 canaries also cost considerably more than 150 health checks. Option C fails because it is the highest-overhead answer of the four: the company would patch, scale and monitor probe instances in every Region, handle their failures, and pay for custom metric ingestion, while still building the availability and latency metrics that Route 53 emits for free.

stem: A company's EC2-based application suddenly started returning HTTP 500 errors after a configuration change pushed via AWS Systems Manager State Manager. The team needs to quickly revert to the previous configuration. The State Manager association applied an SSM document that modified application configuration files on 200 instances. Which approach provides the fastest rollback?

options.text: Use SSM Run Command to execute a command document that restores the configuration files from a backup stored in S3. Set MaxConcurrency to 100% and MaxErrors to 0 to apply the rollback to all 200 instances simultaneously with immediate failure detection.

Create an SSM Automation document that connects to each instance via Session Manager and reverts the configuration file changes. Execute the Automation document with a rate control of 50 instances at a time and a failure threshold of 5% across the fleet.

Terminate all 200 instances and allow the Auto Scaling group to launch replacements with the original launch template UserData. Configure the Auto Scaling group's instance refresh with a minimum healthy percentage of 90% to maintain availability during replacement.

Create a new version of the SSM document containing the previous configuration values. Update the State Manager association to use the new document version and wait for the association to automatically re-apply across all 200 instances at the next scheduled interval.

explanation: A is correct: Run Command executes imperatively and immediately on the targeted managed instances, so restoring the known-good configuration files from the S3 backup begins on all 200 instances at once when MaxConcurrency is 100%, and MaxErrors 0 aborts the invocation the moment any instance fails so the team is not left guessing. That is the shortest path from outage to restored configuration, which is what the question asks for. B is incorrect because SSM Automation adds a document-orchestration layer on top and the option deliberately throttles to 50 instances per wave, so the same rollback takes several sequential batches instead of one parallel pass. C is incorrect because terminating and replacing 200 instances is by far the slowest route - each replacement must launch, run UserData and pass health checks - and it discards instance state during an active incident. D is incorrect because a State Manager association re-applies on its schedule, so waiting for the next interval leaves the broken configuration serving 500s for up to the full association interval; publishing a corrected document version is the right follow-up to stop the bad configuration being re-pushed, but it is not the fastest rollback.

stem: A company needs to implement a centralized secrets management solution for applications running across 20 AWS accounts. Secrets must be encrypted with account-specific KMS keys, rotated automatically, and access must be auditable. Which TWO configurations are required?

options.text: Deploy AWS Secrets Manager in each account with account-specific KMS CMKs for encryption. Enable automatic rotation using Lambda functions deployed in each account's VPC and configure rotation schedules based on the sensitivity classification of each secret.

Enable AWS CloudTrail in all accounts with data events for Secrets Manager API calls. Create a centralized CloudTrail trail that aggregates logs to a security account's S3 bucket, and configure CloudWatch Logs metric filters to alert on unauthorized GetSecretValue calls.

Create a centralized Secrets Manager instance in a shared services account with a single KMS CMK. Configure resource-based policies on each secret to grant cross-account access and share secrets using AWS Resource Access Manager (RAM) for simplified management.

Deploy HashiCorp Vault on ECS Fargate in the shared services account with transit encryption enabled. Configure Vault's AWS auth backend to authenticate applications from each account and use Vault's built-in audit logging to record all secret access events.

explanation: A and B are correct. A satisfies the encryption and rotation requirements: Secrets Manager in each of the 20 accounts lets every secret be encrypted with that account's own KMS customer managed key (a secret can only use a key in its own account and Region), and Secrets Manager's built-in rotation runs a rotation Lambda - placed in the account's VPC so it can reach private RDS endpoints - on a per-secret schedule. B satisfies auditability: GetSecretValue and the other Secrets Manager calls are recorded by CloudTrail, and an organization trail delivering all 20 accounts' logs to one S3 bucket in the security account, with metric filters and alarms on unauthorized or unusual retrievals, gives the centralized, tamper-evident access record. C is incorrect because a single shared CMK in one account directly contradicts the account-specific-key requirement, and AWS RAM does not support sharing Secrets Manager secrets - cross-account access is granted through secret resource policies plus KMS key policies. D is incorrect because self-hosting HashiCorp Vault brings unsealing, HA, upgrade and backup burdens and moves the audit trail out of CloudTrail, when the native services already meet every stated requirement.

stem: A development team wants to implement canary deployments for their Lambda functions using AWS SAM. The deployment should shift 10% of traffic to the new version, monitor for errors for 5 minutes, then shift the remaining 90% if no errors occur. Which SAM configuration implements this?

options.text: Configure the Lambda function with two versions behind an Application Load Balancer target group using weighted target groups. Set the primary target group weight to 90% and the canary target group to 10%, with ALB health checks triggering automatic deregistration.

Configure the Lambda function's DeploymentPreference property with Type set to Canary10Percent5Minutes. Define pre-traffic and post-traffic hooks as Lambda functions and add CloudWatch alarms monitoring the Lambda Errors metric for automatic rollback on failures.

Configure the Lambda function with a provisioned concurrency setting of 10% on the new version. Create an API Gateway canary deployment stage that routes 10% of traffic and use a Step Functions workflow to promote or rollback after a 5-minute evaluation.

Create a Lambda alias with a routing configuration that sends 10% of invocations to the new version. Configure a CloudWatch Events rule to trigger a Lambda function after 5 minutes that updates the alias routing to 100% or rolls back based on error metric evaluation.

explanation: B is correct: DeploymentPreference on an AWS::Serverless::Function makes SAM generate a CodeDeploy Lambda deployment group managing the alias's traffic weights. Canary10Percent5Minutes shifts 10% of alias traffic to the new version, holds five minutes, then shifts the remaining 90%. Alarms listed under Alarms (for example the function's Errors metric) are monitored throughout and CodeDeploy reverts the weights automatically if one fires; PreTraffic and PostTraffic hooks run validation Lambdas around the shift. A is incorrect because weighted target groups are an HTTP construct - an ALB can invoke a Lambda target, but this does not apply to functions invoked by other event sources, and it bypasses versions and aliases, which is how Lambda traffic shifting actually works. C is incorrect because provisioned concurrency controls warm execution environments rather than traffic split, an API Gateway canary stage only covers requests arriving through that API, and the promote-or-rollback logic is hand-built in Step Functions. D is incorrect not because alias routing configuration cannot split traffic - it can - but because the scheduled Lambda that evaluates error metrics and promotes or reverts is exactly the orchestration CodeDeploy already provides through a single SAM property.

stem: A company manages 100 CloudFormation stacks across multiple accounts. They frequently need to update a common parameter (like AMI ID) across all stacks when a new golden AMI is released. Manual updates are error-prone and time-consuming. Which approach automates this cross-stack parameter update?

options.text: Store the AMI ID in a DynamoDB global table replicated across all accounts' Regions. Use CloudFormation custom resources backed by Lambda functions that query DynamoDB for the current AMI ID during stack creation and update operations.

Store the AMI ID in AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store as a public parameter. Reference the parameter in all CloudFormation templates using the AWS::SSM::Parameter::Value dynamic reference. When the parameter is updated, trigger stack updates across all accounts via CodePipeline.

Create a CloudFormation StackSet that deploys a common parameter stack to all accounts. Use cross-stack references with Fn::ImportValue in each application stack to reference the AMI ID. Update the StackSet to propagate the new AMI ID to all accounts automatically.

Use AWS Service Catalog with a central AMI portfolio that publishes the latest AMI ID as a product output. Configure dependent stacks to reference the Service Catalog product output and trigger product updates to propagate the new AMI ID to all provisioned products.

explanation: B is correct: keeping the golden AMI ID in an SSM Parameter Store parameter and declaring the template parameter with the type AWS::SSM::Parameter::Value<AWS::EC2::Image::Id> means every one of the 100 stacks resolves the AMI from a single authoritative source at create or update time. Publishing a new AMI becomes a one-line parameter update, and a pipeline that then issues the stack (or StackSet) updates rolls the change out consistently; because the resolved value appears in the change set, each update remains reviewable before it executes. A is incorrect because a Lambda-backed custom resource plus a DynamoDB global table is a large amount of bespoke, failure-prone infrastructure to store a value Parameter Store already holds and CloudFormation already reads natively. C is incorrect because Fn::ImportValue creates hard export/import coupling: an exported value cannot be modified while any stack imports it, so updating the shared AMI export across 100 dependent stacks is precisely what that coupling prevents. D is incorrect because Service Catalog governs which products teams may launch and does not act as a parameter distribution channel that arbitrary CloudFormation stacks can read an AMI ID from.

stem: A company's microservices architecture uses Amazon API Gateway as the front door. During a downstream service outage, API Gateway continued forwarding requests, causing cascading failures across multiple services. Which pattern prevents cascading failures in this architecture?

options.text: Configure API Gateway with Lambda authorizers that check downstream service health before routing requests. Cache health check results for 30 seconds and return HTTP 503 with a Retry-After header when the downstream service is detected as unhealthy.

Implement the circuit breaker pattern in the integration layer: bound every downstream call with an explicit API Gateway integration timeout and track consecutive failures per downstream service in Amazon ElastiCache. When the threshold is crossed, open the circuit so calls fail fast with a cached fallback instead of being forwarded, and half-open after a cooldown to probe for recovery.

Implement bulkhead isolation by deploying each downstream service behind its own dedicated Network Load Balancer and a separate API Gateway VPC link. Configure NLB cross-zone load balancing and target group health checks with a 5-second interval so that failing service instances are detected and removed from rotation before they can affect neighbouring services.

Implement circuit breaker pattern using API Gateway usage plans with throttling limits per downstream service. Configure burst and rate limits based on each service's capacity and return HTTP 429 responses when limits are exceeded to protect downstream services.

explanation: Option B is correct because it implements the actual circuit breaker semantics the scenario needs. Bounding each call with an explicit integration timeout stops callers from piling up behind a hung downstream service and exhausting connections and Lambda concurrency, which is the mechanism by which one outage cascades. Recording consecutive failures per downstream service in a shared ElastiCache store lets every concurrently executing integration observe the same state, so once the threshold is crossed the circuit opens for all of them and subsequent requests fail fast with a cached fallback rather than being forwarded into the outage. The half-open probe after a cooldown restores traffic automatically when the dependency recovers. Option A fails because a Lambda authorizer is invoked to make an authorization decision about the caller and its result is cached against the caller's identity source, not against downstream health; using it as a health gate means the cached decision is keyed on the wrong thing, and the authorizer's own calls to the failing service add load to the very dependency that is struggling. Option C fails because bulkheads and fast health checks limit which instances receive traffic but do nothing when the whole service is down - the NLB keeps accepting connections and the callers keep blocking on them, so requests still stack up and the failure still propagates. Option D fails because throttling is volume-based, not error-based: usage plans apply to API keys and stage-level rate and burst limits, so a service that is failing while still under its rate limit receives every request, and a healthy service that is merely popular gets throttled.

stem: A company runs a data pipeline that processes files uploaded to S3, transforms them using Lambda, and stores results in DynamoDB. The operations team needs to track the end-to-end processing time for each file and identify bottlenecks. Some files take 10x longer than average. Which observability approach best identifies the processing bottlenecks?

options.text: Configure CloudWatch Container Insights for the Lambda function to collect per-invocation metrics including duration, memory usage, and initialization time. Create a CloudWatch dashboard with percentile statistics showing p99 duration and correlate with file size dimensions.

Configure Amazon Managed Service for Prometheus to scrape custom metrics from the Lambda function using the Prometheus client library. Define recording rules to compute processing duration histograms by file type and size bucket, and visualize in Grafana dashboards.

Enable S3 event notifications to publish to CloudWatch Logs via an SNS topic. Create Lambda function CloudWatch Logs metric filters that extract processing duration and file metadata, then build CloudWatch Logs Insights queries to analyze slow file processing patterns.

Enable AWS X-Ray tracing on the Lambda function and instrument the code with custom subsegments for each processing stage. Annotate traces with the S3 object key and file size, then use X-Ray analytics to filter traces by duration and identify slow processing stages.

explanation: D is correct: the question asks where the time goes inside processing a given file, and X-Ray subsegments wrapped around each stage (S3 GetObject, parse, transform, DynamoDB PutItem) decompose a single invocation's duration into named spans. Annotating the trace with the S3 object key and file size makes those traces indexed and filterable in X-Ray analytics, so the team can isolate only the traces in the 10x tail and see which subsegment expands - for example DynamoDB writes being throttled on the largest files. A is incorrect because Container Insights covers ECS, EKS and Kubernetes, not Lambda; Lambda already emits Duration and Init Duration, and neither exposes the internal stage breakdown nor accepts file size as a metric dimension. B is incorrect because scraping Prometheus metrics from short-lived Lambda invocations is impractical (there is no long-lived endpoint to scrape), and aggregate duration histograms still cannot attribute time to a stage within one invocation. C is incorrect because S3 event notifications cannot publish to CloudWatch Logs, and log metric filters produce aggregate metrics that lack the per-request causal chain a trace provides.

stem: A company's production environment experienced a memory leak in an EC2 application that gradually consumed all available memory over 4 hours before the instance became unresponsive. CloudWatch basic monitoring with 5-minute metrics didn't detect the gradual increase early enough. Which monitoring improvement provides earlier detection?

options.text: Configure Amazon EventBridge with a scheduled rule that invokes a Lambda function every minute to query EC2 instance status checks. Publish custom metrics for StatusCheckFailed_Instance and create an alarm that triggers when status checks fail for 3 consecutive checks.

Enable AWS Systems Manager inventory collection on all EC2 instances with a custom inventory type for memory statistics. Configure SSM State Manager to collect memory data every 5 minutes and create an AWS Config rule that evaluates memory thresholds for compliance.

Install the CloudWatch agent on all EC2 instances configured to collect memory utilization at 1-minute intervals. Create a CloudWatch anomaly detection alarm on the mem_used_percent metric that triggers when memory usage deviates from the expected baseline pattern.

Enable EC2 detailed monitoring to collect CPU metrics at 1-minute intervals instead of the default 5-minute interval. Create a CloudWatch alarm on the CPUUtilization metric with anomaly detection bands and set the alarm to trigger when CPU exceeds normal patterns.

explanation: C is correct: memory utilization is a guest-OS statistic that EC2 does not publish at all, so no change to EC2 monitoring can surface it. Installing the CloudWatch agent and collecting mem_used_percent at a 1-minute interval is what makes the leak observable, and a CloudWatch anomaly detection alarm learns the normal memory profile so a slow upward drift breaks out of the expected band early in the four-hour slide, long before a static high-water threshold would trip. A is incorrect because EC2 instance status checks only fail once the instance is already unresponsive, which is the end of the incident rather than early detection, and polling them from a scheduled Lambda merely re-publishes a metric CloudWatch already provides.
