B is incorrect because SSM Inventory captures configuration and installed-software snapshots for querying rather than time-series metrics, and AWS Config evaluates resource configuration compliance - neither is a metric-alarm pathway for memory utilization. D is incorrect because detailed monitoring only raises the frequency of the metrics EC2 already publishes, and memory is not among them; CPUUtilization does not track a memory leak, since a leaking process can sit at normal CPU right up to the moment memory is exhausted.

stem: A company needs to implement a policy that prevents any IAM user or role from creating resources outside of the approved AWS Regions (us-east-1 and eu-west-1), except for global services like IAM, CloudFront, and Route 53. Which mechanism enforces this restriction across all accounts?

options.text: Configure AWS Config rules that evaluate resource compliance by checking the Region attribute of every resource. Enable auto-remediation using SSM Automation to terminate or delete resources created in non-approved Regions and notify administrators via SNS.

Create an IAM permissions boundary policy that denies actions outside us-east-1 and eu-west-1 using the aws:RequestedRegion condition key. Attach the permissions boundary to all IAM users and roles in each account and exclude global service actions from the deny statement.

Create an SCP in AWS Organizations that denies all actions with a StringNotEquals condition on aws:RequestedRegion for us-east-1 and eu-west-1. Add a NotAction list for global services including iam:*, cloudfront:*, route53:*, and sts:* to exempt them from the Region restriction.

Deploy VPC configurations only in us-east-1 and eu-west-1, leaving other Regions without networking infrastructure. Create IAM policies that deny ec2:CreateVpc and ec2:CreateSubnet in all Regions to prevent teams from establishing networking in unapproved Regions.

explanation: C is correct: an SCP at the organization root or an OU applies to every principal in every member account, including the account root user, and cannot be removed by a local administrator - so it is the only option that enforces the restriction across all accounts. A Deny conditioned on StringNotEquals for aws:RequestedRegion (us-east-1, eu-west-1), written with NotAction listing the global services (iam:*, cloudfront:*, route53:*, sts:*), blocks resource creation everywhere else while leaving those global services working. A is incorrect because AWS Config is detective: the resource is created first and only deleted afterwards, so nothing is prevented, and auto-terminating resources is a hazardous remediation. B is incorrect because permissions boundaries must be attached to each user and role individually, do not apply to the account root user, and can be detached by anyone holding iam:PutRolePermissionsBoundary - they are a delegation control, not an organization-wide guardrail. D is incorrect because most services (S3, DynamoDB, Lambda, SQS and more) need no VPC at all, so withholding networking does not stop them being used in unapproved Regions, and denying ec2:CreateVpc in all Regions would also break the two approved ones.

stem: A company uses AWS CodePipeline for continuous delivery. The production deployment stage requires approval from at least two different team leads within a 4-hour window. If only one approval is received, the deployment should be rejected. Which configuration implements this dual-approval requirement?

options.text: Add a single manual approval action in CodePipeline with an SNS topic that notifies both team leads. Configure a Lambda function as the approval reviewer that tracks approvals in a DynamoDB table and only approves the action when two distinct approvers have responded.

Replace the CodePipeline manual approval with an EventBridge rule that triggers a Step Functions workflow. The workflow sends approval requests via SNS, waits for two callback tokens from distinct approvers within 4 hours, and calls PutApprovalResult on success.

Add two sequential manual approval actions in the production stage of CodePipeline, each assigned to a different SNS topic subscribed by different team leads. Configure each approval action with a 4-hour timeout to ensure both approvals are collected within the time window.

Add a manual approval action in CodePipeline and configure the pipeline execution IAM role to require MFA from two separate IAM users. Attach a condition key in the approval IAM policy requiring aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent from at least two distinct principals.

explanation: C is correct: a CodePipeline manual approval action is resolved by a single ApproveOrReject response, so requiring two people means two approval actions in the stage. Placed in successive run orders, the pipeline advances only after both approve; each action has its own timeout enforcing the 4-hour window, and each points at a different SNS topic to notify a different lead. If the second approval never arrives, that action times out and the execution fails, so a lone approval never deploys. A is incorrect because CodePipeline has no concept of a Lambda 'approval reviewer' attached to an approval action - an approval can only be resolved by a principal calling PutApprovalResult - so the mechanism described does not exist. B is incorrect because it removes the manual approval action and then calls PutApprovalResult, which is self-contradictory: with no approval action in the stage there is nothing for that API to resolve and the pipeline would never pause while the workflow collected callbacks. D is incorrect because aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent asserts only that the single calling principal authenticated with MFA; IAM has no condition key that requires two distinct principals to act on the same request.

stem: A company needs to ensure that all EC2 instances launched in their AWS accounts have the AWS Systems Manager agent installed and are registered as managed instances. Some instances are launched from custom AMIs that don't include the SSM agent. Which approach ensures ALL instances become managed regardless of the AMI used?

options.text: Enable Default Host Management Configuration in AWS Systems Manager for each account so that instances automatically receive Systems Manager permissions from the AmazonSSMManagedEC2InstanceDefaultPolicy through Instance Metadata Service Version 2, removing the need to create and attach an IAM instance profile to every instance in every account.

Create a Lambda function triggered by EC2 RunInstances CloudTrail events via EventBridge. The Lambda function uses EC2 Instance Connect to SSH into new instances and install the SSM agent via remote command execution, then verifies registration in the SSM API.

Bake the SSM agent into every custom AMI used in the accounts and add a UserData script to all launch templates that installs the agent from the regional S3 endpoint if it is missing. Attach an IAM instance profile containing AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore in each launch template so instances register on first boot.

Create an AWS Config rule that checks if instances are registered as SSM managed instances. Configure auto-remediation with the AWS-ConfigureAWSPackage SSM document to install the SSM agent on non-compliant instances and register them with Systems Manager automatically.

explanation: Option C is correct because getting the agent onto an AMI that lacks it is fundamentally an image and launch-configuration problem, and this is the only option that solves it at the source. Baking the agent into the custom AMIs means it is present and starts at boot, the UserData fallback covers any image that slipped through the bakery, and attaching an instance profile carrying AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore in the launch template gives the agent the credentials it needs to call ssm:UpdateInstanceInformation and register. Because both halves are applied to every launch template and every AMI used in the accounts, instances launched by Auto Scaling, by the console, or by IaC all become managed. Option A fails because Default Host Management Configuration does not install anything. It requires SSM Agent version 3.2.582.0 or later to already be running on the instance; what it changes is where the agent gets its credentials, substituting IMDS-delivered permissions for an attached instance profile and then keeping the existing agent updated. An instance launched from an AMI with no agent at all is exactly the case it cannot help. Option B fails because EC2 Instance Connect depends on the ec2-instance-connect package being present in the AMI and on a running sshd plus network reachability from the Lambda function into the VPC, none of which is guaranteed for an arbitrary custom AMI, and pushing SSH access into an automation Lambda is a significant security regression. Option D fails on a chicken-and-egg problem: AWS-ConfigureAWSPackage is an SSM document, and Systems Manager can only run a document on an instance that is already a managed instance, so it cannot remediate the instances that lack the agent.

stem: A company operates an Aurora PostgreSQL database that experiences read-heavy traffic spikes causing reader instances to become overwhelmed. Aurora Auto Scaling is configured but new read replicas take 5-10 minutes to become available. Which approach reduces the impact of sudden read traffic spikes?

options.text: Configure Aurora Auto Scaling with a lower target CPU utilization threshold of 40% to trigger scaling earlier. Add a predictive scaling policy based on historical traffic patterns and maintain a minimum of 3 reader instances during business hours via scheduled scaling actions.

Switch from Aurora PostgreSQL to Aurora PostgreSQL Serverless v2 for the reader instances. Configure the minimum ACU to handle baseline read traffic and the maximum ACU to handle peak traffic, allowing automatic scaling in seconds instead of minutes for new instances.

Create additional Aurora cross-Region read replicas in a secondary Region. Configure the application's database connection pool to distribute read queries across both primary and secondary Region reader endpoints using DNS-based round-robin load balancing.

Add an Amazon ElastiCache for Redis cluster between the application and Aurora for read caching. Implement a cache-aside pattern in the application code with a TTL matching the data freshness requirements, reducing the number of direct queries hitting Aurora readers.

explanation: B is correct: Aurora Serverless v2 changes capacity by adjusting Aurora Capacity Units on an existing instance in fine increments within seconds, rather than provisioning a whole new DB instance. Configuring reader instances as Serverless v2 with a minimum ACU that covers baseline reads and a high maximum lets a reader absorb a sudden spike essentially immediately, which is what removes the 5-10 minute cold-provisioning gap that Aurora Auto Scaling cannot avoid. A is incorrect because a lower CPU target and predictive or scheduled policies only start the same slow provisioning sooner or keep spare instances warm; a spike that does not match the historical pattern still waits 5-10 minutes for new capacity. C is incorrect because cross-Region read replicas add replication lag and cross-Region network latency for reads, DNS round-robin distributes without any awareness of load or health, and the added capacity sits in the wrong Region for latency-sensitive traffic. D is incorrect because an ElastiCache cache-aside layer genuinely offloads repeated reads but requires application changes, helps only for cacheable queries, and serves data that is stale up to the TTL - it does not make the database itself scale faster when the spike is on uncacheable queries.

stem: A company runs a multi-account AWS environment and needs to centralize security-related findings from Amazon GuardDuty, AWS Security Hub, Amazon Inspector, and Amazon Macie into a single dashboard for the security operations team. Which configurations are needed? (Choose two.)

options.text: Configure each service (GuardDuty, Inspector, Macie) to send findings to individual CloudWatch log groups in each account. Create cross-account CloudWatch log subscriptions to aggregate all findings into a central account's CloudWatch Logs for unified querying.

Create an EventBridge rule in the delegated administrator account that matches Security Hub Findings Imported events and targets an Amazon Data Firehose delivery stream writing findings to an S3 bucket. Catalog the bucket in the AWS Glue Data Catalog, query the findings with Amazon Athena, and build the dashboard in Amazon QuickSight.

Create custom EventBridge rules in each account that match security findings from all four services. Configure cross-account event bus targets to forward the findings to a central security account's event bus, and build a Lambda-based aggregation layer that deduplicates repeated findings and renders a consolidated dashboard for the security operations team.

Designate a central security account as the AWS Security Hub delegated administrator through AWS Organizations. Enable Security Hub in all accounts with automatic enablement for new accounts and configure integration with GuardDuty, Inspector, and Macie findings.

explanation: Options D and B are the two configurations required. Option D provides the aggregation layer: designating a delegated administrator through AWS Organizations and enabling Security Hub across all accounts with auto-enablement for new accounts causes GuardDuty, Inspector and Macie findings to be normalized into the AWS Security Finding Format and imported into the central account automatically, including from accounts that join later. Option B provides the dashboard, using the documented export path. An EventBridge rule on Security Hub Findings Imported events streams the normalized findings through Amazon Data Firehose into S3; a Glue Data Catalog table makes them queryable, Athena runs the aggregations, and QuickSight builds the interactive visuals for the security operations team on the Athena data source. Option A fails because these services do not publish findings to CloudWatch log groups - GuardDuty, Inspector and Macie surface findings through their own APIs and EventBridge, not as log events - so there is nothing for a cross-account log subscription to forward, and routing them through Logs would also discard the structured ASFF schema. Option C fails because it rebuilds, badly, what Security Hub already provides: per-account rules for four different services each emit their own native finding shape, so the central bus receives unnormalized, undeduplicated events, and a custom Lambda aggregation layer must then be written and maintained to render a dashboard that QuickSight over Athena delivers out of the box.

stem: A company's ECS service running on Fargate experienced an outage because the tasks failed to pull a container image from Amazon ECR. Investigation revealed that a VPC endpoint for ECR was deleted during a network infrastructure update. Which proactive measure prevents this type of outage?

options.text: Create an AWS Config rule that monitors the existence of required VPC endpoints for ECR, S3, and CloudWatch Logs. Configure auto-remediation with an SSM Automation document that recreates the deleted VPC endpoints and updates the associated security group rules.

Configure CloudFormation stack policies on the network infrastructure stacks that deny Update:Delete actions on VPC endpoint resources. Apply the stack policy during stack creation and require a temporary policy override with change management approval for deletions.

Set up a CloudWatch alarm on the ECS service RunningTaskCount metric to detect when the count drops below the desired count. Configure the alarm to trigger an EventBridge rule that invokes a Lambda function to diagnose ECR connectivity and recreate endpoints.

Deploy the ECS service in public subnets with a NAT gateway as a fallback route for ECR image pulls. Configure the task definition with both the VPC endpoint and public internet ECR registry as image sources using a multi-stage Dockerfile with fallback layers.

explanation: CloudFormation stack policies prevent accidental deletion of critical resources like VPC endpoints by denying delete operations unless explicitly overridden. This proactively prevents the issue. Option A detects and remediates after deletion, but there's still a window where ECS tasks can't pull images. Option C reacts to the symptom (task count drop) rather than preventing the root cause. Option D uses public subnets and NAT gateways which contradicts the VPC endpoint architecture and adds cost.

stem: A company needs to implement a workflow where developers can assume elevated IAM roles for production troubleshooting, but only for 1-hour sessions, only after manager approval, and all actions must be logged with the developer's identity. Which solution implements this just-in-time elevated access?

options.text: Configure AWS Systems Manager Change Manager to define a change template for production access requests. When a manager approves the request, an SSM Automation runbook creates a time-limited IAM role policy with a 1-hour expiry condition and logs via CloudTrail.

Create an IAM role with an inline policy containing a time-based condition using aws:CurrentTime that restricts access to a 1-hour window. Have the developer request access through a Slack integration that calls a Lambda function to update the role's trust policy.

Create an IAM role with the required production permissions and a maximum session duration of 1 hour. Use AWS IAM Identity Center with a permission set that requires MFA and has a session duration of 1 hour, integrated with an approval workflow in ServiceNow via API.

Deploy a custom web application on API Gateway and Lambda that accepts access requests and sends approval emails to managers. Upon approval, the Lambda function calls the STS AssumeRole API to generate temporary credentials and delivers them to the developer securely.

explanation: SSM Change Manager provides a managed approval workflow where managers approve change requests, and SSM Automation creates time-limited access with full CloudTrail logging. Option A integrates external ServiceNow but IAM Identity Center doesn't natively include approval workflows. Option C builds a custom application that duplicates managed service functionality. Option D's time-based condition uses a fixed time window rather than a relative 1-hour session from the time of approval.

stem: A company uses AWS CodeBuild for their CI process. Build times are inconsistent, sometimes completing in 3 minutes and other times taking 15 minutes for the same codebase. Investigation reveals that the variance is caused by dependency downloads from public repositories. Which solution provides consistent build times?

options.text: Set up AWS CodeArtifact as a repository for upstream package registries including npm, PyPI, and Maven Central. Configure CodeBuild projects to use CodeArtifact as the package source, which caches upstream packages and serves them from within the AWS network.

Configure CodeBuild to use a VPC-attached build environment with a NAT gateway that has an Elastic IP. Set up a Squid proxy on an EC2 instance to cache downloaded dependencies and configure the build environment to use the proxy for all HTTP and HTTPS requests.

Create a custom Docker image containing all pre-installed dependencies and store it in Amazon ECR. Use this custom image as the CodeBuild environment image and rebuild the image weekly with updated dependencies using a scheduled CodePipeline pipeline.

Enable CodeBuild local caching with the source cache and custom cache modes enabled. Configure the S3 cache location to store dependency directories and set the cache expiry to 24 hours to ensure dependencies are refreshed daily from upstream repositories.

explanation: A is correct: a CodeArtifact repository can be given an upstream connection to each public registry (npmjs, PyPI, Maven Central). The first request for a package version fetches and stores it in CodeArtifact; every later build resolves it from CodeArtifact over the AWS network at predictable latency, removing the variance caused by public-registry slowness or throttling and protecting builds from yanked packages. B is incorrect because a self-managed Squid proxy on EC2 is infrastructure the team must size, patch and make highly available, and caching HTTPS package downloads effectively requires TLS interception, which adds certificate management on top. C is incorrect because baking dependencies into a CodeBuild image makes them stale between weekly rebuilds - any build needing a newer package falls back to the public registry and the slow path returns - while adding image build and maintenance work. D is incorrect because it conflates the cache types: local caching is tied to a warm build host and is not stored in an S3 cache location, and on any cache miss (a cold host, or the first build after the 24-hour expiry the option deliberately configures) the build downloads from the public registries again, so the 15-minute worst case persists.

stem: A company runs all of its Terraform workflows in Terraform Cloud and wants to implement policy-as-code that prevents developers from creating overly permissive IAM policies (such as policies with '*' actions or '*' resources). The checks must be evaluated inside the managed Terraform Cloud run, between plan and apply, and must block a non-compliant apply without introducing any additional CI/CD tooling or external binaries into the workflow. Which tool meets these requirements?

options.text: Configure AWS IAM Access Analyzer policy validation to check IAM policies created by Terraform. Enable the Access Analyzer integration with the AWS provider and configure it to fail terraform plan when policy validation returns findings with ERROR severity level.

Use HashiCorp Sentinel with Terraform Cloud/Enterprise to write policy rules that inspect the terraform plan output for IAM policy documents containing '*' in actions or resources. Configure the Sentinel policies as hard-mandatory to block non-compliant applies.

Write custom Terraform validation blocks in the IAM policy resource definitions using the condition attribute. Define precondition checks that parse the policy JSON document and fail with an error message if any statement contains wildcard actions or resource ARNs.

Implement Open Policy Agent (OPA) with the Conftest tool to evaluate Terraform plan JSON output against Rego policies. Write Rego rules that parse IAM policy documents and deny plans containing wildcard permissions in action or resource fields.

explanation: Option B is correct because Sentinel is the policy engine embedded in Terraform Cloud and Terraform Enterprise, and it runs as a native stage of the managed run: after the plan is produced and before apply is offered. Sentinel policies read the tfplan and tfstate imports directly, so they can walk every aws_iam_policy and inline policy document in the plan and reject wildcards in Action or Resource, and a hard-mandatory enforcement level makes the failure non-overridable so the apply cannot proceed. Because the engine is part of the platform the company already uses, no extra tooling is introduced, which is the stem's explicit constraint. Option A fails because there is no AWS provider integration that wires IAM Access Analyzer policy validation into terraform plan; ValidatePolicy is an API you call yourself from a separate step, and Access Analyzer findings for deployed policies are evaluated after the resources exist, so neither mode blocks the apply from inside the run. Option C fails because validation and precondition blocks are limited to the resource or module in which they are declared and to Terraform's expression language; they cannot be centrally enforced across all workspaces by a platform team, and a developer can simply omit them from a new module. Option D fails on the stated constraint rather than on capability: OPA with Conftest does evaluate plan JSON and can deny wildcard permissions, but it requires exporting the plan and running the conftest binary in a separate CI job outside the Terraform Cloud run, which is exactly the additional tooling the company has ruled out.

stem: A company operates a real-time data ingestion pipeline using Amazon Kinesis Data Streams. The stream has 20 shards and receives 10,000 records per second. The company needs to ensure zero data loss even if the consumer application is down for up to 24 hours. Which configuration ensures data durability?

options.text: Configure the Kinesis stream with a retention period of 168 hours (7 days) to provide ample buffer beyond the 24-hour consumer downtime requirement. Enable server-side encryption using a KMS CMK and configure enhanced monitoring to track per-shard metrics.

Enable Kinesis Data Streams on-demand capacity mode to automatically scale shards based on throughput. Configure the stream with a retention period of 24 hours and use enhanced fan-out consumers to ensure dedicated throughput for each consumer application.

Deploy a Kinesis Data Firehose delivery stream as an additional consumer that writes all records to an S3 bucket in real-time. Configure Firehose with a buffering interval of 60 seconds and enable S3 bucket versioning and server-side encryption for data durability.

Configure the producer application to write records to both Kinesis Data Streams and an SQS FIFO queue simultaneously. If the Kinesis consumer fails, configure a backup Lambda consumer to read from the SQS queue and reprocess the records into the pipeline.

explanation: A is correct: Kinesis Data Streams retains records 24 hours by default and can be extended to 168 hours (and up to 365 days with long-term retention). At 168 hours, even a full 24-hour consumer outage leaves every record in the stream; on restart the application resumes from its last checkpointed sequence number and replays the backlog, with days of safety margin. Encryption and enhanced monitoring are sensible extras that do not affect durability. B is incorrect because 24 hours of retention exactly equals the maximum tolerated outage, leaving zero margin - any extra delay in detecting the failure or restarting the consumer silently drops records - and on-demand capacity and enhanced fan-out address throughput, not retention. C is incorrect because a Firehose consumer does durably copy records to S3, but recovery then requires building and testing a separate S3 replay path rather than simply resuming the stream consumer, and Firehose is itself a consumer bounded by the same stream retention if it falls behind. D is incorrect because dual-writing to both Kinesis and SQS doubles cost, creates a consistency problem when one write succeeds and the other fails, and imposes FIFO ordering and per-message-group throughput constraints on a 10,000 records/second pipeline - to solve what one retention setting already solves.

stem: A company needs to implement real-time alerting on CloudTrail events that match specific patterns, such as root account logins, IAM policy changes, or security group modifications. Alerts must be delivered within 2 minutes of the event occurring. Which architecture provides the lowest latency alerting?

options.text: Configure CloudTrail to deliver events to an S3 bucket with event notifications enabled. Set up S3 event notifications to trigger a Lambda function that parses the CloudTrail log file and sends SNS notifications when matching patterns are found in the events.

Configure CloudTrail to deliver events to CloudWatch Logs with a log group in the same Region. Create CloudWatch Logs metric filters for each event pattern (root login, IAM changes, security group changes) and set up CloudWatch alarms with 1-minute evaluation periods.

Configure CloudTrail Lake to ingest all management events into the event data store. Create scheduled CloudTrail Lake queries that run every minute to search for root logins, IAM changes, and security group modifications, and publish results to an SNS topic.

Enable Amazon EventBridge integration with CloudTrail for management events. Create EventBridge rules with event patterns matching root account signin, IAM policy changes, and security group modifications, with SNS topics as targets for immediate notification delivery.

explanation: D is correct: CloudTrail publishes management events to the default EventBridge bus in near real time (seconds), so rules matching the 'AWS Console Sign In via CloudTrail' detail-type for root ConsoleLogin and 'AWS API Call via CloudTrail' for IAM policy actions and AuthorizeSecurityGroupIngress can target SNS directly, well inside the 2-minute goal. A is incorrect because CloudTrail batches log files to S3 roughly every 5 minutes (often longer), so the S3 notification and Lambda parse cannot even begin until that delivery delay has elapsed. B is incorrect because CloudTrail-to-CloudWatch Logs delivery latency plus metric-filter evaluation plus alarm evaluation periods stacks up to several minutes, and it needs a separate filter/alarm pair per pattern. C is incorrect because CloudTrail Lake events become queryable only after ingestion lag (minutes), and per-minute scheduled queries add polling delay and scan cost on top of that lag.

stem: A company's Auto Scaling group frequently launches instances that fail their ELB health check and are replaced, producing a rapid cycle of launching and terminating instances. This results in high costs and an inability to maintain the desired capacity. The health check grace period is already set to 900 seconds, and engineers have confirmed that the instances never pass the health check even when left running for 30 minutes. Which approach stabilizes the Auto Scaling group?

options.text: Switch the Auto Scaling group from ELB health checks to EC2 status checks to avoid premature termination. Configure a CloudWatch alarm on the Auto Scaling GroupInServiceInstances metric to alert when capacity drops below the desired count for investigation.

Increase the health check grace period on the Auto Scaling group to 600 seconds to allow more time for instance initialization. Configure the ALB target group health check with a longer interval of 30 seconds and increase the healthy threshold to 5 consecutive checks.

Enable Auto Scaling instance scale-in protection for all instances in the group to prevent termination. Configure a warm pool with a pool size equal to the desired capacity to maintain pre-initialized instances ready for immediate launch when failures occur.

Temporarily suspend the ReplaceUnhealthy Auto Scaling process to stop the launch-terminate cycle. Investigate the root cause by reviewing the instance system logs in the EC2 console and CloudWatch agent logs, then fix the underlying issue before resuming the process.

explanation: Option D is correct because the instances never become healthy no matter how long they run, which means this is a defect on the instance rather than a timing problem. Suspending the ReplaceUnhealthy process stops Auto Scaling from terminating instances that fail the health check, which both halts the cost bleed and, crucially, leaves a failing instance alive long enough to be examined. The engineer can then pull the system log from the EC2 console and the application and CloudWatch agent logs to find why the health check endpoint never returns success, fix that, and resume the process. Option A fails because EC2 status checks only verify that the hypervisor and instance networking are functioning; switching to them would mark a completely broken application as healthy, so the group would hold its capacity while serving errors, which hides the incident rather than resolving it. Option B fails on the numbers given: the grace period is already 900 seconds, so reducing it to 600 makes the situation worse, and lengthening the target group interval or raising the healthy threshold only changes how quickly a verdict is reached for instances that will never pass. Option C fails because scale-in protection applies to instances Auto Scaling chooses to terminate during a scale-in event; it does not prevent the replacement of instances that have been marked unhealthy, so the cycle continues. A warm pool would additionally pre-provision more copies of the same broken configuration, increasing cost without fixing anything.

stem: A company needs to ensure that all Amazon EBS volumes are encrypted with a customer-managed KMS key. Existing unencrypted volumes must be identified and encrypted, and future unencrypted volume creation must be prevented. Which combination of actions achieves this?

options.text: Configure AWS CloudTrail to log CreateVolume API calls and create an EventBridge rule that triggers a Lambda function to encrypt newly created unencrypted volumes. Use Amazon Inspector to scan for unencrypted EBS volumes and generate findings for remediation.

Create an SCP that denies ec2:CreateVolume unless the aws:RequestTag/Encrypted condition is true. Deploy a Lambda function on a daily schedule that scans all EBS volumes using the DescribeVolumes API and creates encrypted copies of any unencrypted volumes found.

Implement a CloudFormation hook that validates EBS volume resources for encryption before stack operations. Deploy an AWS Config rule with auto-remediation that uses a Lambda function to snapshot, encrypt, and replace unencrypted volumes across all accounts.

Enable EBS encryption by default in each account's EC2 settings with the desired KMS CMK. Deploy an AWS Config rule encrypted-volumes to detect existing unencrypted volumes and use SSM Automation to create encrypted snapshots and replace unencrypted volumes.

explanation: D is correct: enabling EBS encryption by default per account and Region with the chosen customer managed KMS key forces every newly created volume to be encrypted regardless of how it is created (console, CLI, SDK, Auto Scaling, CloudFormation). The AWS Config managed rule encrypted-volumes then flags the pre-existing unencrypted volumes, and an SSM Automation runbook snapshots each one, copies the snapshot with the CMK, and swaps in the encrypted replacement. A is incorrect because an existing volume cannot be encrypted in place, so the Lambda cannot 'encrypt newly created unencrypted volumes', and Amazon Inspector scans for software vulnerabilities and network reachability, not EBS encryption state. B is incorrect because EBS encryption is not expressed as a request tag; the relevant IAM condition key is ec2:Encrypted, so the SCP as written does not deny unencrypted volume creation, and a daily scan leaves a detection gap plus orphaned unencrypted originals. C is incorrect because CloudFormation hooks only intercept CloudFormation stack operations, so volumes created directly via the console, API, or Auto Scaling bypass the guardrail entirely.

stem: A company needs to implement a GitOps workflow for their Kubernetes applications running on Amazon EKS. Application manifests are stored in a CodeCommit repository, and any change to the manifests should automatically sync to the EKS cluster within 5 minutes. The platform team also requires a built-in web console that shows the live sync status and health of every Kubernetes resource across all of the company's clusters, with RBAC-controlled manual sync and rollback that on-call operators can trigger without shell access to the clusters. Which approach implements this GitOps pattern?

options.text: Configure an EventBridge rule that matches CodeCommit repository state change events. Target a Lambda function that clones the repository, compares manifests against the cluster state using the Kubernetes API, and applies diffs using the kubectl binary in a Lambda layer.

Install Flux CD on the EKS cluster configured to watch the CodeCommit repository for manifest changes. Configure Flux with a sync interval of 1 minute and enable automated image updates with the Flux image automation controller for container image promotions.

Create a CodePipeline triggered by CodeCommit changes that runs a CodeBuild project to apply Kubernetes manifests. Configure CodeBuild with kubectl and the EKS cluster's kubeconfig to run kubectl apply on the changed manifest files from the repository.

Deploy ArgoCD on the EKS cluster and configure an Application resource pointing to the CodeCommit repository with a sync policy of automated pruning. Set the sync interval to 3 minutes and configure health checks for each Kubernetes resource in the application.

explanation: Option D is correct because ArgoCD is the only choice that delivers both halves of the requirement. It is a true pull-based GitOps controller running inside the cluster, so an Application resource pointing at the CodeCommit repository with an automated sync policy and pruning continuously reconciles the cluster against Git, and a 3-minute reconciliation interval comfortably meets the 5-minute objective. ArgoCD also ships a first-party web UI that renders the resource tree with per-resource health and sync status across every registered cluster, and its built-in RBAC model lets operators be granted sync and rollback actions on specific projects without any kubectl access. Option A fails because it is not GitOps at all: a Lambda function invoked by an event performs a one-shot push, so nothing reconciles drift between commits, and cloning repositories and running kubectl from a Lambda layer within the 15-minute limit is fragile and offers no health visibility. Option B fails on the console requirement rather than on the sync requirement - Flux at a 1-minute interval reconciles from CodeCommit perfectly well - but Flux ships as a set of controllers with no built-in UI or RBAC-controlled operator console, so the company would have to adopt and operate a separate third-party dashboard to get what the stem asks for. Option C fails because CodePipeline running kubectl apply is push-based CI/CD: it only acts when the pipeline runs, so manual changes or drift in the cluster persist unnoticed until the next commit, and it provides no continuous reconciliation, no per-resource health view and no rollback console.

stem: A company is using AWS CloudFormation and needs to create a stack that provisions resources in a specific order: first a VPC, then subnets, then an RDS instance in those subnets, and finally a Lambda function that needs the RDS endpoint. The RDS instance takes 15 minutes to provision. How should the template be structured to handle the dependencies and long provisioning time?

options.text: Create the VPC and subnets in one template deployed first. Use a separate template with a CloudFormation WaitCondition and WaitConditionHandle that pauses for 15 minutes before creating the Lambda function, allowing the RDS instance time to provision.

Split the resources into four nested stacks executed sequentially. Use CloudFormation stack outputs and Fn::GetAtt on AWS::CloudFormation::Stack resources to pass the VPC ID, subnet IDs, and RDS endpoint between nested stacks as parameters.

Define all resources in a single template without explicit DependsOn, relying solely on Fn::Ref and Fn::GetAtt intrinsic functions to establish implicit dependencies. CloudFormation automatically determines the correct creation order from these resource references.

Define all resources in the template with explicit DependsOn attributes creating the chain VPC -> Subnets -> RDS -> Lambda. Pass the database endpoint into the Lambda environment variables through a template parameter whose default value is the endpoint DNS name recorded from the previous deployment of the stack.

explanation: Option C is correct because CloudFormation builds its dependency graph from intrinsic function references. When the subnets Ref the VPC, the DB subnet group Refs the subnets, and the Lambda environment variable uses Fn::GetAtt on the RDS instance endpoint, CloudFormation infers the exact ordering the stem describes and creates each resource only after its dependencies report CREATE_COMPLETE. That also handles the 15-minute provisioning time automatically: CloudFormation blocks on the RDS instance until the service reports it available, so no timing logic of any kind is needed and the Lambda function receives a real endpoint. Option A fails because a WaitCondition paired with a WaitConditionHandle waits for a signal sent to a pre-signed URL, not for a wall-clock duration; a timeout is a failure bound rather than a sleep. Hard-coding 15 minutes is also fragile, since a slower restore or a larger instance class would leave the Lambda function created before the database exists. Option B fails because four nested stacks add a parent template, four child templates and parameter plumbing to express a purely linear dependency that a single template already expresses for free, increasing deployment time and rollback complexity without any benefit. Option D fails on the endpoint itself: a template parameter defaulted to a value recorded from the previous deployment is a static string, so on the first deployment there is no value and on any deployment where RDS is replaced the Lambda function is configured with a stale endpoint pointing at a database that no longer exists. The DependsOn chain sequences the resources correctly but cannot supply a value the template never reads from the resource.

stem: A company runs a critical API on Amazon API Gateway with a Lambda backend. During a Lambda service disruption in us-east-1, the API was completely unavailable for 45 minutes. The company requires an RTO of 5 minutes for this API. Which architecture provides the required resilience?

options.text: Deploy the Lambda function with provisioned concurrency in us-east-1 to ensure warm execution environments. Configure API Gateway with a caching layer and set the cache TTL to 300 seconds so that cached responses are served during Lambda service disruptions.

Deploy the API Gateway and Lambda function in both us-east-1 and us-west-2. Configure Route 53 with a failover routing policy and health checks on each Regional API Gateway endpoint. Route 53 automatically fails over to the healthy Region within 60 seconds of detection.

Deploy the Lambda function in us-east-1 and configure API Gateway with a Lambda@Edge function as a fallback integration. If the primary Lambda returns an error, configure API Gateway to retry the request against the Lambda@Edge function running in the nearest CloudFront edge location.

Deploy the API Gateway and Lambda function in us-east-1. Create an API Gateway Regional endpoint in us-west-2 as a standby and configure a CloudWatch alarm that triggers a Step Functions workflow to deploy the Lambda function to us-west-2 when disruption is detected.

explanation: B is correct: an independent API Gateway plus Lambda stack in us-west-2 with Route 53 failover records and health checks makes recovery a DNS operation. Standard health checks mark an endpoint unhealthy after roughly 30 seconds (three 10-second checks), and with a short record TTL clients are on the secondary Region well inside the 5-minute RTO with no human action. A is incorrect because provisioned concurrency keeps execution environments warm but does nothing during a Regional Lambda service impairment, and API Gateway caching only replays previously cached GET responses for the TTL window - writes and cache misses fail. C is incorrect because Lambda@Edge is a CloudFront feature invoked by CloudFront viewer/origin events; API Gateway cannot use it as an integration fallback or retry target. D is incorrect because deploying the function to us-west-2 only after an alarm fires adds build and deployment time to the outage and leaves an untested standby, so the 5-minute RTO cannot be met.

stem: A company uses AWS Lambda functions that occasionally experience cold start latency exceeding 10 seconds for Java-based functions. The team needs to monitor cold start frequency and duration separately from warm invocation metrics. Which monitoring approach isolates cold start metrics?

options.text: Enable Lambda provisioned concurrency set to the expected baseline invocation rate. Monitor the ProvisionedConcurrencySpilloverInvocations CloudWatch metric to track how many invocations exceed provisioned capacity and experience cold starts during traffic spikes.

Configure AWS X-Ray tracing on the Lambda function and create a custom X-Ray group filtering for traces that include the Initialization subsegment. Use X-Ray analytics to compute the cold start percentage and average initialization duration across all traced invocations.

Create a CloudWatch Logs metric filter on the Lambda function log group that matches the REPORT log line containing 'Init Duration'. Extract the init duration value as a custom metric and create alarms when the average cold start duration exceeds the 10-second threshold.

Enable Lambda Insights as a Lambda layer and configure the enhanced monitoring extension. Lambda Insights automatically reports Init Duration metrics separately from invocation duration, allowing CloudWatch dashboards to display cold start frequency and duration independently.

explanation: D is correct: the Lambda Insights layer runs as an extension that emits an embedded-metric-format performance record for every invocation, and that record carries init_duration_ms separately from duration and billed_duration. Cold starts therefore appear as their own metric with their own count, and the built-in Lambda Insights dashboards chart cold start frequency and initialization time independently of warm invocation latency, with no per-function wiring. A is incorrect because provisioned concurrency is a mitigation rather than a measurement: ProvisionedConcurrencySpilloverInvocations counts invocations that exceeded provisioned capacity but never reports how long any initialization actually took. B is incorrect because X-Ray traces are sampled by default, so the Initialization subsegment yields a partial and statistically skewed view, and X-Ray groups filter traces rather than producing a durable cold-start metric for alarming. C is incorrect as the best answer because it hand-builds a metric filter per function against unstructured REPORT text, and the extracted value gives init duration only - cold start count relative to total invocations and memory pressure still require additional filters, which is exactly the work Lambda Insights removes.

stem: A company's production DynamoDB table started returning ProvisionedThroughputExceededException errors during a flash sale event. The table is configured with provisioned capacity and Auto Scaling with a target utilization of 70%. Which immediate action resolves the throttling while the team investigates capacity planning?

options.text: Increase the Auto Scaling maximum capacity units for both read and write capacity. Reduce the target utilization from 70% to 50% to trigger scaling earlier and configure the scaling cooldown period to 60 seconds for faster scale-up response during traffic surges.

Switch the DynamoDB table to on-demand capacity mode using the UpdateTable API. On-demand mode instantly adapts to traffic spikes by serving up to double the previous peak traffic, eliminating provisioned throughput exceptions without manual capacity adjustments.

Enable DynamoDB reserved capacity for the table at the expected peak read and write throughput. Configure CloudWatch alarms on ConsumedReadCapacityUnits and ConsumedWriteCapacityUnits to alert when consumption approaches 80% of the reserved capacity allocation.

Add a DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) cluster in front of the table to absorb read traffic. Configure the DAX cluster with a cache TTL of 300 seconds and enable item-level caching for GetItem and BatchGetItem operations to reduce direct table read capacity consumption.

explanation: B is correct: UpdateTable can switch a live table from provisioned to on-demand (pay-per-request) mode without downtime, and on-demand instantly absorbs traffic up to double the table's previous peak while continuously raising that peak as load grows, so ProvisionedThroughputExceededException stops immediately without capacity math during the sale. A is incorrect because DynamoDB Auto Scaling is driven by CloudWatch alarms and Application Auto Scaling, so it adds capacity over minutes; lowering the target to 50 percent and shortening cooldowns speeds it up only marginally and cannot track a flash-sale step change. C is incorrect because DynamoDB reserved capacity is purely a billing commitment against provisioned throughput - it buys a discount, not additional throughput - so throttling continues unchanged. D is incorrect because DAX only offloads eligible read traffic and only after cluster creation (minutes) and cache warm-up; it does nothing for write throttling and is not an immediate mitigation.

stem: A company stores sensitive customer PII in an Amazon S3 bucket. The security team needs to automatically discover and classify PII data, identify any PII that's been shared in public or cross-account S3 buckets, and generate compliance reports monthly. Which service combination meets these requirements?

options.text: Configure AWS Config rules with the s3-bucket-public-read-prohibited and s3-account-level-public-access-blocks rules. Use Amazon Textract to extract text from documents in the S3 bucket and apply custom regex patterns to identify PII fields in the extracted content.

Enable S3 Storage Lens with advanced metrics and recommendations to identify publicly accessible buckets. Configure S3 Inventory reports to list all objects and use Amazon Athena queries with regex patterns to scan inventory metadata for PII-related object key naming conventions.

Deploy Amazon Comprehend to analyze S3 objects for PII entities using the DetectPiiEntities API. Create a Lambda function to scan new objects triggered by S3 event notifications and store PII classification results in a DynamoDB table for monthly compliance reporting.

Enable Amazon Macie to scan the S3 buckets for PII using managed data identifiers. Configure Macie to generate sensitive data discovery results and use the Macie policy findings to identify publicly accessible or cross-account shared buckets containing PII.

explanation: D is correct: Macie is the managed S3 data classification service. Managed data identifiers detect PII such as names, national ID numbers, and payment card data inside object content, discovery jobs can be scheduled monthly with results written to S3 for compliance reporting, and Macie's separate policy findings flag buckets that are publicly accessible, shared with external accounts, or missing encryption - covering both halves of the requirement in one service. A is incorrect because Config rules evaluate only bucket-level public access configuration, and Textract plus hand-written regex is an OCR pipeline you must build, tune, and operate with no managed classification and no cross-account exposure detection. B is incorrect because Storage Lens and S3 Inventory report metadata only (keys, size, encryption, ownership); querying object key names in Athena never inspects object content, so PII in generically named files is missed entirely. C is incorrect because Comprehend DetectPiiEntities classifies text you explicitly feed it, requiring custom Lambda orchestration, file-format handling, and cost control, and it has no visibility into bucket policies or ACLs to detect public or cross-account sharing.

stem: A company runs integration tests in their CodePipeline that require a fully deployed infrastructure environment. Creating the test environment takes 20 minutes and costs $50 per run. The team runs 30 pipeline executions daily. Which strategy reduces testing costs while maintaining test quality?

options.text: Create a persistent shared test environment that is reset between pipeline runs using CloudFormation stack updates. Configure CodePipeline to run integration tests against the shared environment and use a DynamoDB-based locking mechanism to serialize concurrent test executions.

Replace full integration tests with contract tests using Pact framework in a CodeBuild stage. Run lightweight consumer-driven contract tests that validate API interfaces between services without deploying full infrastructure, and run full integration tests only before production.

Configure CodePipeline with a manual approval gate before the integration test stage. Require developers to batch multiple code changes into a single pipeline execution and run integration tests only when explicitly approved, reducing the number of daily executions.

Use AWS CloudFormation with spot instances for the test environment infrastructure. Configure CodeBuild to create the environment using Spot Instance request templates and reduce the test suite to only critical path tests, cutting environment runtime by 50%.

explanation: B is correct: consumer-driven contract tests run entirely inside a CodeBuild container against recorded provider expectations, so the 20-minute, 50-dollar environment is not built on all 30 daily executions. The interface regressions that integration tests most often catch (breaking request/response shape changes between services) are still caught on every commit, and one full integration run before production preserves the final end-to-end gate, so quality is maintained while cost drops sharply. A is incorrect because a single shared environment plus a DynamoDB lock serializes 30 executions per day behind one environment, creating long queues, state leakage between runs, and flaky results that erode test trust. C is incorrect because manual approval gates and batching changes cut cost only by cutting feedback: defects surface later in larger batches and are harder to attribute to a specific commit. D is incorrect because Spot Instances shave part of the compute cost but leave the 20-minute provisioning time and the full-stack dependency intact, and trimming the suite to critical-path tests explicitly reduces test quality, which the requirement forbids.

stem: A company uses AWS CDK to define their infrastructure and wants to share a common set of constructs (VPC patterns, security configurations, monitoring setups) across 20 development teams. The shared constructs must be versioned and teams should be able to pin to specific versions. Which approach enables this shared construct library?

options.text: Build a shared CDK app that deploys common infrastructure (VPC, security, monitoring) to each account. Have teams import the deployed resources using Fn::ImportValue in their CDK stacks, creating cross-stack dependencies between the shared and team-specific infrastructure.

Create a CDK construct library as an npm package published to AWS CodeArtifact. Version the package using semantic versioning and configure each team's CDK project to reference the construct library as a dependency with a pinned version in their package.json file.

Create CloudFormation modules from the shared constructs and publish them to the CloudFormation registry as private modules. Have teams reference the modules in their CDK templates using CfnResource constructs with the module type and version constraints.

Store the shared CDK constructs in a central CodeCommit repository. Configure each team's CDK project to use git submodules referencing specific tags in the shared repository, and run cdk synth to verify construct compatibility during each team's CI/CD build.

explanation: B is correct: a CDK construct library is ordinary TypeScript/Python code, so packaging it as an npm module and publishing it to AWS CodeArtifact provides semantic versioning, immutable published versions, upstream npmjs proxying, and IAM-controlled access. Each of the 20 teams pins a version in package.json and adopts new versions on its own schedule, which is precisely the versioning and pinning requirement. A is incorrect because deploying shared infrastructure and consuming it through Fn::ImportValue shares resources, not constructs: an exported output cannot be changed while any stack imports it, which tightly couples all 20 teams to the shared stack's lifecycle. C is incorrect because CloudFormation registry modules are template fragments - teams lose CDK's L2/L3 abstractions, type checking, and unit testability, and CDK can only consume them through raw CfnResource escape hatches. D is incorrect because git submodules pin a commit rather than participating in dependency resolution, offer no transitive dependency or version-conflict handling, and require every team's build environment to carry Git credentials for the central repo.

stem: A company runs a stateless web application on an Auto Scaling group behind an ALB. During deployment, the team replaces instances with a rolling update. Users report brief 502 errors because in-flight requests are cut off when an instance is terminated before it finishes responding. The team must keep the existing Auto Scaling group and the rolling update strategy, and wants to fix the root cause of the truncated requests. Which configuration eliminates the 502 errors during rolling deployments?

options.text: Add a lifecycle hook on the EC2_INSTANCE_TERMINATING event with a heartbeat timeout of 300 seconds. Configure the application to stop accepting new connections when it receives the termination signal and complete all in-flight requests before sending the CONTINUE signal.

Configure the Auto Scaling group with an instance refresh operation using a minimum healthy percentage of 100%. Set the instance warmup time to 300 seconds and configure the ALB health check with a 10-second interval and 5-second timeout for faster health detection.

Switch from a rolling update to a blue/green deployment strategy using CodeDeploy with an ALB. Configure CodeDeploy to create a replacement target group, shift traffic using ALB listener rules, and terminate original instances only after all connections are drained.

Reduce the ALB target group deregistration delay from the default 300 seconds to 30 seconds so instances leave the target group quickly, and increase the Auto Scaling group default cooldown to 300 seconds so instance replacements are spaced further apart.

explanation: Option A is correct. An EC2_INSTANCE_TERMINATING lifecycle hook holds the instance in Terminating:Wait while the ALB deregisters it, and the application uses that window to stop accepting new work and finish every in-flight request before calling CompleteLifecycleAction with CONTINUE. That is the AWS-recommended graceful-shutdown pattern and it removes the truncated-response cause of the 502s without changing the deployment strategy. Option B is wrong: instance refresh with 100% minimum healthy percentage and faster health checks changes how quickly replacements are launched and detected, but nothing about it lets an instance finish requests that are already in flight when termination begins. Option C is wrong for this stem: blue/green with CodeDeploy is a different deployment strategy, and the team must keep rolling updates and its existing Auto Scaling group. Option D is wrong and actively harmful: 300 seconds is already the default deregistration delay, so cutting it to 30 seconds truncates in-flight requests sooner and increases errors, while the Auto Scaling cooldown governs scaling activity spacing and has no effect on connection draining.

stem: A company needs to implement cost anomaly detection that alerts the finance team when any AWS service's daily spend increases by more than 20% compared to the 30-day average. The alert must include the specific service, account, and estimated impact. Which approach provides this cost monitoring?

options.text: Deploy a Lambda function on a daily schedule that queries AWS Cost Explorer API for service-level daily costs. Compare each service's cost against the 30-day rolling average and send formatted SNS notifications when any service exceeds the 20% threshold.

Configure AWS Cost Anomaly Detection with a monitor that tracks costs by AWS service. Set the alert threshold to 20% above the expected spend and configure SNS notifications to the finance team with anomaly details including service name, account ID, and root cause analysis.

Set up AWS Budgets with a daily cost budget for each AWS service and configure budget alerts at 120% of the 30-day average daily spend. Enable budget action notifications via SNS and configure the budget to include account-level breakdowns in the alert emails.

Create a CloudWatch alarm on the EstimatedCharges billing metric in us-east-1 with anomaly detection enabled. Configure the alarm to trigger when daily charges deviate by more than 20% from the expected band and send notifications via SNS with metric dimensions.

explanation: B is correct: AWS Cost Anomaly Detection builds ML baselines per monitor - here an AWS services monitor that segments spend by service - detects deviations from expected spend automatically, and alert subscriptions can be configured to fire when the anomaly exceeds a percentage above expected. The SNS/email payload includes the service, the linked account, the anomaly time window, the total dollar impact, and root-cause attribution, matching every element the finance team asked for. A is incorrect because it reimplements a managed service: you own the Cost Explorer API calls, the rolling-average math, false-positive suppression, and message formatting, and Cost Explorer data itself lags by hours. C is incorrect because AWS Budgets compares actual spend against a static budgeted amount you define per service; the threshold does not follow a moving 30-day average, so it requires continuous manual retuning as baselines drift. D is incorrect because the EstimatedCharges billing metric is published only in us-east-1 at roughly 6-hour granularity with coarse ServiceName dimensions and no linked-account dimension, so it delivers neither the timeliness nor the account-level attribution required.

stem: During a Regional AWS service event, a company's application in us-east-1 became degraded. The team had no visibility into whether the issue was with their application or the AWS service. They need a way to quickly determine if AWS service issues are impacting their workloads during incidents. Which approach provides this visibility?

options.text: Deploy synthetic monitoring using CloudWatch Synthetics canaries that test critical application endpoints every minute. Compare canary failure patterns against the AWS Service Health Dashboard status page and create a custom dashboard showing both canary and service health side by side.

Subscribe to AWS Health Dashboard RSS feeds for all services used by the application. Configure a Lambda function to poll the feeds every minute and compare service health events against the application's error patterns stored in CloudWatch Logs for correlation analysis.

Enable AWS Health events integration with Amazon EventBridge in the application account. Create EventBridge rules that match health events for the services used (EC2, RDS, Lambda) and correlate them with application CloudWatch alarms using a centralized incident dashboard.

Configure Amazon CloudWatch Internet Monitor for the application's VPC endpoints. Monitor internet traffic paths for performance anomalies and use the Internet Monitor dashboard to distinguish between AWS infrastructure issues and application-level problems during incidents.

explanation: C is correct: AWS Health delivers account-specific events - both public service events that affect your particular resources and account-scoped notifications - to the default EventBridge bus. Rules matching the aws.health source for EC2, RDS, and Lambda can drive an incident dashboard or chat channel where those events sit beside the application's CloudWatch alarms, answering 'is this AWS or us?' programmatically and within seconds of AWS posting the event. A is incorrect because the public Service Health Dashboard status page is not account-scoped and typically lags actual impact, and eyeballing canary failures against a status page is a manual correlation with no signal about your affected resource IDs. B is incorrect because the RSS feeds carry the same generic, non-account-specific information, and polling them from Lambda adds latency and undifferentiated code for data EventBridge already pushes. D is incorrect because CloudWatch Internet Monitor measures internet-path performance and availability between end users and your AWS-hosted application; it reports nothing about the health of the EC2, RDS, or Lambda services themselves.

stem: A company needs to implement network-level isolation for their production EKS workloads. Different microservice teams should only be able to communicate with their own services and explicitly approved cross-team services. Which approach enforces this network segmentation within the EKS cluster?

options.text: Implement Kubernetes NetworkPolicy resources with a default-deny ingress and egress policy in each namespace. Create specific NetworkPolicy rules that allow traffic only between pods with matching team labels and explicitly approved cross-team service selectors.

Configure AWS App Mesh with virtual services for each microservice and define traffic policies using virtual routers. Create route rules that restrict traffic to same-team virtual services by default and require explicit route entries for cross-team service communication.

Deploy each team's services in separate EKS node groups with dedicated security groups. Configure security group rules to allow traffic only within each team's node group and add specific rules for approved cross-team communication based on the node group security group IDs.

Deploy AWS Network Firewall in the VPC subnets hosting the EKS nodes. Create stateful rule groups that inspect traffic between pod CIDR ranges and allow only approved source-destination pairs based on team ownership of the pod IP address ranges.

explanation: A is correct: Kubernetes NetworkPolicy is enforced by the CNI at the pod level (the Amazon VPC CNI supports it natively on EKS, as do Calico and Cilium). A default-deny ingress and egress policy per namespace plus allow rules whose podSelector and namespaceSelector match team labels expresses exactly 'own team's services plus explicitly approved cross-team services', and it holds regardless of which node a pod is scheduled onto. B is incorrect because App Mesh shapes Layer 7 routing for traffic that already flows through Envoy sidecars; a pod can still open a direct TCP connection to any other pod IP, so mesh route rules are traffic management, not enforced network isolation. C is incorrect because security groups attach to ENIs and nodes, so unless security groups for pods is used, all pods sharing a node share its security group - far too coarse for per-service isolation, and pinning each team to dedicated node groups wastes capacity and still cannot separate services within a team. D is incorrect because AWS Network Firewall inspects traffic that is routed through its endpoints; same-node and intra-subnet pod-to-pod traffic never reaches it, and it has no awareness of Kubernetes labels, namespaces, or the ephemeral pod IPs it would need to write team-based rules.

stem: A company wants to automate the process of creating and distributing hardened AMIs to all AWS accounts in their organization. The AMI pipeline should build from a base Amazon Linux 2 AMI, apply CIS benchmarks, install monitoring agents, and share the AMI with all accounts. Which service orchestrates this AMI pipeline?

options.text: Create an AWS Systems Manager Automation document that launches an instance, applies State Manager associations for CIS benchmarks and agent installation, creates an AMI, and shares it. Schedule the Automation document using a maintenance window for monthly builds.

Use EC2 Image Builder to create an image pipeline with a recipe that includes CIS benchmark components, CloudWatch agent installation, and SSM agent configuration. Configure the distribution settings to share the output AMI with all accounts in the AWS Organization.

Deploy HashiCorp Packer on a CodeBuild project to build the hardened AMI from a JSON template. Configure Packer to run Ansible playbooks for CIS benchmarks and agent installation, then use a Lambda function to share the AMI across Organization accounts.

Create a CodePipeline with a CodeBuild stage that launches an EC2 instance from the base AMI. Use SSM Run Command to apply CIS benchmarks and install agents, then create an AMI from the instance and share it using the ModifyImageAttribute API across accounts.

explanation: B is correct: EC2 Image Builder is the managed golden-AMI factory. A recipe composes the Amazon Linux 2 parent image with AWS-managed hardening components (including STIG and CIS Benchmark components) and build components that install the CloudWatch and SSM agents; test components validate the output image; the pipeline runs on a schedule or when the parent image is updated; and distribution settings automatically copy, share, and launch-permission the resulting AMI to every account in the Organization, with full image versioning and change tracking. A is incorrect because an Automation document can build an AMI, but you hand-write the launch, harden, snapshot, share, and cleanup steps and the per-account sharing loop, and it provides no recipe versioning or built-in test phase. C is incorrect because Packer plus Ansible is a self-managed toolchain: you own the build agents, plugin and playbook versions, and a custom Lambda to fan out image sharing - undifferentiated work for a capability AWS already manages. D is incorrect for the same reason: CodePipeline plus CodeBuild plus Run Command plus ModifyImageAttribute is a hand-built reimplementation of Image Builder, with no component library, no image testing stage, and no Organizations-aware distribution.

stem: A company is migrating from AWS CloudFormation to Terraform for infrastructure management. They need to import 100 existing AWS resources currently managed by CloudFormation into Terraform without recreating them. Which TWO steps are necessary to accomplish this migration?

options.text: Write Terraform resource configurations matching the existing AWS resources' current state. Run terraform import for each resource to associate the Terraform state with the existing AWS resources, then run terraform plan to verify no changes are detected.

Delete the CloudFormation stacks with DeletionPolicy set to Retain on all resources to preserve them in AWS. This detaches the resources from CloudFormation management, allowing Terraform to take ownership without resource recreation or state conflicts.

Use the terraformer tool to automatically generate Terraform configuration files and state from existing AWS resources. Review the generated HCL code for accuracy, refactor to follow team coding standards, and run terraform plan to confirm state alignment.

Export the CloudFormation template to a Terraform configuration file using the cfn-tf-converter tool. Import the converted configuration directly into Terraform without modifications and run terraform apply to synchronize the Terraform state with existing resources.

explanation: A and B together are correct. B comes first: setting DeletionPolicy (and UpdateReplacePolicy) to Retain on every resource and then deleting the CloudFormation stacks leaves the physical AWS resources intact while removing CloudFormation's ownership, so two tools never believe they manage the same resource. A then adopts them: author HCL that matches each resource's current attributes, run terraform import (or an import block) so the Terraform address is bound to the existing physical ID, and confirm with terraform plan that no changes are reported - proof that the configuration matches reality and nothing will be recreated. C is incorrect because terraformer only generates configuration and state from live resources; it does nothing about the CloudFormation stacks that still own them, so a later stack update, rollback, or drift remediation would fight Terraform. D is incorrect because there is no supported cfn-tf-converter import path, and running terraform apply against an empty state would attempt to create duplicate resources rather than adopt the existing ones - import, not apply, is what associates state with existing infrastructure.

stem: A company operates an Amazon Aurora MySQL Global Database with a primary cluster in us-east-1 and a secondary cluster in eu-west-1. They need to test their disaster recovery procedure by performing a managed failover from us-east-1 to eu-west-1 with minimal data loss. Which approach performs the DR test correctly?

options.text: Use the Aurora Global Database managed planned failover feature to promote the eu-west-1 secondary cluster to primary. This process synchronizes the clusters before switching, ensuring zero data loss, and demotes the original primary to a secondary cluster automatically.

Initiate an unplanned failover by stopping the writer instance in the us-east-1 primary cluster. The Aurora Global Database automatically detects the failure and promotes the eu-west-1 secondary cluster to primary within the configured RPO, typically under 1 second of data loss.

Detach the eu-west-1 secondary cluster from the global database using the RemoveFromGlobalCluster API. Promote the detached cluster to a standalone Aurora cluster, update the application connection strings to point to the eu-west-1 endpoint, and manually recreate replication.

Create a manual snapshot of the us-east-1 primary cluster and copy it to eu-west-1. Restore the snapshot as a new Aurora cluster in eu-west-1, configure it as the new primary, and update DNS records to point to the restored cluster's endpoint.

explanation: A is correct: Aurora Global Database managed planned failover is the supported way to rehearse regional DR. Aurora stops writes on the us-east-1 primary, waits for the eu-west-1 secondary to fully catch up so replication lag reaches zero, then promotes eu-west-1 to primary and demotes the original primary to a secondary - the global cluster topology and replication survive the switch, with no data loss and no manual reconfiguration. B is incorrect because stopping the writer triggers the unplanned detach-and-promote path, whose RPO equals whatever replication lag was outstanding (typically about a second, not zero); that is a failure-injection exercise, not the minimal-data-loss managed failover requested, and it leaves the global topology broken afterward. C is incorrect because RemoveFromGlobalCluster permanently detaches the secondary into a standalone cluster, severing replication so it must be rebuilt from scratch; it is the manual escape hatch used when the managed path is unavailable. D is incorrect because snapshot copy and restore yields an RPO equal to the age of the snapshot and takes far longer than a managed failover, and it produces a divergent cluster rather than exercising the global database failover mechanism the DR plan relies on.

stem: A company needs to analyze VPC Flow Logs to identify the top talkers (source IPs generating the most traffic), detect port scanning attempts, and visualize traffic patterns over time. The analysis must cover 30 days of flow log data across 50 VPCs. Which solution provides this analysis capability?

options.text: Configure VPC Flow Logs to publish to a Kinesis Data Stream. Use Amazon Managed Service for Apache Flink to run continuous SQL queries that identify real-time top talkers and port scanning attempts, with results stored in Amazon Timestream for time-series visualization.

Enable VPC Flow Logs integration with Amazon Detective. Use Detective's built-in behavioral analysis to identify unusual traffic patterns including top talkers and port scanning attempts, and export findings to Amazon QuickSight for custom traffic pattern dashboards.

Configure VPC Flow Logs to publish to S3 in Parquet format with Hive-compatible partitioning. Use Amazon Athena with SQL queries to analyze top talkers, port scanning patterns, and traffic trends across the 30-day dataset with partitioned queries for cost efficiency.

Configure VPC Flow Logs to publish to CloudWatch Logs. Use CloudWatch Logs Insights queries with aggregation functions to identify top source IPs by byte count, detect port scanning by counting distinct destination ports per source IP, and graph traffic patterns over time.

explanation: C is correct: VPC Flow Logs can be delivered straight to S3 in Parquet with Hive-compatible partitioning, so Athena reads only the columns it needs and prunes to the partitions a query touches. Top talkers (SUM(bytes) GROUP BY srcaddr), port scanning (COUNT(DISTINCT dstport) per srcaddr within a time window), and traffic trends over time are all ordinary SQL, and 30 days across 50 VPCs stays inexpensive in both storage and per-query scanning. A is incorrect because Kinesis Data Streams plus Managed Service for Apache Flink plus Timestream is a real-time streaming pipeline: substantially more expensive and operationally heavy than the retrospective 30-day analysis actually required, and windowed streaming SQL cannot answer arbitrary ad-hoc historical questions. B is incorrect because Amazon Detective ingests flow logs to support entity- and finding-centric security investigations driven by GuardDuty; it offers no arbitrary aggregation for top talkers and no export path to QuickSight. D is incorrect because CloudWatch Logs ingestion and storage of flow logs at this volume is the most expensive option, and Logs Insights scans raw log data with per-query time and concurrency limits, making 30-day cross-VPC aggregation slow and costly.

stem: A company's Lambda function processes messages from an SQS queue. After a code deployment, the function started throwing unhandled exceptions, causing messages to be retried repeatedly. The team needs to implement a mechanism to automatically detect and respond to this type of deployment failure. Which approach provides the earliest detection?

options.text: Configure the Lambda function with a dead-letter queue (DLQ) SQS queue and create a CloudWatch alarm on the DLQ's ApproximateNumberOfMessagesVisible metric. When messages appear in the DLQ, trigger a Lambda function to analyze the error and notify the development team.

Create a CloudWatch alarm on the Lambda function Errors metric with a threshold of 10 errors in a 1-minute period. Configure the alarm to trigger an EventBridge rule that invokes a Lambda function to automatically roll back the deployment using the CodeDeploy rollback API.

Enable AWS X-Ray tracing on the Lambda function and configure X-Ray insights to detect fault rate anomalies. Set up an EventBridge rule matching X-Ray insight notifications and target an SNS topic subscribed by the on-call team for immediate fault spike awareness.

Monitor the SQS queue's ApproximateNumberOfMessagesVisible metric and create a CloudWatch alarm when the count exceeds a threshold. Configure the alarm to trigger an SNS notification to the on-call team and an EventBridge rule to pause the SQS event source mapping.

explanation: B is correct: the Lambda Errors metric is emitted per invocation at 1-minute granularity, so an alarm on 10 errors in a single 1-minute period fires within roughly a minute of the bad version beginning to throw - the earliest signal available for this failure mode.
