It publishes a bucket inventory with sensitivity scores plus findings to Security Hub and EventBridge, which is the compliance reporting required. A is incorrect because Inspector assesses software vulnerabilities and network reachability for EC2, ECR images, and Lambda; it has no S3 object-content classification and no PII or PHI data identifiers. C is incorrect because Glue crawlers infer schema and Glue Data Quality validates author-written rules against structured datasets only, with no cross-account discovery model and no managed sensitive-data classifiers. D is incorrect because per-account Comprehend endpoints with S3-triggered Lambdas is bespoke infrastructure in 30 accounts that classifies only newly written text objects, leaving all existing data unscanned.

stem: A company's CodePipeline frequently fails at the deploy stage because of CloudFormation parameter mismatches between environments. The team passes parameters via JSON files, but the files sometimes have incorrect values for the target environment. Which approach prevents parameter mismatch errors?

options.text: Use CloudFormation StackSets to deploy the same template across all environments simultaneously. Define parameter overrides at the StackSet level for each target account and Region, ensuring parameters are managed centrally rather than in separate JSON files.

Create separate CloudFormation templates for each environment with hardcoded parameter values. Maintain each template in a dedicated branch of the CodeCommit repository and configure CodePipeline to use the environment-specific branch as the source for each deploy stage.

Store environment-specific parameters in AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store with a hierarchical path structure (/app/dev/dbname, /app/prod/dbname). Reference SSM parameters in CloudFormation using the AWS::SSM::Parameter::Value<String> parameter type for automatic resolution.

Add a CodeBuild validation stage before each deploy action that parses the parameter JSON file and validates values against a schema using a JSON Schema validator. Fail the pipeline if any parameter value doesn't match the expected format or allowed values for the target environment.

explanation: C is correct because storing values in Parameter Store under an environment-scoped hierarchy and declaring the template parameter as AWS::SSM::Parameter::Value<String> means the template carries only the path; CloudFormation resolves the current value from Parameter Store in the target account at create or update time. There is no per-environment JSON artifact to drift, and the value is owned by the environment rather than by the pipeline. A is incorrect because StackSets exist to deploy one template across many accounts and Regions with per-target parameter overrides, which are still hand-maintained values, and StackSets are the wrong tool for promoting a change through dev, test, and prod stages of a pipeline. B is incorrect because hardcoded per-environment templates in separate branches multiply the template by the number of environments, so every fix must be merged everywhere and branch drift becomes the new failure mode. D is incorrect because schema validation catches malformed or out-of-range values but a well-formed yet wrong value - a dev database name in the prod file - passes validation and still fails at deploy.

stem: A company manages their Kubernetes cluster configuration using Helm charts stored in a CodeCommit repository. They want version-controlled Helm releases with rollback capability and validation of chart values before deployment. The team already operates a CodePipeline for this application, runs no GitOps controllers in the EKS cluster today, and wants the LEAST additional in-cluster infrastructure to build and operate. Which Helm management approach provides these capabilities on EKS?

options.text: Create a CodePipeline that runs helm lint and helm template in a CodeBuild validation stage. Add a CodeBuild deploy stage that runs helm upgrade --install with the --atomic flag, which automatically rolls back on deployment failure and validates chart rendering before apply.

Deploy Flux CD with the Helm controller on the EKS cluster. Define HelmRelease custom resources that reference the Helm charts in CodeCommit with specific version pins. Flux automatically deploys charts, validates values against JSON schemas, and supports rollback to previous releases.

Deploy a custom Helm deployment operator on EKS that watches for ConfigMap changes in a dedicated namespace. Store Helm values in ConfigMaps and trigger the operator to run helm upgrade when values change, with automatic rollback if the deployment health check fails.

Store Helm charts in an ECR Helm repository instead of CodeCommit. Configure ArgoCD with a Helm source pointing to the ECR repository and enable ArgoCD's auto-sync with self-healing. ArgoCD validates chart values and provides one-click rollback to any previous release.

explanation: A is correct and adds nothing at all to the cluster. helm lint catches chart and values errors, helm template renders the manifests so the supplied values are validated before anything is applied, and helm upgrade --install --atomic makes the release transactional - if the upgrade fails or times out, Helm automatically rolls back to the previous revision. Helm keeps release history as secrets in the cluster, so an operator-initiated helm rollback is available afterwards, and the entire workflow runs inside the CodePipeline the team already owns. B does satisfy the functional requirements - Flux's helm-controller pins chart versions, validates values against values.schema.json, and performs upgrade remediation with rollback - but it violates the least-additional-infrastructure constraint, because it means deploying, upgrading, and operating the source-controller and helm-controller plus their CRDs and RBAC when a pipeline already exists. C requires the team to build and maintain a bespoke operator that reinvents release history, values validation, and rollback that Helm already provides, and ConfigMap-driven triggers offer no chart version pinning. D adds ArgoCD and also contradicts the stem by relocating the charts out of the CodeCommit repository into an ECR OCI registry, moving the source of truth the team already established.

stem: A company runs a mission-critical application that writes to both DynamoDB and S3. A transaction must either succeed in both or fail in both to maintain data consistency. If the DynamoDB write succeeds but the S3 write fails, the transaction should be rolled back. Which pattern ensures data consistency across both services?

options.text: Use DynamoDB Streams to trigger a Lambda function that writes to S3 after each DynamoDB write succeeds. If the S3 write fails, the Lambda function deletes the DynamoDB item and sends the event to a dead-letter queue for retry and investigation.

Write to S3 first and use S3 event notifications to trigger a Lambda function that writes to DynamoDB. Configure the Lambda function with a DLQ for failed DynamoDB writes and implement a reconciliation process that scans for orphaned S3 objects without matching DynamoDB items.

Implement a two-phase commit protocol using a coordinator Lambda function. The coordinator first sends prepare requests to both DynamoDB and S3, and if both acknowledge, sends commit requests. If either fails to prepare, the coordinator sends abort requests to both services.

Implement the saga pattern using Step Functions. Define a state machine that writes to DynamoDB first, then writes to S3. If the S3 write fails, execute a compensating transaction that deletes the DynamoDB item. Use Step Functions error handling for automatic compensation.

explanation: D is correct because no distributed transaction spans DynamoDB and S3, so the achievable guarantee is eventual atomicity through a saga. A Step Functions state machine makes the sequence explicit and durable: write DynamoDB, then write S3, with a Catch on the S3 state routing to a compensating task that deletes or tombstones the DynamoDB item. Step Functions' retry and catch semantics plus its execution history make the compensation itself reliable and auditable rather than best-effort. A is incorrect because DynamoDB Streams fire asynchronously after the item is already committed and visible to readers, and a stream or Lambda failure can leave the item permanently orphaned with no orchestrator retrying the compensation. B is incorrect because writing S3 first has the mirror-image problem, and the option openly relies on a reconciliation scan to find orphans - detection after the fact, not rollback. C is incorrect because two-phase commit requires participants exposing prepare, commit, and abort with locking, and neither DynamoDB nor S3 offers a prepare phase, so the described coordinator cannot exist.

stem: A company needs log-based alerting for an application running on Amazon ECS. When the application logs contain the pattern 'CRITICAL ERROR: database connection timeout', the on-call operations engineer must be paged within 30 seconds of the line being written to CloudWatch Logs. Which approach provides the FASTEST alerting on this log pattern?

options.text: Configure a CloudWatch Logs subscription filter that forwards matching log entries to a Lambda function. The Lambda function parses the log event, extracts relevant details, and immediately publishes an alert to an SNS topic with the log entry details and timestamp.

Configure a CloudWatch Logs metric filter that matches the pattern 'CRITICAL ERROR: database connection timeout'. Create a custom CloudWatch metric from the filter and set up a CloudWatch alarm with a 1-minute period that triggers an SNS notification when the metric exceeds 0.

Create a CloudWatch Logs Insights scheduled query that runs every 2 minutes searching for the error pattern. Configure the query to publish results to an SNS topic when matching log entries are found, including the count and most recent occurrence timestamp.

Configure CloudWatch Logs to send all logs to a Kinesis Data Stream. Deploy a Kinesis Data Analytics application with a SQL query that detects the error pattern in real-time and publishes matched events to a Lambda function that sends SNS alerts immediately.

explanation: A is correct. A CloudWatch Logs subscription filter evaluates the filter pattern as events are ingested into the log group and streams matches to the Lambda function within seconds; the function then publishes to SNS immediately. The only latency in the path is log agent delivery plus one Lambda invocation, which fits comfortably inside the 30-second requirement. B is the conventional pattern but cannot meet this SLA: the metric filter must first publish a data point, CloudWatch must ingest that data point, and the alarm must then complete at least one full 1-minute evaluation period before it transitions to ALARM and notifies SNS, which routinely puts end-to-end notification at two to three minutes. C is slower still and partly fictitious: CloudWatch Logs Insights has no built-in scheduled query that publishes to SNS - that requires an EventBridge schedule plus a Lambda wrapper - and a 2-minute polling cadence by itself already exceeds the 30-second requirement by a wide margin. D is not faster than the native subscription filter while adding a Kinesis data stream and a streaming SQL application for a single fixed-string match, multiplying cost and operational surface; Kinesis Data Analytics for SQL applications has also reached end of support, so it is not a valid design going forward.

stem: A company operates an e-commerce platform and needs to implement automated scaling of their DynamoDB table capacity based on upcoming promotional events. Marketing schedules flash sales 24 hours in advance, and the table needs 10x capacity during these events. Which approach pre-scales DynamoDB capacity for planned events?

options.text: Switch the DynamoDB table to on-demand capacity mode 30 minutes before the event. On-demand mode handles traffic spikes up to double the previous peak without provisioning. After the event, switch back to provisioned capacity mode during the next low-traffic period.

Use Application Auto Scaling scheduled actions for the DynamoDB table. Create scheduled actions that increase provisioned capacity 30 minutes before the flash sale starts and decrease capacity 1 hour after the sale ends, matching capacity to the expected event demand pattern.

Create an EventBridge scheduled rule 30 minutes before each flash sale that invokes a Lambda function. The Lambda function calls the UpdateTable API to increase provisioned capacity to the required level and creates another scheduled event to reduce capacity after the sale.

Configure DynamoDB Auto Scaling with a target utilization of 50% and maximum capacity set to 10x the baseline. The lower target utilization triggers scaling at 50% capacity, providing headroom for sudden traffic increases during the flash sale without pre-scaling.

explanation: B is correct because Application Auto Scaling manages DynamoDB provisioned capacity, and its scheduled actions set a new MinCapacity and MaxCapacity at a specified time using at() or cron() expressions. Raising the floor before the sale means the table already holds 10x capacity when the first request arrives - no warm-up and no throttling while a target-tracking policy catches up - and a second scheduled action lowers it afterward. A is incorrect because on-demand mode instantly absorbs only up to roughly twice the previous peak and throttles beyond that while partitions adapt, and capacity mode switches are rate-limited to once per 24 hours per table, making a switch-before-and-after pattern unworkable for frequent flash sales. C is incorrect because an EventBridge schedule plus a Lambda calling UpdateTable rebuilds scheduled actions in custom code with its own IAM, error handling, and conflicts with any attached scaling policy. D is incorrect because target tracking is reactive: it scales only after CloudWatch shows sustained consumption and scale-up takes minutes, so the opening burst is throttled regardless of the maximum.

stem: A company needs to implement a solution that allows developers to access production AWS resources for debugging but only through a controlled, time-limited session that is fully recorded. All commands and API calls must be captured for audit review. Which solution provides audited production access?

options.text: Create a bastion host in the production VPC with SSH access through AWS Systems Manager port forwarding. Configure the bastion with script recording that uploads terminal sessions to S3 and IAM policies that grant temporary credentials through STS AssumeRole with a 1-hour duration.

Configure AWS Systems Manager Session Manager for EC2 and ECS access. Session Manager records all terminal sessions to S3 and CloudWatch Logs. Use IAM Identity Center with time-limited permission sets that grant 1-hour access to production accounts after MFA verification.

Deploy Amazon WorkSpaces virtual desktops for production access. Configure WorkSpaces with session recording enabled and install the AWS CLI with pre-configured production credentials. Restrict WorkSpaces access to the company's corporate IP range using WorkSpaces access control rules.

Deploy AWS Cloud9 IDE environments in the production VPC for developer access. Configure Cloud9 with IAM roles that have read-only production permissions and enable CloudTrail to log all API calls made from the Cloud9 environment for audit compliance review.

explanation: B is correct because Session Manager opens shells over the SSM Agent's outbound channel - no inbound ports, no bastion, no SSH keys - and with logging enabled it streams the full keystroke and output transcript of every session to S3 and CloudWatch Logs, optionally KMS-encrypted, alongside StartSession and TerminateSession records in CloudTrail. Pairing that with IAM Identity Center permission sets whose session duration is capped at one hour and gated by MFA delivers the time-limited, fully recorded access required, and every API call made with those credentials is separately captured in CloudTrail. A is incorrect because a bastion is still an EC2 host to manage, and SSM port forwarding tunnels raw SSH whose contents Session Manager cannot record, so the recording would be bespoke and user-bypassable. C is incorrect because WorkSpaces has no native recording of CLI activity, and embedding pre-configured production credentials in a desktop creates long-lived credentials, the opposite of time-limited access. D is incorrect because Cloud9 terminal commands are not recorded anywhere - CloudTrail captures API calls but not shell activity - and read-only permissions block the debugging the scenario requires.

stem: A company wants to implement automated security scanning in their CI/CD pipeline for infrastructure-as-code templates. The scanning must check CloudFormation and Terraform templates for misconfigurations like open security groups, unencrypted resources, and overly permissive IAM policies before deployment. Which tool provides this multi-format IaC security scanning?

options.text: Integrate Checkov (by Bridgecrew) into the CodeBuild buildspec.yml as a pre-deployment validation step. Checkov scans both CloudFormation and Terraform templates against hundreds of built-in policies for security misconfigurations and outputs results in JUnit format for CodeBuild reports.

Use AWS CloudFormation Guard (cfn-guard) to validate CloudFormation templates and integrate tfsec for Terraform template scanning. Run both tools in a CodeBuild stage with custom rule sets matching the company's security standards and fail the build on policy violations.

Configure Amazon CodeGuru Security to scan IaC templates in the CodeCommit repository. CodeGuru Security analyzes infrastructure code for security vulnerabilities and misconfigurations, posting findings as pull request comments and blocking merges for critical security issues.

Deploy AWS Config rules in a sandbox account that evaluate resources created from the templates. Deploy the templates to the sandbox, run Config evaluations, and fail the pipeline if any Config rules report non-compliance with security standards for the deployed resources.

explanation: Checkov provides unified scanning for both CloudFormation and Terraform templates with hundreds of built-in security policies. JUnit output integrates with CodeBuild's test reporting for visibility. Option B uses two separate tools (cfn-guard and tfsec) which works but requires maintaining two tool configurations. Option C's CodeGuru Security focuses on application code, not IaC template scanning. Option D deploys then evaluates which is slower and more expensive than pre-deployment scanning.

stem: A company uses AWS CDK and wants to implement a custom construct that creates a standardized VPC with public subnets, private subnets, NAT Gateways, and VPC Flow Logs. The construct must be reusable across multiple stacks and enforce that certain properties like CIDR ranges don't overlap with existing VPCs. Which CDK pattern implements this reusable, validated construct?

options.text: Create a CDK L3 construct class that extends Construct and composes L2 constructs for VPC, Subnets, NAT Gateways, and Flow Logs. Add validation logic in the constructor that checks CIDR ranges against a DynamoDB table of existing VPC CIDRs and throws an error on overlap.

Create a CDK Stack subclass that encapsulates the VPC resources. Other stacks reference the VPC stack's outputs using cross-stack references. Add a CDK Aspect that validates CIDR ranges during synthesis by checking the CDK context for a list of existing VPC CIDRs.

Create a CDK Pipeline construct that provisions the VPC through a CodePipeline. The pipeline includes a CodeBuild stage that validates CIDR ranges against existing VPCs by querying the EC2 DescribeVpcs API, then deploys the CloudFormation stack if validation passes.

Create a CloudFormation module containing the VPC resources and register it in the CloudFormation registry. Reference the module in CDK using the CfnResource construct type and pass CIDR ranges as module parameters with AllowedPattern constraints for format validation.

explanation: A is correct because an L3 pattern construct - a class extending Construct that composes the L2 Vpc, NAT gateway, and FlowLog constructs - is CDK's unit of reuse: it is instantiated inside any stack, exposes a typed props interface, and its constructor runs arbitrary code, so the CIDR-overlap check against the DynamoDB registry executes at synth time and can throw before a template is emitted. B is incorrect because subclassing Stack forces every consumer to take on an extra stack plus cross-stack exports that create hard-to-remove dependencies, and Aspects are attached by the consumer and visit the tree late, making them the wrong place for constructor-time input validation. C is incorrect because putting validation in a CDK Pipelines CodeBuild step surfaces the failure late in a pipeline run instead of at synth, and it turns the VPC into a pipeline artifact rather than a construct any stack can instantiate. D is incorrect because a CloudFormation registry module wrapped in CfnResource forfeits CDK typing, IDE completion, and programmatic checks - AllowedPattern can only validate the CIDR's string format, never whether it overlaps an existing VPC.

stem: A company's serverless application uses API Gateway with Lambda and processes 10,000 requests per second. The Lambda functions make synchronous calls to a legacy on-premises system that can only handle 100 requests per second. How should the architecture be designed to bridge the throughput gap?

options.text: Deploy Amazon MQ (ActiveMQ) as a message broker between Lambda and the on-premises system. Configure ActiveMQ with a queue that rate-limits delivery to 100 messages per second using the AMQ delivery policy and return immediate acknowledgments from Lambda.

Implement a token bucket rate limiter in the Lambda function using a DynamoDB table to track request tokens. Each Lambda invocation checks for available tokens and either processes the request or returns a retry response. Tokens are replenished at a rate of 100 per second.

Configure API Gateway with throttling set to 100 requests per second matching the on-premises capacity. Return HTTP 429 responses for excess requests and implement client-side retry logic with exponential backoff to eventually process all requests through the throttled pipeline.

Place an SQS queue between Lambda and the on-premises system. Lambda sends requests to SQS, and a separate consumer Lambda reads from the queue at a controlled rate of 100 messages per second using reserved concurrency of 100. Return async acknowledgments to API Gateway callers.

explanation: D is correct because the mismatch is a producer/consumer rate problem and SQS is the buffer that absorbs it. The API-facing Lambda enqueues and returns immediately, decoupling the 10,000 rps front end and API Gateway's 29-second integration limit from the backend, while a separate consumer Lambda with reserved concurrency of 100 bounds in-flight calls to the legacy system at roughly 100 concurrent requests. The queue holds the backlog durably for up to 14 days and drains at whatever rate the legacy system sustains. A is incorrect because Amazon MQ is a broker you must size and patch, and ActiveMQ has no simple per-queue delivery-rate policy of the kind described, so it adds operational burden for buffering SQS provides serverlessly. B is incorrect because a DynamoDB token bucket concentrates 10,000 rps of conditional writes on a single hot item - itself a throttling hotspot - and token-less requests are rejected rather than buffered. C is incorrect because throttling API Gateway to 100 rps rejects roughly 99 percent of requests with 429s, and client retries cannot converge when arrival rate is 100x capacity, so the work is effectively dropped.

stem: A company runs AWS Fargate tasks that generate application logs in a custom format. The operations team needs to parse these logs to extract request IDs, user IDs, and response times as structured fields for querying. Which log processing approach structures the custom log format?

options.text: Configure the Fargate task with a Fluent Bit sidecar container using the FireLens log driver. Define a Fluent Bit parser configuration with a regex pattern matching the custom log format and configure the output plugin to send structured JSON logs to CloudWatch Logs.

Configure the Fargate task to send logs to a Kinesis Data Firehose delivery stream. Add a Lambda transformation function that parses the custom log format using regex, converts it to structured JSON, and forwards the enriched logs to CloudWatch Logs for querying.

Send the custom logs to CloudWatch Logs using the awslogs driver. Create CloudWatch Logs Insights queries with the parse command and regex patterns to extract request IDs, user IDs, and response times from the raw log lines during query time without pre-processing.

Modify the application code to output logs in JSON format instead of the custom format. Include request_id, user_id, and response_time as top-level JSON fields. CloudWatch Logs automatically recognizes JSON-formatted logs and enables field-based filtering without additional parsing.

explanation: A is correct because FireLens routes container stdout and stderr to a Fluent Bit sidecar, which is where parsing must happen on Fargate since no host-level agent is possible. A parser defined with Format regex and named capture groups turns each custom-format line into a record with request_id, user_id, and response_time keys, and the cloudwatch_logs output writes it as JSON, so CloudWatch Logs discovers the fields and Logs Insights filters and aggregates on them without a parse expression - and the same structured stream can be fanned out to other destinations. B is incorrect because Firehose plus a Lambda transform produces the same JSON but adds two services, per-record transform cost, and buffering latency for work the sidecar does inline. C is incorrect because the awslogs driver ships raw lines and a Logs Insights parse expression re-runs the regex on every query, scanning more data, and named fields extracted at query time cannot be used by metric filters or subscription filters. D is incorrect because emitting JSON from the application requires changing and redeploying application code, which the scenario's fixed custom format rules out.

stem: A company's production RDS MySQL database is running low on storage, with only 10% free space remaining and growing by 2% per day. The team needs to address this before the database runs out of space in 5 days. Which immediate action and long-term solution should be implemented?

options.text: Immediately modify the RDS instance to increase allocated storage manually. While the storage modification is in progress, identify and purge unnecessary data, old logs, and temporary tables. For long-term, configure CloudWatch alarms on FreeStorageSpace to alert at 20% remaining.

Enable RDS storage autoscaling with a maximum storage threshold 3x the current allocation. Storage autoscaling automatically increases storage when free space drops below 10% of allocated storage, preventing out-of-space errors. For long-term, analyze and optimize table sizes and indexes.

Enable RDS Performance Insights to identify queries causing excessive storage growth. Analyze the Top SQL by temporary space usage and optimize the queries to reduce disk consumption. For long-term, archive old data to S3 using DMS and implement table partitioning.

Take a manual snapshot of the database and restore it to a new RDS instance with larger storage. Promote the restored instance and update DNS to point to the new instance. For long-term, implement automated log rotation and enable compression on large tables.

explanation: B is correct because RDS storage autoscaling is a no-downtime setting change: once MaxAllocatedStorage is set, RDS automatically grows allocated storage when free space falls below 10 percent of allocated storage for 5 minutes, adding the greater of 5 GiB or 10 percent of current allocation. With free space already at 10 percent and shrinking 2 percent per day it triggers essentially immediately and keeps protecting the instance as data grows, buying time for the longer-term archival and index work. A is incorrect because a manual storage increase is a one-time fix that a human must repeat at every recurrence, storage cannot be modified again for several hours after a change, and a CloudWatch alarm only notifies - it adds no capacity. C is incorrect because Performance Insights surfaces query load and temporary space usage, which is useful root-cause analysis, but analysis frees no storage and the instance still fills within 5 days. D is incorrect because snapshot-and-restore to a larger instance means a lengthy restore, a write-stopping cutover to avoid data loss, and a DNS switch - hours of risk for something a live modification handles online.

stem: A company needs to implement an automated compliance framework that evaluates their multi-account AWS environment against multiple standards including CIS, PCI DSS, and NIST 800-53 simultaneously. Non-compliant findings must be centrally managed with remediation tracking. Which service provides multi-standard compliance evaluation?

options.text: Deploy Amazon Inspector across all accounts with scanning for all three compliance benchmarks. Inspector evaluates EC2 instances, container images, and Lambda functions against CIS, PCI DSS, and NIST 800-53 controls, generating findings in Security Hub for centralized management.

Configure AWS Config with conformance packs for each compliance standard. Deploy CIS, PCI DSS, and NIST 800-53 conformance packs through Organizations and use the Config compliance dashboard to view per-rule compliance status across all accounts and standards.

Enable AWS Security Hub with all three security standards (CIS, PCI DSS, NIST 800-53) enabled across all accounts via Organizations. Security Hub evaluates resources against all standards simultaneously and provides a centralized findings dashboard with workflow status tracking for remediation.

Deploy AWS Audit Manager with assessment frameworks for CIS, PCI DSS, and NIST 800-53. Audit Manager collects evidence from Config, CloudTrail, and Security Hub to assess compliance, generating audit-ready reports with evidence attachments for each compliance standard.

explanation: C is correct: Security Hub is the purpose-built multi-standard posture service. Enabling it through Organizations with the CIS AWS Foundations Benchmark, PCI DSS, and NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 standards makes Security Hub run all enabled controls continuously against every account, aggregate findings in ASFF into a delegated administrator account, and track remediation through the finding workflow status (NEW, NOTIFIED, SUPPRESSED, RESOLVED) plus per-standard compliance scores. A is incorrect because Inspector performs vulnerability scanning (CVEs in EC2, ECR images, Lambda) and does not evaluate CIS/PCI/NIST account-level configuration controls. B is incorrect because conformance packs give per-rule compliance status but no finding-level workflow states or remediation tracking, and packs must be authored and maintained per standard. D is incorrect because Audit Manager gathers evidence to produce audit reports for auditors; it does not run continuous control evaluation with an operational remediation queue.

stem: A company has 30 development teams, each with their own CodePipeline. The DevOps team needs to monitor all pipelines centrally, detect stalled pipelines, and alert when any pipeline has been in a failed state for more than 30 minutes. Which monitoring approach provides this central pipeline oversight?

options.text: Configure CloudWatch cross-account observability to share CodePipeline metrics from all accounts. Create a CloudWatch composite alarm that evaluates the pipeline execution failure metric across all pipelines, triggering when any pipeline shows sustained failure for 30 minutes.

Deploy Amazon DevOps Guru across all development accounts to monitor CodePipeline resources. DevOps Guru uses ML to detect anomalous pipeline behavior including prolonged failure states and generates insights with recommended remediation actions for pipeline issues.

Create a Lambda function on a 5-minute schedule in the monitoring account. The function calls the ListPipelineExecutions API across all accounts using cross-account IAM roles and checks for pipelines with failed executions older than 30 minutes, sending SNS alerts for stalled pipelines.

Create EventBridge rules matching CodePipeline execution state change events across all accounts. Forward events to a central monitoring account's event bus. Deploy a Lambda function that tracks pipeline states in DynamoDB and alerts via SNS when any pipeline remains failed for 30 minutes.

explanation: D is correct: CodePipeline emits execution state-change events (STARTED, SUCCEEDED, FAILED, SUPERSEDED) to EventBridge in real time. Forwarding those events from all 30 accounts to a central event bus gives one stream of truth, and a Lambda function that records the last state and timestamp per pipeline in DynamoDB can evaluate duration and alert via SNS once a pipeline has stayed FAILED for 30 minutes. A is incorrect because CodePipeline publishes no 'time spent in failed state' metric, and composite alarms combine the states of other alarms rather than evaluating a metric across arbitrary pipelines. B is incorrect because DevOps Guru analyzes operational metrics for supported resources such as Lambda, RDS, and DynamoDB; CodePipeline execution state is not an ML anomaly signal it monitors, and it cannot express a 30-minute threshold. C is incorrect because polling ListPipelineExecutions for every pipeline in every account adds up to 5 minutes of detection lag, burns API quota, and still needs the same cross-account trust plus custom state tracking.

stem: A company needs to implement a solution that automatically detects when CloudFormation stacks drift from their template definitions and reverts the drift. The solution must work across 20 AWS accounts and handle both direct resource modifications and deletions. Which approach provides automated drift detection and correction?

options.text: Configure CloudTrail to monitor resource modification API calls. Create EventBridge rules that match API calls modifying CloudFormation-managed resources and trigger Lambda functions that immediately call UpdateStack to revert unauthorized changes to the template state.

Deploy AWS Config with the cloudformation-stack-drift-detection-check rule across all accounts. Configure auto-remediation with an SSM Automation document that triggers CloudFormation UpdateStack to reconcile drifted resources back to their template-defined configuration.

Schedule CloudFormation drift detection on all stacks using an EventBridge rule that triggers a Lambda function hourly. The Lambda runs DetectStackDrift for each stack and, when drift is detected, executes a stack update with the same template to force resources back into the defined state.

Deploy AWS Control Tower with guardrails that prevent modifications to CloudFormation-managed resources. Use SCPs to deny direct API access to resources that are managed by CloudFormation stacks, ensuring all changes must go through CloudFormation template updates.

explanation: B is correct: the AWS managed rule cloudformation-stack-drift-detection-check invokes CloudFormation drift detection for each in-scope stack and records COMPLIANT/NON_COMPLIANT results in Config. Deployed as an organization Config rule it covers all 20 accounts with one deployment, and Config's remediation action can invoke an SSM Automation document that reconciles the stack, with retries and central compliance history for both modified and deleted resources. A is incorrect because a CloudTrail/EventBridge rule sees only the raw API call and cannot tell whether the affected resource belongs to a CloudFormation stack, so it would fire on legitimate changes and needs custom lookup logic. C is incorrect because it re-implements what the managed Config rule already does, requires deploying and operating the schedule in every account, gives no central compliance record, and DetectStackDrift is asynchronous and rate-limited across many stacks. D is incorrect because SCPs and guardrails only block changes; they neither detect nor correct drift that already exists, and blanket denies break emergency operations.

stem: A company's application uses an Application Load Balancer with connection-based routing. During a deployment, the ALB continued sending new connections to instances being drained, causing errors. The deregistration delay was set to 300 seconds, but some long-lived connections exceeded this timeout. How should the team handle long-lived connections during deployments?

options.text: Switch from connection-based to request-based routing by disabling sticky sessions on the target group. Configure the ALB to use round-robin request distribution so each HTTP request can be routed to any healthy instance regardless of the original connection target.

Increase the ALB deregistration delay to 3600 seconds to accommodate the longest-lived connections. Configure the ALB idle timeout to 4000 seconds matching the maximum connection duration and enable connection draining on the target group with the extended timeout.

Implement graceful shutdown in the application that closes WebSocket and long-lived HTTP connections with a close frame when the instance receives a SIGTERM signal. Set the deregistration delay to 30 seconds after implementing graceful shutdown for faster deployments.

Configure the Auto Scaling group with a lifecycle hook on EC2_INSTANCE_TERMINATING. The lifecycle hook pauses termination while the application closes long-lived connections. After all connections are closed, the application calls CompleteLifecycleAction to allow termination.

explanation: D is correct: an EC2_INSTANCE_TERMINATING lifecycle hook puts the instance in Terminating:Wait, so Auto Scaling will not terminate it while the application drains WebSocket or other long-lived connections. The application (or an agent) extends the pause with RecordLifecycleActionHeartbeat and calls CompleteLifecycleAction the moment the last connection closes, so shutdown is bounded by real connection lifetime rather than a fixed timer. A is incorrect because an upgraded WebSocket or keep-alive connection is pinned to one target for its lifetime; disabling stickiness changes only how new connections are placed and does nothing for connections already open. B is incorrect because a 3600-second deregistration delay plus a 4000-second idle timeout makes every deployment wait for the worst case even when almost all connections are short, and it is still a hard cap that cuts off anything longer. C is incorrect because graceful shutdown alone gives no guarantee that clients disconnect within 30 seconds, and shortening the deregistration delay makes premature termination more likely, not less.

stem: A company runs a Kubernetes application on Amazon EKS and needs to collect pod-level CPU, memory, network, and disk I/O metrics. The metrics must be available in CloudWatch for dashboarding and alarming. Which approach collects Kubernetes pod-level metrics in CloudWatch?

options.text: Enable CloudWatch Container Insights for the EKS cluster by deploying the CloudWatch agent as a DaemonSet. Container Insights automatically collects pod-level CPU, memory, network, and disk metrics and publishes them to CloudWatch with Kubernetes metadata dimensions.

Deploy the Kubernetes Metrics Server on the EKS cluster to collect pod-level resource metrics. Configure a custom Lambda function that periodically queries the Metrics Server API and publishes the pod metrics to CloudWatch using the PutMetricData API.

Install Prometheus on the EKS cluster using the Prometheus Helm chart and configure it to scrape kubelet and cAdvisor metrics from each node. Set up a Prometheus CloudWatch exporter that forwards selected pod metrics to CloudWatch for dashboarding and alarming.

Configure the ADOT (AWS Distro for OpenTelemetry) collector as a DaemonSet on EKS. Configure the collector with the kubeletstats receiver for pod metrics and the CloudWatch EMF exporter to publish metrics as embedded metric format logs in CloudWatch for automatic metric extraction.

explanation: Container Insights with the CloudWatch agent DaemonSet provides automated pod-level metric collection with Kubernetes metadata dimensions (pod name, namespace, service). It's the native AWS solution for EKS metrics. Option B uses Metrics Server which is for HPA, not for CloudWatch metric publishing. Option C deploys Prometheus with a custom exporter adding infrastructure complexity. Option D uses ADOT which works but Container Insights provides a simpler, purpose-built solution for this use case.

stem: A company needs to create a post-incident review process that automatically collects relevant data when an incident occurs. The data should include CloudWatch metrics around the incident timeframe, relevant CloudTrail events, deployment history, and configuration changes. Which approach automates incident data collection?

options.text: Configure CloudWatch dashboards with annotation markers for incidents. When an incident occurs, manually add time-range annotations on the dashboard and use the CloudWatch API to export metric data for the incident period. Attach the exported data to a JIRA ticket for review.

Create a Step Functions workflow triggered by incident creation events. The workflow parallel-executes Lambda functions that query CloudWatch GetMetricData, CloudTrail LookupEvents, CodePipeline ListPipelineExecutions, and AWS Config GetResourceConfigHistory, storing results in a DynamoDB table.

Use AWS Systems Manager Incident Manager with response plans that include runbook automation. Configure the runbook to automatically collect CloudWatch metrics, query CloudTrail for relevant events, retrieve CodePipeline execution history, and compile the data into an incident timeline document in S3.

Enable Amazon Detective for the AWS accounts. Detective automatically collects and analyzes CloudTrail logs, VPC Flow Logs, and GuardDuty findings to build a behavior graph. During incidents, use Detective's investigation capabilities to visualize the timeline of relevant events.

explanation: C is correct: Incident Manager response plans can attach SSM Automation runbooks that execute automatically when an incident is created. One runbook can call GetMetricData/GetMetricWidgetImage for the incident window, LookupEvents against CloudTrail, ListPipelineExecutions for deployment history, and GetResourceConfigHistory from Config, then write the compiled timeline to S3 and attach it to the incident record that Incident Manager already maintains for the post-incident analysis. A is incorrect because dashboard annotation and metric export are manual steps and collect metrics only, missing CloudTrail, deployment, and configuration data. B is incorrect because it hand-builds the same collection with Step Functions and Lambda, and storing raw results in DynamoDB produces no incident record, timeline, or post-incident analysis artifact. D is incorrect because Detective ingests only CloudTrail, VPC Flow Logs, and GuardDuty findings for security investigation; it has no view of deployments or Config changes and requires an analyst to drive the investigation.

stem: A company deploys Lambda functions that access sensitive data in DynamoDB. The security team requires that Lambda functions can only access specific DynamoDB tables based on the function's purpose, and that no function should have broader permissions than needed. Which IAM strategy enforces fine-grained Lambda-to-DynamoDB access?

options.text: Create dedicated IAM execution roles for each Lambda function with resource-level permissions scoped to specific DynamoDB table ARNs. Each role grants only the required actions (GetItem, PutItem, Query) on only the tables that function needs, following least-privilege principle.

Configure DynamoDB resource-based policies on each table that allow access only from specific Lambda function execution role ARNs. Attach a shared execution role to all Lambda functions and rely on the table-level policies to enforce which functions can access which tables.

Create a single shared IAM execution role with DynamoDB full access (dynamodb:*) for all Lambda functions. Add condition keys in the role policy that restrict access based on the calling Lambda function's ARN using the aws:SourceArn condition key for table-level access control.

Create IAM permission boundaries for each Lambda function's execution role. The permission boundaries define the maximum allowed DynamoDB tables and actions, while the execution role's policies grant the subset of permissions within the boundary for the function's specific needs.

explanation: A is correct. A dedicated execution role per function, with every statement scoped to specific table ARNs and only the actions that function actually performs, is the direct expression of least privilege. What a function may do is visible in its own role, IAM Access Analyzer and last-accessed data can be reviewed per function, and no function inherits another function's access. B relies on a mechanism that is real - DynamoDB has supported resource-based policies on tables and indexes since March 2024 - but the design fails because every function shares one execution role: the table policy sees an identical principal ARN for all of them and cannot distinguish one function from another, and the shared identity policy must still grant the union of all needed permissions, so no individual function's role is narrowed and auditing which function can reach which table becomes materially harder. C does not work: aws:SourceArn is populated when an AWS service makes a request on your behalf, not on data-plane calls a function makes with its own execution role credentials, so the condition never matches for DynamoDB requests from function code, and granting dynamodb:* on the shared role is the opposite of least privilege. D inverts the purpose of the control: a permissions boundary only caps the maximum permissions a role can receive and grants nothing itself, so per-function roles with resource-scoped policies are still required underneath; boundaries are a useful guardrail for delegated role creation but are not the mechanism that enforces this access model.

stem: A development team uses AWS CodeBuild to build container images. Build times have increased to 25 minutes because each build downloads the same base dependencies. The team wants to reduce build times without changing their Dockerfile structure. Which CodeBuild optimization reduces dependency download time?

options.text: Enable CodeBuild S3 caching with the Docker layer cache path configured. S3 caching persists Docker layers across any build host in the fleet, so all builds benefit from cached layers regardless of which host executes the build operation.

Switch to CodeBuild batch builds that run multiple build phases in parallel containers. Configure the install phase to download dependencies in a parallel container while the build phase prepares the build environment, reducing total elapsed time.

Enable CodeBuild local caching with Docker layer cache mode. This caches Docker image layers between builds on the same build host, so subsequent builds reuse cached layers for unchanged dependency installation steps in the Dockerfile.

Configure CodeBuild to use a custom build image stored in Amazon ECR that already contains the base dependencies pre-installed. Create a scheduled pipeline that rebuilds the custom image weekly with the latest dependency versions for consistency.

explanation: C is correct: CodeBuild local caching with LOCAL_DOCKER_LAYER_CACHE keeps the Docker layer cache on the build host between builds, so when CodeBuild reuses a host the unchanged dependency-installation layers in the Dockerfile hit the cache instead of downloading again. It requires privileged mode but no Dockerfile changes. A is incorrect because the S3 cache copies declared file paths only; it does not support Docker layer caching, and the S3 upload/download round trip would add time rather than remove it. B is incorrect because batch builds run several independent build jobs (build graph, matrix, or fanout) in parallel; they do not split the install and build phases of a single build, and each job still downloads its own dependencies. D is incorrect because the CodeBuild image is the environment the build runs in, not the base image of the container being built, so pre-installed packages there do not shorten the docker build inside it, and a weekly rebuild adds maintenance and version drift.

stem: A company manages infrastructure across 50 AWS accounts using AWS CloudFormation StackSets. A recent deployment failed in 5 accounts due to insufficient IAM permissions. The team needs to ensure StackSet operations succeed across all accounts before proceeding. Which StackSet configuration prevents partial deployments?

options.text: Configure the StackSet operation preferences with a failure tolerance of 0 and a maximum concurrent accounts setting of 1. This stops the entire StackSet operation immediately if any single account fails, preventing partial deployments across the remaining target accounts.

Enable automatic execution in the StackSet and configure it with self-managed permissions. Create the required AWSCloudFormationStackSetExecutionRole in each account with identical permissions to ensure consistent deployment capabilities across all target accounts.

Set the StackSet operation to use the SEQUENTIAL region ordering with a failure tolerance of 10%. Deploy to a test account first using account-level targeting, then proceed with the full StackSet deployment after validating the test account deployment succeeds.

Configure the StackSet to use service-managed permissions with AWS Organizations. Enable automatic deployment for the target organizational units so that new accounts automatically receive the stack and existing accounts maintain consistent configurations.

explanation: A is correct. A failure tolerance of 0 tells CloudFormation to stop the StackSet operation the moment a single account fails, so the operation cannot quietly succeed in 45 accounts and fail in 5. CloudFormation also enforces that MaxConcurrentCount must be no greater than FailureToleranceCount + 1, so with a tolerance of 0 the maximum concurrent account count must be 1 - the operation proceeds one account at a time, which is precisely the behavior needed to halt on the first failure. B addresses the specific root cause of this outage by ensuring an identically permissioned AWSCloudFormationStackSetExecutionRole exists in every target account, but it leaves the operation preferences untouched, so any other class of failure still leaves the fleet in a partially deployed state. C explicitly permits a partial rollout: a 10 percent failure tolerance across 50 accounts allows five accounts to fail before the operation stops - exactly the situation the team just experienced - and SEQUENTIAL ordering controls the order in which Regions are processed, not per-account failure behavior. D configures service-managed permissions and automatic deployment to accounts that later join the target OUs, which helps with account onboarding but sets no failure tolerance and does nothing to stop a partially applied operation.

stem: A company runs a stateful application on EC2 instances behind a Network Load Balancer. The application maintains in-memory session data that takes 60 seconds to synchronize to a shared Redis cluster during shutdown. How should the team ensure graceful instance termination during Auto Scaling scale-in events?

options.text: Set the NLB target group deregistration delay to 120 seconds to allow time for session synchronization during scale-in. The NLB stops sending new connections while existing connections drain, giving the application time to sync session data to Redis.

Enable EC2 instance stop protection on all instances in the Auto Scaling group. When a scale-in event triggers, the stop protection creates a 120-second delay during which the application receives a warning notification and synchronizes session data to the Redis cluster.

Configure the Auto Scaling group termination policy to use OldestInstance and set the default cooldown period to 120 seconds. The cooldown period delays termination long enough for the application to detect the scale-in event and synchronize sessions to Redis.

Configure an Auto Scaling lifecycle hook on the EC2_INSTANCE_TERMINATING event with a heartbeat timeout of 120 seconds. The application listens for the lifecycle notification via SQS, triggers session synchronization to Redis, then calls CompleteLifecycleAction when finished.

explanation: D is correct: an EC2_INSTANCE_TERMINATING lifecycle hook holds the instance in Terminating:Wait for the heartbeat timeout and publishes a notification to SNS/SQS/EventBridge. The application consumes that notification, flushes the in-memory session state to Redis, and calls CompleteLifecycleAction, so termination happens only after the 60-second synchronization has actually finished. A is incorrect because the deregistration delay governs only how long the load balancer keeps draining existing connections; it never tells the application that termination is imminent, so no synchronization is triggered. B is incorrect because there is no 'stop protection' behavior of that kind: EC2 stop protection blocks StopInstances calls, does not apply to Auto Scaling termination, and emits no warning notification or delay. C is incorrect because the cooldown period throttles how soon the group starts the next scaling activity; it does not postpone termination of the instance already selected for scale-in, and OldestInstance only chooses which instance dies.

stem: A company's microservices application produces logs in different formats: JSON from Node.js services, structured text from Java services, and unstructured output from legacy Python services. All logs need to be parsed into a consistent schema in CloudWatch Logs for unified querying. Which approach normalizes heterogeneous log formats?

options.text: Create CloudWatch Logs Insights queries that use the parse command to extract fields from each log format at query time. Define saved queries for JSON, structured text, and unstructured formats so operators can analyze logs using the appropriate query for each service.

Deploy a Kinesis Data Firehose delivery stream with Lambda transformation. Services send logs to Firehose, the Lambda function detects log format and normalizes each record into a consistent JSON schema, then Firehose delivers normalized logs to CloudWatch Logs.

Configure CloudWatch Logs metric filters with multiple pattern syntaxes for each log group. Create separate metric filters for JSON, structured text, and unstructured formats that extract fields into CloudWatch metrics using the appropriate pattern matching syntax.

Deploy FluentBit as a sidecar container for each microservice. Configure FluentBit with format-specific parsers (JSON parser, regex parser, multiline parser) and use the modify filter to transform all parsed records into a unified JSON schema before sending to CloudWatch Logs.

explanation: D is correct: Fluent Bit sidecars parse at ingestion, where format knowledge lives. A JSON parser handles the Node.js output, a regex parser handles the Java structured text, and a multiline/regex parser handles the legacy Python output; the modify/rename filters then map every record onto one field schema before the cloudwatch_logs output writes it, so CloudWatch Logs stores uniformly structured JSON that a single Logs Insights query can read. A is incorrect because query-time parse leaves the stored data heterogeneous, requires operators to know each service's format, and prevents a single unified query. B is incorrect because Kinesis Data Firehose cannot deliver to CloudWatch Logs (its destinations are S3, Redshift, OpenSearch, Iceberg, Splunk, and HTTP endpoints), so the described pipeline cannot be built. C is incorrect because metric filters emit numeric CloudWatch metrics from matching lines; they never rewrite or normalize the log events themselves.

stem: A company wants a trunk-based development workflow in which every commit to the main branch flows through one delivery pipeline and is released to production after passing all quality gates, with no manual approval step anywhere in the path to production. The pipeline must run automated tests and security scanning, and it must be able to detect a bad release in production and reverse it without human intervention. Which TWO components are essential for this trunk-based CI/CD pipeline? (Choose two.)

options.text: Implement CodeDeploy with a canary deployment configuration (10% traffic for 15 minutes) for the production stage. CloudWatch alarms on error rate and latency automatically trigger rollback if the canary phase detects degraded performance in the deployment.

Create feature branch pipelines that build and test each feature branch independently before merging to main. After merge, a separate release pipeline deploys the main branch to production without additional testing since feature branches were already tested.

Configure CodeBuild to run DAST scanning by deploying to a staging environment and running OWASP ZAP against the staging endpoints. The build stage fails if any critical or high-severity vulnerabilities are detected, blocking the deployment from proceeding.

Configure CodePipeline with a source stage connected to the main branch, followed by CodeBuild stages for unit tests, integration tests, and SAST scanning. Configure the stages so that any failing test or any high-severity SAST finding fails the stage and halts the pipeline before the production deployment stage runs.

Set up Git branch protection rules requiring at least two code review approvals and a passing CI build before any commit can be merged to the main branch. This pre-merge quality gate ensures only reviewed and tested code enters the trunk.

explanation: A and D are the two essential pipeline components. D supplies the automated quality gates inside the trunk pipeline itself: every commit to main enters one pipeline, and unit tests, integration tests, and SAST run as blocking stages, so a commit that fails any check never reaches the deployment stage - and because the gates are automated, no manual approval sits in the path to production. A supplies the safe release and the automatic reversal the stem demands: a CodeDeploy canary that shifts 10 percent of traffic for 15 minutes with CloudWatch alarms on error rate and latency rolls the deployment back on its own when the canary degrades, which is what makes deploying every commit without a human watching acceptable. B contradicts both trunk-based development and safety: it depends on long-lived feature branches and then deploys the merged trunk with no retesting, so a defect introduced by the merge itself is never caught. C is a supplementary gate, not an essential one - DAST with OWASP ZAP requires standing up and deploying to a staging environment on every commit, adding many minutes to a pipeline meant to run on every push, and the blocking security check is already provided by the SAST stage in D. E is a repository policy rather than a pipeline component, and requiring two human reviews before every merge reintroduces exactly the manual gate and queueing that this continuous-delivery model is designed to eliminate.

stem: A company needs to automate the remediation of publicly accessible S3 buckets detected by AWS Config. When a bucket's Block Public Access settings are disabled, the system must automatically re-enable them within 5 minutes. Which approach provides the fastest automated remediation?

options.text: Enable AWS Security Hub with the S3 security standards checks. Configure Security Hub automated response with a custom action that triggers a Lambda function to re-enable Block Public Access when Security Hub generates a finding for a publicly accessible S3 bucket.

Deploy a Lambda function on a 5-minute CloudWatch Events schedule that lists all S3 buckets and checks their Block Public Access configuration. The function calls PutPublicAccessBlock to re-enable settings on any bucket where Block Public Access is partially or fully disabled.

Create an EventBridge rule that matches S3 PutBucketPublicAccessBlock API calls in CloudTrail where the configuration disables any Block Public Access setting. The rule triggers a Lambda function that immediately calls PutPublicAccessBlock to re-enable all four settings.

Configure the AWS Config rule s3-account-level-public-access-blocks-periodic to evaluate S3 bucket public access. Set up auto-remediation with the AWS-EnableS3BucketPublicAccessBlock SSM Automation document to re-enable Block Public Access settings on non-compliant buckets.

explanation: C is correct: CloudTrail delivers management events to EventBridge within roughly a minute, so a rule matching PutBucketPublicAccessBlock (and DeletePublicAccessBlock) fires as soon as the setting is weakened. The Lambda target calls PutPublicAccessBlock to restore all four flags, which is event-driven and comfortably inside the 5-minute requirement without scanning anything. A is incorrect because a Security Hub custom action is an operator-initiated button in the console, not an automatic trigger, and Security Hub control findings can lag hours behind the change. B is incorrect because listing every bucket and calling GetPublicAccessBlock on each one every 5 minutes means detection lag of up to a full cycle plus scan time, and it throttles as the bucket count grows. D is incorrect because s3-account-level-public-access-blocks-periodic is a periodic rule evaluating the account-level Block Public Access settings, not per-bucket settings, and periodic evaluation (1 hour at best, 24 hours by default) cannot meet a 5-minute target.

stem: A company needs to rotate database credentials stored in AWS Secrets Manager every 30 days for an Amazon RDS PostgreSQL database. The application uses connection pooling and must not experience downtime during rotation. Which rotation strategy ensures zero-downtime credential rotation?

options.text: Configure Secrets Manager automatic rotation with a 30-day schedule using the alternating users rotation strategy. This strategy creates two database users and alternates between them during rotation, so the previous credentials remain valid while the new ones are activated.

Create a Lambda function triggered by an EventBridge scheduled rule every 30 days. The function generates a new password, updates the RDS master user password, then updates the Secrets Manager secret value. The application detects the change via secret version staging labels.

Configure Secrets Manager automatic rotation with a 30-day schedule and enable multi-Region secret replication. The rotation Lambda updates credentials in the primary region first, then replication propagates changes to other regions, ensuring consistent credentials globally.

Configure Secrets Manager automatic rotation with a 30-day schedule using the single user rotation strategy. Enable the rotation Lambda function to update the password and wait for all existing database connections to close naturally before the old password becomes invalid.

explanation: A is correct: the alternating users strategy clones the original user (user and user_clone) and, on each rotation, changes the password of whichever user is currently inactive, then flips AWSCURRENT to that user. The other user's credentials remain valid and stay available under AWSPREVIOUS, so pooled connections and any client that cached the old secret keep authenticating successfully until they refresh - true zero downtime. B is incorrect because a hand-written rotator that resets the RDS master password invalidates the old password immediately for every new connection, gives no AWSPENDING/AWSCURRENT staging semantics, and applications do not automatically 'detect' staging label changes. C is incorrect because multi-Region replication copies a secret to other Regions; it addresses geography, not the overlap window that prevents authentication failures during rotation. D is incorrect because single-user rotation changes the one password in place and Secrets Manager cannot wait for existing connections to close, so any client reconnecting with the cached old password fails.

stem: A team uses AWS CDK to define infrastructure and wants to prevent deployments that would delete or replace stateful resources like RDS databases and DynamoDB tables. The protection must be enforced in the CI/CD pipeline before any changes are applied. Which CDK feature prevents accidental stateful resource deletion?

options.text: Enable CDK stack termination protection by setting terminationProtection: true in the Stack props. This prevents the entire stack from being deleted accidentally but allows individual resource updates and replacements to proceed through normal deployments.

Run cdk diff in the pipeline and parse the output for resource replacements or deletions of stateful resource types. Fail the pipeline if the diff shows any RDS or DynamoDB resources being destroyed or replaced, blocking the deployment from proceeding.

Configure OPA (Open Policy Agent) policies in the pipeline that evaluate the CDK-synthesized CloudFormation template. The OPA policies check for Delete or Replace change types on RDS and DynamoDB resources and deny the deployment if detected.

Add the CfnResource.addDeletionPolicy(DeletionPolicy.RETAIN) to all stateful resources in the CDK code. This sets the CloudFormation DeletionPolicy to Retain, ensuring resources are preserved even if removed from the CDK stack, preventing accidental data loss.

explanation: B is correct: cdk diff compares the synthesized template against the deployed stack using a CloudFormation change set, so its output explicitly flags resources that will be destroyed or replaced and marks destructive changes. Parsing that output in the pipeline and failing the build when an RDS or DynamoDB resource shows replace/destroy blocks the deployment before CloudFormation executes anything. A is incorrect because terminationProtection only refuses DeleteStack; a stack update that replaces the database inside the stack proceeds normally. C is incorrect because the synthesized template is a static description of desired state - it contains no Delete/Replace change types, since replacement is only determined by comparing against the deployed stack, so OPA over the template cannot see it. D is incorrect because DeletionPolicy: RETAIN merely orphans the resource instead of deleting it (and UpdateReplacePolicy is a separate setting); the deployment still succeeds and the stack still stops managing the database.

stem: A company uses Terraform to manage infrastructure across development, staging, and production environments. Each environment has identical resource definitions but different configurations (instance sizes, replica counts). The team wants to eliminate code duplication across environments. Which Terraform approach reduces environment code duplication?

options.text: Implement Terragrunt with a directory hierarchy where each environment folder contains a terragrunt.hcl that references the shared Terraform module and provides environment-specific input variables. Terragrunt's generate blocks create provider and backend configurations per environment.

Use Terraform workspaces to manage environments within a single configuration directory. Define environment-specific values using conditional expressions based on terraform.workspace, such as instance_type = terraform.workspace == 'prod' ? 'm5.xlarge' : 't3.medium'.

Create a Terraform module containing all shared resource definitions. Each environment directory contains a main.tf that calls the module with environment-specific variable values from a terraform.tfvars file. Module versioning ensures environments can be updated independently.

Create separate Terraform configurations for each environment using symbolic links to share common .tf files. Each environment directory contains symlinks to shared resource files plus environment-specific variable definition files that override default values for that environment.

explanation: C is correct: a shared module holds the resource definitions once, and each environment directory is a thin root module that calls it with a tfvars file supplying instance sizes and replica counts. Each environment keeps its own state and backend, pinned module versions let dev take a change before prod does, and this is native Terraform with no extra tooling. A is incorrect because Terragrunt is a third-party wrapper that adds another binary, DSL, and upgrade path for a problem native modules plus tfvars already solve; it is a reasonable scaling choice but not the minimal one here. B is incorrect because workspaces share one configuration, one backend key prefix, and usually one set of provider credentials; encoding differences as terraform.workspace conditionals spreads environment logic through the code and becomes unreadable as differences multiply. D is incorrect because symlinks are not a Terraform feature - they break on some platforms, confuse module resolution and provider lock files, and offer no versioning of the shared code.

stem: A company's application uses Amazon Aurora MySQL with a primary instance in us-east-1 and read replicas. The RPO requirement is 1 second and the RTO requirement is 1 minute for the database tier. The current single-Region setup meets RPO but a regional failure would exceed the RTO. Which Aurora configuration meets both RPO and RTO requirements?

options.text: Configure Aurora cross-Region read replicas in us-west-2 using MySQL binary log replication. During a regional failure, promote the cross-Region read replica to a standalone Aurora cluster and update the application's database endpoint to the new cluster.

Enable Aurora Backtrack on the primary cluster and configure automated snapshots with cross-Region copy to us-west-2. During a regional failure, restore the latest snapshot in us-west-2 to create a new Aurora cluster and point the application to the restored endpoint.

Set up AWS Database Migration Service with continuous replication from the Aurora primary to a standby Aurora cluster in us-west-2. DMS captures changes via CDC and applies them to the standby cluster with near-zero lag for disaster recovery failover.

Create an Aurora Global Database with a secondary cluster in us-west-2. Aurora Global Database replicates data with less than 1 second lag using dedicated storage-level replication. During a regional failure, promote the secondary cluster to primary within approximately 1 minute.

explanation: D is correct: Aurora Global Database replicates at the storage layer using dedicated infrastructure, giving typical cross-Region lag under one second, which satisfies the 1-second RPO. Managed planned failover or unplanned cross-Region failover promotes the us-west-2 secondary to a full read/write primary in roughly a minute, meeting the RTO, and the secondary already exists so nothing has to be provisioned during the event. A is incorrect because Aurora MySQL cross-Region read replicas use binlog replication, whose lag grows with write volume and typically exceeds a second, and manual promotion plus endpoint changes takes well over a minute. B is incorrect because Backtrack is an in-Region rewind feature that provides no cross-Region capability, and restoring a copied snapshot creates a new cluster in 15-30+ minutes with an RPO equal to the snapshot interval. C is incorrect because DMS CDC adds a replication instance to size, monitor, and fail over, its lag is not guaranteed sub-second, and it provides no managed promotion.

stem: A company needs to detect when API Gateway latency exceeds the 99th percentile baseline by more than 2 standard deviations, without manually setting static thresholds. The detection must automatically adapt to changing traffic patterns throughout the day. Which CloudWatch feature provides adaptive latency anomaly detection?

options.text: Deploy a Lambda function on a 5-minute schedule that queries the API Gateway Latency metric using GetMetricStatistics with the p99 statistic. The function calculates a rolling 7-day average and standard deviation, then publishes a custom alarm when latency exceeds 2 standard deviations.

Enable API Gateway detailed metrics and create CloudWatch Logs Insights queries that analyze latency distributions. Schedule the query to run every 5 minutes via EventBridge and trigger an SNS notification when the p99 latency exceeds the calculated dynamic threshold.

Configure a CloudWatch composite alarm that combines multiple static threshold alarms for different time periods. Set daytime thresholds at 500ms and nighttime thresholds at 200ms to account for different traffic patterns during peak and off-peak hours.

Create a CloudWatch anomaly detection model on the API Gateway Latency metric. CloudWatch automatically learns the metric's expected pattern including daily and weekly seasonality, and generates dynamic upper and lower bounds that adapt to normal traffic pattern variations.

explanation: D is correct: CloudWatch anomaly detection trains a model on up to two weeks of the API Gateway Latency metric, learning hourly, daily, and weekly seasonality, and emits an expected band. An alarm on ANOMALY_DETECTION_BAND with a band width of 2 fires exactly when the observed value deviates by more than two standard deviations from the learned norm, and the band moves with traffic so no static threshold is ever set. A is incorrect because it rebuilds anomaly detection by hand: a flat rolling mean and standard deviation ignores time-of-day seasonality, so it alarms every peak and misses off-peak regressions. B is incorrect because Logs Insights queries log events, not metrics; API Gateway latency is a CloudWatch metric, and the 'dynamic threshold' would still have to be computed by custom code. C is incorrect because two hard-coded day/night thresholds are still static - they do not adapt to gradual traffic growth, seasonal peaks, or shifting business hours.

stem: A company has a monorepo hosted in GitHub and connected to AWS through an AWS CodeConnections connection. The repository contains 15 microservices, each in its own directory with its own buildspec.yml, and most commits touch only one service. The team wants only the services whose source code changed in the latest commit to be built and deployed, using native CodePipeline capabilities with the least custom scripting to maintain. Which approach implements selective service building for the monorepo?

options.text: Configure a CodeBuild project with a buildspec that runs git diff to identify changed directories. Use a shell script to iterate through changed service directories and execute each service's buildspec.yml conditionally, skipping services without changes.

Create 15 separate CodePipeline pipelines, one per service. Configure each V2-type pipeline's CodeConnections source action with a git push trigger that includes a file path filter for that service's directory, so the pipeline starts only when files under that path change.

Deploy a Lambda function triggered by repository push events delivered through EventBridge. The function analyzes the commit diff to identify changed service directories and starts only the relevant CodeBuild projects for changed services, skipping unchanged services entirely.

Configure a single CodePipeline with 15 parallel CodeBuild actions in the build stage. Each CodeBuild project checks for changes in its service directory using git diff and exits early with a success status if no relevant files were modified in the latest commit.

explanation: B is correct. With a V2-type pipeline, a CodeConnections source action supports git push triggers with file path include and exclude filters, so a pipeline is started only when a commit actually touches the directory that pipeline owns. This is a native CodePipeline capability requiring no scripting, and each service gets its own execution history, stage model, and rollback surface. A pushes selection logic into a shell script the team must write and maintain, and it is fragile in CodeBuild: the source is cloned at a fixed depth by default, so a git diff against the previous commit is unreliable unless the clone depth and git-credential-helper are configured, and the pipeline still executes on every commit regardless. C reimplements path filtering in a Lambda function outside CodePipeline, so the builds it launches are invisible to the pipeline's stage model - no stage gating, no artifact handoff, no approval or deployment actions - and it is the largest volume of custom code among the options. D honors selectivity only nominally: all 15 CodeBuild actions are still provisioned and executed on every commit, each paying container startup and source download before exiting, so build minutes and pipeline duration scale with the number of services rather than with the size of the change.

stem: A company needs to implement automated incident escalation. If a critical CloudWatch alarm is not acknowledged within 15 minutes, the notification must escalate from the on-call engineer to the engineering manager, then to the VP of Engineering after 30 minutes. Which service provides tiered escalation?

options.text: Configure PagerDuty integration with CloudWatch alarms via SNS. Create a PagerDuty escalation policy with three levels: on-call engineer (immediate), engineering manager (15 minutes), and VP of Engineering (30 minutes). PagerDuty manages acknowledgment tracking and escalation timing.

Create an SNS topic with three subscriptions: the on-call engineer, engineering manager, and VP of Engineering. Configure CloudWatch alarm actions to publish to the SNS topic immediately, then use SNS message filtering to delay delivery to higher-level contacts based on elapsed time.

Configure AWS Systems Manager Incident Manager with an escalation plan that defines three escalation stages. Stage 1 contacts the on-call engineer immediately, Stage 2 contacts the engineering manager after 15 minutes, and Stage 3 contacts the VP after 30 minutes of no acknowledgment.

Deploy a Step Functions workflow triggered by the CloudWatch alarm. The workflow sends an initial notification to the on-call engineer, waits 15 minutes using a Wait state, checks for acknowledgment in DynamoDB, and sends escalation notifications if the incident remains unacknowledged.

explanation: C is correct: Incident Manager escalation plans are built exactly for tiered paging.
