Configure the FIFO queue with a receive request attempt ID that consumers set on each ReceiveMessage call. After restart, consumers use the same attempt ID to receive the same batch of messages they were processing before the restart, ensuring no messages are skipped.

Configure the FIFO queue with message group IDs based on transaction account numbers. Each account's transactions are processed in order within their message group. After consumer restart, consumers resume processing each message group from where they left off based on FIFO ordering guarantees.

Enable FIFO queue dead-letter queue with a max receive count of 1 to prevent reprocessing. Configure content-based deduplication to automatically detect and eliminate duplicate transaction messages that may be redelivered after consumer restart during the deployment window.

explanation: C is correct because SQS FIFO guarantees ordering only within a MessageGroupId. Using the transaction's account number as the group ID keeps each account's transactions strictly ordered while allowing parallelism across accounts. While consumers are down, messages simply accumulate; after restart, any message whose visibility timeout expired becomes visible again at the head of its group, and SQS will not deliver later messages in that group until the in-flight one is deleted - so ordering survives the restart automatically. A is incorrect because deduplication scope of messageGroup with high-throughput FIFO changes the deduplication and throughput model but does not establish the grouping key that provides the ordering guarantee, and it says nothing about restart behavior. B is incorrect because ReceiveRequestAttemptId only deduplicates a retried ReceiveMessage network call within a 5-minute window; it is not a durable cursor and has no bearing on message ordering. D is incorrect because a maxReceiveCount of 1 diverts a message to the DLQ after a single expired receive - during a consumer restart, in-flight financial transactions would be pulled out of the ordered stream - and content-based deduplication can silently discard legitimately identical transactions.

stem: A payments platform runs its API tier on Amazon ECS, an Aurora PostgreSQL cluster, and an SQS queue that buffers settlement jobs. During load spikes the API 5XX error rate alone routinely crosses 5% for a minute or two, Aurora CPU alone crosses 80% during nightly reindexing, and queue depth alone crosses 1,000 messages whenever a downstream partner is slow. Paging on any single one of these signals has produced weeks of noisy alerts, so the on-call team now wants an incident declared and an SNS page sent only while all three conditions are true at the same time. The team also wants each of the three signals to remain independently visible on dashboards for troubleshooting, and wants to avoid writing and maintaining custom evaluation code. Which CloudWatch configuration declares the incident only when all three conditions hold simultaneously?

options.text: Create a CloudWatch metric math expression that combines the API error rate, database CPU, and queue depth metrics into a single derived metric. Set an alarm on the derived metric that triggers when the calculated value exceeds a threshold representing all three conditions being met.

Create individual CloudWatch alarms for API error rate, database CPU, and queue depth. Then create a CloudWatch composite alarm that combines all three alarms using AND logic. The composite alarm only enters ALARM state when all three child alarms are simultaneously in ALARM state.

Configure CloudWatch Synthetics canary that checks all three metrics every minute. The canary script queries the CloudWatch GetMetricData API for all three metrics and reports a failure only when all three conditions exceed their thresholds simultaneously in the same evaluation period.

Create an EventBridge rule with multiple event patterns matching each of the three CloudWatch alarm state changes. Configure the rule with an input transformer that checks if all three alarms transitioned to ALARM state within a 5-minute window, triggering the incident declaration.

explanation: Option B is correct. A CloudWatch composite alarm evaluates a rule expression over the states of child alarms using AND, OR and NOT, so ALARM(api) AND ALARM(db) AND ALARM(queue) enters ALARM only while all three child alarms are simultaneously in ALARM. The three child alarms still exist independently for dashboards, and the SNS action is attached to the composite alarm only, which removes the per-signal noise with no custom code. Option A fails because the three series have incompatible units and scales (a percentage, a CPU percentage and a message count); metric math has no Boolean AND, so any single expression such as a sum or product can be pushed over a fixed threshold by one metric alone - it cannot express simultaneity. Option C misuses Synthetics, which is designed to run canary scripts against endpoints for availability and latency; polling GetMetricData from a canary is custom evaluation code the team wants to avoid, and it duplicates alarm evaluation with worse reliability and no alarm history. Option D fails because EventBridge rules match individual events statelessly - an input transformer only reshapes the JSON of the one event being delivered and cannot correlate three separate alarm state-change events or track which alarms are still in ALARM.

stem: A company needs to implement database schema migrations as part of their CI/CD pipeline for an Aurora PostgreSQL database. Schema changes must be versioned, reversible, and applied automatically during deployment. The team needs to ensure migrations run only once and in the correct order. Which approach integrates database migrations into the deployment pipeline?

options.text: Configure Aurora's stored procedures to manage schema versioning. Deploy migration stored procedures through CloudFormation and invoke them via a post-deployment EventBridge rule. The stored procedures check a versions table and apply pending changes within database transactions.

Use CloudFormation custom resources to execute database migration scripts during stack updates. The custom resource Lambda connects to Aurora, runs migration SQL files stored in S3, and reports success or failure to CloudFormation. Stack rollback reverts migrations on failure.

Add a CodeBuild stage in the pipeline that runs a database migration tool (Flyway or Liquibase) against the Aurora database. The tool tracks applied migrations in a metadata table, applies only pending migrations in version order, and supports rollback scripts for each migration.

Store SQL migration scripts in the application repository versioned with sequential numbering. Configure a Lambda function triggered by CodePipeline that connects to Aurora and executes pending SQL scripts using the Data API. Track applied migrations in a DynamoDB table.

explanation: C is correct because Flyway and Liquibase maintain a schema-history table inside the target database, so each migration is applied exactly once and in version order, with a lock that serializes concurrent runners; both support versioned changes plus undo/rollback changesets. Executing them from a CodeBuild stage puts migrations in the correct place in the deployment sequence with access to the pipeline artifact, VPC and IAM credentials. A is incorrect because stored procedures push migration logic into the database where it is hard to version, diff, code-review and test, and the hand-written versions table duplicates what a migration tool already does reliably. B is incorrect because CloudFormation custom resources tie DDL to stack lifecycle: CloudFormation rollback cannot undo already-committed SQL, and a failing custom resource can leave the stack in UPDATE_ROLLBACK_FAILED with the schema half migrated. D is incorrect because a Lambda plus DynamoDB tracker is a bespoke migration engine with a 15-minute timeout, no distributed locking and no rollback semantics, and the Data API is a poor fit for long-running DDL.

stem: A company needs to implement automated runbooks that guide operators through incident resolution steps. Each runbook step must be executable with AWS API calls, and the runbook must track which steps have been completed. If an operator loses connectivity, another operator must be able to resume the runbook from the last completed step. Which service provides managed incident runbooks with step tracking?

options.text: Create AWS Step Functions workflows that define runbook steps as individual states. Each state executes an AWS API call via SDK integrations. Step Functions tracks workflow state, and operators can view the visual workflow to identify the current step and resume execution after connectivity restoration.

Deploy a custom runbook application using Amazon DynamoDB to track step completion status. Create Lambda functions for each runbook step that execute AWS API calls. The application UI shows completed and pending steps, allowing any operator to continue from the last recorded completion point.

Use AWS Systems Manager Incident Manager with automation runbooks attached to response plans. Incident Manager runbooks define sequential steps with SSM Automation actions. Step completion is tracked in the incident timeline, and any operator can view progress and resume from the last completed step.

Configure AWS Systems Manager Automation documents with multi-step runbook definitions. Each step executes AWS API calls with approval gates for human review. SSM Automation tracks step execution status, and operators can monitor progress through the SSM console during incident resolution.

explanation: C is correct because an Incident Manager response plan attaches SSM Automation runbooks to the incident: the runbook's steps make AWS API calls, and the execution and per-step status are recorded on the incident record and timeline. Because that state lives with the incident rather than in one operator's session, any responder with access can open the incident, see the last completed step, and resume or continue - exactly the handoff requirement. A is incorrect because Step Functions tracks workflow state well but has no incident context, no engagement or on-call handoff, and no notion of an operator resuming a human-driven runbook. B is incorrect because a DynamoDB, Lambda and custom UI build reimplements Incident Manager and leaves the team owning the availability of their own incident tooling. D is incorrect because a standalone SSM Automation document does track step status and supports approval steps, but the execution is not tied to an incident - there is no shared incident record, timeline correlation, or engagement plan for handing work between responders.

stem: A company needs to detect and alert on unusual IAM activity patterns, such as API calls from new IP addresses, access key usage from unexpected geographic locations, or privilege escalation attempts. The detection must use machine learning to establish baselines and identify anomalies without manual rule creation. Which service provides ML-based IAM activity anomaly detection?

options.text: Enable Amazon GuardDuty with IAM threat detection. GuardDuty analyzes CloudTrail management events using machine learning to detect anomalous IAM activity including console logins from unusual locations, API calls from new IP ranges, and credential compromise indicators.

Enable IAM Access Analyzer to continuously monitor IAM policies and resource sharing. Access Analyzer uses automated reasoning to identify unintended external access grants and generates findings when IAM roles, S3 buckets, or other resources are accessible from outside the organization.

Configure AWS CloudTrail Insights to detect unusual API call volume patterns. CloudTrail Insights analyzes management event patterns and alerts when IAM-related API call rates deviate significantly from established baselines, indicating potential privilege escalation or unauthorized access.

Deploy Amazon Detective to build a behavior graph from CloudTrail, VPC Flow Logs, and GuardDuty findings. Detective's ML models identify unusual IAM activity patterns by comparing current behavior against established baselines for each IAM principal across the monitored accounts.

explanation: A is correct because GuardDuty consumes CloudTrail management events, VPC Flow Logs and DNS logs and applies machine-learned per-principal baselines, emitting IAM-focused findings such as UnauthorizedAccess:IAMUser/ConsoleLoginSuccess.B for anomalous geographies, InstanceCredentialExfiltration for keys used off-instance, and Discovery/Persistence anomaly findings for unusual API patterns - all without the team authoring any rules. B is incorrect because IAM Access Analyzer applies automated reasoning to policy documents to find unintended external or unused access; it is static analysis of configuration, not runtime behavioral anomaly detection. C is incorrect because CloudTrail Insights baselines API call volume and error rates, so it flags unusual rates but misses single-call anomalies such as a first-ever login from a new country or an API call from a new IP range. D is incorrect because Detective builds a behavior graph for investigating findings raised by other services; it is an investigation tool and does not itself generate IAM anomaly alerts.

stem: A company needs to implement a policy-as-code framework that evaluates Terraform plans before applying changes. Policies must verify that no public S3 buckets are created, all EC2 instances use approved AMI IDs, and resource naming follows the company convention. Which TWO components are needed for Terraform policy enforcement? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Configure a CI/CD pipeline stage that runs the policy evaluation tool after terraform plan and before terraform apply. The stage fails the pipeline if any policy violations are detected, preventing non-compliant infrastructure changes from being applied to the AWS environment.

Deploy AWS Config rules in the target accounts that evaluate S3 bucket access, EC2 AMI compliance, and resource naming after Terraform creates the resources. Configure auto-remediation to fix non-compliant resources immediately after Terraform provisioning completes.

Integrate OPA (Open Policy Agent) with Rego policies into the CI/CD pipeline. The pipeline runs terraform plan, converts the plan to JSON, and evaluates it against Rego policies that check S3 access, AMI compliance, and naming conventions before allowing terraform apply.

Write Sentinel policies that validate the Terraform plan output for S3 bucket public access settings, EC2 AMI IDs against an approved list, and resource naming patterns. Sentinel evaluates policies against the Terraform plan before apply, blocking non-compliant changes.

Use tfsec static analysis tool to scan Terraform configuration files for security misconfigurations. tfsec checks for public S3 buckets, validates security group rules, and identifies potential compliance violations in the Terraform HCL code before any plan or apply operation.

explanation: OPA with Rego policies (Option B) provides flexible policy evaluation against Terraform plan JSON output. A CI/CD pipeline stage (Option C) gates the apply step on policy compliance, blocking non-compliant changes. Option A uses Sentinel which requires Terraform Cloud/Enterprise. Option D evaluates after resource creation rather than preventing non-compliant creation. Option E scans static configuration but doesn't evaluate the actual plan including computed values and variable interpolation.

stem: A company runs a microservices application where one service depends on an external third-party API that occasionally experiences outages lasting 5-30 minutes. During outages, the dependent service retries aggressively, consuming CPU and creating cascading failures. Which resilience pattern prevents cascading failures from third-party API outages?

options.text: Configure an API Gateway with a caching layer in front of the third-party API calls. Cache successful API responses for 30 minutes so that during outages, the service receives cached responses instead of failures. Invalidate the cache when the third-party API recovers.

Implement request rate limiting on the dependent service to cap the number of outbound API calls per second. During outages, the rate limiter prevents aggressive retries by queuing excess requests. When the API recovers, queued requests are sent at the limited rate.

Implement a circuit breaker pattern in the dependent service. After a threshold of consecutive third-party API failures, the circuit opens and immediately returns a fallback response without calling the external API. Periodically test the API with a half-open state to detect recovery.

Deploy an SQS queue between the dependent service and the third-party API. Instead of calling the API directly, the service sends requests to the queue. A separate consumer processes queue messages against the API with exponential backoff retry, decoupling the service from API availability.

explanation: C is correct because a circuit breaker counts consecutive failures and timeouts, and once the threshold trips it opens - subsequent calls return a fallback immediately without occupying a thread, socket or CPU cycle on retries. A periodic half-open probe tests the third-party API and closes the breaker when it recovers, so the service self-heals after the 5-30 minute outage. This directly removes the retry storm that is causing the cascade. A is incorrect because caching only helps repeated reads of the same keys: writes and cache misses still hit the dead API, and a 30-minute TTL guarantees stale responses for data that changes. B is incorrect because rate limiting caps outbound throughput but each permitted request still blocks on a dead endpoint until timeout, and queueing the excess grows memory and latency - the resource pressure is relocated, not eliminated. D is incorrect because SQS only helps fire-and-forget work: synchronous callers needing a response cannot use it, the consumer still retries against the failed API, and it requires re-architecting the interaction as asynchronous.

stem: A company needs to detect when their application's error rate increases significantly compared to the previous deployment. After each deployment, the error rate should be compared against the pre-deployment baseline for 15 minutes. If the error rate is 3x higher than the baseline, an automatic rollback should trigger. Which monitoring approach compares post-deployment error rates against baselines?

options.text: Create a CloudWatch anomaly detection model on the application's error rate metric. During deployment, the anomaly detection band represents the expected error rate range. Configure a CloudWatch alarm that triggers rollback when the error rate exceeds the upper anomaly detection band by 3x.

Configure a CodeDeploy deployment with CloudWatch alarms using metric math. Create a metric math expression that compares the current 5-minute error rate against the average error rate from the 1-hour window before the deployment. Set the alarm threshold at 3x the baseline value.

Deploy a Lambda function triggered by the CodeDeploy deployment start event. The function records the current error rate as a baseline in SSM Parameter Store. After 15 minutes, another Lambda invocation compares the current error rate against the stored baseline and triggers rollback if 3x exceeded.

Configure the deployment pipeline to record pre-deployment error rates in a CloudWatch custom metric. Create a composite alarm that evaluates both the custom baseline metric and the live error rate metric, triggering when the live metric exceeds 3x the baseline custom metric value.

explanation: Option C is correct because it is the only design that actually captures a value and compares against it later. A Lambda function hooked to the CodeDeploy deployment-start event snapshots the current error rate into SSM Parameter Store, and a second invocation 15 minutes later reads that stored number, compares the live rate against 3x it, and calls StopDeployment with autoRollbackEnabled if the ratio is breached. Option B is not implementable: CloudWatch metric math provides no time-shift or offset function, so no expression can reference the average of a series from the hour preceding the deployment - metric math only operates on the series inside the alarm's current evaluation range, and alarm thresholds are static scalars, not values read from another period. Option A is wrong because an anomaly detection band is a trained model of normal seasonal behavior, not the specific pre-deployment baseline the stem requires; band-based alarms are configured with a band width multiplier around the predicted value, so there is no way to express '3x the measured pre-deployment rate'. Option D fails because composite alarms combine the ALARM/OK states of child alarms with Boolean logic - they cannot compare the numeric value of one metric against a multiple of another metric's value, and a child alarm cannot take its threshold from a metric.

stem: A company needs to manage multiple related CodePipeline pipelines that share common stages (source, security scanning) but have different deployment targets (EC2, ECS, Lambda). The team wants to avoid duplicating the common stages across all pipelines. Which approach enables pipeline stage reuse?

options.text: Define all pipelines using CloudFormation with shared template snippets for common stages. Use CloudFormation Mappings and Conditions to include the correct deployment stage based on a DeploymentTarget parameter. Each pipeline stack is instantiated with a different parameter value.

Deploy Terraform modules for the common pipeline stages and separate modules for each deployment type. The root Terraform configuration composes shared and deployment-specific modules, creating individual pipelines that share common stage definitions through module reuse.

Create a single CodePipeline with conditional execution logic using CodeBuild. The CodeBuild stage determines the deployment target based on repository metadata and invokes the appropriate deployment action (EC2 deploy, ECS deploy, or Lambda deploy) using the AWS CLI.

Create a shared CodePipeline for common stages (source, security scanning) that outputs artifacts to S3. Create separate deployment pipelines triggered by the shared pipeline's success event via EventBridge. Each deployment pipeline's source stage reads the artifact from the shared pipeline's S3 output.

explanation: D is correct because running source and security scanning once in a shared pipeline and publishing the validated artifact to S3, then matching the CodePipeline Pipeline Execution State Change SUCCEEDED event in EventBridge to start each target-specific pipeline, means the common stages exist and execute exactly once. Deployment pipelines start from the vetted artifact, can run concurrently, and evolve independently per target. A is incorrect because CloudFormation Mappings and Conditions reuse template text only - each stack still instantiates its own source and scan stages, so the scan runs redundantly for every pipeline. B is incorrect because Terraform modules have the same limitation: code reuse without execution reuse, so the common stages are still duplicated at runtime in each pipeline. C is incorrect because a single pipeline whose CodeBuild step shells out to deployment CLIs hides the deployments from CodePipeline's stage model - no per-target approvals, rollback or visibility - and serializes all three targets inside one execution.

stem: A company detected that an S3 bucket containing sensitive data was briefly made public due to a misconfiguration. Although the bucket was secured within 10 minutes, the company needs to determine if any data was accessed during the exposure window. Which AWS service provides the access analysis needed for this investigation?

options.text: Query CloudTrail S3 data events for the bucket during the 10-minute exposure window. Data events log every GetObject request including the source IP address, user agent, and timestamp. Filter for requests from unknown IP addresses or anonymous principals to identify potential unauthorized access.

Check S3 server access logs for the bucket during the 10-minute window. Server access logs record all requests made to the bucket including anonymous requests, providing IP addresses, request types, and HTTP response codes for every object access during the exposure period.

Use Amazon Detective to investigate the S3 bucket exposure incident. Detective's behavior graph analyzes CloudTrail and VPC Flow Logs to identify unusual access patterns to the S3 bucket, showing which entities accessed the bucket and whether the access originated from outside the organization.

Enable Amazon Macie on the S3 bucket and run a sensitive data discovery job for the exposure period. Macie analyzes the bucket contents to identify what sensitive data was exposed and generates findings about the sensitivity level of potentially accessed objects during the public exposure.

explanation: CloudTrail S3 data events provide detailed request-level logging including source IP, principal, and timestamp for every GetObject request. This directly shows whether any unauthorized access occurred during the exposure window. Option B identifies what data is sensitive but doesn't show who accessed it during the exposure. Option C requires S3 server access logs to be pre-enabled and has delivery delays. Option D investigates patterns but requires CloudTrail data events as its underlying data source.

stem: A company needs to implement least-privilege access for their CI/CD pipeline's IAM role. The pipeline deploys CloudFormation stacks that create various AWS resources. The team wants to restrict the pipeline role to only the permissions needed for the specific resources defined in the templates. Which approach implements least-privilege for the CloudFormation deployment role?

options.text: Create a CloudFormation service role with only the specific IAM permissions needed to create, update, and delete the resources defined in the templates. Pass this service role to CloudFormation via the RoleARN parameter. The pipeline role only needs cloudformation:* and iam:PassRole permissions.

Analyze CloudTrail logs from previous deployments to identify the exact API calls made during stack operations. Create an IAM policy with only those specific actions and resources. Attach the policy to the pipeline role, providing historically-validated least-privilege permissions.

Configure the pipeline IAM role with PowerUserAccess managed policy which provides broad AWS access excluding IAM management. This prevents the pipeline from modifying IAM resources while allowing it to create all other AWS resource types defined in CloudFormation templates.

Use IAM Access Analyzer policy generation to create a policy based on the pipeline role's actual API activity over 90 days. Access Analyzer generates a least-privilege policy based on observed actions, which can replace the current broad permissions on the pipeline role.

explanation: A is correct because CloudFormation assumes the service role passed in RoleARN and uses that role's permissions for every resource action, so the resource-creation permissions live in a role scoped precisely to the resource types the templates declare. The pipeline principal then needs only cloudformation actions plus iam:PassRole - and PassRole can be conditioned on that single role ARN, so pipeline credentials cannot be used to create resources directly. B is incorrect because mining CloudTrail from past deployments is reactive: it captures only the actions previously exercised and breaks the first time a template adds a new resource type or takes an untested delete or rollback path. C is incorrect because PowerUserAccess grants nearly every non-IAM service action, which is the opposite of least privilege. D is incorrect because Access Analyzer policy generation is limited to CloudTrail's 90-day lookback and, like option B, is observational - it lags newly introduced resource types and requires the role to remain over-permissioned throughout the observation period.

stem: A company manages AWS resources using both CloudFormation and Terraform in different teams. Some resources need to be shared between the two tools (e.g., a VPC created by CloudFormation is referenced by Terraform-managed EC2 instances). How should the teams share resource information between CloudFormation and Terraform?

options.text: Store shared resource identifiers in AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store. CloudFormation writes resource IDs to Parameter Store using custom resources after stack creation. Terraform reads Parameter Store values using the aws_ssm_parameter data source for cross-tool reference.

Export CloudFormation stack outputs for shared resources (VPC ID, subnet IDs) using the Export field. In Terraform, use the aws_cloudformation_export data source to read the exported values and reference them in Terraform resource configurations for cross-tool resource sharing.

Configure Terraform to import CloudFormation-managed resources into its state using terraform import. Both tools then manage the shared resources simultaneously, with CloudFormation handling creation and updates while Terraform references the imported resources for dependent configurations.

Create a shared state file in S3 that both CloudFormation and Terraform can read. CloudFormation writes resource identifiers to the S3 file using a Lambda-backed custom resource, and Terraform reads the file using the aws_s3_object data source to retrieve shared resource information.

explanation: B is correct because adding an Export name to a CloudFormation stack output publishes the value at the account and Region level, and Terraform's aws_cloudformation_export data source reads that export by name at plan time. This is a clean, read-only, one-way reference: Terraform never takes ownership of the VPC, and CloudFormation refuses to delete or change an exported output while another consumer depends on it. A is incorrect because Parameter Store works but requires a Lambda-backed custom resource to write and clean up the values, adding moving parts for something CloudFormation exports provide natively. C is incorrect because terraform import brings the resource into Terraform state, so both tools believe they own it; the next apply or stack update will fight over drift and a terraform destroy could delete CloudFormation-managed infrastructure. D is incorrect because a hand-rolled JSON document in S3 is a bespoke side channel with the same custom-resource overhead, no versioning or type safety, and no protection against removing a value that a consumer still needs.

stem: A company needs to implement a retry strategy for Lambda functions that process events from an SQS queue. Some processing failures are transient (database connection timeouts) while others are permanent (malformed message data). The team wants to retry transient failures but immediately dead-letter permanent failures. Which SQS and Lambda configuration handles both failure types?

options.text: Configure the Lambda function with reserved concurrency and retry behavior at the function level. Set MaximumRetryAttempts to 3 for transient failures. Implement error handling that publishes permanent failures to an SNS topic for alerting while the function returns success to SQS.

Configure the SQS queue with a redrive policy (maxReceiveCount of 3) and a dead-letter queue. In the Lambda function code, catch transient errors and throw them to trigger SQS retry. For permanent errors, delete the message from the queue and log the error to CloudWatch Logs.

Configure the SQS queue with a maxReceiveCount of 5, a dead-letter queue, and a visibility timeout longer than the function timeout. For transient errors, let the error propagate out of the handler (or return the record in batchItemFailures) so the message becomes visible again and is retried until maxReceiveCount routes it to the DLQ. For permanent errors, send the message to the DLQ explicitly and return successfully.

Configure the Lambda event source mapping with a maximum retry attempts of 3 and a destination configuration for failures pointing to an SQS dead-letter queue. The Lambda function throws exceptions for transient failures and returns success for permanent failures after logging them.

explanation: Option C is correct and now describes the mechanism accurately. With an SQS event source mapping, the Lambda poller deletes a message only when the handler returns normally; if the error propagates (or the record is listed in the batchItemFailures partial-batch response), the message is not deleted, becomes visible again after the visibility timeout, and is redelivered until maxReceiveCount sends it to the DLQ - that is the transient path. For permanent errors the function explicitly SendMessage's the payload to the DLQ and then returns successfully, so the poller deletes the original immediately with no wasted retries. Setting the visibility timeout above the function timeout prevents duplicate concurrent delivery. Option A is wrong because reserved concurrency is a throttling control and MaximumRetryAttempts is an asynchronous-invocation setting that does not apply to SQS event source mappings; publishing to SNS and returning success also leaves no durable copy of the poison message. Option B correctly throws for transient errors but destroys permanent failures - deleting the message and writing a log line discards the payload, whereas the stem requires dead-lettering it. Option D invents configuration: MaximumRetryAttempts and on-failure destinations on an event source mapping exist only for stream sources such as Kinesis and DynamoDB Streams, not for SQS, and returning success for permanent failures deletes them without dead-lettering.

stem: A company needs to implement real-time alerting when their application's p99 latency exceeds 500ms. The application processes 100,000 requests per minute, and the alerting must be based on actual percentile calculations, not averages or approximations. Which CloudWatch metric configuration provides accurate percentile-based alerting?

options.text: Publish request latency as a CloudWatch high-resolution custom metric using the PutMetricData API with StorageResolution set to 1 second. Create a CloudWatch alarm on the p99 statistic of the metric with a 1-minute evaluation period and a threshold of 500 milliseconds.

Publish request latency values using CloudWatch Embedded Metric Format in application logs. EMF automatically creates high-resolution metrics that support percentile statistics. Create a CloudWatch alarm evaluating the p99 statistic with a 500ms threshold and 1-minute period.

Create a CloudWatch Logs metric filter that extracts latency values from application logs and publishes them as a CloudWatch metric. Set the metric filter to capture the numeric latency value and create an alarm on the p99 statistic of the extracted metric at 500ms.

Deploy a Lambda function on a 1-minute schedule that queries the application's health endpoint for latency statistics. The function publishes the reported p99 latency as a custom CloudWatch metric. Create an alarm on the metric's Average statistic with a 500ms threshold.

explanation: CloudWatch Embedded Metric Format publishes metric values from logs that support percentile statistics including p99. At 100K requests per minute, EMF efficiently handles high-volume metric publishing without individual PutMetricData API calls. Option A uses PutMetricData which at 100K requests/minute would be extremely expensive and may hit API throttling limits. Option C's metric filters extract single values and don't support percentile calculations on the raw metric. Option D publishes pre-calculated p99 which loses the raw data needed for CloudWatch's native percentile calculation.

stem: A company needs to automatically generate and publish API documentation whenever changes are merged to the main branch of their API repository. The documentation must be generated from OpenAPI specifications stored in the repository and published to an internal documentation portal hosted on S3 with CloudFront. Which pipeline configuration automates API documentation publishing?

options.text: Configure a CodePipeline triggered by main branch commits. Add a CodeBuild stage that validates the OpenAPI specification using swagger-cli, generates HTML documentation using Redoc or Swagger UI, and deploys the generated static files to the S3 documentation bucket with CloudFront invalidation.

Deploy API Gateway with documentation export enabled. Configure API Gateway to import the OpenAPI specification on each deployment and use the GetExport API to generate documentation. Store the exported documentation in S3 and serve through CloudFront with automatic cache invalidation.

Configure AWS Amplify to host the documentation portal connected to the API repository. Amplify automatically detects changes to OpenAPI specification files and rebuilds the documentation site using a built-in OpenAPI documentation generator, deploying updates to the Amplify-hosted endpoint.

Create a Lambda function triggered by CodeCommit main branch push events. The function reads the OpenAPI specification from the repository, calls the Swagger Editor API to generate HTML documentation, and uploads the generated files to S3 with appropriate cache control headers.

explanation: A is correct because a CodePipeline source action on the main branch plus one CodeBuild stage covers the whole workflow: swagger-cli validate fails the build on an invalid OpenAPI document, Redoc or Swagger UI renders static HTML, aws s3 sync uploads to the documentation bucket, and CreateInvalidation clears the CloudFront cache so readers see the new docs immediately. Everything is versioned, repeatable and auditable. B is incorrect because API Gateway's documentation export emits an OpenAPI document, not a rendered portal, and it would require deploying the API to API Gateway purely as a documentation-generation step. C is incorrect because Amplify Hosting builds whatever the build spec says but has no built-in OpenAPI documentation generator that automatically detects spec files - the generation step still has to be written. D is incorrect because it depends on an external Swagger Editor API that is not a supported integration, and Lambda's package size and execution limits make it a fragile host for a documentation toolchain.

stem: A company needs to automatically remediate findings from AWS Security Hub. When Security Hub detects that an RDS instance has deletion protection disabled, the system must automatically enable deletion protection within 5 minutes. Which integration automates Security Hub finding remediation?

options.text: Configure AWS Config auto-remediation on the rds-instance-deletion-protection-enabled rule. When Config detects a non-compliant RDS instance, it triggers an SSM Automation document that calls the RDS ModifyDBInstance API to enable deletion protection automatically.

Create a Security Hub custom action that operators can manually invoke on RDS deletion protection findings. The custom action sends an event to EventBridge which triggers a Lambda function to enable deletion protection. Operators review findings and click the custom action button.

Deploy a Step Functions workflow triggered by a 5-minute EventBridge schedule. The workflow lists all Security Hub findings for RDS deletion protection, filters for active findings, and executes remediation by calling ModifyDBInstance for each non-compliant RDS instance found in the findings.

Configure Security Hub with automated response and remediation using EventBridge rules. Create an EventBridge rule matching Security Hub findings for RDS deletion protection. The rule triggers a Lambda function that calls ModifyDBInstance to enable deletion protection on the non-compliant instance.

explanation: D is correct because Security Hub publishes every finding to EventBridge as a Security Hub Findings - Imported event; a rule filtered on the RDS deletion-protection control fires within seconds of import and invokes Lambda to call ModifyDBInstance with DeletionProtection set to true, easily inside the five-minute objective, and the function can write the workflow status back to the finding. A is incorrect because although Config auto-remediation would technically fix the resource, the requirement is to remediate Security Hub findings - Config is a separate detection path with its own evaluation cadence and would miss findings that reach Security Hub from other integrations. B is incorrect because a Security Hub custom action requires a human to select the finding and click the action, making it manual by definition. C is incorrect because a 5-minute polling schedule means worst-case remediation of five minutes plus workflow execution time, wastes GetFindings calls on every tick, and re-processes the same findings unless you build additional state tracking.

stem: A company needs to implement a solution that detects when sensitive data like credit card numbers or personal identifiers appear in S3 buckets that are not classified as containing PII. The detection must run continuously across all S3 buckets in the organization. Which service provides automated sensitive data discovery in S3?

options.text: Deploy Amazon Comprehend with PII detection configured for S3 object processing. Create a Lambda function triggered by S3 PutObject events that sends each uploaded object to Comprehend for PII analysis. Comprehend identifies credit card numbers and personal identifiers in the object content.

Configure AWS Config with a custom rule that evaluates S3 bucket contents for sensitive data patterns. The Config rule's Lambda function downloads objects from each bucket and runs regex pattern matching for credit card numbers and personal identifiers, reporting non-compliant buckets.

Enable Amazon Macie across all accounts in the organization using delegated administrator. Configure automated sensitive data discovery jobs that continuously scan S3 buckets for credit card numbers, personal identifiers, and other PII patterns using Macie's managed data identifiers.

Enable Amazon GuardDuty S3 protection across all organization accounts. GuardDuty monitors S3 data access patterns and detects when objects containing sensitive data are accessed by unusual principals or from unexpected locations, generating findings for potential data exposure incidents.

explanation: C is correct because Macie is the purpose-built sensitive data discovery service for S3: enabled organization-wide through a delegated administrator, it maintains an inventory of every bucket in every account and runs automated sensitive data discovery continuously, sampling objects and matching managed data identifiers such as CREDIT_CARD_NUMBER and national identifiers. It produces findings and bucket-level sensitivity scores, which is exactly how you surface PII sitting in buckets not classified as containing PII. A is incorrect because Comprehend PII detection is per-document NLP invoked object by object, subject to document size and throughput limits, with no bucket inventory and no coverage of objects that already exist before the trigger is wired up. B is incorrect because Config evaluates configuration items, not object contents; a Lambda that downloads and regex-scans bucket contents hits timeout and memory limits and cannot scale to organization-wide S3 data. D is incorrect because GuardDuty S3 Protection analyzes CloudTrail S3 data events for anomalous access patterns and never inspects object content, so it cannot determine whether a bucket holds credit card numbers.

stem: A company uses AWS CDK to define their infrastructure. The team needs to share common constructs (custom VPC, standard ECS cluster, monitoring stack) across 10 application teams. Each team should use the latest version of shared constructs without copying code. Which CDK approach enables construct sharing across teams?

options.text: Create a monorepo containing all application CDK projects and shared constructs. Use npm workspaces to share construct packages between projects within the monorepo. All teams develop in the same repository, ensuring everyone uses the same version of shared constructs.

Publish shared constructs as an internal npm package (for TypeScript CDK) to a private CodeArtifact repository. Each application team adds the package as a dependency in their CDK project. Package versioning allows teams to upgrade shared constructs independently on their own schedule.

Create a shared CDK app repository containing all common constructs. Each application team clones the repository and copies construct files into their CDK projects. Teams periodically pull updates from the shared repository and merge construct changes into their local copies.

Deploy shared constructs as CloudFormation modules registered in the CloudFormation registry. Application teams reference the modules using AWS::CloudFormation::ModuleDefaultVersion in their CDK templates, inheriting the shared resource definitions without CDK-specific dependencies.

explanation: B is correct because CDK constructs are ordinary library code, so publishing them as a versioned npm package to a private CodeArtifact repository gives each of the 10 teams a normal dependency with semantic versioning, changelogs, transitive resolution and the ability to track the latest compatible version or pin deliberately. CodeArtifact also handles authentication, upstream npmjs proxying, and per-team read permissions. A is incorrect because a monorepo with npm workspaces does share code, but it forces all 10 application teams into a single repository and release cadence - an organizational constraint the requirement does not impose. C is incorrect because copying construct files is exactly the code duplication the requirement forbids: there is no version metadata, teams drift apart, and every update becomes a manual merge. D is incorrect because CloudFormation registry modules are template fragments that cannot express CDK L2/L3 abstractions, aspects or synthesis-time logic, and CDK cannot consume them as constructs.

stem: A company's production application uses Amazon MQ (ActiveMQ) as a message broker. The broker runs in a single-instance configuration and the team experienced a 45-minute outage when the broker instance had a hardware failure. The team needs to reduce the broker's recovery time to under 60 seconds. Which Amazon MQ configuration provides rapid failover?

options.text: Deploy a network of brokers with two Amazon MQ instances configured as a mesh topology. Messages are replicated between both brokers, and clients connect to both using failover transport URIs. If one broker fails, clients automatically reconnect to the surviving broker.

Reconfigure the Amazon MQ broker as an active/standby deployment across two Availability Zones. The active/standby configuration maintains a synchronized standby instance that automatically takes over within seconds when the active broker fails, providing sub-minute failover.

Enable Amazon MQ storage redundancy by selecting the EBS storage option with Multi-AZ replication. EBS replication ensures message data is preserved across AZ failures, and the broker instance restarts automatically from the replicated storage in the standby AZ after a hardware failure.

Switch from Amazon MQ to Amazon SQS which provides built-in high availability across multiple AZs without instance management. SQS automatically distributes messages across multiple servers and AZs, eliminating single-point-of-failure risk inherent in broker-based messaging.

explanation: B is correct because Amazon MQ for ActiveMQ active/standby is a managed two-Availability-Zone deployment in which both brokers share a replicated durable message store; if the active broker or its AZ fails, the standby takes over the same endpoints and a client using the failover: transport URI reconnects and resumes in well under a minute, versus the roughly 45 minutes a single-instance broker took to be rebuilt. A is incorrect because a network of brokers is a scaling and store-and-forward topology, not a high-availability one: messages persisted on the failed broker remain unavailable until it returns, and each node is still a single instance unless it is itself active/standby. C is incorrect because there is no Amazon MQ EBS Multi-AZ storage redundancy option - single-instance brokers use EBS in one AZ - and durable storage alone does not bring a failed broker back within seconds. D is incorrect because replacing Amazon MQ with SQS abandons JMS/AMQP/MQTT semantics, topics, selectors and transactions, making it an application rewrite rather than a broker configuration change.

stem: A company runs an EKS cluster and needs to correlate Kubernetes events (pod scheduling failures, node NotReady, OOMKilled) with application performance metrics to troubleshoot cluster issues. Kubernetes events must be searchable and correlated with CloudWatch metrics. Which approach captures and correlates Kubernetes events?

options.text: Enable the EKS control plane logging for the scheduler, controller-manager, and API server components. These logs capture pod scheduling decisions, node health changes, and OOM events. Query the control plane logs in CloudWatch Logs Insights alongside application performance data.

Configure the Kubernetes event exporter to forward cluster events to CloudWatch Logs. Create separate log groups for Kubernetes events and application logs. Use CloudWatch Logs Insights cross-log-group queries to correlate events with application metrics during troubleshooting.

Deploy Prometheus with the kube-state-metrics exporter to capture Kubernetes object state including events. Configure Grafana dashboards that display Kubernetes events alongside Prometheus metrics. Use the CloudWatch Prometheus data source to query both Kubernetes events and application metrics.

Deploy the CloudWatch agent with Container Insights enhanced observability on the EKS cluster. Container Insights collects Kubernetes events, pod metrics, and node metrics into CloudWatch. Use CloudWatch Logs Insights to query Kubernetes events alongside performance metrics in a single view.

explanation: D is correct because Container Insights with enhanced observability (via the CloudWatch Observability EKS add-on) deploys the CloudWatch agent and Fluent Bit to collect node, pod and container metrics in embedded metric format and ships Kubernetes events into a CloudWatch Logs group in the same Container Insights hierarchy. A single Logs Insights query can therefore join event records such as FailedScheduling, NodeNotReady and OOMKilled with the performance data emitted alongside them. A is incorrect because EKS control plane logging covers apiserver, scheduler and controller-manager activity but not kubelet-generated events such as OOMKilled, and it carries no pod resource metrics to correlate against. B is incorrect because a third-party event exporter puts events into a log group but leaves you owning its deployment and lifecycle, with no metric correlation - you build the join yourself. C is incorrect because kube-state-metrics exposes object state as metrics rather than the event stream, running Prometheus and Grafana adds a parallel monitoring stack, and there is no CloudWatch Prometheus data source that would surface Kubernetes events.

stem: A company deploys AWS Lambda functions using CloudFormation and needs to implement canary deployments that route 10% of traffic to the new version for 10 minutes before full cutover. If the canary version's error rate exceeds 1%, the deployment must automatically roll back. Which Lambda deployment configuration provides this canary behavior?

options.text: Configure the Lambda function with a CodeDeploy deployment preference of Canary10Percent10Minutes in the CloudFormation template. Add a CloudWatch alarm monitoring the Lambda function's Errors metric for the canary version. CodeDeploy automatically rolls back if the alarm triggers during the canary window.

Create a Lambda function alias with weighted routing at 90/10 between the production and canary versions. Configure a CloudWatch alarm on the canary alias's error rate. Manually update the alias weights to 0/100 after the 10-minute canary period if no alarm triggers.

Deploy two Lambda function versions behind an API Gateway stage with canary settings at 10% traffic. API Gateway routes 10% of requests to the canary deployment. After 10 minutes, promote the canary to production or roll back based on CloudWatch alarm evaluation of the error rate.

Configure a Step Functions workflow that orchestrates the canary deployment. The workflow publishes a new Lambda version, updates the alias to route 10% traffic, waits 10 minutes while monitoring errors, and either completes the cutover or rolls back based on the CloudWatch alarm evaluation.

explanation: CodeDeploy with Canary10Percent10Minutes in CloudFormation provides managed canary deployment for Lambda. CodeDeploy handles traffic shifting, alarm monitoring, and automatic rollback natively. Option B requires manual weight updates and doesn't provide automatic rollback. Option C uses API Gateway canary which is separate from Lambda version management. Option D builds custom orchestration when CodeDeploy provides this natively through SAM/CloudFormation deployment preferences.

stem: A company needs to implement a war room communication channel that automatically activates when a critical incident is declared. The channel must include the on-call engineer, the service owner, and the incident commander, with access to relevant runbooks and dashboards. Which AWS service provides automated incident communication?

options.text: Configure AWS Systems Manager Incident Manager with response plans that define engagement contacts (on-call engineer, service owner, incident commander). When an incident is created, Incident Manager automatically notifies all contacts via SMS, email, or voice call and creates a shared incident timeline.

Create an SNS topic with subscriptions for the on-call engineer, service owner, and incident commander. Configure CloudWatch alarm actions to publish to the SNS topic when critical alarms trigger. Include runbook links and dashboard URLs in the SNS message template for quick access.

Deploy Amazon Chime SDK with a chatbot that creates a new chat room when a critical incident is detected. The chatbot automatically invites the required participants, posts relevant runbook links, and shares CloudWatch dashboard screenshots in the incident chat room for collaborative troubleshooting.

Configure PagerDuty integration via SNS to manage incident escalation and communication. PagerDuty creates incident channels in Slack, pages the on-call team, and provides a mobile app for incident management. AWS EventBridge forwards CloudWatch alarm events to PagerDuty for incident creation.

explanation: Incident Manager provides integrated incident management with automatic contact engagement, escalation plans, runbook integration, and shared incident timeline. It's the native AWS service for war room coordination. Option B sends notifications but doesn't provide incident management or collaborative response. Option C requires Chime SDK development for chat-based collaboration. Option D uses third-party PagerDuty when Incident Manager provides native incident communication.

stem: A company must guarantee that every AWS API call made from instances in their VPC negotiates TLS 1.2 or higher, and that calls attempting older TLS versions cannot succeed. The requirement applies to all AWS service endpoints the workloads reach, not just Amazon S3. Which approach actually controls the minimum TLS version used for those AWS API calls?

options.text: Configure VPC endpoints for all AWS services with endpoint policies that include a condition requiring aws:SecureTransport to be true. This ensures all traffic through the VPC endpoints uses HTTPS, but additional SDK configuration is needed to enforce the minimum TLS version.

Configure the AWS SDK and CLI on all instances to use a minimum TLS version of 1.2 in the SDK configuration. Set the TLS minimum version in the shared AWS configuration file (~/.aws/config) or in the application's SDK client configuration code across all services.

Create an SCP that denies all AWS API actions unless the s3:TlsVersion condition key indicates TLS 1.2 or higher. Apply the SCP across the organization to enforce minimum TLS requirements for all service API calls from all accounts and VPCs in the organization.

Create an SCP with a condition key aws:TlsVersion that denies API calls when the TLS version is less than 1.2. Apply the SCP to all organizational units. This blocks any API call made over TLS versions older than 1.2 regardless of the AWS service endpoint being called.

explanation: Option B is correct: the TLS version is the outcome of a handshake negotiated by the client, so the only place it can be pinned is the client. Setting the minimum TLS version in the shared config file or in the SDK client configuration (and keeping the SDK on a current version, since modern AWS SDKs already default to TLS 1.2) is what guarantees no call is attempted with an older protocol; the server side already refuses anything below TLS 1.2 at AWS endpoints, and CloudTrail's tlsDetails field can be used to audit for stragglers. Option A only asserts that the request arrived over HTTPS - aws:SecureTransport is a Boolean and carries no version information - and the option itself concedes that SDK configuration is still required. Option C uses s3:TlsVersion, a service-specific condition key that Amazon S3 alone populates; in a Deny that covers all actions, the key is simply absent for every non-S3 request, so a StringLessThan style condition either never matches (enforcing nothing) or, with a NumericLessThan on a missing key, produces unpredictable results while still covering only S3. Option D relies on aws:TlsVersion, which is not a real global condition key - the AWS global condition key reference contains aws:SecureTransport but no TLS version key - so the SCP cannot be authored as described.

stem: A company uses CloudFormation and needs to create a stack that provisions resources in a specific order with explicit dependencies. An RDS database must be fully available before an ECS service starts, because the ECS task definition references the database endpoint. Which CloudFormation feature ensures correct resource creation ordering?

options.text: Use CloudFormation stack policy to define the creation order. Set the stack policy to allow RDS creation first and ECS service creation second. The policy enforces sequential resource provisioning in the specified order during both stack creation and update operations.

Add a CloudFormation WaitCondition between the RDS and ECS resources. The WaitCondition pauses stack creation until the database passes a health check signal sent by a Lambda-backed custom resource, ensuring the database is not only created but also fully operational.

Use the DependsOn attribute on the ECS service resource to explicitly declare a dependency on the RDS database resource. CloudFormation creates the RDS database first and waits for it to complete before creating the ECS service, ensuring the database endpoint is available.

Pass the database endpoint into the ECS task definition as a template parameter whose value is copied by hand from the RDS console after the database is created. Because the task definition contains no Ref or Fn::GetAtt pointing at the database resource, CloudFormation can create both resources in parallel and the stack completes faster.

explanation: Option C is correct and matches the stem's requirement for an explicit dependency. DependsOn on the ECS service tells CloudFormation not to begin creating that resource until the RDS resource reaches CREATE_COMPLETE, and for an RDS DB instance CREATE_COMPLETE means the instance is available and its endpoint is resolvable. Option A misdescribes stack policies: they are JSON documents that allow or deny update actions against resources during stack updates only. They play no role in creation, and they cannot express sequencing. Option B misuses WaitCondition, which blocks only until it receives the configured number of success signals; a WaitCondition must itself be sequenced with DependsOn to sit between two resources, and the extra Lambda-backed custom resource duplicates a guarantee CloudFormation already provides, since an RDS instance is available at CREATE_COMPLETE. Option D actively removes the dependency: hand-copying the endpoint into a parameter leaves no reference between the two resources, so CloudFormation is free to create the ECS service before or concurrently with the database, which is exactly the failure the stem is trying to prevent - and the pasted endpoint becomes stale whenever the instance is replaced.

stem: A company needs to implement a bulkhead pattern for their microservices application on ECS. Each service should have isolated resource pools so that one service's resource exhaustion doesn't affect other services. Which ECS configuration provides service-level resource isolation?

options.text: Deploy each microservice in a separate ECS cluster with its own VPC. Cluster-level isolation ensures that one service's resource exhaustion cannot affect another service's cluster. Use VPC peering for inter-service communication between the isolated clusters and VPCs.

Configure ECS task definitions with hard resource limits (CPU and memory) for each microservice. Set the task-level CPU and memory limits to cap resource consumption per task, preventing any single service's tasks from consuming excessive cluster resources during load spikes.

Use ECS Service Connect to manage inter-service communication with connection limits per service. Service Connect's built-in rate limiting prevents one service from overwhelming another with requests, implementing the bulkhead pattern at the network communication layer between microservices.

Deploy each microservice as a separate ECS service with its own capacity provider. Configure each capacity provider with a dedicated Auto Scaling group that has independent scaling policies, instance types, and maximum capacity limits, providing complete compute isolation per service.

explanation: D is correct because giving each microservice its own ECS capacity provider backed by a dedicated Auto Scaling group creates physically separate compute pools with independent scaling policies, instance types and maximum capacity - the defining property of a bulkhead. A service that exhausts its pool consumes only its own ASG's capacity and cannot displace or starve tasks belonging to other services. A is incorrect because a separate cluster and VPC per service does isolate but at a much higher cost: VPC peering or Transit Gateway, duplicated networking, and per-cluster operational overhead - heavier than the compute isolation the question asks for. B is incorrect because task-level CPU and memory limits bound one task, yet every service still draws from the same shared cluster capacity pool, so a service that scales out to hundreds of individually compliant tasks still starves its neighbors. C is incorrect because Service Connect provides service discovery, traffic telemetry and client-side routing between services; it is not a compute resource pool and does not cap a service's CPU or memory consumption.

stem: A company needs to implement distributed tracing for their serverless application that uses API Gateway, Lambda, DynamoDB, and SQS. The team needs end-to-end visibility of requests flowing through all four services. Which X-Ray configuration provides complete serverless trace visibility?

options.text: Deploy AWS Distro for OpenTelemetry (ADOT) Lambda layer in each function. Configure ADOT to collect traces from all service interactions and export them to X-Ray. ADOT provides vendor-neutral instrumentation that captures traces across API Gateway, Lambda, DynamoDB, and SQS.

Enable X-Ray active tracing on the API Gateway stage and on every Lambda function, and instrument the function code with the X-Ray SDK so DynamoDB and SQS calls are recorded as subsegments. Trace context propagates from the gateway into the function and through SQS message attributes, giving one end-to-end trace.

Enable CloudWatch ServiceLens for the serverless application. ServiceLens automatically discovers and maps the service dependencies between API Gateway, Lambda, DynamoDB, and SQS. It provides end-to-end trace visualization without requiring explicit X-Ray SDK instrumentation in the code.

Configure the X-Ray daemon as a Lambda layer in each function. The daemon collects trace segments from the Lambda execution environment and forwards them to the X-Ray service. Enable API Gateway access logging with trace ID propagation to correlate gateway and function traces.

explanation: Option B is correct and now states only real settings. Active tracing is a stage-level setting on API Gateway and a function-level setting on Lambda; DynamoDB and SQS have no tracing configuration of their own and appear in the trace as subsegments emitted by the instrumented caller, which is exactly what the X-Ray SDK (or ADOT auto-instrumentation) produces when it patches the AWS SDK client. X-Ray propagates the trace header from the gateway into the function and Lambda's SQS integration carries the AWSTraceHeader message attribute, so the whole path resolves into one trace with per-service latency. Option A is a working way to instrument the Lambda side, but the ADOT layer runs inside the function and cannot create API Gateway's own segment - that still requires enabling active tracing on the stage - so as written it does not deliver the gateway portion of the end-to-end trace. Option C inverts the dependency: ServiceLens is a visualization surface over X-Ray traces, CloudWatch metrics and logs, so it shows nothing until X-Ray tracing is enabled and segments are being emitted. Option D is factually wrong about the runtime: the X-Ray daemon is built into the Lambda execution environment and is never deployed as a layer, and correlating access logs by trace ID gives log correlation, not a segmented distributed trace.

stem: A company's development team accidentally deployed a broken Lambda function version that caused production errors. The team needs a deployment safety mechanism that automatically detects increased errors within the first 5 minutes of deployment and rolls back to the previous working version. Which Lambda deployment feature provides this automatic safety net?

options.text: Implement feature flags using AWS AppConfig to control which Lambda function version serves production traffic. The feature flag gradually enables the new version for increasing percentages of requests. If errors increase, manually toggle the feature flag to revert to the previous version.

Deploy Lambda versions using CloudFormation with the AutoPublishAlias property in an AWS::Serverless::Function resource. Configure DeploymentPreference with Alarms pointing to a CloudWatch alarm on the Lambda Errors metric. CodeDeploy automatically rolls back if the alarm triggers during deployment.

Configure Lambda function aliases with CodeDeploy traffic shifting using the Linear10PercentEvery1Minute deployment configuration. Add a pre-traffic hook Lambda function that invokes the new version with synthetic test events and fails the deployment if the responses are wrong. No alarms are associated with the deployment group.

Configure Lambda provisioned concurrency on the new version before shifting traffic. Use a custom health check endpoint in the Lambda function that returns the function's health status. Deploy a Step Functions workflow that monitors the health endpoint and reverts the alias if failures are detected.

explanation: Option B is correct. AutoPublishAlias on AWS::Serverless::Function publishes a new version and points the alias at it on every deploy, and DeploymentPreference with an Alarms list hands the shift to CodeDeploy, which watches those CloudWatch alarms for the whole traffic-shifting window and automatically shifts 100% of traffic back to the previous version the moment any listed alarm enters ALARM. That is the built-in, declarative safety net the stem asks for. Option C uses the same CodeDeploy traffic-shifting machinery but deliberately attaches no alarms: a pre-traffic hook runs once before any production traffic is shifted, so it can catch a version that is broken on synthetic input, but it cannot detect an error rate that only appears under real production traffic during the 5-minute window - there is nothing monitoring the live deployment, so nothing triggers a rollback. Option A relies on a human noticing the errors and toggling the flag, which is explicitly not automatic. Option D builds a bespoke control loop - provisioned concurrency is a cold-start setting and is irrelevant to safety, a self-reported health endpoint will not report the errors real callers are seeing, and the Step Functions workflow is undifferentiated custom code duplicating what CodeDeploy already provides.

stem: A company needs to implement an automated response to a DDoS attack detected by AWS Shield Advanced. The response must include activating additional CloudFront capacity, enabling WAF rate limiting, and notifying the security team. Which TWO actions should be configured for automated DDoS response? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Configure Shield Advanced automatic application layer DDoS mitigation on the CloudFront distribution. Shield Advanced automatically creates and deploys WAF rules that block attack traffic patterns, adapting the rules as the attack evolves without manual intervention from the security team.

Create an EventBridge rule matching Shield Advanced DDoS attack events. The rule triggers a Lambda function that enables a pre-configured WAF rate-limiting rule, scales up origin capacity via Auto Scaling API calls, and sends SNS notifications to the security team with attack details.

Contact the AWS Shield Response Team (SRT) through an AWS Support case to request manual DDoS mitigation. SRT engineers analyze the attack pattern and implement custom WAF rules and network-level mitigations specific to the attack. This requires a Business or Enterprise Support plan.

Enable CloudFront automatic scaling which handles DDoS traffic volume increases natively. CloudFront's globally distributed edge network absorbs volumetric attacks without additional configuration. Register the CloudFront distribution with Shield Advanced for enhanced L7 attack visibility.

Configure AWS WAF with a rate-based rule permanently enabled at a high threshold. During a DDoS attack, the rate-based rule automatically blocks IP addresses exceeding the request rate threshold. No additional activation is needed since the rule is always active and evaluating incoming requests.

explanation: A is correct because Shield Advanced automatic application-layer DDoS mitigation, enabled on the protected CloudFront distribution, allows Shield to author and place WAF rules in a Shield-managed rule group as it detects attack signatures, and to keep adapting those rules as the attack shifts - with no human in the loop. B is correct because Shield Advanced surfaces DDoS attack events and the DDoSDetected metric, so an EventBridge rule can match the attack event and invoke Lambda to perform the remaining requirements: enabling the pre-staged WAF rate-based rule, scaling origin capacity via the Auto Scaling API, and publishing attack details to SNS for the security team. C is incorrect because engaging the Shield Response Team through a support case is a human escalation whose latency depends on the support plan - the opposite of an automated response. D is incorrect because there is no CloudFront automatic scaling setting to enable, and while CloudFront inherently absorbs volumetric traffic, this option performs none of the three required response actions. E is incorrect because an always-on rate-based rule is a useful static baseline but cannot scale origin capacity or notify anyone, and a high fixed threshold will not catch a widely distributed low-and-slow Layer 7 attack.

stem: A company needs to ensure that all EC2 instances launched in their accounts have the AWS Systems Manager Agent installed and are registered as managed instances. Instances without SSM Agent must be detected and remediated. Which approach ensures universal SSM Agent coverage across all EC2 instances?

options.text: Deploy EC2 Image Builder pipelines that include SSM Agent installation as a mandatory build component. All teams must use Image Builder AMIs for their EC2 launches. Image Builder validates SSM Agent presence in the test phase before distributing the AMI for production use.

Configure AWS Config with the ec2-instance-managed-by-systems-manager rule to detect unregistered instances. Auto-remediate with the AWS-AttachIAMToInstance Automation document, which attaches an instance profile containing AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore, and enable Systems Manager Default Host Management Configuration so instances with the preinstalled agent register automatically.

Mandate the use of Amazon Linux 2 or Windows AMIs that include SSM Agent pre-installed. Create an SCP that denies ec2:RunInstances unless the AMI is from the approved list. Ensure all approved AMIs include SSM Agent and the AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore managed IAM policy.

Configure a VPC endpoint for Systems Manager in all VPCs. Deploy a Lambda function triggered by EC2 RunInstances CloudTrail events that attaches the AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore policy to the instance's IAM role and verifies SSM Agent registration within 5 minutes of launch.

explanation: Option B is correct and now remediates something that is actually remediable from the control plane. The overwhelming cause of an instance failing ec2-instance-managed-by-systems-manager is missing IAM permissions, not a missing binary - current Amazon Linux, Ubuntu and Windows AMIs ship the agent preinstalled. AWS Config continuously detects the non-compliant population, the AWS-AttachIAMToInstance Automation document associates an instance profile carrying AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore via EC2 APIs (no agent required), and Default Host Management Configuration registers instances automatically without any per-instance role at all. Option A puts the agent in the AMI but provides no detection and no enforcement - it depends on every team voluntarily consuming Image Builder output, and instances launched from any other AMI are never found. Option C is brittle and incomplete: an AMI allow-list SCP must be maintained per Region and rewritten on every AMI release, a managed IAM policy cannot be baked into an AMI (it must be attached to an instance profile at launch), and the SCP cannot detect an instance whose agent later stops or whose profile is removed. Option D cannot fix the common case - if the instance was launched with no IAM role, there is no role to attach a policy to - and being CloudTrail-event driven it never touches instances that already exist.

stem: A company uses Terraform and needs to manage sensitive values like database passwords and API keys in their configurations. These values must not appear in Terraform state files or plan output in plaintext. Which Terraform approach securely handles sensitive values?

options.text: Use environment variables prefixed with TF_VAR_ to pass sensitive values to Terraform. Environment variables are never written to state files or displayed in plan output. Configure CI/CD pipelines to inject secrets as environment variables from a secure vault during Terraform execution.

Declare variables as sensitive using the sensitive = true flag in the variable block. Terraform redacts sensitive values from plan and apply output. Store the actual values in a terraform.tfvars file excluded from version control, and encrypt the Terraform state file at rest in S3.

Encrypt the terraform.tfvars file using AWS KMS before committing to version control. Decrypt the file in the CI/CD pipeline before running Terraform. This ensures sensitive values are encrypted at rest in the repository while being available in plaintext during Terraform execution.

Store sensitive values in AWS Secrets Manager and reference them using the aws_secretsmanager_secret_version data source. This keeps sensitive values out of the Terraform configuration files entirely, though they still appear in the Terraform state file after being retrieved.

explanation: B is correct because marking a variable sensitive = true makes Terraform redact its value from plan and apply output and refuse to expose it through unmarked outputs, which is what keeps secrets out of CI logs; keeping real values in a gitignored tfvars file keeps them out of version control; and enabling server-side encryption (plus a restrictive bucket policy and state locking) on the S3 backend protects the state file, which always stores values in plaintext internally regardless of how they were supplied. Together these are the standard controls for this requirement. A is incorrect because TF_VAR_ variables are still assigned to Terraform variables, so the resulting attribute values are persisted to state exactly like any other input - the claim that they never reach state is false, and an unmarked variable is still printed in plan output. C is incorrect because KMS-encrypting tfvars protects the value only at rest in the repository; once decrypted for the run it appears in plan output unless also marked sensitive, and it still lands in state. D is incorrect because the aws_secretsmanager_secret_version data source writes the retrieved SecretString into state in plaintext - the option itself concedes this - and it does nothing about plan output.

stem: A company needs to implement health checks for an ECS Fargate service behind an ALB. The application takes 90 seconds to fully initialize after the container starts. During initialization, the health check endpoint returns HTTP 503. The current configuration causes containers to be terminated before they finish initializing. Which health check configuration prevents premature container termination?

options.text: Set the ALB target group deregistration delay to 120 seconds. The deregistration delay provides a buffer period during which the ALB continues routing traffic to the container while it initializes, preventing the container from being terminated due to failed health checks during startup.

Configure the ALB target group health check with a health check grace period in the ECS service definition set to 120 seconds. The grace period prevents the ECS service from marking tasks as unhealthy during the initial startup period, allowing the full 90-second initialization to complete.

Configure the container health check in the ECS task definition with a start period of 120 seconds. The start period disables health checking during the initial startup phase, allowing the container to complete its 90-second initialization before health checks begin evaluating container status.
