Increase the ALB target group health check interval to 120 seconds with an unhealthy threshold of 3. This means the first health check failure won't occur until 120 seconds after registration, giving the container time to initialize before being evaluated as unhealthy.

explanation: B is correct because the ECS service's healthCheckGracePeriodSeconds instructs the service scheduler to ignore Elastic Load Balancing (and Route 53) health check failures for the configured window after a task reaches RUNNING. Setting it to 120 seconds covers the 90-second initialization, so ECS stops replacing tasks that are merely still starting, while normal health-check sensitivity resumes afterwards. A is incorrect because deregistration delay controls how long the ALB drains in-flight connections to a target being removed; it has no effect during registration or startup. C is incorrect because the container health check startPeriod suppresses only the container-level (Docker) health check - the terminations here originate from the ALB target group marking the target unhealthy and the ECS service replacing it, which startPeriod does not gate. D is incorrect because a 120-second interval with a threshold of 3 delays the first unhealthy verdict but then delays detection of genuinely failed targets by up to six minutes for the rest of the task's life, treating the symptom rather than declaring a startup grace window.

stem: A company needs to set up automated canary testing that continuously validates their production API endpoints from multiple geographic locations. The canaries must check endpoint availability, response time, and response content accuracy every 5 minutes. If any canary fails, the team must be alerted immediately. Which CloudWatch feature provides multi-location endpoint monitoring?

options.text: Configure CloudWatch Internet Monitor for the application's CloudFront distribution. Internet Monitor provides visibility into internet availability and performance from the perspective of end users across different geographic locations, alerting when connectivity issues affect specific regions.

Configure CloudWatch Synthetics canaries that run Node.js or Python scripts on a 5-minute schedule from multiple AWS regions. Each canary script validates HTTP status codes, response latency, and response body content. Failed canary runs trigger CloudWatch alarms that send SNS notifications.

Create Route 53 health checks for each API endpoint configured to run from multiple geographic locations. Health checks verify HTTP status codes and search for expected strings in the response body. Configure health check alarms that send SNS notifications when checks fail consecutively.

Deploy Lambda functions in multiple AWS regions that call the production API endpoints every 5 minutes via EventBridge scheduled rules. Each function validates the response and publishes custom CloudWatch metrics for availability and latency. Create alarms on the custom metrics for failure alerting.

explanation: B is correct because CloudWatch Synthetics canaries are managed Lambda-based scripts (Node.js with Puppeteer or Python with Selenium) that can be scheduled at rate(5 minutes) and deployed independently in each Region you want to probe from. The script asserts on HTTP status codes, measures duration and inspects response body content, and Synthetics automatically emits SuccessPercent, Duration and Failed metrics plus screenshots, HAR files and logs, so alarms and SNS notification are pure configuration. A is incorrect because Internet Monitor reports internet-path availability and performance for the city/network combinations your users come from; it does not execute request assertions against a specific endpoint or validate response bodies. C is incorrect because Route 53 health checks do run from multiple locations and support string matching, but the match is a single string within the first 5,120 bytes, with no scripting, no multi-step flows and only fixed 10- or 30-second intervals. D is incorrect because deploying per-Region Lambdas on EventBridge schedules rebuilds Synthetics by hand, leaving you to implement metric publishing, artifact capture and failure diagnostics yourself.

stem: A company needs to implement a blue/green deployment strategy for their application running on an Auto Scaling group behind an ALB. During the deployment, both the blue (current) and green (new) environments must run simultaneously. Traffic must be switched atomically from blue to green after validation. Which approach implements ALB-based blue/green deployment for Auto Scaling groups?

options.text: Create two Auto Scaling groups (blue and green) registered to different ALB target groups. Deploy the new version to the green ASG. After validation, modify the ALB listener rule to forward traffic from the blue target group to the green target group, achieving atomic traffic switching.

Configure Route 53 weighted routing with two record sets pointing to two different ALBs. Deploy the new version behind the secondary ALB. Gradually shift Route 53 weights from the primary to the secondary ALB over time, completing the blue/green transition after validation.

Configure CodeDeploy with an in-place deployment type and the OneAtATime deployment configuration. CodeDeploy updates instances in the Auto Scaling group one at a time, deregistering each from the ALB, updating the application, and re-registering after validation passes.

Use CloudFormation with an UpdatePolicy that enables AutoScalingRollingUpdate. Set MinInstancesInService to 100% of the desired capacity. CloudFormation launches new instances with the updated configuration before terminating old instances, providing rolling blue/green behavior.

explanation: A is correct because two Auto Scaling groups each registered to their own target group behind the same ALB lets blue and green run simultaneously for validation, and a single ModifyListener or ModifyRule call repoints the listener's forward action from the blue target group to the green one. That change is applied atomically by the ALB with no DNS or client involvement, and rollback is the same call in reverse. B is incorrect because Route 53 weighted routing shifts traffic through DNS, so resolvers and clients honor cached TTLs - the cutover is gradual and non-atomic, and the old version keeps receiving traffic after the weights change. C is incorrect because CodeDeploy in-place with OneAtATime updates the existing instances progressively; that is a rolling deployment in which both versions serve traffic and there is no single switch point. D is incorrect because AutoScalingRollingUpdate replaces instances in batches within the same ASG and target group - also a rolling update - and it cannot hold a complete, validated green environment before switching.

stem: A company needs to implement a mechanism that automatically reverts IAM policy changes that grant overly permissive access. If any IAM policy is modified to include a wildcard (*) action on a wildcard (*) resource, the change must be automatically reverted to the previous policy version. Which approach detects and reverts overly permissive IAM policy changes?

options.text: Deploy IAM Access Analyzer with custom policy validation. Access Analyzer continuously evaluates all IAM policies for overly permissive configurations. When a policy with wildcard action and resource is detected, Access Analyzer generates a finding that triggers auto-remediation via EventBridge and Lambda.

Create an EventBridge rule matching IAM PutUserPolicy, PutRolePolicy, and CreatePolicyVersion CloudTrail events. The rule triggers a Lambda function that evaluates the new policy document. If the policy contains Action:* with Resource:*, the function reverts to the previous policy version.

Configure AWS Config with a custom rule that evaluates IAM policy documents for wildcard permissions. When a non-compliant policy is detected, Config auto-remediation triggers an SSM Automation document that retrieves the previous policy version from CloudTrail and restores it to the IAM entity.

Create an SCP that denies iam:PutUserPolicy, iam:PutRolePolicy, and iam:CreatePolicyVersion unless the policy document excludes Action:* with Resource:*. The SCP uses the iam:PolicyDocument condition key to evaluate policy content before the change is applied.

Enable AWS CloudTrail with IAM event monitoring. Create a CloudWatch Logs metric filter that matches IAM policy modification API calls. Set a CloudWatch alarm that triggers an SNS notification to the security team when any IAM policy is modified for manual review and reversion.

explanation: B is correct because CloudTrail delivers PutUserPolicy, PutRolePolicy and CreatePolicyVersion management events to EventBridge in near real time, and the event's requestParameters contain the policy document itself. A Lambda target can parse the document and, when it finds Action "*" on Resource "*", revert by calling SetDefaultPolicyVersion back to the prior managed-policy version or re-putting the previous inline document, achieving detection plus automatic reversion. A is incorrect because IAM Access Analyzer's policy validation and custom policy checks emit findings and are useful in a pipeline, but Access Analyzer performs no remediation and has no concept of the previous policy version to restore. C is incorrect because AWS Config custom rules evaluate on configuration-item delivery or a periodic schedule, adding minutes of latency, and an SSM Automation document cannot retrieve a restorable prior policy from CloudTrail - CloudTrail records the new document, whereas IAM itself retains up to five managed-policy versions. D is incorrect because there is no iam:PolicyDocument condition key that lets an SCP inspect the JSON body of a policy being written; SCPs restrict actions and can use context keys such as iam:PermissionsBoundary, but they cannot parse policy content. E is incorrect because a metric filter and SNS alarm produce only a human notification, with no automatic reversion, which is the stated requirement.

stem: A company needs to implement network-level encryption for all traffic between EC2 instances within their VPC. The encryption must be transparent to applications running on the instances without requiring application code changes. Which AWS feature provides transparent inter-instance encryption?

options.text: Deploy AWS PrivateLink endpoints for inter-instance communication. PrivateLink encrypts traffic using TLS as it traverses the AWS network between instances. Applications connect to PrivateLink endpoints instead of direct instance addresses for encrypted communication.

Enable AWS Nitro Enclaves on all EC2 instances for encrypted processing. Nitro Enclaves create isolated compute environments that encrypt all data in use, including network traffic between enclaves running on different instances within the VPC, transparent to applications.

Configure VPC Flow Logs with encryption enabled to encrypt all network traffic metadata. Deploy IPSec VPN tunnels between all instance pairs using strongSwan VPN software. The VPN tunnels encrypt all inter-instance traffic transparently at the network layer below the application.

Enable VPC encryption in-transit by launching instances on Nitro-based instance types. Nitro instances automatically encrypt traffic between instances in the same VPC using AES-256 encryption at the network interface level, requiring no application changes or certificate management.

explanation: D is correct because on supported Nitro-based instance types AWS transparently encrypts VPC traffic between instances with AES-256 at the Nitro card, for traffic that stays within the same VPC (and across peered VPCs or Transit Gateway within a Region). Encryption happens below the guest operating system, so there is no agent, certificate management or application change - exactly the transparency the requirement calls for. A is incorrect because PrivateLink provides private connectivity to a service endpoint; it does not apply to general instance-to-instance traffic, and any encryption there is a property of the protocol the service speaks, not of PrivateLink. B is incorrect because Nitro Enclaves carve out isolated CPU and memory for confidential processing and deliberately have no network interface at all - only a vsock channel to the parent instance - so they cannot encrypt VPC traffic between instances. C is incorrect because VPC Flow Logs record flow metadata and cannot encrypt anything, and building strongSwan IPsec tunnels between every instance pair is a self-managed O(n squared) mesh, which is the opposite of transparent.

stem: A company needs to implement a GitOps workflow for their CloudFormation infrastructure. When a CloudFormation template is updated in the Git repository, the changes must be automatically previewed as a change set, reviewed by a human, and then executed. Which pipeline architecture implements GitOps for CloudFormation?

options.text: Deploy ArgoCD configured to watch the Git repository containing CloudFormation templates. ArgoCD detects template changes and synchronizes the CloudFormation stack state with the Git-defined desired state. ArgoCD provides a UI for reviewing and approving the synchronization before execution.

Configure AWS Service Catalog with a CloudFormation product backed by the Git repository. When templates change, Service Catalog updates the product version. Administrators review and approve the new product version in the Service Catalog console before users can provision updated stacks.

Create an EventBridge rule triggered by Git repository push events. The rule invokes a Lambda function that validates the template with cfn-lint, creates a CloudFormation stack update directly, and sends an SNS notification after the update completes for post-deployment review.

Configure CodePipeline with a source stage connected to the Git repository. Add a CloudFormation action that creates a change set in review mode. Add a manual approval stage where reviewers examine the change set. After approval, add a CloudFormation execute change set action to apply changes.

explanation: D is correct because this is the canonical CloudFormation GitOps pipeline: a source action on the Git repository, a CloudFormation action with ActionMode CHANGE_SET_REPLACE that computes the diff without applying it, a manual approval action where reviewers inspect exactly which resources will be added, modified or replaced, and finally a CHANGE_SET_EXECUTE action gated behind that approval. Git is the source of truth and every change is previewed and human-approved before execution. A is incorrect because ArgoCD reconciles Kubernetes manifests through the Kubernetes API and has no CloudFormation provider, so it cannot create or execute change sets. B is incorrect because Service Catalog governs which products users may provision and versions them, but administrators review a product version rather than a change set showing resource-level modifications to a live stack, and it does not deploy automatically on push. C is incorrect because it lints the template and then applies the stack update immediately, notifying after the fact - there is no change-set preview and no human gate, which are the two things the requirement asks for.

stem: A company runs a containerized application on EKS that needs to handle Pod disruptions gracefully during cluster upgrades and node replacements. The application requires at least 3 out of 5 replicas to be available at all times during planned maintenance. Which Kubernetes resource prevents excessive Pod disruption during maintenance?

options.text: Configure the deployment's strategy with maxUnavailable set to 2 and maxSurge set to 2 in the rollingUpdate section. This limits the number of pods that can be unavailable during deployment updates to 2, maintaining at least 3 available pods during the rolling update process.

Create a PodDisruptionBudget (PDB) with minAvailable set to 3 for the application's deployment. During node drain operations for cluster upgrades, the PDB prevents the Kubernetes scheduler from evicting pods below the minimum threshold, ensuring at least 3 replicas remain running.

Set the deployment's replicas to 7 with a Horizontal Pod Autoscaler minimum of 5. The additional replicas provide buffer capacity during node drains, ensuring that even if 2 pods are evicted during maintenance, the application maintains at least 5 running pods above the minimum threshold.

Configure pod anti-affinity rules that spread the 5 replicas across different nodes and availability zones. During node maintenance, only one replica is affected per node drain, naturally maintaining at least 4 available replicas while the evicted pod reschedules to a healthy node.

explanation: B is correct because a PodDisruptionBudget with minAvailable: 3 is enforced by the Kubernetes Eviction API, which is what kubectl drain and the managed node group, Karpenter and cluster-upgrade paths use. An eviction that would drop healthy replicas below three is rejected, so the drain blocks or proceeds only as replacement pods become Ready - guaranteeing the availability floor through planned maintenance. A is incorrect because maxUnavailable and maxSurge apply solely to the Deployment's own rolling update; they place no constraint on evictions initiated externally by a node drain. C is incorrect because extra replicas add headroom but nothing prevents a drain from evicting an arbitrary number of pods at once - without a PDB every eviction request is granted. D is incorrect because anti-affinity spreads pods to limit the blast radius of a single node failure, but a rolling cluster upgrade drains nodes in sequence and, with no PDB, can evict faster than replacements become Ready; strict anti-affinity can even prevent rescheduling if no compliant node has capacity.

stem: A company needs to monitor the performance of their Aurora PostgreSQL database and identify the top SQL queries consuming the most CPU and I/O resources. The analysis must not impact database performance and should provide historical query performance data for trend analysis. Which Aurora feature provides SQL-level performance monitoring?

options.text: Configure CloudWatch Enhanced Monitoring for the Aurora cluster at 1-second granularity. Enhanced Monitoring provides OS-level metrics including CPU, memory, and I/O per process. Map the PostgreSQL backend processes to specific queries using pg_stat_activity for query-level attribution.

Enable Aurora PostgreSQL's pg_stat_statements extension to collect query execution statistics. Query the pg_stat_statements view to identify top CPU-consuming and I/O-intensive queries. Export the data to CloudWatch custom metrics for historical dashboarding and trend analysis.

Enable Performance Insights on the Aurora cluster with a retention period of 2 years. Performance Insights collects SQL-level metrics including CPU, I/O, and wait events per query. The Top SQL tab shows the queries consuming the most resources, with historical data for trend analysis.

Enable Aurora audit logging with the pgaudit extension. Configure pgaudit to log all DML and DDL statements with execution duration. Stream audit logs to CloudWatch Logs and use Logs Insights queries to calculate aggregate CPU and I/O time per SQL query pattern.

explanation: C is correct because Performance Insights is purpose-built for this: it samples active sessions roughly once per second with negligible overhead, attributes database load (average active sessions) to individual SQL statements, wait events, hosts and users, and the Top SQL view ranks statements by load with the CPU versus I/O wait breakdown. Enabling long-term retention (up to 24 months) preserves the history needed for trend analysis. A is incorrect because Enhanced Monitoring reports OS process metrics only; mapping a PostgreSQL backend PID to a statement through pg_stat_activity is a point-in-time snapshot with no historical attribution, and OS metrics do not decompose into per-statement CPU and I/O. B is incorrect because pg_stat_statements does aggregate per-statement counters, but you must poll it, compute deltas, publish custom metrics and handle resets - a manual rebuild of Performance Insights that still lacks wait-event attribution. D is incorrect because pgaudit logs statement text and adds meaningful write overhead at volume, and audit records show what ran, not how much CPU or I/O each statement consumed.

stem: A company needs to implement a deployment pipeline that deploys the same application to multiple AWS regions sequentially. The pipeline must deploy to us-east-1 first, run smoke tests, then deploy to eu-west-1, run smoke tests, and finally deploy to ap-southeast-1. If any region's deployment or tests fail, subsequent regions must not be deployed. Which CodePipeline configuration implements sequential multi-region deployment?

options.text: Create three separate CodePipelines, one per region. Configure EventBridge rules so that successful completion of the us-east-1 pipeline triggers the eu-west-1 pipeline, and successful eu-west-1 completion triggers the ap-southeast-1 pipeline. Each pipeline runs independently in its target region.

Create a Step Functions workflow that orchestrates the multi-region deployment. The workflow deploys to each region sequentially using CodeDeploy API calls, runs smoke tests via Lambda invocations, and stops the workflow if any step fails, preventing deployment to subsequent regions.

Create a single CodePipeline with a parallel deployment stage containing three CodeDeploy actions, one per region. Add a test stage after the deployment stage that runs smoke tests against all three regions simultaneously. The pipeline fails if any region's tests do not pass within the timeout.

Create a single CodePipeline with sequential stages for each region: deploy-us-east-1, test-us-east-1, deploy-eu-west-1, test-eu-west-1, deploy-ap-southeast-1, test-ap-southeast-1. Each deploy stage uses a cross-region CodeDeploy action, and test stages use CodeBuild with region-specific test configurations.

explanation: D is correct because CodePipeline executes stages strictly in order and a failed action halts the execution, so alternating deploy and CodeBuild smoke-test stages per Region gives exactly the required sequencing and the required stop-on-failure behavior. CodePipeline supports cross-Region actions natively (with an artifact store in each Region), so one pipeline with a single execution history and one rollback story covers all three Regions. A is incorrect because three EventBridge-chained pipelines do preserve ordering but split the deployment across three separate executions with no unified view, no single rollback, and additional failure modes in the chaining rules themselves. B is incorrect because a parallel deployment stage violates the sequential requirement outright: all three Regions receive the new version before any smoke test runs, so a bad build reaches every Region. C is incorrect because Step Functions can orchestrate this but duplicates orchestration CodePipeline already provides, giving up native artifact handling, source triggering and approval actions.

stem: A company needs to implement a chaos engineering experiment that tests their application's behavior when calls to a specific DynamoDB table experience increased latency. The experiment must be controlled, must not require application code changes, and must stop automatically if the application's error rate exceeds 5%. Which approach provides controlled, managed fault injection for this test?

options.text: Use AWS Fault Injection Service (FIS) with an experiment template that runs the aws:ssm:send-command action with the AWSFIS-Run-Network-Latency document on the hosts running the application, delaying traffic to the DynamoDB endpoint. Add a stop condition using a CloudWatch alarm on the application's error rate; FIS halts the experiment automatically when the alarm reaches 5%.

Create a Lambda function that periodically writes large items to the target DynamoDB table to consume write capacity and cause throttling. Monitor the table's ThrottledRequests metric and the application error rate. Stop the Lambda function manually if the application error rate exceeds 5%.

Modify the application's DynamoDB client to add artificial sleep delays before each API call during the experiment. Configure a feature flag in AppConfig that controls the injected latency duration. Monitor CloudWatch alarms and toggle the feature flag off if the error rate exceeds the threshold.

Deploy a DynamoDB proxy layer using AWS AppSync that intercepts all DynamoDB requests. Add artificial latency in the AppSync resolvers during the experiment window. Monitor the application error rate in CloudWatch and manually disable the latency injection if errors exceed 5%.

explanation: Option A is correct and now uses an action FIS actually supports. FIS has no DynamoDB latency action - its only DynamoDB action is aws:dynamodb:global-table-pause-replication - so latency toward a DynamoDB endpoint is injected on the client side of the call using aws:ssm:send-command with the AWSFIS-Run-Network-Latency document, which applies traffic control rules on the EC2 or ECS hosts for traffic to the specified destination. This keeps the experiment inside the managed FIS framework, so it is templated, reproducible, time-boxed, and governed by a CloudWatch alarm stop condition that halts and rolls back the experiment automatically at 5% error rate. Option B injects the wrong fault - consuming write capacity produces throttling exceptions, not latency - and it requires a human to notice the threshold and stop the Lambda, so there is no automatic stop condition. Option C violates the no-code-change constraint by putting sleep calls in the application client, and toggling a feature flag is a manual abort rather than an automated stop condition. Option D changes the production architecture just to test it, AppSync is a GraphQL API rather than a transparent DynamoDB proxy, and the abort is again manual.

stem: A company needs to implement centralized security findings management across 50 AWS accounts. Findings from GuardDuty, Inspector, Macie, IAM Access Analyzer, and Firewall Manager must be aggregated into a single dashboard with the ability to track remediation progress. Which service provides centralized finding aggregation?

options.text: Deploy Amazon Detective in the management account to aggregate and correlate security findings from all services across the organization. Detective's behavior graph provides investigation capabilities and timeline visualization for tracking security findings and their remediation across all accounts.

Create an Amazon OpenSearch Service cluster for centralized finding storage. Configure each security service across all accounts to stream findings to the OpenSearch cluster via Kinesis Data Firehose. Build OpenSearch dashboards for finding aggregation, visualization, and remediation tracking.

Deploy AWS Security Hub with organization-wide enablement using a delegated administrator account. Security Hub aggregates findings from GuardDuty, Inspector, Macie, Access Analyzer, and Firewall Manager into a unified dashboard with workflow status tracking for remediation progress across all accounts.

Configure each security service to send findings to a centralized CloudWatch Logs log group in the management account. Create CloudWatch Logs Insights dashboards that aggregate findings across all services and accounts with saved queries for tracking remediation status.

explanation: C is correct because Security Hub is the aggregation layer for AWS security findings: GuardDuty, Inspector, Macie, IAM Access Analyzer and Firewall Manager are native integrations that publish findings in the AWS Security Finding Format automatically. With an organization delegated administrator and auto-enable for new accounts, all 50 accounts roll up to a single console (and cross-Region aggregation consolidates Regions), and every finding carries a Workflow status of NEW, NOTIFIED, RESOLVED or SUPPRESSED for remediation tracking. A is incorrect because Detective ingests CloudTrail, VPC Flow Logs and GuardDuty findings to build a behavior graph for deep investigation of a specific finding; it is not a multi-service finding aggregator and has no remediation workflow states. B is incorrect because an OpenSearch cluster fed by Firehose means building and operating ingestion, index mappings, dashboards and status tracking for a capability Security Hub delivers with a setting, and several of these services do not stream to Firehose directly. D is incorrect because Logs Insights over a shared log group gives text search, not normalized ASFF findings, deduplication, severity normalization or per-finding workflow state.

stem: A company deploys infrastructure using Terraform with multiple provider configurations for different AWS regions. The team needs to ensure that provider configurations are consistent across all environments and that no developer accidentally uses a provider configuration that connects to a production region from a development workspace. Which Terraform approach prevents cross-environment provider misconfiguration?

options.text: Implement separate Terraform root modules for each environment, each with its own provider configuration hard-coded to the correct region. Developers work in their environment's directory, and the provider configuration cannot be accidentally changed because it's committed to version control.

Use Terraform workspaces combined with variable maps that select the appropriate AWS region based on the active workspace. Define a provider configuration that references the workspace-specific region variable, ensuring each workspace automatically connects to its designated environment's region.

Use Terraform Cloud with workspace-level variable sets that define the AWS region and credentials for each environment. Workspace-level variables override any local provider configuration, ensuring that operations in each workspace always target the correct environment regardless of local settings.

Create a custom Terraform provider wrapper that validates the target region against the current workspace before executing any API call. The wrapper rejects operations if the workspace name doesn't match the expected region configuration, preventing cross-environment operations.

explanation: Option A is correct and is the separation HashiCorp recommends. Separate root modules give each environment its own directory, its own backend and state, its own credentials, and a provider block whose region is committed to version control and reviewed like any other change. Targeting production then requires deliberately changing directory, so there is no in-band state a developer can get wrong. Option B is the pattern HashiCorp explicitly warns against for environment separation: all workspaces share one backend, one configuration and one set of credentials, so a stale or forgotten 'terraform workspace select' means the very next apply reaches into production with production's region resolved automatically from the map - the mechanism that is supposed to protect you is the mechanism that silently redirects you. Option C makes a false claim: Terraform Cloud variable sets supply input variables and environment variables, and they do not override a provider block, so a region written in the configuration still wins; it also requires adopting Terraform Cloud, which the stem never establishes. Option D is not implementable - providers are plugins that Terraform core invokes over a defined plugin protocol, and there is no supported interception layer that inspects the workspace name before each API call short of forking the AWS provider.

stem: A company needs to implement a saga pattern for a distributed transaction that spans three microservices: Order, Payment, and Inventory. If the Payment service fails after the Order is created, the system must automatically compensate by cancelling the order. Which AWS service orchestrates the saga pattern with compensation?

options.text: Deploy Amazon EventBridge with event-driven choreography between services. Each service publishes success or failure events. Create EventBridge rules that route failure events to compensating actions. The Payment service's failure event triggers the Order service's CancelOrder handler.

Use AWS Step Functions to orchestrate the saga workflow. Define states for CreateOrder, ProcessPayment, and ReserveInventory with catch blocks that trigger compensating transactions (CancelOrder, RefundPayment) when any step fails. Step Functions manages the state machine and error handling.

Implement a distributed transaction coordinator using DynamoDB as the transaction log. A Lambda function monitors the transaction state in DynamoDB and triggers compensating actions when any service reports a failure. DynamoDB streams notify the coordinator of state changes in real-time.

Configure SQS queues between each service pair for request and compensation messages. The Order service sends a message to the Payment queue. If Payment fails, it sends a compensation message to the Order compensation queue. Each service independently handles its compensation logic.

explanation: B is correct because Step Functions is the orchestrated-saga engine: each service call is a Task state, and Retry/Catch blocks route failures to explicit compensating Task states in a defined order, so a ProcessPayment failure after CreateOrder deterministically drives CancelOrder. The service durably holds saga state across long-running steps, and the execution history is an audit trail showing exactly which compensations ran. A is incorrect because EventBridge choreography can implement a saga, but the compensation logic is scattered across every service's rules and handlers with no central state - ordering of multi-step compensation, partial compensation failures, and debugging all become the application's problem. C is incorrect because a DynamoDB transaction log with a Lambda coordinator is a hand-built Step Functions, requiring you to implement timeouts, retries, idempotency and stuck-saga recovery yourself. D is incorrect because point-to-point SQS compensation queues share choreography's drawbacks and add none of the visibility; at-least-once delivery also makes non-idempotent compensations such as refunds hazardous.

stem: A company needs to implement log-based alerting that detects specific error patterns across multiple microservices. When a specific error message like 'ConnectionRefused' appears more than 10 times within 5 minutes across any combination of services, an alert must fire. Which CloudWatch Logs feature provides cross-service log pattern alerting?

options.text: Configure CloudWatch Logs subscription filters on each log group that forward matching 'ConnectionRefused' entries to a Kinesis Data Stream. Deploy a Lambda consumer that counts events within 5-minute tumbling windows and publishes an SNS alert when the count exceeds 10 across all services.

Enable CloudWatch Contributor Insights on all microservice log groups with a rule matching 'ConnectionRefused' entries. Contributor Insights aggregates the error occurrences across all log groups and provides a top contributors view. Create a CloudWatch alarm when the total contributor count exceeds 10.

Create a CloudWatch Logs metric filter on each microservice's log group that matches the 'ConnectionRefused' pattern. Publish a custom CloudWatch metric with a value of 1 for each match. Create a CloudWatch alarm on the SUM of the metric with a 5-minute period and threshold of 10.

Create a CloudWatch Logs Insights query that searches for 'ConnectionRefused' across all microservice log groups within a 5-minute window. Schedule the query to run every 5 minutes via EventBridge and trigger an SNS alert if the query returns more than 10 matching log entries.

explanation: C is correct because a metric filter on each log group can publish to the same metric namespace and metric name, so CloudWatch aggregates matches from all microservices into one time series. An alarm on the SUM statistic with a 5-minute period and a threshold of 10 then fires on the combined cross-service count, with no polling, no glue code and no per-query scan cost. A is incorrect because subscription filters into a Kinesis Data Stream plus a windowing Lambda consumer would work but means operating a stream, handling shard scaling, checkpointing and tumbling-window boundaries for something metric filters do natively. B is incorrect because Contributor Insights ranks top contributors by a dimension (which host, which IP is causing the errors) and its rule metrics are UniqueContributors, MaxContributorValue and SampleCount - it is not designed for a simple total-count threshold, and it bills per log event processed. D is incorrect because Logs Insights is an interactive, ad-hoc query engine; scheduling it every five minutes adds Lambda glue, incurs a data-scan charge on every run, and query concurrency limits and timeouts make it unreliable as a continuous alarm source.

stem: A company needs to implement a deployment approval workflow where deployments to production require approval from at least 2 out of 3 designated approvers. The pipeline must wait for the required approvals and proceed automatically once 2 approvals are received. Which CodePipeline configuration supports multi-approver workflows?

options.text: Configure a manual approval action in CodePipeline with an SNS topic that notifies all three approvers. The first approver to approve or reject determines the action outcome. To require multiple approvals, create two sequential approval actions, each notifying different approver subsets.

Deploy a custom approval workflow using Step Functions integrated with CodePipeline. The workflow sends approval requests to all three approvers via email, tracks responses in DynamoDB, and signals CodePipeline approval when 2 out of 3 responses are received within the timeout period.

Configure CodePipeline with a Lambda invoke action that creates approval requests in a custom DynamoDB-backed approval system. The Lambda function polls DynamoDB for approval responses every minute and returns success to CodePipeline when 2 approvals are recorded from the 3 designated approvers.

Create three parallel manual approval actions in a single CodePipeline stage. Each action is assigned to one of the three approvers. CodePipeline requires all parallel actions to succeed for the stage to pass. Configure two of the three to be required and one optional using action run conditions.

explanation: Step Functions with CodePipeline integration provides custom approval logic including multi-approver tracking. The workflow manages approval collection in DynamoDB and signals CodePipeline when the 2-of-3 threshold is met. Option A's sequential approvals require both to approve (not 2-of-3 selection). Option C builds a similar custom system but without Step Functions' built-in waiting and state management. Option D's parallel actions require all to pass; CodePipeline doesn't support optional parallel actions natively.

stem: A company needs to implement automated capacity scaling during incidents. When an Incident Manager incident is created with severity 'Critical', the system must automatically scale up the application's ECS service desired count by 50% and increase the Aurora cluster's read replica count by 2. Which approach automates incident-driven capacity scaling?

options.text: Create an EventBridge rule matching Incident Manager incident creation events with Critical severity. The rule triggers a Step Functions workflow that parallel-executes ECS service scaling via UpdateService API and Aurora replica creation via CreateDBInstance API, with error handling for each action.

Configure CloudWatch composite alarms that trigger both the incident creation in Incident Manager and scaling actions simultaneously. The alarm actions include Lambda functions that scale ECS services and Aurora replicas independently of the incident management workflow.

Configure Incident Manager response plans with SSM Automation runbooks that execute scaling actions. The runbook includes steps to call ECS UpdateService to increase desired count and RDS CreateDBInstanceReadReplica to add Aurora replicas. The runbook executes automatically when the incident is created.

Deploy an Auto Scaling policy on the ECS service triggered by a custom CloudWatch metric that represents incident severity. When Incident Manager creates a Critical incident, a Lambda function publishes a high-value metric that triggers the scaling policy to increase the desired count by 50%.

explanation: C is correct because an Incident Manager response plan can reference SSM Automation runbooks that start automatically when an incident is created against that plan, so no separate event plumbing is needed. The runbook's aws:executeAwsApi steps call ECS UpdateService with the increased desiredCount and RDS CreateDBInstanceReadReplica for the two additional Aurora replicas, and the run's progress and output are attached to the incident so responders can see what the automation did. A is incorrect because an EventBridge rule feeding Step Functions reimplements the response-plan-to-runbook integration Incident Manager already provides, and the automation's status would not appear on the incident record. B is incorrect because firing scaling from the alarm in parallel with incident creation decouples the scaling from the incident lifecycle: it scales even when no Critical incident is declared, and no record of the action is attached to the incident. D is incorrect because publishing a synthetic severity metric so an Application Auto Scaling policy reacts is indirect and imprecise - target-tracking and step policies compute their own capacity from the metric, so a literal +50% is not expressible - and it does nothing at all for the Aurora read replicas.

stem: A company needs to implement a canary analysis pipeline stage that compares the new version's performance metrics against the current production version using statistical analysis. The canary must run for 30 minutes with 10% traffic before an automated go/no-go decision is returned to the pipeline. The team wants to achieve this with the LEAST custom development. Which approach implements statistical canary analysis in the deployment pipeline?

options.text: Deploy a Lambda function that collects CloudWatch metrics from both the canary and baseline versions during the 30-minute window. The function performs a Mann-Whitney U statistical test comparing the metric distributions and publishes a pass/fail result to CodePipeline for automated decision making.

Deploy Kayenta (open-source canary analysis tool) alongside the pipeline. Kayenta collects metrics from both canary and baseline versions, performs automated statistical comparison using configurable scoring, and reports a canary health score. Integrate Kayenta's verdict into CodePipeline via Lambda.

Configure CodeDeploy with a Canary10Percent30Minutes deployment for an ECS service. Add CloudWatch alarms on error rate and latency metrics. CodeDeploy monitors the alarms during the 30-minute canary window and automatically rolls back if any alarm breaches the static threshold.

Create a Step Functions workflow that deploys the canary version with 10% traffic. The workflow waits 30 minutes, then queries CloudWatch metrics for both versions. A comparison Lambda calculates the average difference between canary and baseline metrics and approves if within 10% tolerance.

Configure API Gateway canary settings to route 10% of traffic to the new deployment. Use CloudWatch Contributor Insights to compare the top latency contributors between canary and baseline versions. After 30 minutes, review the Contributor Insights report to decide whether to promote the canary.

explanation: Option B is correct. Kayenta, the automated canary analysis service from the Spinnaker project, is purpose-built for exactly this problem: it queries the same metrics for the canary and baseline groups over a configured interval, applies a configurable statistical comparison per metric, and emits an aggregate canary score against a pass threshold. It is off-the-shelf software, so the only code the team writes is a thin Lambda that relays the verdict as a CodePipeline job result - the least custom development of the options that actually compare against a baseline. Option A does satisfy the statistical requirement but requires the team to build and own metric collection, the Mann-Whitney U implementation, thresholding and pipeline signalling, which is the most custom development on offer. Option C is disqualified by the stem: CodeDeploy's Canary10Percent30Minutes evaluates static CloudWatch alarm thresholds against the new version alone and never compares it to the production baseline, so it performs no statistical analysis. Option D is both custom orchestration and statistically unsound - comparing means with a flat 10% tolerance ignores variance and sample size, so it is not a statistical test. Option E ends in a human reading a report rather than an automated decision, and Contributor Insights ranks top contributors to a log-derived metric; it does not perform a canary-versus-baseline hypothesis test.

stem: A company needs to implement infrastructure testing for their Terraform configurations. The tests must verify that deployed infrastructure actually works correctly (not just that the template is valid). Security groups must allow expected traffic, IAM roles must have correct permissions, and endpoints must be reachable. Which testing approach validates deployed infrastructure behavior?

options.text: Run terraform validate and terraform plan to verify configuration syntax and preview changes. Use tfsec to scan for security misconfigurations. Combine these pre-deployment checks in the CI/CD pipeline to catch issues before any infrastructure is deployed to AWS.

Use Terratest (a Go testing framework) to write integration tests that deploy infrastructure using Terraform, run validation checks against the deployed resources (HTTP requests, SSH connections, IAM policy simulation), and then destroy the infrastructure after tests pass.

Use Terraform's built-in check blocks and precondition/postcondition assertions to validate resource attributes after deployment. Check blocks verify that outputs match expected values and postconditions ensure deployed resources have the correct configuration properties.

Deploy the Terraform configuration to a sandbox account and run InSpec compliance profiles against the deployed resources. InSpec tests verify security group rules, IAM permissions, and endpoint connectivity. Destroy the sandbox environment after validation completes successfully.

explanation: Terratest deploys real infrastructure, runs behavioral tests (HTTP requests, SSH, API calls) against it, and tears it down. This validates that deployed infrastructure actually works, not just that the configuration is syntactically correct. Option B only validates configuration files, not deployed behavior. Option C uses InSpec which tests compliance properties but Terratest is the standard for full Terraform integration testing. Option D's check blocks verify attributes but don't perform behavioral testing like making HTTP requests or testing connectivity.

stem: A company's application depends on an Amazon ElastiCache Redis cluster for caching. During a Redis node failure, the application must gracefully degrade by serving requests directly from the database instead of failing completely. Which application architecture pattern implements graceful cache degradation?

options.text: Deploy a read-through caching layer using DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) in front of the database. DAX provides a fully managed caching layer with built-in high availability. Replace ElastiCache Redis with DAX to eliminate the need for application-level cache degradation handling.

Deploy ElastiCache with Multi-AZ and automatic failover enabled. During a node failure, the replica is automatically promoted to primary within seconds. The application's Redis client library reconnects to the new primary endpoint, resuming cached reads without requiring database fallback.

Configure the application to use Redis Sentinel mode that monitors Redis node health. When Sentinel detects a node failure, it triggers a custom failover script that switches the application's cache endpoint to a backup Redis cluster running on EC2 instances in a separate Availability Zone.

Implement a cache-aside pattern with fallback logic in the application. When the Redis call fails or times out (with a short timeout of 500ms), the application catches the exception and queries the database directly. Log the cache miss for monitoring while continuing to serve the user request.

explanation: D is correct because graceful degradation is an application-side property: with cache-aside plus a short 500 ms client timeout wrapped in a try/catch, a Redis node failure or failover window becomes a slightly slower request served from the database rather than a user-visible error, and logging the fallback keeps the degradation measurable. This is the only option that keeps requests succeeding while the cache is genuinely unavailable. A is incorrect because DAX is a DynamoDB-specific accelerator that sits only in front of DynamoDB; it cannot cache arbitrary relational queries, and replacing the cache tier still leaves the question of behavior when that tier is down unanswered. B is incorrect because Multi-AZ with automatic failover shortens the outage but does not remove it - calls still fail during replica promotion and client topology refresh, and the requirement is explicitly about behaving correctly when Redis calls fail. C is incorrect because ElastiCache manages failover itself and does not expose Redis Sentinel; running Sentinel with a custom failover script against a self-managed backup cluster is unsupported, duplicates managed functionality, and introduces split-brain risk.

stem: A company needs to implement end-user experience monitoring for their web application. The monitoring must capture real user metrics including page load time, time to first byte, first contentful paint, and JavaScript errors from actual browser sessions. Which AWS service provides real user monitoring?

options.text: Deploy Amazon CloudWatch RUM (Real User Monitoring) by adding the CloudWatch RUM web client snippet to the application's HTML pages. RUM collects performance metrics and errors from actual user browser sessions and publishes them to CloudWatch for dashboarding and alerting.

Enable CloudFront real-time logs that capture viewer request and response metrics including TTFB and transfer time. Stream the logs to Kinesis Data Firehose for analysis in Amazon Athena. Calculate page load metrics from the CloudFront log data for user experience monitoring.

Deploy the CloudWatch agent on the application's web servers to collect server-side response time metrics. Configure the agent to capture HTTP request duration, response codes, and server processing time. Publish these metrics to CloudWatch for server-side performance monitoring and alerting.

Configure CloudWatch Synthetics canaries that simulate user interactions with the web application from multiple regions. The canaries measure page load time, TTFB, and FCP using headless Chrome browsers and report performance metrics to CloudWatch for monitoring and alerting.

explanation: A is correct: the CloudWatch RUM web client runs in the visitor's browser, reads the Navigation Timing, Paint Timing and Performance Observer APIs, and reports page load time, TTFB, FCP and uncaught JavaScript errors from real sessions to CloudWatch for dashboards and alarms. B is incorrect because CloudFront real-time logs contain only edge-side fields such as time-taken and bytes; the edge cannot observe browser rendering milestones like FCP or client-side JS exceptions. C is incorrect because the CloudWatch agent measures server-side processing on the web tier and sees nothing that happens after the response leaves the server. D is incorrect because Synthetics canaries are scripted headless-browser probes from fixed AWS locations — synthetic measurements that miss the device, network, geography and browser diversity that defines real user monitoring.

stem: A company is migrating their CI/CD pipeline from Jenkins to AWS-native services. The Jenkins pipeline builds Docker images, runs unit and integration tests, performs SAST scanning, and deploys to Amazon ECS. The company keeps its source code in GitHub and its packages in an existing JFrog Artifactory repository, and will continue to use both after the migration. Which two AWS services replace Jenkins pipeline orchestration and Jenkins build and test execution? (Choose two.)

options.text: AWS CodePipeline replaces Jenkins pipeline orchestration for defining the CI/CD workflow stages. CodePipeline manages the source, build, test, and deploy stages with integrations to CodeBuild, CodeDeploy, and third-party tools, replacing Jenkins pipeline-as-code definitions.

AWS CodeBuild replaces Jenkins build agents for compiling code, building Docker images, running unit and integration tests, and performing SAST scanning. CodeBuild provides managed build environments with Docker support and scales automatically without maintaining build server infrastructure.

AWS CodeCommit replaces Jenkins source code management integration. CodeCommit provides Git-based repositories that integrate natively with CodePipeline, replacing Jenkins SCM plugins for source code checkout and webhook-triggered builds from repository events.

AWS CodeArtifact replaces Jenkins artifact management for storing build outputs. CodeArtifact provides managed repositories for npm, Maven, and Python packages, replacing Jenkins artifact archiving and providing dependency caching for faster builds across the CI/CD pipeline.

AWS CodeDeploy replaces Jenkins deployment plugins for managing ECS deployments. CodeDeploy provides blue/green and rolling deployment strategies for ECS services with automatic rollback capabilities, replacing Jenkins deployment scripts and manual deployment orchestration.

explanation: The stem asks for the two services that take over the two named Jenkins responsibilities: pipeline orchestration and build/test execution. Option A covers orchestration - CodePipeline models the stages, their order, transitions and approvals, and invokes the action providers, which is what a Jenkinsfile's stage graph did. Option B covers execution - CodeBuild runs the buildspec in a managed container with Docker support, so compiling, building images, running unit and integration tests and invoking a SAST tool all move onto CodeBuild instead of self-managed Jenkins agents. Option C is source control, which the migration does not need: the company keeps GitHub, CodePipeline connects to it directly through AWS CodeConnections, and CodeCommit is in any case closed to new customers. Option D is package repository management, and the company is keeping JFrog Artifactory; CodeArtifact also runs no build or test steps and orchestrates nothing. Option E is a real and useful part of the target architecture for the ECS blue/green rollout, but deployment is neither orchestration nor build/test execution, so it is outside what the stem asks for.

stem: A company's Lambda function processes messages from a Kinesis Data Stream. Occasionally, a single malformed record in the stream causes the Lambda function to throw an error, blocking all subsequent records in the shard from being processed. The team needs the function to skip problematic records while continuing to process valid ones. Which Lambda event source mapping configuration handles poison pill records?

options.text: Configure the Lambda event source mapping with bisect-on-function-error enabled and maximum retry attempts of 2. When a batch fails, Lambda splits the batch in half and retries each half separately. This isolates the problematic record into increasingly smaller batches until it can be identified and skipped.

Configure the Lambda event source mapping with a maximum record age of 60 seconds. Records older than 60 seconds are automatically expired from the event source mapping and skipped. This prevents any single record from blocking the stream for more than 60 seconds.

Implement try-catch error handling in the Lambda function code that catches exceptions for individual record processing. When a record fails, log the error and continue processing the remaining records in the batch. Return a partial batch response indicating which records succeeded.

Configure the Lambda event source mapping with a destination for failures pointing to an SQS queue. After the maximum retry attempts, Lambda sends the failed batch metadata to the SQS destination and advances the stream iterator past the problematic records to continue processing.

explanation: A is correct: with BisectBatchOnFunctionError the event source mapping splits a failing batch in half and retries each half independently; repeated halving isolates the single poison record, and once MaximumRetryAttempts (2) is exhausted for that sub-batch Lambda discards it (to the on-failure destination if configured) and advances the shard iterator so valid records keep flowing. B is incorrect because MaximumRecordAgeInSeconds expires records purely by age, discarding every valid record that ages out behind the blockage — data loss, not isolation. C is incorrect because in-handler try/catch cannot cover failures outside the handler (runtime deserialization, out-of-memory, timeout), and the question asks for event source mapping configuration, not application code. D is incorrect because an on-failure destination without bisecting records metadata for the whole failed batch, so the poison record is never isolated and every good record in that batch is dropped with it.

stem: A company needs to implement a zero-trust network model for their ECS services where every service-to-service communication is authenticated and authorized. Services must present verifiable identity credentials, and authorization decisions must be based on the calling service's identity, not network location. Which AWS service implements service-to-service authentication for ECS?

options.text: Deploy AWS App Mesh with mutual TLS authentication between all virtual services. App Mesh's Envoy proxy sidecars authenticate service identity using X.509 certificates issued by ACM Private CA. Authorization policies control which services can communicate based on verified service identities.

Configure security groups for each ECS service that restrict inbound traffic to specific security group IDs. Security group references verify the source service's identity at the network level, ensuring only authorized services can establish connections to the target service.

Deploy Amazon VPC Lattice with service network policies that authenticate and authorize service-to-service communication. VPC Lattice uses IAM-based authentication where each ECS service assumes a role, and service network policies evaluate IAM identity for authorization decisions.

Implement API Gateway with Lambda authorizers between all ECS services. Each service call goes through API Gateway which validates a JWT token issued to the calling service. The Lambda authorizer verifies the token's claims and generates an IAM policy allowing or denying access.

explanation: VPC Lattice provides native service-to-service authentication using IAM-based identity. Services authenticate with their IAM role, and service network policies authorize communication based on the calling service's IAM identity, implementing zero-trust principles. Option A uses App Mesh with mTLS which provides transport-level authentication but not IAM-based authorization policies. Option B uses security groups which are network-based, not identity-based access control. Option D adds API Gateway between every service which adds latency and complexity.

stem: A company uses CloudFormation and needs to update their stack without any downtime. The stack includes an ALB, ECS service, and RDS database. The update changes the ECS task definition and adds a new CloudWatch alarm. Which CloudFormation update strategy minimizes deployment risk?

options.text: Create a CloudFormation change set from the updated template. Review the change set to verify which resources will be modified, replaced, or added. Execute the change set only after confirming that no resources will be replaced or deleted unexpectedly during the update operation.

Delete the existing CloudFormation stack and create a new stack with the updated template. This ensures a clean deployment without update complications. Use the DeletionPolicy: Retain attribute on the RDS database to preserve data during the stack deletion and recreation process.

Run terraform import to bring the CloudFormation-managed resources under Terraform management temporarily. Make the changes using Terraform's plan and apply workflow which provides more granular control over resource updates. Migrate back to CloudFormation after the update.

Update the stack directly using the aws cloudformation update-stack CLI command with the new template. CloudFormation automatically determines the minimum changes needed and applies them. If the update fails, CloudFormation automatically rolls back all changes to the previous stack state.

explanation: A is correct: a change set is a dry run — CloudFormation computes the resource-level diff, labels each entry Add, Modify or Remove, and for Modify reports whether Replacement is True, False or Conditional. Reviewing it surfaces any property change that would replace a resource and cause downtime, so the template can be fixed before anything is touched. B is incorrect because deleting the stack destroys the ALB and ECS service outright; DeletionPolicy: Retain merely orphans the RDS instance, which is then unmanaged and must be re-imported. C is incorrect because moving a live stack into Terraform and back adds enormous risk and effort for a routine task-definition and alarm change. D is incorrect because update-stack applies the diff blind — the first sign of an unintended replacement is the replacement itself, and automatic rollback does not undo the outage that already happened.

stem: A company needs to implement automated recovery for their EC2-based application when the underlying host hardware fails. The application stores state in EBS volumes. Recovery must preserve the EBS volumes and the instance's Elastic IP address. Which EC2 feature provides automated host-failure recovery?

options.text: Configure an EventBridge rule matching EC2 instance state change events for the specific instance. When the instance transitions to 'stopped' due to hardware failure, the rule triggers a Lambda function that starts the instance and reassociates the Elastic IP if it was disassociated.

Configure EC2 auto-recovery using a CloudWatch alarm that monitors the StatusCheckFailed_System metric. When the system status check fails (indicating host hardware issues), the alarm action triggers EC2 instance recovery which relaunches the instance on new hardware with the same EBS volumes and EIP.

Enable EC2 instance store-backed automatic recovery in the instance's placement group. When a host failure is detected, EC2 automatically migrates the instance to a healthy host within the same placement group, preserving the instance's memory state, EBS volumes, and network configuration.

Deploy the EC2 instance in an Auto Scaling group with minimum, maximum, and desired capacity all set to 1. When the instance fails a health check, Auto Scaling terminates the failed instance and launches a replacement instance. Configure the ASG to use the same EBS volumes and EIP.

explanation: B is correct: a CloudWatch alarm on StatusCheckFailed_System with the ec2:recover action triggers EC2 automatic recovery, migrating the instance to healthy hardware while keeping the same instance ID, private IPv4 address, Elastic IP association, EBS volume attachments and instance metadata — exactly what the requirement preserves. A is incorrect because host hardware failure surfaces as a failed system status check rather than a clean transition to 'stopped', so the state-change rule usually never fires, and it cannot help an instance that is impaired but still running. C is incorrect because no 'instance store-backed automatic recovery' exists in placement groups, and live migration preserving memory state is not offered for standard EC2 instances. D is incorrect because an ASG replaces the instance with a brand-new one — new instance ID, fresh root volume from the AMI — and cannot reattach a specific pre-existing EBS volume or EIP without extra lifecycle-hook automation.

stem: A company runs a multi-tenant SaaS application and needs to track per-tenant resource consumption for billing purposes. Each tenant's API requests, compute time, storage usage, and data transfer must be individually metered. Which approach implements per-tenant usage metering?

options.text: Publish per-tenant custom CloudWatch metrics using Embedded Metric Format with a TenantId dimension. Each API request logs tenant-specific resource consumption (compute time, storage, transfer) as EMF metrics. Use CloudWatch metric math to aggregate per-tenant monthly consumption for billing.

Configure AWS Marketplace Metering Service to report per-tenant usage. The application calls the MeterUsage API for each tenant after processing requests, reporting consumption dimensions like API calls, compute hours, and data transfer. Marketplace handles billing based on metered usage.

Deploy a custom metering Lambda function triggered by each API request. The function records tenant ID, resource type, and consumption amount in a DynamoDB table partitioned by tenant. A monthly Lambda function aggregates each tenant's consumption from DynamoDB and generates billing reports.

Enable AWS Cost Explorer with cost allocation tags. Tag all resources with a TenantId tag. Cost Explorer aggregates costs by tenant tag, providing per-tenant resource consumption breakdowns for API compute, storage, and data transfer that can be used for tenant billing calculations.

explanation: A is correct: EMF lets the request handler write one structured JSON log line carrying the raw consumption values plus a TenantId dimension. CloudWatch extracts these into metrics with no PutMetricData request charge, and metric math rolls each tenant's monthly totals up for invoicing. Tenant context is attached where the work happens, the only place API count, compute time, storage delta and transfer are attributable. B is incorrect because the Marketplace Metering Service (MeterUsage) reports usage only for subscriptions sold through AWS Marketplace; it cannot bill tenants the company contracts with directly. C is incorrect because it re-implements metric aggregation on DynamoDB — a write per request, tenant-partition hot spotting, and a custom monthly rollup job — to produce what EMF plus metric math already gives. D is incorrect because cost allocation tags report AWS spend, not application usage, and shared resources such as one ECS service or DynamoDB table cannot be split per tenant by tag.

stem: A company needs to implement artifact promotion across environments. Build artifacts created in the dev environment must be promoted to staging and then to production without rebuilding. Each environment must verify the artifact's integrity before deployment. Which artifact management approach ensures consistent artifact promotion?

options.text: Store build artifacts in Amazon S3 with versioning enabled. Tag artifacts with environment metadata (dev-approved, staging-approved). Each environment's pipeline verifies the S3 object version and tag before deployment. Promote by adding environment tags, never by rebuilding the artifact.

Push container images to a single Amazon ECR repository with environment-specific tags (v1.2.3-dev, v1.2.3-staging, v1.2.3-prod). Each environment's pipeline pulls the image by its environment-specific tag. Promote by retagging the image for the next environment without rebuilding.

Store artifacts in separate S3 buckets per environment (dev-artifacts, staging-artifacts, prod-artifacts). The dev pipeline builds and uploads to the dev bucket. Promotion copies the artifact between buckets. Each environment's pipeline downloads from its dedicated artifact bucket for deployment.

Use AWS CodeArtifact to store build packages. Publish the artifact to a dev repository. Each environment has its own CodeArtifact repository. Promote artifacts by copying from the dev repository to staging repository to production repository using the CopyPackageVersions API.

explanation: B is correct: pushing once and then adding tags promotes the identical manifest and layers — the immutable sha256 digest never changes, so production runs bit-for-bit what dev validated, and each pipeline can resolve and pin that digest as its integrity check. Nothing is rebuilt, so no dependency or base-image drift creeps in. A is incorrect because S3 object tags are mutable metadata on an artifact identified by version ID rather than content hash; integrity checking requires separately tracked checksums, and the scheme does not address container deployment. C is incorrect because copying between per-environment buckets creates a new object in each bucket, duplicating storage and destroying the single-identity guarantee — a copy can diverge from its source undetected. D is incorrect because CodeArtifact is a package repository for build-time dependencies (npm, Maven, PyPI); CopyPackageVersions promotes libraries, not deployable container images.

stem: A company needs to implement an automated runbook that diagnoses why an ECS service's tasks are failing to start. The runbook must check common failure causes: insufficient capacity, image pull failures, IAM role issues, and security group misconfigurations. Which service automates this diagnostic runbook?

options.text: Create a CloudWatch dashboard that displays ECS service events, task stop reasons, ECR pull metrics, IAM authentication failures, and VPC flow log data. Operations teams manually review the dashboard when task failures occur to diagnose the root cause from the consolidated metrics view.

Create an SSM Automation document with sequential steps that: query ECS service events for failure messages, check the cluster's available CPU and memory capacity, verify ECR image accessibility, validate the task IAM role permissions, and test security group connectivity using VPC Reachability Analyzer.

Configure ECS Service Connect health checks that monitor task startup behavior. Service Connect automatically detects common startup failures and generates detailed diagnostic reports including image pull errors, IAM permission denials, and network connectivity issues for each failed task.

Deploy a Lambda function triggered by ECS task state change events for STOPPED status. The function queries the ECS DescribeTasks API to get the stop reason, checks CloudWatch Logs for container agent errors, and publishes a diagnostic report to an SNS topic with identified failure causes.

explanation: B is correct: an SSM Automation runbook encodes the diagnostic sequence as versioned, parameterized, ordered steps. aws:executeAwsApi steps call DescribeServices/DescribeTasks for stop reasons, DescribeClusters and DescribeContainerInstances for remaining CPU and memory, and ECR/IAM APIs to test image accessibility and role permissions, while aws:executeScript starts a Reachability Analyzer path analysis. It runs identically for any operator and can be triggered from EventBridge or an OpsItem. A is incorrect because a dashboard only co-locates telemetry — a human still performs every diagnostic step, so nothing is automated. C is incorrect because ECS Service Connect provides service discovery and traffic telemetry for already-running tasks; it does not diagnose why tasks fail to start and emits no such report. D is incorrect because the Lambda covers only stop reasons and log scraping, never checking cluster capacity, IAM permissions or security group reachability, so it is a notifier rather than the multi-cause runbook required.

stem: A company needs to ensure that EC2 instances can only access specific S3 buckets through a VPC endpoint, and that the S3 buckets can only be accessed from the VPC (not from the public internet). Which combination of policies enforces bidirectional access restriction?

options.text: Configure a security group on the VPC endpoint that restricts inbound traffic to specific EC2 instance security groups. Configure the S3 bucket policy with a condition requiring the x-amz-source-account header to match the AWS account ID, ensuring only authorized accounts access the bucket.

Configure the VPC endpoint policy to allow access only to the specific S3 bucket ARNs. Configure the S3 bucket policy with a condition that denies all access unless the request comes through the VPC endpoint (aws:sourceVpce condition). This enforces restrictions in both directions.

Configure the VPC endpoint with a route table association limited to specific subnets. Create an S3 bucket policy that allows access only from the VPC's CIDR range using the aws:SourceIp condition. This restricts which instances can reach S3 and which networks S3 accepts traffic from.

Attach an IAM policy to the EC2 instance role that allows s3:GetObject and s3:PutObject only on the specific bucket ARNs. Configure the S3 bucket ACL to grant access only to the EC2 instance role's canonical user ID for bucket-level access control.

explanation: B is correct: the two policies constrain opposite ends of the path. The VPC endpoint policy is evaluated on every request traversing the endpoint, so scoping it to specific bucket ARNs stops instances reaching any other bucket through it. The bucket policy's explicit Deny with StringNotEquals on aws:SourceVpce rejects any request that did not arrive via that endpoint, blocking the internet and other networks. Together the restriction is bidirectional. A is incorrect because a gateway endpoint for S3 has no security group — it works through route table entries — and x-amz-source-account is not a network-path condition. C is incorrect because aws:SourceIp evaluates the public source IP; requests via a VPC endpoint do not present the VPC CIDR to S3, so the condition never matches and access simply breaks. D is incorrect because IAM policies and bucket ACLs authorize principals, not network paths — the bucket stays reachable from the internet, and ACLs cannot reference IAM roles.

stem: A company needs to manage environment-specific secrets (database URLs, API keys) for CloudFormation stacks across dev, staging, and production environments. Secrets must not be hardcoded in templates or committed to version control. The values are set once by the platform team and do not require automatic rotation or cross-account sharing, and with several hundred secrets across the three environments the company wants the LOWEST ongoing storage cost. Which approach securely provides environment-specific secrets to CloudFormation stacks?

options.text: Store secrets in AWS Secrets Manager with environment-prefixed names (/dev/db-url, /staging/db-url, /prod/db-url). Reference secrets in CloudFormation templates using dynamic references ({{resolve:secretsmanager:/dev/db-url:SecretString}}). CloudFormation resolves the reference at deployment time without exposing the value.

Store secrets in a KMS-encrypted S3 object per environment. Create a Lambda-backed custom resource that retrieves and decrypts the secrets from S3 during stack creation. The custom resource passes the decrypted values to other resources as outputs within the CloudFormation stack.

Create a CloudFormation template parameter for each secret with the NoEcho attribute set to true. Pass secret values as parameter overrides in the deployment command. NoEcho prevents the values from being displayed in the console or CloudFormation events, protecting them from exposure.

Store secrets in AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store as SecureString parameters encrypted with KMS. Reference parameters in CloudFormation using dynamic references ({{resolve:ssm-secure:/dev/db-url}}). CloudFormation resolves the encrypted parameter at deployment time without storing the value in the template.

explanation: Option D is correct. SecureString parameters in Parameter Store are KMS-encrypted at rest, are IAM- and path-scoped per environment, and are resolved by CloudFormation at deploy time through the {{resolve:ssm-secure:...}} dynamic reference, so no value ever appears in the template or in version control. Standard-tier parameters carry no per-parameter monthly charge, which is what makes this the lowest-cost option for several hundred static secrets. Option A is technically equivalent in security and resolution mechanics, and would be preferred if rotation, cross-account sharing or generated passwords were needed - but Secrets Manager bills roughly $0.40 per secret per month plus API charges, so at this scale it loses on the stated cost requirement while its differentiating rotation feature goes unused. Option B builds a custom resource to do what dynamic references do natively, and worse, custom resource response data is stored in the stack and readable via DescribeStackResource, so the decrypted secrets end up exposed. Option C only masks values in the console and in DescribeStacks output; the secrets still have to be supplied on the deploy command line, where they land in shell history and CI job logs, and NoEcho does nothing to solve where the values are stored between deployments.

stem: A company's API receives traffic from clients worldwide and needs to minimize latency for all users. The API backend runs on ECS in us-east-1. The team wants to reduce latency for users in Europe and Asia-Pacific without deploying the backend in multiple regions. Which AWS service reduces global client latency for a single-region backend?

options.text: Deploy AWS Global Accelerator with an endpoint group pointing to the ALB in us-east-1. Global Accelerator routes client traffic through the nearest AWS edge location and uses the AWS backbone network to reach us-east-1, reducing internet latency for European and Asia-Pacific users.

Deploy API Gateway edge-optimized endpoint in front of the ECS backend. Edge-optimized API Gateway uses CloudFront edge locations to accept API requests closest to the client, then routes to the us-east-1 backend through the AWS network for reduced internet traversal latency.

Place Amazon CloudFront in front of the ALB with caching enabled for API responses. CloudFront serves cached responses from edge locations nearest to users, reducing latency for repeated requests. Configure appropriate cache TTLs based on API response freshness requirements.

Configure Route 53 latency-based routing with health checks for the ALB endpoint. Route 53 routes users to the lowest-latency AWS endpoint. Since only us-east-1 exists, all traffic routes there, but Route 53's latency measurement provides optimal DNS resolution performance.
