explanation: A is correct: Global Accelerator advertises two static anycast IPs from AWS edge locations, so a client in Frankfurt or Singapore enters the AWS network after a short internet hop and the rest of the distance to the us-east-1 ALB travels the AWS backbone. Internet hops, loss and jitter drop for every request — cacheable or not — while the ALB and ECS backend are unchanged. B is incorrect because an edge-optimized API Gateway endpoint forces all traffic through API Gateway, adding a managed-service hop, per-request charges and a 29-second integration limit, and requires re-fronting the existing ALB architecture. C is incorrect because CloudFront only helps when a response is cacheable; dynamic per-user API responses hit the origin every time. D is incorrect because latency-based routing selects among multiple regional endpoints — with only us-east-1 deployed every answer is identical — and DNS never changes the network path.

stem: A company needs to detect configuration drift in their production environment. When someone manually modifies an AWS resource that is managed by CloudFormation, the change must be detected within 15 minutes and an alert sent to the operations team. Which approach detects configuration drift in near-real-time?

options.text: Deploy CloudFormation Guard policies that validate resource configurations against expected values. Run cfn-guard validate on a 15-minute schedule that compares actual resource configurations (retrieved via describe APIs) against the expected configurations defined in the CloudFormation templates.

Schedule CloudFormation drift detection on all production stacks using an EventBridge rule that triggers every 15 minutes. The rule invokes a Lambda function that calls DetectStackDrift for each stack and sends SNS alerts when drift is detected on any stack resource.

Enable AWS Config continuous recording for all resource types. Create AWS Config rules that compare the current resource configuration against the CloudFormation template's expected configuration. Config evaluates changes within minutes and flags drifted resources as non-compliant.

Create EventBridge rules matching CloudTrail API events for resource modification actions (ModifyDBInstance, UpdateSecurityGroup, PutBucketPolicy). The rules trigger a Lambda function that checks if the modified resource is part of a CloudFormation stack and alerts if the change was not made through CloudFormation.

explanation: EventBridge with CloudTrail API event matching detects resource modifications in near-real-time. The Lambda function determines if the modified resource belongs to a CloudFormation stack, providing immediate drift detection. Option B runs drift detection every 15 minutes which meets the SLA but is less immediate than event-driven detection. Option C uses Config which evaluates changes but can't directly determine if a change was made outside CloudFormation. Option D requires custom tooling to compare describe API output against templates.

stem: A company needs to implement a testing strategy where every pull request automatically deploys a temporary preview environment that reviewers can access. The environment must be destroyed automatically when the pull request is merged or closed. Which approach creates ephemeral PR preview environments?

options.text: Use AWS Amplify hosting with branch previews enabled. Amplify automatically creates a preview deployment for each pull request branch with a unique URL. When the pull request is merged or closed, Amplify automatically deletes the preview deployment and its associated resources.

Configure CodeBuild to trigger on pull request events. The buildspec creates a CloudFormation stack named with the PR number, deploys the application, and comments the preview URL on the pull request. A Lambda function triggered by PR close/merge events deletes the corresponding CloudFormation stack.

Create a CodePipeline for each active pull request using a Lambda function triggered by PR events. Each pipeline deploys to a unique ECS service. When the PR is merged, another Lambda function deletes the pipeline and associated ECS resources to clean up the preview environment.

Deploy an EKS cluster with a namespace per pull request. Use Argo CD to automatically create a namespace and deploy the PR branch when a pull request is opened. Argo CD deletes the namespace when the PR is merged, cleaning up all Kubernetes resources in the PR-specific namespace.

explanation: B is correct: a CodeBuild project subscribed to pull-request events builds the branch and deploys a CloudFormation stack named for the PR, so each PR gets a fully isolated set of real AWS resources; the buildspec posts the URL back as a PR comment, and a Lambda on the PR closed/merged event calls DeleteStack, guaranteeing teardown with no orphaned environments. A is incorrect because Amplify Hosting PR previews cover only Amplify-hosted web apps and Amplify-defined backends — they cannot stand up an arbitrary application's VPC, ECS services or databases. C is incorrect because creating and destroying an entire CodePipeline per pull request is heavyweight, slow, and quickly hits pipeline-per-account quotas for something that lives only as long as a review. D is incorrect because it presumes an EKS platform, and Argo CD does not create per-PR namespaces on its own — that needs an ApplicationSet with a pull-request generator.

stem: A company experienced a production outage caused by an expired TLS certificate on their ALB. The team needs to implement proactive monitoring that alerts 30 days before any ACM certificate expires, with escalation to the security team at 7 days. Which monitoring approach provides certificate expiration alerting?

options.text: Enable ACM certificate renewal notifications in the ACM console. ACM automatically sends email notifications to the domain owner when certificates approach expiration. Configure the domain owner email to forward to both the operations team and security team distribution lists.

Deploy a Lambda function on a daily schedule that calls the ACM ListCertificates and DescribeCertificate APIs. The function calculates days until expiration for each certificate and sends SNS notifications at the 30-day and 7-day thresholds with different severity levels for team routing.

Create a CloudWatch alarm on the ACM DaysToExpiry metric for each certificate. Set the alarm threshold at 30 days for initial notification via SNS. Create a second alarm at 7 days that sends escalation notifications to the security team's SNS topic with a higher severity prefix.

Configure AWS Config with the acm-certificate-expiration-check rule set to evaluate certificates 30 days before expiration. Create EventBridge rules matching Config compliance change events that trigger Lambda for 30-day alerting via SNS and 7-day escalation via a different SNS topic.

explanation: C is correct: ACM publishes a per-certificate DaysToExpiry metric to the AWS/CertificateManager namespace, so one alarm with a threshold below 30 gives the initial notice and a second below 7 pointed at the security team's SNS topic gives the escalation — native metrics, two tiers, no code. A is incorrect because ACM's built-in expiry emails go to WHOIS registrant, admin and technical contacts on a fixed schedule with no 30/7-day tiering or per-team routing, and they are routinely filtered or unread, which is how the outage happened. B is incorrect because it hand-builds a daily poller to recompute a value CloudWatch already emits, adding a Lambda, schedule, IAM and up to 24 hours of detection granularity for no benefit. D is incorrect because the Config managed rule acm-certificate-expiration-check evaluates a single configured threshold and reports one compliance state, so two tiers need two rules plus EventBridge and Lambda glue on top of periodic rather than continuous evaluation.

stem: A company needs to implement a policy that automatically quarantines newly launched EC2 instances until they pass a security compliance check. New instances must be placed in a restricted security group that allows only SSM Agent communication. After passing compliance checks, instances are moved to their operational security group. Which approach automates instance quarantine and release?

options.text: Deploy a launch template that specifies the quarantine security group as the default. All new instances start in the restricted group. An SSM State Manager association runs compliance checks every 5 minutes on new instances and updates the security group to operational upon passing all checks.

Configure AWS Config with required-tags and approved-ami rules. New instances that fail Config evaluation are flagged as non-compliant. Config auto-remediation attaches the quarantine security group. When instances become compliant after patching, a separate auto-remediation restores the operational group.

Use EC2 Instance Connect Endpoint to restrict network access for new instances. New instances can only be accessed through the Instance Connect Endpoint until compliance checks pass. After compliance verification, the endpoint restriction is removed and instances receive normal network connectivity.

Create an EventBridge rule matching EC2 RunInstances CloudTrail events. The rule triggers a Lambda function that immediately replaces the instance's security group with the quarantine group. SSM Automation runs compliance checks, and upon passing, another Lambda restores the operational security group.

explanation: D is correct: CloudTrail delivers RunInstances to EventBridge within about a minute, so the rule invokes a Lambda that calls ModifyInstanceAttribute to move the instance onto the quarantine security group before the workload finishes booting — regardless of who launched it or through which API path. SSM Automation then runs the compliance checks and restores the operational group on success, closing the loop with no human step. A is incorrect because a launch template governs only launches that reference it; instances started from the console, another template or a different ASG bypass quarantine entirely, and a State Manager association cannot run before the instance is already on the network. B is incorrect because Config evaluates on configuration-item delivery or a schedule, adding minutes of unquarantined exposure, and required-tags/approved-ami test metadata rather than security posture. C is incorrect because EC2 Instance Connect Endpoint is an inbound SSH/RDP path; it constrains neither the instance's inbound nor its outbound traffic, so it is not quarantine.

stem: A company needs to implement a service catalog that allows development teams to self-service provision approved infrastructure patterns (VPC, ECS cluster, RDS database) while ensuring governance controls are enforced. Teams should choose from pre-approved templates without needing CloudFormation expertise. Which service provides governed self-service infrastructure provisioning?

options.text: Create a custom web application using API Gateway and Lambda that presents a catalog of infrastructure options. When developers select an option, the Lambda function deploys the corresponding CloudFormation stack using pre-configured parameters and an admin IAM role.

Share CloudFormation templates in a central S3 bucket with documentation for each template's parameters. Developers download templates and deploy them using the CloudFormation console with their own IAM permissions. Template parameters include defaults that enforce governance requirements.

Deploy AWS Service Catalog with portfolios containing CloudFormation-based products for each approved infrastructure pattern. Share portfolios with development teams via Organizations. Launch constraints ensure products deploy with controlled IAM roles and pre-configured parameter values.

Deploy Terraform Cloud with a private module registry containing approved infrastructure modules. Development teams create Terraform workspaces and reference modules from the registry. Sentinel policies enforce governance rules before Terraform applies any infrastructure changes.

explanation: C is correct: Service Catalog packages each approved template as a product in a portfolio, portfolios are shared to accounts or OUs through Organizations, and a launch constraint makes provisioning assume a service-managed IAM role — so a developer needs only servicecatalog permissions, not rights to create VPCs, ECS clusters or RDS instances. Template constraints bound parameter values and provisioned products are tracked centrally for update or termination. A is incorrect because it rebuilds Service Catalog's portfolios, constraints and provisioned-product tracking in Lambda, and a broad admin role behind an API is a privilege-escalation surface. B is incorrect because parameter defaults are only suggestions a developer can override, and deploying with their own permissions means they must already hold the underlying create rights — exactly what governance should prevent. D is incorrect because Terraform Cloud with Sentinel adds a separate commercial toolchain, state backend and licensing beside the existing CloudFormation estate and still expects teams to write HCL.

stem: A company needs to implement parallel test execution in their CI/CD pipeline to reduce the 45-minute test suite runtime. The test suite contains 900 independent unit tests that can run in any order. Which CodeBuild configuration enables parallel test execution?

options.text: Configure a CodeBuild batch build with fan-out mode that splits the 900 tests across 9 parallel build tasks, each running 100 tests. Use a build graph with a final fan-in task that aggregates test results from all parallel tasks and reports the overall pass/fail status.

Configure a single CodeBuild project with a BUILD_GENERAL1_2XLARGE compute type that provides 72 vCPUs. Use a test runner configured to run tests in parallel threads, utilizing all available CPU cores to execute the 900 tests concurrently on the single build instance.

Create 9 separate CodeBuild projects, each configured to run a subset of 100 tests. Configure CodePipeline with a parallel action group containing all 9 CodeBuild actions. Each action runs independently and the pipeline stage succeeds only when all 9 actions complete successfully.

Configure CodeBuild with a buildspec that uses GNU Parallel to split the test suite into batches and execute them concurrently on the build instance. GNU Parallel distributes test execution across available CPU cores, reducing wall-clock time proportional to the number of cores.

explanation: CodeBuild batch builds with fan-out mode distribute tests across multiple independent build environments, providing true parallel execution with separate compute resources. The fan-in aggregation step collects results from all workers. Option B runs on a single instance which is limited by the instance's CPU capacity. Option C creates separate projects which are harder to manage than a single batch build configuration. Option D runs on a single instance like Option B, limited by local compute resources.

stem: A company uses AWS CDK and needs to implement custom validation logic that runs during cdk synth. The validation must check that all S3 buckets in the stack have versioning enabled and that no security group allows ingress from 0.0.0.0/0 on port 22. If validation fails, synthesis must stop with an error. Which CDK mechanism provides custom validation during synthesis?

options.text: Write CloudFormation Guard rules that validate the synthesized template output. Run cfn-guard validate against the cdk.out directory after cdk synth completes. Guard rules check for S3 versioning and SSH security group rules, failing the CI/CD pipeline if violations are found.

Create a custom CDK plugin that hooks into the synthesis lifecycle. The plugin runs after all constructs are synthesized and validates the CloudFormation template JSON for S3 bucket and security group properties. The plugin throws an error to block deployment if violations are detected.

Implement the IValidation interface on custom constructs and register validators using node.addValidation(). The validation method inspects construct properties during synthesis and throws errors for S3 buckets without versioning or security groups with open SSH access, blocking cdk synth.

Add Aspects to the CDK app that traverse the construct tree during synthesis. The Aspect's visit() method inspects each construct, checking S3 bucket versioning and security group ingress rules. Use Annotations.of(construct).addError() for violations, which causes cdk synth to fail with errors.

explanation: D is correct: an Aspect registered with Aspects.of(app).add(...) is invoked once per node during the prepare phase of synthesis, so visit() sees every construct in the tree including L2/L3 constructs the team did not author. Annotations.of(node).addError() records an error the CLI reports and makes cdk synth exit non-zero before any template is deployed — exactly the required behavior. A is incorrect because cfn-guard runs against cdk.out after synthesis already succeeded; it can fail a pipeline but cannot stop cdk synth, and it inspects generated CloudFormation rather than construct intent. B is incorrect because CDK plugins are a CLI extensibility point for credential and context providers — there is no supported synthesis-lifecycle plugin hook for template validation. C is incorrect because node.addValidation() with IValidation attaches a validator to one construct at a time, so it only fires where a developer remembered to register it and cannot sweep the whole app.

stem: A company's Lambda function processes orders and writes to both DynamoDB and SQS. If the DynamoDB write succeeds but the SQS send fails, the system has an inconsistent state. The team needs a guarantee that an SQS message is eventually sent for every committed order and for no order that was not committed, and wants to achieve this with the LEAST operational overhead. Which pattern meets these requirements?

options.text: Implement the outbox pattern: write both the order and the SQS message payload to DynamoDB in a single TransactWriteItems call. A separate Lambda function polls the outbox table and sends messages to SQS, deleting outbox entries after successful SQS send confirmation.

Use DynamoDB Transactions to write the order to DynamoDB. Enable DynamoDB Streams on the table and configure a Lambda function trigger on the stream. The stream-triggered Lambda sends the SQS message, ensuring the SQS send only occurs after the DynamoDB write is committed.

Use Step Functions Express Workflow to orchestrate the Lambda function. Define parallel states for DynamoDB write and SQS send with error handling. If either operation fails, Step Functions rolls back the other operation using compensating transactions defined in catch blocks.

Configure the Lambda function with an SQS destination for successful invocations. The function writes to DynamoDB and returns the SQS message payload. Lambda automatically sends the payload to the SQS destination after the function completes successfully with the DynamoDB write committed.

explanation: Option B is correct. DynamoDB Streams emits a record for every committed write and only for committed writes, and the Lambda event source mapping retries the stream shard until the handler succeeds, so the SQS send is guaranteed to happen exactly for orders that were durably written. Because the stream and its trigger are fully managed, there is no poller, no schedule, no outbox table and no cleanup logic to own - the least operational overhead of any correct option. Option A is the canonical transactional outbox and gives the same all-or-nothing guarantee, but the team must build and operate the relay: a second table, a polling or scheduled consumer, idempotent delete-after-confirm logic, backlog monitoring and its own failure handling. It is correct but strictly more overhead, which is what the stem's qualifier decides on. Option C provides no atomicity: parallel states can each fail independently, and an SQS send cannot be compensated once the message is visible to consumers, so the 'rollback' is fictional; it also adds an orchestration layer per order. Option D misuses Lambda destinations - they apply only to asynchronous invocations, they deliver Lambda's own invocation record rather than a custom message body, and they are in no way tied to the DynamoDB write, so a committed write with a later delivery failure still loses the message.

stem: A company's CloudWatch bill has increased significantly due to custom metric publishing from 200 microservices. Each service publishes 20 custom metrics with 5 dimensions each, resulting in thousands of unique metric combinations. The team needs to reduce CloudWatch costs while maintaining essential monitoring. Which approach reduces custom metric costs?

options.text: Switch from custom metrics to CloudWatch Embedded Metric Format (EMF) logs. EMF metrics are extracted from logs which are cheaper to store than custom metrics. Configure log retention policies to delete EMF logs after metric extraction, further reducing storage costs.

Reduce the metric publishing frequency from every minute to every 5 minutes. Standard resolution metrics (60-second) cost the same as high-resolution metrics but reducing publishing frequency reduces the PutMetricData API call volume and associated request charges.

Consolidate metrics across services by publishing to shared metric namespaces with a ServiceName dimension. Instead of 200 separate namespaces, use a single namespace where the ServiceName dimension identifies the source. This reduces the number of unique metrics billed by CloudWatch.

Reduce the number of dimensions on custom metrics from 5 to 2 essential dimensions. Fewer dimension combinations result in fewer unique metric time series, significantly reducing the CloudWatch custom metric cost. Aggregate less-critical dimensions in application logs for ad-hoc analysis.

explanation: D is correct: CloudWatch bills a custom metric per unique combination of namespace, metric name and dimension set, so every distinct set of dimension values is its own billed time series. With five dimensions the series count is the cross-product of their cardinalities; cutting to the two dimensions alarms and dashboards actually query collapses that cross-product and reduces cost roughly in proportion, with the remaining detail kept in logs for Logs Insights. A is incorrect because EMF is only a different ingestion path — the extracted metrics bill at the same per-custom-metric rate, and deleting the source logs does not un-bill them. B is incorrect because publish frequency affects only PutMetricData request charges; the per-metric monthly charge is unchanged by resolution or interval. C is incorrect because the namespace is just one component of a metric's identity — folding 200 namespaces into one while adding a ServiceName dimension yields the same number of unique series and the same cost.

stem: A company needs to implement a secure software supply chain for their container-based application. They must verify that only approved container images are deployed to production ECS clusters and that images haven't been tampered with since building. Which two measures establish container supply chain security? (Choose two.)

options.text: Configure ECR lifecycle policies that automatically delete untagged images and images older than 30 days. This prevents deployment of outdated or unauthorized images by ensuring only recent, actively maintained images are available in the repository for ECS task launches.

Enable ECR image scanning with Amazon Inspector to detect vulnerabilities in container images. Configure the CI/CD pipeline to fail if critical vulnerabilities are found, ensuring only vulnerability-free images are pushed to the production ECR repository for ECS deployment.

Enable ECR immutable image tags on the production repository. Immutable tags prevent existing image tags from being overwritten with different content, ensuring that a specific image tag always references the exact same image layers that were originally pushed to the repository.

Deploy separate ECR repositories for development and production environments. Use ECR replication policies to copy approved images from the development repository to the production repository. ECS production clusters pull only from the production ECR repository for deployment.

Sign container images with AWS Signer using Notation after they are built and scanned in the CI/CD pipeline. Add a pipeline gate that verifies the signature against the signing profile's trust policy before the image digest is written into the ECS task definition, so an unsigned or modified image fails verification and the deployment stops.

explanation: Options E and C are correct. Option E now describes a real enforcement path: AWS Signer signs OCI images using Notation and stores the signature alongside the image in ECR, and because ECS itself has no image-signature verification, the verification must happen where it can gate the release - in the pipeline, before the resolved image digest is written into the task definition. That establishes provenance and detects tampering after build. Option C complements it: enabling tag immutability on the production repository means a tag can never be repointed to different content, closing the window where an approved tag is quietly overwritten between approval and deployment. Option A is repository hygiene - deleting untagged and aged images says nothing about who built an image or whether it was altered, and an attacker's freshly pushed image is by definition recent. Option B is valuable but orthogonal: scanning tells you an image has no known CVEs, and a tampered or entirely substituted image can scan perfectly clean. Option D separates repositories but ECR replication copies on push mechanically; it performs no approval check and no integrity verification, so a compromised development image replicates into production just as readily.

stem: A company's application uses a multi-AZ RDS MySQL database. During a planned AZ maintenance event, the database failed over to the standby instance, causing a 30-second application outage. The team needs to minimize application impact during planned RDS failover events. Which application-level change reduces failover impact?

options.text: Implement a read-write splitting architecture with RDS read replicas. Route read queries to the read replica and write queries to the primary. During primary failover, read operations continue uninterrupted through the replica while writes are queued in SQS until the new primary is available.

Switch to Amazon Aurora MySQL which provides faster failover than standard RDS MySQL. Aurora's failover typically completes in under 30 seconds due to its distributed storage architecture. Configure the Aurora cluster endpoint for automatic failover without application changes.

Configure the application's database connection pool with aggressive connection validation and rapid failure detection. Set the validation query timeout to 5 seconds, enable test-on-borrow, and configure the pool to create new connections immediately when existing connections are detected as broken.

Enable RDS Proxy between the application and the RDS database. RDS Proxy maintains a connection pool and handles failover transparency by holding application connections during failover and reconnecting them to the new primary, reducing application-visible downtime to seconds.

explanation: D is correct: RDS Proxy terminates the application's connections itself and multiplexes them over its own pool. During a Multi-AZ failover the proxy detects the endpoint change, reconnects its backend connections to the promoted standby, and holds the application's sockets open with in-flight requests queued rather than reset — AWS measures this as cutting application-visible failover time by up to about 66%, with no code change beyond the endpoint. A is incorrect because read replicas do nothing for writer failover, and queueing writes to SQS turns a synchronous transactional path into an asynchronous one with ordering and read-your-writes problems. B is incorrect because migrating to Aurora is an engine change whose typical failover is roughly 30 seconds — the same outage already observed — so it does not meet the goal. C is incorrect because aggressive validation only detects the broken connection sooner; every connection is still torn down, re-established and re-authenticated, and test-on-borrow adds latency in steady state.

stem: A company needs to implement centralized key management where a single KMS key is used to encrypt data across multiple AWS accounts in their organization. The key must be managed in a security account and shared with workload accounts. Which KMS key sharing approach enables cross-account encryption?

options.text: Create a KMS grant for each workload account that delegates specific cryptographic operations to the account's IAM roles. Grants provide temporary, revocable permissions without modifying the key policy, allowing fine-grained control over which accounts can use the key.

Create a KMS key in the security account with a key policy that grants kms:Encrypt, kms:Decrypt, and kms:GenerateDataKey permissions to IAM roles in the workload accounts. Workload account resources reference the key ARN from the security account when encrypting data.

Create KMS key replicas in each workload account using KMS multi-Region key replication. The primary key in the security account is replicated to workload accounts, providing each account with a local key replica that shares the same key material for consistent encryption.

Share the KMS key using AWS Resource Access Manager (RAM) to share the key resource with specific organizational units. RAM sharing enables workload accounts in the shared OUs to use the key for encryption operations without key policy modifications in the security account.

explanation: B is correct: a KMS key lives in one account, and cross-account use needs both halves — the key policy in the security account must allow the workload account or its roles to call kms:Encrypt, kms:Decrypt and kms:GenerateDataKey*, and the workload account's IAM policies must allow the same actions on the key ARN. Workload resources then reference the full cross-account key ARN. This is the documented pattern for a central organization key. A is incorrect because a grant can only be created by a principal the key policy already authorizes and delegates to a named grantee for temporary programmatic use — it supplements the key policy rather than establishing the cross-account authorization. C is incorrect because multi-Region replicas are replicated across Regions within the same account; there is no cross-account replication, and a replica still needs its own key policy. D is incorrect because AWS RAM does not support KMS keys as a shareable resource type — KMS cross-account access is expressed solely in the key policy.

stem: A company uses CloudFormation and needs to deploy a Lambda function that depends on a custom Lambda Layer. The layer contains shared utility libraries that are built and updated independently from the function. The team wants the function's stack update to pick up the newest layer build reliably every time. Which approach manages Lambda Layer versions in CloudFormation?

options.text: Publish the layer to a shared Lambda Layer ARN that all functions reference using a fixed ARN without a version qualifier. When the layer is updated, all functions automatically use the latest layer version on their next invocation without requiring function or stack updates.

Store the layer ZIP file in S3 with versioning enabled. Reference the S3 bucket, key, and version ID in the AWS::Lambda::LayerVersion resource. Use a CloudFormation parameter to specify the S3 object version ID, updated in the pipeline each time the layer code changes.

Define the Lambda Layer using AWS::Lambda::LayerVersion in the same stack as the function, pointing its Content at a fixed S3 bucket and key that the layer build overwrites. CloudFormation creates a new layer version each time the layer code is rebuilt, and Ref returns the layer version ARN including the new version number.

Define the Lambda Layer as a separate CloudFormation stack that exports the layer ARN including version number. The function's stack imports the layer ARN using Fn::ImportValue. When the layer stack is updated with new code, the exported ARN includes the new version number automatically.

explanation: Option B is correct because it makes the change detectable. CloudFormation only replaces an AWS::Lambda::LayerVersion (and therefore publishes a new layer version) when a property in the template actually changes; passing the S3 object version ID as a parameter guarantees the Content property differs on every layer build, so a new layer version is published and Ref hands the function the new versioned ARN. It also keeps the layer artifact decoupled from the function's source. Option C is the trap: if the pipeline overwrites the same bucket and key, the Content property is byte-for-byte identical between deployments, CloudFormation sees no change, no new layer version is published, and the stack silently keeps running the stale layer - the stem's requirement fails exactly when it matters. Option A is invalid Lambda behavior: a function must reference a fully qualified layer version ARN, there is no unqualified 'latest' layer reference, and layers are resolved at function configuration time rather than per invocation. Option D breaks on update: CloudFormation refuses to modify or delete an exported output value while another stack imports it, so republishing the layer in its own stack with a new versioned ARN fails until every importing stack is first detached.

stem: A company needs to implement a multi-region active-passive disaster recovery strategy with an RPO of 15 minutes and an RTO of 30 minutes. The application uses EC2 instances, an ALB, and Amazon S3 for data storage. The DR region must be cost-optimized during normal operations. Which DR architecture minimizes cost while meeting RPO and RTO requirements?

options.text: Configure S3 cross-region replication for data and create daily AMI backups copied to the DR region. During a disaster, restore the latest AMI in the DR region, launch EC2 instances, configure the ALB, and update Route 53 to point to the DR region's ALB for traffic routing.

Deploy a warm standby in the DR region with a scaled-down Auto Scaling group (1 instance) behind a pre-configured ALB. Enable S3 cross-region replication for continuous data synchronization. During failover, scale up the ASG to production capacity and switch DNS to the DR ALB.

Deploy a pilot light configuration in the DR region with the minimum required infrastructure: an AMI copied from the primary region, a pre-configured launch template, and S3 cross-region replication. During failover, launch EC2 instances from the AMI and create an ALB to serve traffic.

Deploy identical production infrastructure in the DR region with Route 53 failover routing. Keep the DR instances stopped during normal operations to minimize cost. During failover, start all instances and wait for health checks to pass before Route 53 routes traffic to the DR region.

explanation: C is correct: pilot light keeps only the essentials always on — S3 Cross-Region Replication, which typically completes in minutes and comfortably meets a 15-minute RPO, plus a copied AMI and a launch template — with no EC2 or ALB running, so idle cost is essentially storage. On declaration, launching from the pre-baked AMI and creating the ALB takes minutes, inside the 30-minute RTO. A is incorrect because daily AMI backups make the recovery point for anything captured in the AMI up to 24 hours old, violating the 15-minute RPO regardless of S3 replication. B is incorrect because warm standby runs an instance and an ALB continuously; it meets both targets but costs more than pilot light, and the question asks for the cheapest option that still meets them. D is incorrect because a stopped fleet still pays for every instance's EBS volumes plus a full-size ALB while recovering no faster than launching from an AMI — strictly more expensive for the same outcome.

stem: A company needs to implement structured logging across all their Lambda functions to enable efficient log querying. All logs must include a correlation ID, request timestamp, function name, and log level in a consistent JSON format. Which approach standardizes Lambda logging across all functions?

options.text: Configure CloudWatch Logs Insights to parse unstructured Lambda logs into the required fields at query time. Create saved queries that extract correlation ID, timestamp, function name, and log level from free-text log messages using the parse command for structured analysis.

Use AWS Lambda Powertools (Python/TypeScript/Java) Logger utility across all functions. Powertools Logger automatically includes function name, request ID, and timestamp in structured JSON format. Configure the Logger with custom keys for correlation ID and log level for consistent output.

Deploy a centralized log processing Lambda function triggered by CloudWatch Logs subscription filters. The function receives raw logs from all Lambda functions, parses them, adds missing structured fields (correlation ID, timestamp, log level), and republishes them as structured JSON to a destination log group.

Create a shared Lambda Layer containing a custom logging library that formats all log output as JSON with the required fields. Each Lambda function imports the logging library from the layer and uses it instead of the standard console.log or print statements.

explanation: B is correct: Powertools for AWS Lambda's Logger is built for the runtime — it emits JSON on every statement, auto-injects cold_start, function_name, function_memory_size, function_arn and the request ID via inject_lambda_context, supports append_keys for a correlation ID, and can pull a correlation ID from the event with a configured JMESPath. It is AWS-maintained for Python, TypeScript, Java and .NET, so one convention covers a polyglot fleet. A is incorrect because parsing at query time only reshapes text that was already emitted — fields never logged cannot be recovered, and metric filters, subscriptions and every other consumer still see unstructured data. C is incorrect because a subscription-filter Lambda cannot invent a correlation ID the function never recorded, and it doubles ingestion cost while adding a second log group and a failure point. D is incorrect because a hand-rolled layer must be built, versioned and maintained per runtime with context enrichment wired manually, duplicating a supported library.

stem: A company needs to implement a release management process where deployments to production require change tickets to be created, approved, and linked to the deployment. The pipeline must verify that an approved change ticket exists before proceeding with the production deployment. Which approach integrates change management with the deployment pipeline?

options.text: Configure a ServiceNow integration with CodePipeline using a Lambda function. Before the production deployment stage, the Lambda creates a change request in ServiceNow, waits for approval via webhook callback, and signals CodePipeline to proceed when the ServiceNow change request is approved.

Integrate CodePipeline with AWS Systems Manager Change Manager. Create a change request template that requires approval before deployment. The pipeline invokes Change Manager to create and wait for approval of a change request before executing the production deployment stage.

Add a manual approval action in CodePipeline that requires the approver to enter the change ticket number in the comments field. After approval, a Lambda function validates the ticket number against the ITSM system's API and proceeds with deployment only if the ticket is in approved status.

Create an EventBridge rule that sends deployment events to a Slack channel for change advisory board review. The CAB approves or rejects the deployment in Slack, and a Slack bot integration signals CodePipeline to proceed or stop based on the CAB's decision in the channel.

explanation: B is correct: Systems Manager Change Manager is the native change-control service — a change template defines required approver levels, honours change calendars and freeze windows, and produces an auditable change request for every deployment. CodePipeline invokes it to create the request and blocks the production stage until it reaches Approved, so an approved ticket provably exists and is linked before deployment. A is incorrect because it bolts a third-party ITSM plus bespoke webhook-callback plumbing onto the pipeline when an AWS-native, already-integrated change workflow exists. C is incorrect because a free-text ticket number typed into a manual approval is unverified at the moment of approval — validating afterwards means approval was already granted, and the field can be mistyped or fabricated. D is incorrect because a Slack thread is not a change record: no template, no enforced approver hierarchy, no calendar enforcement, and no auditable linkage between deployment and a governed change request.

stem: A company needs to implement a mechanism that automatically pauses deployments during active production incidents. When an Incident Manager incident is open with Critical severity, no CodePipeline deployments to production should proceed. Deployments should resume automatically when the incident is resolved. Which approach implements incident-aware deployment gating?

options.text: Add a Lambda invoke action before the production deployment stage in each pipeline. The Lambda function queries Incident Manager for active Critical incidents. If an active incident exists, the Lambda throws an error causing the stage to retry. When the incident is resolved, the retry succeeds.

Store the incident status in an SSM Parameter Store parameter. EventBridge rules update the parameter when incidents are created or resolved. The CodePipeline production stage includes a Lambda action that reads the parameter and blocks deployment if the parameter indicates an active incident.

Configure CloudWatch composite alarms that combine application health alarms with incident status. When the composite alarm is in ALARM state, add it as a gating condition on the CodePipeline manual approval action. Operators cannot approve deployments while the composite alarm indicates an active incident.

Create an EventBridge rule matching Incident Manager incident lifecycle events. When a Critical incident is created, the rule triggers a Lambda function that disables the production deployment stage in all CodePipeline pipelines. When the incident is resolved, another event re-enables the deployment stages.

explanation: D is correct: Incident Manager emits incident lifecycle events (created, updated, resolved) to EventBridge. A rule filtered on Critical severity invokes a Lambda that calls DisableStageTransition on the production stage of every pipeline, parking in-flight executions at the stage boundary rather than failing them, and the resolution event calls EnableStageTransition. The gate is applied centrally, needs no edit to any pipeline definition, and reverses itself. A is incorrect because a Lambda action that throws puts the stage into Failed — CodePipeline does not auto-retry, so an operator must manually retry and the execution is recorded as failed meanwhile. B is incorrect because it still requires inserting a gating Lambda action into every pipeline, and the SSM parameter is duplicated state that can drift from Incident Manager's real status. C is incorrect because alarms cannot be attached to a manual approval action as a blocking condition — that is not a CodePipeline feature — and it reintroduces the human step the requirement wants removed.

stem: A company needs to implement data protection for their S3 buckets containing sensitive financial data. The protection must prevent accidental deletion, ensure encryption at rest, and maintain access logs for audit purposes. Which three S3 configurations together satisfy these requirements? (Choose three.)

options.text: Configure S3 Intelligent-Tiering storage class for automatic cost optimization. Intelligent-Tiering moves objects between access tiers based on usage patterns, reducing storage costs for infrequently accessed financial data while maintaining immediate retrieval capability when needed.

Enable S3 Transfer Acceleration to speed up data uploads to the bucket. Transfer Acceleration uses CloudFront edge locations for faster data transfer, reducing the risk of upload failures that could cause data loss during large financial data ingestion operations.

Enable default SSE-KMS encryption with a customer-managed KMS key on the S3 bucket. Configure the KMS key policy to restrict decryption to specific IAM roles. All objects stored in the bucket are automatically encrypted with the customer-managed key without requiring client-side configuration.

Enable S3 Versioning and configure S3 Object Lock in governance mode with a 1-year retention period. Versioning preserves all object versions, and Object Lock prevents deletion during the retention period. MFA Delete can be enabled for additional protection against version deletion.

Configure S3 server access logging to record all requests made to the bucket. Access logs include requester identity, operation performed, timestamp, and response status. Store access logs in a separate logging bucket with its own retention and access controls for audit compliance.

explanation: The stem lists three distinct requirements and options C, D and E each satisfy exactly one of them. Option D covers 'prevent accidental deletion': versioning means a delete creates a delete marker rather than destroying data, Object Lock in governance mode blocks version deletion for the retention period (overridable only by principals holding s3:BypassGovernanceRetention), and MFA Delete adds a further barrier. Option C covers 'encryption at rest': bucket default encryption with SSE-KMS and a customer-managed key encrypts every new object automatically, and the key policy gives an independent, auditable decryption boundary. Option E covers 'access logs for audit': S3 server access logging records requester, operation, time and response for every request, and writing to a separate logging bucket keeps the audit trail outside the control of anyone editing the data bucket (CloudTrail data events are an equally valid alternative in practice). Option A is a storage-cost feature - Intelligent-Tiering changes what you pay, not what is protected, and it neither prevents deletion nor encrypts nor logs. Option B is an upload-performance feature; failed uploads are simply retried by the client and never result in data loss, so it addresses none of the three requirements.

stem: A company needs to manage Terraform state for 100 different application stacks. Each stack's state must be isolated to prevent accidental cross-stack state corruption, while using a shared S3 backend. Which Terraform backend configuration provides state isolation?

options.text: Create separate S3 buckets for each application stack's Terraform state. Each bucket has its own DynamoDB table for state locking. This provides complete physical isolation between stacks' state files, preventing any possibility of cross-stack state corruption.

Use Terraform workspaces within a single root module to manage all 100 stacks. Each workspace has its own state file stored at env:/workspace-name/terraform.tfstate in the shared S3 bucket. Switch workspaces using terraform workspace select before running operations.

Configure each Terraform stack with a unique S3 key path in the backend configuration (e.g., stacks/app-name/terraform.tfstate). All stacks share the same S3 bucket and DynamoDB lock table, but each has its own state file path preventing cross-stack state interference.

Configure Terraform with a Consul backend that provides key-value state storage with ACL-based access control. Each application stack stores its state in a unique Consul key path, and Consul ACLs prevent cross-stack state access based on the operator's authentication credentials.

explanation: C is correct: the S3 backend's key attribute names the object path of one state file, so a distinct key per stack such as stacks/<app>/terraform.tfstate isolates all 100 states inside one bucket. Locking remains correct because the DynamoDB lock item's LockID is the full bucket/key path, so runs against different stacks never contend while two runs against the same stack do. One bucket carries versioning, encryption and a single policy, and IAM can still scope teams by key prefix. A is incorrect because 100 buckets and 100 lock tables multiply quota pressure, policy sprawl, configuration and cost for isolation a key prefix already provides. B is incorrect because workspaces are for variations of one configuration (dev/stage/prod of the same root module); 100 different application stacks share no common root module, and forcing them into one means a single blast radius. D is incorrect because a Consul backend means operating, securing and backing up a Consul cluster when S3 with DynamoDB locking already satisfies the requirement.

stem: A company's microservices application experiences cascading timeouts when a downstream service becomes slow. Service A calls Service B with a 30-second timeout. Service B calls Service C with a 30-second timeout. When Service C is slow, both Service B and Service A timeout after 30 seconds each, causing a 60-second user-facing latency. How should the team configure timeouts to prevent cascading delays?

options.text: Implement timeout budgets where each downstream call has a shorter timeout than its caller. Set Service A's timeout to 10 seconds, Service B's call to Service C timeout to 5 seconds. This ensures downstream timeouts cascade up quickly, preventing accumulated delay for the end user.

Remove timeouts from inter-service calls and implement circuit breakers instead. Circuit breakers detect slow downstream services and fail fast without waiting for timeouts. After the circuit opens, requests immediately return a fallback response without attempting the downstream call.

Configure all services with the same 5-second timeout for downstream calls. Equal timeouts across all services prevent any single slow service from consuming more than 5 seconds. Add retry with backoff on each service to handle transient failures within the reduced timeout window.

Configure API Gateway with a 30-second overall request timeout. Each downstream service processes requests asynchronously by queuing work in SQS and returning immediately. The API Gateway waits for the final response from a completion queue within its 30-second timeout window.

explanation: A is correct: a timeout budget gives each hop strictly less time for its downstream call than it has itself, leaving margin for its own work. With A at 10s and B's call to C at 5s, a slow C is abandoned by B at 5s and B returns an error or fallback well inside A's budget, so the user waits about 5 seconds instead of the 60 produced by two 30s timeouts in series. Propagating the remaining budget as a deadline keeps this correct as chains deepen. B is incorrect because removing timeouts leaves requests blocked indefinitely on hung sockets while the breaker is still accumulating failures — a breaker needs a timeout to classify a call as failed, so it complements rather than replaces one. C is incorrect because uniform timeouts still accumulate (three hops at 5s is 15s), and retries at every layer multiply load on the degraded service. D is incorrect because SQS-backed async processing changes the API contract and consistency model, and API Gateway's integration timeout still caps the wait.

stem: A company needs to implement real-time alerting on VPC Flow Log data to detect port scanning activity. The alert must fire when any single source IP attempts connections to more than 100 distinct destination ports within a 5-minute window. Which approach enables real-time flow log analysis for port scan detection?

options.text: Enable Amazon GuardDuty which analyzes VPC Flow Logs for network threats including port scanning. GuardDuty's Recon:EC2/PortProbeUnprotectedPort finding type detects port probe activity and generates findings when instances are being scanned from external or internal source IPs.

Stream VPC Flow Logs to CloudWatch Logs and use a subscription filter to forward entries to a Kinesis data stream. Deploy an Amazon Managed Service for Apache Flink application (formerly Kinesis Data Analytics) with a 5-minute tumbling window query that counts distinct destination ports per source IP and invokes Lambda when the count exceeds 100.

Create CloudWatch Logs metric filters on the VPC Flow Log log group that extract source IP and destination port fields. Create a CloudWatch anomaly detection alarm on the metric to detect unusual patterns of port diversity per source IP that deviate from normal baseline behavior.

Enable VPC Flow Logs delivered to S3 with a 5-minute aggregation interval. Configure Amazon Athena scheduled queries that analyze the flow log data for port scanning patterns every 5 minutes. When a source IP exceeds 100 distinct destination ports, Athena triggers an SNS notification.

explanation: Option B is correct because a streaming analytics engine is the only thing in this list that can compute per-key cardinality over a bounded window. Flow log records reach CloudWatch Logs, a subscription filter forwards them continuously to Kinesis Data Streams, and a Managed Service for Apache Flink application groups by source IP over a 5-minute tumbling window, counts distinct destination ports, and invokes Lambda for any group exceeding 100 - which is precisely the rule in the stem, evaluated in near real time. Option A cannot meet a quantified rule: Recon:EC2/PortProbeUnprotectedPort is an unconfigurable managed detector that fires on probes of unprotected ports based on AWS's own heuristics and threat intelligence, and GuardDuty exposes no port-count, window length or threshold to tune, so '100 distinct ports in 5 minutes' cannot be expressed. Option C fails on capability: metric filters emit a numeric value per matching log event and cannot compute distinct-value cardinality grouped by source IP, and layering anomaly detection on top replaces the company's explicit deterministic threshold with a learned band. Option D is batch, not real time - flow logs are delivered to S3 with several minutes of publishing latency on top of the aggregation interval, and Athena has no native scheduled-query-to-SNS trigger, so an external scheduler would be required anyway.

stem: A company needs a strategy that lets internal users exercise new API features before external customers see them. Internal users must get the new behavior while external users keep the current behavior, and both groups must call the same API endpoint. The company will not deploy or operate a second copy of the application, and the segment decision must be derived from the authenticated user's own attributes rather than from a header or cookie that the client supplies. Which deployment pattern enables user-segment-based feature exposure?

options.text: Configure API Gateway with canary settings that route a percentage of traffic to the new stage. Add a Lambda authorizer that inspects request headers for an internal user identifier and routes internal users to the canary deployment. External users are routed to the production stage.

Implement feature flags using AWS AppConfig with user-segment targeting. The API application checks the feature flag for each request, evaluating the user's attributes against segment rules. Internal users see new features while external users see the existing functionality from the same deployment.

Configure CloudFront with Lambda@Edge on the viewer request event. The Lambda function inspects the request for internal user cookies or headers and modifies the Origin header to route internal users to the new version's origin while external users are routed to the current version's origin.

Deploy both API versions behind an ALB. Create ALB listener rules with header-based routing that checks for an X-Internal-User header. Internal users include the header in their requests and are routed to the new version's target group. External users are routed to the current version.

explanation: Option B is correct and is the only option compatible with all three constraints. AppConfig feature flags with segment targeting keep a single deployed artifact serving one endpoint; the application evaluates the flag per request against the authenticated principal's attributes (for example the identity provider claim marking an employee), so internal users execute the new code path while everyone else executes the current one. No second copy of the application exists and the decision comes from server-side identity, not from anything the caller can set. Option A fails on two counts: API Gateway canary settings shift a random percentage of traffic to the canary release and cannot be steered per user, and a Lambda authorizer returns an allow/deny policy and context - it performs no routing between stages. Option C requires a second origin running the new version, which is the second copy the company refuses to operate, and it keys off cookies or headers that the client controls. Option D likewise stands up a second target group running a second copy, and it depends on internal users voluntarily attaching an X-Internal-User header, which any external caller can forge to obtain the unreleased behavior.

stem: A company needs to implement automated cost anomaly response. When AWS Cost Anomaly Detection identifies unexpected spending increases, the system must automatically restrict the affected service's usage and notify the FinOps team. Which approach automates cost anomaly response?

options.text: Enable Trusted Advisor cost optimization checks and configure EventBridge rules matching Trusted Advisor findings. When Trusted Advisor identifies cost optimization opportunities like idle resources, trigger Lambda functions to automatically stop or terminate the identified unused resources.

Create a CloudWatch alarm on the AWS EstimatedCharges metric with anomaly detection. When the alarm triggers, a Lambda function analyzes Cost Explorer data to identify the spending anomaly source and sends a detailed report to the FinOps team with recommended actions for cost reduction.

Configure Cost Anomaly Detection with SNS notifications. Create an EventBridge rule matching Cost Anomaly Detection alerts. The rule triggers a Step Functions workflow that applies a restrictive SCP to the affected account, scales down Auto Scaling groups, and sends detailed notification to the FinOps team.

Configure AWS Budgets with actual cost budget alerts. When spending exceeds the budget threshold, Budgets triggers a Lambda function via SNS that identifies the highest-cost service and applies IAM policies denying further resource creation for that service until the FinOps team reviews.

explanation: C is correct: Cost Anomaly Detection applies machine learning per monitor and delivers alerts to SNS, which EventBridge can match to start a Step Functions state machine. The workflow gives an ordered, retryable, auditable response — attach a restrictive SCP to the offending account, scale the identified Auto Scaling groups down, and publish an enriched notification to FinOps — with explicit error handling between steps. A is incorrect because Trusted Advisor cost checks surface chronically idle or oversized resources on a slow refresh cadence; they say nothing about a sudden spend spike and would not fire on the anomaly. B is incorrect because EstimatedCharges is a coarse billing metric published roughly every six hours for account or service totals, so anomaly detection on it lags and cannot attribute the spike to a linked account, usage type or resource. D is incorrect because AWS Budgets fires on a fixed threshold someone must guess and maintain — missing an anomalous spike that stays under budget and crying wolf during legitimate growth.

stem: A company needs to implement a solution that prevents developers from escalating their own IAM privileges. Developers must be able to create IAM roles for their Lambda functions, but those roles must not have more permissions than the developer's own role. Which IAM feature enforces this privilege boundary?

options.text: Create an IAM permission boundary policy that defines the maximum permissions a Lambda execution role can have. Require developers to attach this permission boundary when creating IAM roles by using a condition key (iam:PermissionsBoundary) in the developer's IAM policy.

Create an SCP that denies iam:CreateRole unless the role's trust policy only trusts lambda.amazonaws.com. This prevents developers from creating roles that could be assumed by entities other than Lambda, limiting privilege escalation through role assumption by other principals.

Implement IAM Access Analyzer to continuously validate that developer-created roles don't exceed the developer's own permissions. Access Analyzer generates findings when a created role has broader permissions, and auto-remediation removes the excess permissions from the offending role.

Configure AWS Organizations SCPs that deny all iam:CreateRole actions for developers. Instead, provide a Service Catalog product that creates Lambda execution roles with pre-approved permission sets. Developers provision roles through Service Catalog without direct IAM access.

explanation: Permission boundaries define the maximum permissions that any IAM entity can have. By requiring developers to attach a permission boundary when creating roles (enforced via condition key), the created roles cannot exceed the boundary's permissions regardless of what policies the developer attaches. Option B limits trust policies but doesn't restrict the role's permissions. Option C detects overly permissive roles after creation, not at creation time. Option D blocks all role creation which is too restrictive.

stem: A company manages its infrastructure with CloudFormation. One stack must also provision objects in two third-party SaaS platforms as part of the same deployment: a Datadog monitor and a PagerDuty service. The integration must handle the full stack lifecycle, so that a stack update changes the SaaS objects and deleting the stack deletes them. This is a one-off integration used only by this stack; the team has no plans to reuse it in other templates or share it with other teams, and wants the solution that takes the LEAST development effort to build and operate. Which approach meets these requirements?

options.text: Register a third-party CloudFormation resource type using the CloudFormation registry. Develop a resource handler in Java or Python that implements create, update, and delete operations against the SaaS API. Register the handler as a custom type (e.g., ThirdParty::Datadog::Monitor) usable in templates.

Create an SSM Automation document that provisions the third-party resource. Reference the SSM document in CloudFormation using AWS::SSM::Document and trigger it with an EventBridge rule on stack lifecycle events. The automation handles creation, update, and deletion based on the event type.

Use a CloudFormation macro that transforms the template during processing. The macro's Lambda function intercepts custom resource definitions, calls the third-party API to provision resources, and injects the provisioned resource identifiers back into the transformed CloudFormation template.

Create a Lambda-backed CloudFormation custom resource (AWS::CloudFormation::CustomResource). The Lambda function handles Create, Update, and Delete events by calling the third-party SaaS API. The function sends a response to the CloudFormation pre-signed S3 URL indicating success or failure.

explanation: Option D is correct: a Lambda-backed AWS::CloudFormation::CustomResource is the lowest-effort way to wire a one-off SaaS integration into a stack. CloudFormation invokes the function with a RequestType of Create, Update, or Delete along with the resource properties, the function calls the Datadog and PagerDuty APIs, and it signals the pre-signed S3 response URL, so a stack delete also deletes the SaaS objects. Option A is the more robust and reusable mechanism, and vendors do publish exactly such public-registry extensions, but authoring one with the CloudFormation CLI requires a JSON resource schema, create/read/update/delete/list handlers, contract tests, and a packaged submission and activation per account and Region - far more development effort than a single non-reusable integration justifies. Option B fails because AWS::SSM::Document only stores the document; CloudFormation never executes it, and there is no per-resource stack lifecycle event stream in EventBridge that maps cleanly onto Create, Update, and Delete of one logical resource, so deletions would silently be missed. Option C fails because a macro runs during template transformation, before any resource is provisioned; it cannot participate in the resource lifecycle at all and it receives nothing when the stack is deleted, leaving orphaned SaaS objects.

stem: A company runs a critical batch processing job on an EC2 Spot Instance fleet. Spot interruptions cause job failures and require restarting the entire batch from the beginning. Each batch takes 4 hours to complete. Which approach minimizes the impact of Spot interruptions on long-running batch jobs?

options.text: Switch from Spot Instances to On-Demand Instances for the batch processing job. On-Demand Instances are not subject to interruption and guarantee availability for the full 4-hour batch duration. Use Reserved Instances or Savings Plans to reduce the cost of the On-Demand compute.

Configure the Spot Fleet with a diversified allocation strategy across multiple instance types and Availability Zones. Launch instances from at least 6 different capacity pools to reduce the probability that all instances are interrupted simultaneously during the 4-hour batch window.

Implement checkpointing in the batch application that saves processing state to S3 every 10 minutes. When a Spot interruption notice is received (2 minutes before termination), the application saves its current checkpoint. On restart, the job resumes from the latest checkpoint instead of starting over.

Use EC2 Spot Fleet with allocation strategy set to capacity-optimized to launch instances from pools with the lowest interruption probability. Configure the fleet to maintain the desired capacity by automatically replacing interrupted instances with instances from alternative capacity pools.

explanation: C is correct: periodically writing state to S3, plus a final checkpoint when the two-minute Spot interruption notice (or the earlier rebalance recommendation) arrives via IMDS or EventBridge, bounds lost work to one checkpoint interval. A replacement instance reads the latest checkpoint and resumes mid-batch, so a 4-hour job survives reclamation. It is the only option that changes the cost of an interruption rather than its probability. A is incorrect because it abandons the Spot discount entirely — Savings Plans still price far above Spot — and treats an application design gap as a purchasing decision. B is incorrect because diversifying across pools lowers the chance of a mass reclamation, but any single reclaimed instance still loses all uncheckpointed in-progress work. D is incorrect for the same reason: capacity-optimized allocation picks the deepest pools and the fleet does replace interrupted instances, but the replacement restarts the batch from zero because no state was persisted.

stem: A company needs to implement a service dependency map that automatically discovers and visualizes all service-to-service communication patterns in their microservices application. The map must update in real-time as new services are added or communication patterns change. Which observability tool provides automatic service dependency mapping?

options.text: Enable AWS X-Ray with active tracing on all services. X-Ray's service map automatically discovers service dependencies from trace data, showing request flows, latency distributions, and error rates between services. The map updates in real-time as new traces reveal communication patterns.

Deploy Prometheus with the Grafana service map plugin on the EKS cluster. Prometheus collects service mesh metrics from Istio or App Mesh sidecars, and Grafana's service map visualization displays real-time communication patterns between services with traffic volume indicators.

Deploy Amazon CloudWatch ServiceLens to visualize service topology. ServiceLens combines CloudWatch metrics, logs, and X-Ray traces to create an integrated service map that shows service health, dependencies, and performance metrics in a single unified view.

Configure VPC Flow Logs and use Amazon Detective to build a network communication graph. Detective analyzes flow log data to identify service-to-service communication patterns based on IP addresses and ports, creating a visual dependency map of all network interactions.

explanation: A is correct: with active tracing and X-Ray SDK or ADOT instrumentation each segment records caller and callee identity, so X-Ray derives the service map purely from observed traces — a node appears the moment a new service emits or receives a traced request, and each edge carries direction, latency distribution, request rate and error/fault/throttle rates. Discovery is automatic and continuously updated. B is incorrect because it presupposes EKS plus a service mesh (Istio or App Mesh) and a self-managed Prometheus/Grafana stack; it is neither AWS-managed nor applicable to services outside the mesh. C is incorrect because ServiceLens is a CloudWatch console experience layered over X-Ray traces, metrics and logs — the automatic dependency discovery it renders is X-Ray's, so X-Ray is the mechanism asked for. D is incorrect because Detective is a security investigation service over GuardDuty, CloudTrail and flow logs; an IP-to-IP graph cannot resolve to logical services behind shared load balancers, NAT or ephemeral container IPs.

stem: A company needs to ensure that their CodePipeline deployments to production can be audited. Every deployment must record who triggered it, what artifacts were deployed, which approval was given, and when each stage completed. Where does CodePipeline store this deployment audit trail?

options.text: Configure CodePipeline to send execution events to CloudWatch Logs. Each pipeline execution creates log entries for stage transitions, action results, and approval responses. The logs include the IAM principal, artifact versions, and timestamps for comprehensive audit trail storage.

Configure CodePipeline notifications to an SNS topic that fans out to a Lambda function. The Lambda function records all pipeline events including trigger source, artifact details, approvals, and stage completions in a DynamoDB audit table with TTL-based retention management.

Enable AWS Config recording for CodePipeline resources. Config tracks changes to pipeline configurations and captures pipeline execution state changes as configuration items. The Config timeline shows who modified pipelines and when deployments occurred with configuration snapshots.

CodePipeline execution history records all stage transitions, action executions, approval decisions, and artifact details. CloudTrail logs all CodePipeline API calls including StartPipelineExecution with the triggering principal. Together they provide a complete deployment audit trail.

explanation: D is correct: CodePipeline retains per-pipeline execution history with each execution's stage and action states, start and end times, action outcomes, the manual approval's approver, comment and timestamp, and the source revision and artifact identifiers that flowed through. CloudTrail independently records every API call including StartPipelineExecution and PutApprovalResult with the calling IAM principal, source IP and time. Together they answer who, what, which approval and when, with nothing to build. A is incorrect because CodePipeline does not natively write execution logs to CloudWatch Logs — that requires EventBridge or notification rules plus a Lambda writer, so the option describes a capability that does not exist as stated. B is incorrect because it builds a parallel audit store, with a DynamoDB TTL that actively deletes audit records, duplicating data the service already retains authoritatively. C is incorrect because Config records resource configuration, so it captures edits to the pipeline definition; executions are events, not configuration items, and never appear on the Config timeline.

stem: A company runs a web application on an Auto Scaling group whose health check type is already set to ELB, behind an Application Load Balancer. Instances are repeatedly marked unhealthy, terminated, and replaced, yet the application team reports that every instance serves real user traffic correctly for as long as it is alive. The Auto Scaling group's health check grace period is 900 seconds and instances finish initializing in about 3 minutes, but targets are deregistered roughly 20 minutes after launch. Target group monitoring shows the health check requests are connecting successfully with no timeouts, and an engineer who curls the configured health check path and port receives an HTTP 302 redirect to the login page while the application is serving traffic normally. The constant churn is causing service disruption. What is the most likely cause and fix?

options.text: The instance's security group blocks the health check traffic from the load balancer. Fix by adding an inbound rule to the instance security group that allows traffic from the load balancer's security group on the health check port, enabling the ELB to reach the health check endpoint.

The ELB health check path returns a non-200 status code when the application is healthy. Fix by updating the health check path to an endpoint that returns HTTP 200 when the application is ready, and configuring the health check to accept the correct HTTP response code range.

The Auto Scaling group is using EC2 status checks instead of ELB health checks. Fix by switching to ELB health checks which verify application-level health. EC2 status checks only verify hardware and system-level health, missing application-level issues.

The health check grace period is shorter than the application startup time. Fix by increasing the health check grace period to exceed the application's full initialization time, preventing Auto Scaling from marking instances as unhealthy before they finish starting up.

explanation: Option B is correct. The evidence shows the health check reaches the instance but the configured path answers with HTTP 302, a redirect to the login page. An ALB target group counts only responses inside its configured matcher range - HTTP 200 by default - as healthy, so a 302 marks the target unhealthy; the target group deregisters it, and because the Auto Scaling group uses the ELB health check type it terminates and replaces the instance. The fix is to point the health check at an unauthenticated readiness endpoint that returns 200, or to widen the accepted success codes to include the redirect. Option A fails because a security group block would appear as connection timeouts and no instance would ever pass a health check or serve traffic; the stem states the checks connect successfully and instances serve users for roughly 20 minutes first. Option C fails because the group is already configured with the ELB health check type, so there is nothing to change and the diagnosis does not match the stated configuration. Option D fails because the 900-second grace period is far longer than the roughly 3-minute startup, and terminations occur about 20 minutes after launch - long after any grace period would have expired - so startup timing cannot be the cause.

stem: A company needs to implement automated compliance scanning that validates their AWS environment against the CIS AWS Foundations Benchmark. The scanning must run continuously and provide a compliance score with details on which controls pass and fail. Which service provides CIS benchmark compliance evaluation?

options.text: Enable AWS Security Hub with the CIS AWS Foundations Benchmark security standard. Security Hub continuously evaluates AWS resources against CIS controls using automated security checks. The compliance dashboard shows overall score and per-control pass/fail status with remediation guidance.

Configure AWS Config conformance packs using the CIS AWS Foundations Benchmark conformance pack template. The conformance pack deploys Config rules that evaluate resources against CIS controls and provides a compliance dashboard showing per-rule compliance status across all resources.

Deploy AWS Audit Manager with the CIS AWS Foundations Benchmark assessment framework. Audit Manager collects evidence from Config, CloudTrail, and Security Hub to assess compliance against each CIS control. It generates audit-ready reports with evidence attachments for compliance documentation.

Run Amazon Inspector CIS benchmark assessments on all EC2 instances. Inspector evaluates instance configurations against CIS Operating System benchmarks for Linux and Windows. The findings show which CIS controls pass and fail at the operating system configuration level.

explanation: A is correct: Security Hub ships the CIS AWS Foundations Benchmark as a built-in standard. Enabling it activates the controls, which are evaluated continuously by Config-backed detective checks as configurations change, and Security Hub presents a per-standard security score plus PASSED/FAILED status and remediation guidance for every control, aggregated across accounts and Regions via Organizations. B is incorrect only in degree: a Config conformance pack deploys CIS-aligned rules and shows rule-level compliance, but it reports raw rule results without a benchmark score or per-control remediation guidance, and it is the evaluation layer Security Hub already orchestrates. C is incorrect because Audit Manager assembles evidence for point-in-time audit reports against a framework — an evidence-collection tool, not a continuously scored compliance dashboard. D is incorrect because Inspector's CIS scans target operating system hardening benchmarks inside EC2 instances, a different benchmark family from the account-level CIS AWS Foundations Benchmark.

stem: A company needs to implement a multi-account infrastructure deployment strategy using CloudFormation. They have a management account, a shared services account, and 20 workload accounts. VPC configurations must be deployed consistently across all workload accounts. Which TWO CloudFormation features enable this multi-account deployment? (Select TWO.)
