Option B fails because it moves the decision outside the cluster - Container Insights metrics arrive with delay, and a Lambda function shelling out to kubectl rollout undo needs cluster credentials and network reachability, which is slower and more fragile than an in-cluster controller. Option D fails because progressDeadlineSeconds and minReadySeconds only detect pods that never become Ready; pods that start cleanly and then return 5% errors pass their readiness probes, and Kubernetes performs no automatic rollback based on application error rate.

stem: A company needs to implement a solution that automatically generates IAM policies based on actual service usage. The team wants to replace overly permissive wildcard policies with least-privilege policies that only include the permissions actually used by each role. Which service generates usage-based IAM policies?

options.text: Configure AWS Config with the iam-policy-no-statements-with-full-access rule. Config identifies IAM policies with wildcard actions. For each flagged policy, manually review the associated role's CloudTrail activity to determine which specific permissions are needed and create a replacement policy.

Enable IAM Access Analyzer policy generation. Access Analyzer reviews CloudTrail logs for the last 90 days to identify the actual AWS service actions and resources used by each IAM role. It generates a least-privilege policy based on observed activity that can replace the existing overly permissive policy.

Enable AWS CloudTrail and query the trail logs to manually identify which API actions each IAM role has called. Create custom IAM policies that include only the observed API actions and resource ARNs. Replace the wildcard policies with the custom least-privilege policies.

Use IAM Access Analyzer to review existing IAM policies for findings about overly permissive access. Access Analyzer identifies policies that grant access to external principals or unused permissions. Use the findings to manually reduce policy permissions to the minimum required.

explanation: B is correct: IAM Access Analyzer policy generation reads CloudTrail for a specified role over a period of up to 90 days, determines which services and actions were actually called and, for supported services, which resource ARNs were touched, and emits a ready-to-review least-privilege IAM policy scoped to that observed activity. That is exactly the usage-based policy generation the question asks for. A is incorrect because that Config rule only flags policies containing wildcard actions: it yields a compliance finding, while reading CloudTrail, choosing the action set and authoring the replacement policy all remain manual. C is incorrect because querying trails by hand is precisely what policy generation automates; at scale it is slow and error-prone, since eventName values must be mapped to IAM actions and resource ARNs by the engineer. D is incorrect because it conflates different Access Analyzer features: external-access and unused-access findings report that permissions are unused or that a resource is reachable externally, but they produce findings rather than a generated replacement policy.

stem: A company uses CloudFormation to deploy EKS clusters and needs to run kubectl commands as part of the stack deployment to create Kubernetes resources (namespaces, RBAC roles, ConfigMaps). CloudFormation doesn't natively support Kubernetes resource creation. Which approach deploys Kubernetes resources through CloudFormation?

options.text: Deploy Helm charts containing the Kubernetes resources using a CloudFormation custom resource that invokes the Helm CLI. The custom resource Lambda installs Helm, authenticates to the EKS cluster, and runs helm install to create the namespaces, RBAC roles, and ConfigMaps from the chart.

Add a CodeBuild project as a CloudFormation resource that runs kubectl commands after the EKS cluster is created. The CodeBuild buildspec configures kubeconfig and creates Kubernetes resources. Use DependsOn to ensure the CodeBuild project runs after the cluster is fully provisioned.

Create a Lambda-backed custom resource that uses the Kubernetes Python client library. The custom resource Lambda function authenticates to the EKS cluster using the aws-iam-authenticator and creates Kubernetes resources based on the properties passed from the CloudFormation template.

Use the AWSQS::Kubernetes::Resource custom CloudFormation resource type from the CloudFormation Public Registry. This registered type allows defining Kubernetes resources directly in CloudFormation templates and handles authentication, creation, update, and deletion of Kubernetes objects.

explanation: Option D is correct. AWSQS::Kubernetes::Resource is an AWS-published extension in the CloudFormation Public Registry that any account can activate in any Region where it is offered. Once activated, namespaces, RBAC objects, and ConfigMaps are declared as ordinary template resources, and the type's handlers authenticate to the cluster and perform create, update, and delete, so the Kubernetes objects participate in the stack lifecycle and are removed when the stack is deleted. Option C is the closest runner-up but is inferior: a Lambda with the Kubernetes client reimplements exactly this capability, leaving the team to own packaging, aws-iam-authenticator wiring, VPC access to a private cluster endpoint, response signalling to the pre-signed URL, and correct update and delete semantics that the registry type already provides and AWS maintains. Option B fails because a CodeBuild project resource is only a definition - CloudFormation creating it does not run a build, DependsOn does not trigger one, and anything a build does create lives outside the stack and is never cleaned up on delete. Option A fails because bundling Helm into a custom resource adds a chart, release state, and a CLI runtime to maintain for a handful of primitive objects.

stem: A company needs to ensure that their Lambda function can handle sudden traffic spikes of 10x normal load. The function currently experiences throttling during spikes because the burst concurrency limit is reached before auto-scaling can provision additional execution environments. Which Lambda configuration handles traffic bursts?

options.text: Deploy Lambda on a dedicated compute environment using Lambda SnapStart (for Java) or container image optimization. SnapStart reduces cold start time to under 200ms, allowing Lambda to scale faster during traffic spikes by initializing new execution environments more quickly.

Request an increase in the Lambda regional burst concurrency limit through a service quota request. The default burst limit of 500-3000 (depending on region) may be insufficient for 10x traffic spikes. A higher burst limit allows more concurrent executions to start simultaneously.

Implement an SQS queue in front of the Lambda function to buffer traffic spikes. Configure the SQS-Lambda event source mapping with a maximum batching window and batch size. SQS absorbs the traffic spike while Lambda processes messages at its available concurrency rate.

Configure provisioned concurrency for the Lambda function at a level matching the expected peak traffic. Provisioned concurrency pre-initializes execution environments that are always ready to handle requests, eliminating cold starts and throttling during sudden traffic spikes.

explanation: D is correct: provisioned concurrency pre-initializes and keeps warm a configured number of execution environments that have already completed INIT. Requests up to that number are served immediately and are not subject to the concurrency scaling ramp, so a 10x spike lands on environments that already exist rather than demanding a burst of new ones. Application Auto Scaling on the provisioned concurrency utilization metric keeps the level tracking demand. A is incorrect because SnapStart and leaner images shorten each new environment's initialization, but the throttling here comes from the rate at which Lambda will create additional environments, and faster init does not raise that rate. B is incorrect because the burst/concurrency scaling rate is a fixed per-function, per-Region behavior that AWS does not raise through a quota request; the adjustable quota is total account concurrency, which is a different limit and is not what is being hit. C is incorrect because fronting the function with SQS converts synchronous requests into asynchronous batch processing: it protects the backend but adds queueing latency and cannot serve a real-time 10x request spike.

stem: A company needs to implement infrastructure drift detection as part of their CI/CD pipeline. Before any deployment, the pipeline must verify that the current state of infrastructure matches the expected state defined in the IaC templates. If drift is detected, the deployment must be blocked until drift is resolved. Which pipeline stage detects infrastructure drift?

options.text: Add a CodeBuild stage that runs terraform plan and checks for unexpected differences between the current state and the desired configuration. If terraform plan shows changes not related to the current deployment, the stage fails indicating drift that must be resolved before proceeding.

Add a Lambda invoke stage that compares the current resource configurations (retrieved via describe APIs) against the expected configurations stored in a DynamoDB baseline table. If differences are detected, the stage fails and publishes the drift report to SNS for resolution.

Add a CodeBuild stage that runs AWS Config compliance checks on all infrastructure resources. If any Config rules show non-compliant resources that should be compliant according to the IaC templates, the stage fails indicating configuration drift that requires investigation.

Add a CodeBuild stage that calls CloudFormation DetectStackDrift for all stacks managed by the pipeline. Parse the drift detection results and fail the pipeline if any resources show MODIFIED or DELETED drift status, blocking deployment until the drift is manually resolved.

explanation: A is correct: terraform plan refreshes state against the live AWS resources and diffs the result against the configuration, so it surfaces out-of-band changes and intended changes together. Running it as a gate with -detailed-exitcode, which returns 2 when a diff exists, lets the CodeBuild stage fail the pipeline whenever the plan contains anything beyond the change being deployed, and since this estate is Terraform-managed its state is the authoritative baseline. B is incorrect because a DynamoDB baseline table is a second, hand-maintained copy of desired state that must be updated after every legitimate deployment and will inevitably diverge from the real state file. C is incorrect because Config rules test whether resources satisfy compliance conditions such as encrypted or not public, which is a different question from whether live configuration matches the template: a resource can be fully compliant and badly drifted. D is incorrect because DetectStackDrift only covers CloudFormation-managed stacks, cannot see Terraform-managed resources, is asynchronous with per-account rate limits, and does not support every resource type and property.

stem: A company needs to implement a disaster recovery testing program that validates their DR procedures quarterly without affecting production. The tests must verify that applications can be restored in the DR region and that data integrity is maintained, and no test may change production routing, production data, or production replication. Which TWO approaches enable non-disruptive DR testing? (Choose two.)

options.text: Perform an actual Route 53 failover to the DR region during a maintenance window. Run the production workload from the DR region for 1 hour, validating all functionality. Then fail back to the primary region by switching Route 53 routing back to the original endpoints.

Create Aurora Global Database clones in the DR region for testing. Aurora cloning creates a copy of the database using copy-on-write without affecting the production database performance. Test application connectivity and data integrity against the clone, then delete it after validation.

Use AWS Fault Injection Service (FIS) to simulate an AZ failure in the production region. Verify that the application automatically fails over to the DR region as expected. Monitor the failover process and validate that data consistency is maintained throughout the simulated failure.

Use AWS Elastic Disaster Recovery (DRS) to maintain continuous replication of production EC2 instances. Launch DR drill instances in the DR region from the replicated data without affecting production replication. Validate application functionality on the drill instances and terminate them after testing.

Restore the most recent RDS automated snapshot directly over the production database cluster in the primary region during the quarterly test window, then run integration tests against it. Because the snapshot and the running cluster hold the same data, the restore proves both recoverability and data integrity.

explanation: Options B and D are correct. Option D uses AWS Elastic Disaster Recovery's drill capability: launching drill instances in the DR Region from the continuously replicated data proves that servers boot and applications run there, and AWS explicitly keeps replication from production running untouched during a drill, so nothing in production is affected and the drill instances are simply terminated afterwards. Option B uses Aurora cloning, which creates a copy-on-write clone sharing the source cluster's storage rather than copying it, so connectivity, schema, and data integrity can be validated against real data with no impact on production performance, and the clone is deleted when the test ends. Option A fails because an actual Route 53 failover moves live customer traffic into the DR Region, which is production impact regardless of the maintenance window, and it changes production routing - explicitly out of bounds. Option C fails because FIS injects the fault into the production Region against production workloads, which is a legitimate resilience exercise but a disruptive one, and an AZ failure validates zonal behavior rather than regional restore. Option E fails and is actively dangerous: restoring a snapshot over the production cluster destroys current production data and takes the database offline for the duration of the restore.

stem: A company needs to enforce that all Lambda functions in their organization use specific VPC configurations and cannot access the public internet directly. Functions must only communicate through VPC endpoints and private subnets. Which enforcement mechanism ensures Lambda VPC compliance?

options.text: Create an SCP that denies lambda:CreateFunction and lambda:UpdateFunctionConfiguration unless the VpcConfig parameter includes approved subnet IDs and security group IDs. The SCP condition keys validate that Lambda functions are configured with the required VPC settings.

Create CloudFormation Hooks that validate Lambda function VPC configuration before provisioning. The hooks check that all AWS::Lambda::Function resources include VpcConfig with approved subnet and security group references, blocking creation of non-VPC Lambda functions.

Deploy Lambda functions exclusively through a Service Catalog product that pre-configures VPC settings. Deny direct lambda:CreateFunction API access for developers through IAM policies, forcing all Lambda creation through the governed Service Catalog provisioning workflow.

Configure AWS Config with a custom rule that evaluates whether Lambda functions have VPC configuration with approved subnets and security groups. Enable auto-remediation that updates non-compliant functions with the required VPC configuration using an SSM Automation document.

explanation: A is correct: Lambda publishes request-level condition keys, notably lambda:VpcIds, lambda:SubnetIds and lambda:SecurityGroupIds, that IAM evaluates on CreateFunction and UpdateFunctionConfiguration. An SCP denying those actions unless the request carries approved subnet and security group IDs is enforced before the API executes and applies to every principal in every member account, including developers, CI/CD roles, CloudFormation service roles and root, so no tool choice can bypass it. B is incorrect because CloudFormation Hooks fire only for CloudFormation and CDK provisioning: a function created via the console, CLI, SDK or Terraform never encounters one. C is incorrect because Service Catalog plus an IAM deny governs the humans, but the Service Catalog launch role and any pipeline role still hold lambda:CreateFunction, and identity-based denies must be attached to and maintained on every principal. D is incorrect because a Config rule is detective: the non-compliant function exists and can be invoked with internet access until remediation runs, and forcibly rewriting VpcConfig can break the function instead of preventing the mistake.

stem: A company uses Terraform with a remote S3 backend and needs to recover from a corrupted state file. The state file was accidentally overwritten with invalid content, and terraform plan shows all resources as needing creation (which would duplicate existing infrastructure). How should the team recover the Terraform state?

options.text: Delete the corrupted state file and run terraform init to reinitialize the backend. Then run terraform plan to discover existing resources. Terraform's reconciliation engine will detect existing resources and create a new state file that matches the deployed infrastructure.

Deploy new infrastructure using terraform apply --target for each resource. After creating duplicate resources, import the original resource IDs using terraform state push with a manually constructed state file that maps resource addresses to the original AWS resource identifiers.

Use terraform import to re-import all existing resources into a new empty state file. For each resource in the Terraform configuration, run terraform import with the resource address and AWS resource ID. This rebuilds the state file from the actual infrastructure.

Restore the previous version of the state file from S3 bucket versioning. The S3 backend bucket should have versioning enabled. Use the S3 console or CLI to restore the state file to the last known good version. Run terraform plan to verify the restored state matches actual infrastructure.

explanation: D is correct: the S3 backend is normally hosted on a versioned bucket precisely for this failure. Listing the object's versions and restoring the last good version to the current key recovers the complete state, every resource address, ID, attribute and dependency, in a single operation, and a subsequent terraform plan reporting no changes confirms it matches the deployed infrastructure. A is incorrect because it describes behavior Terraform does not have: init only configures the backend, and plan against an empty state reports every resource as to-be-created. Terraform never discovers or adopts existing infrastructure on its own. B is incorrect because deliberately creating duplicate resources causes an outage and unnecessary cost, and hand-building a state file to push afterwards is the riskiest possible recovery path. C is incorrect because re-importing is a legitimate fallback only when no backup exists: it is one command per resource instance, including every count and for_each element, with provider-specific ID formats, and any resource missed is left unmanaged and recreated on the next apply.

stem: A company needs to implement a pipeline that automatically creates hotfix branches, applies critical patches, and deploys hotfixes to production bypassing the normal staging environment testing. The hotfix pipeline must still run unit tests and security scans. Which pipeline design supports hotfix deployments?

options.text: Configure the existing production pipeline with a conditional stage that detects hotfix branch patterns. When a hotfix branch triggers the pipeline, the condition skips the staging deployment and testing stages. The pipeline proceeds directly from build/test to production deployment.

Create a separate CodePipeline for hotfixes triggered by commits to hotfix/* branches. The pipeline includes source, CodeBuild (unit tests + security scan), manual approval, and direct production deployment stages. The staging environment stage is omitted for faster hotfix delivery.

Modify the existing pipeline to add a fast-track parallel path. When a hotfix commit is detected, both the normal path (staging + production) and the fast-track path (tests + production) execute simultaneously. The fast-track deploys to production while staging validation continues.

Create a Step Functions workflow triggered by a manual API call for hotfix scenarios. The workflow runs CodeBuild for tests and scanning, creates a change set for production deployment, waits for approval, and executes the deployment. This bypasses the normal CodePipeline entirely.

explanation: B is correct: a dedicated pipeline triggered on hotfix/* keeps the mandatory gates (build, unit tests, security scan, manual approval) while simply not containing a staging stage. The shortened path is explicit and auditable, each pipeline stays a simple linear definition, and the normal release pipeline's behavior is unchanged. A is incorrect because CodePipeline has no native branch-conditional skip: emulating one requires a Lambda action that force-succeeds or trigger/rule gymnastics, producing a pipeline whose executed path varies per run and whose execution history is hard to interpret or audit. C is incorrect because running the fast-track and normal paths simultaneously updates production while staging validation is still in flight, so the validation result arrives only after the risk has already been taken. D is incorrect because a Step Functions workflow can technically perform the steps, but abandoning CodePipeline for the highest-risk deployments discards the artifact store, source integration, approval actions and release history, and it requires a manual API call rather than a branch push.

stem: A company runs a WebSocket-based real-time application on ECS behind an ALB. During deployments, active WebSocket connections are dropped when old tasks are terminated. Users experience disconnections and must manually reconnect. How should the team handle WebSocket connections during ECS deployments?

options.text: Switch from ALB to Network Load Balancer for WebSocket traffic. NLB maintains long-lived TCP connections with connection draining that keeps existing connections active during target deregistration. Configure a deregistration delay matching the WebSocket session duration.

Configure the ALB target group with a long deregistration delay (3600 seconds) matching the maximum WebSocket session duration. During deployment, the ALB stops sending new WebSocket connections to draining tasks while existing connections continue until they naturally close or the delay expires.

Configure ECS with a lifecycle hook that sends a close frame to all active WebSocket connections before task termination. The application notifies connected clients about the pending shutdown, allowing them to gracefully reconnect to a new task before the old task is terminated.

Implement WebSocket reconnection logic in the client application with exponential backoff. When the server closes the WebSocket connection during deployment, the client automatically reconnects to a new healthy task. Session state is preserved in ElastiCache for seamless reconnection.

explanation: B is correct: a WebSocket is a single long-lived TCP connection upgraded from HTTP. When ECS deregisters a task, the target enters draining: the ALB sends it no new connections but keeps established ones open until they close or the deregistration delay expires. Raising that delay toward the 3600-second maximum, with the ECS service's stopTimeout set to match, lets existing sessions finish naturally while new sessions land on the replacement tasks. A is incorrect because NLB is no better here: it also honors a deregistration delay, does not gracefully close TCP targets, and giving up the ALB forfeits host/path routing, WAF integration and HTTP-level features for no gain. C is incorrect because ECS has no per-connection lifecycle hook. The available mechanism is SIGTERM plus stopTimeout, and the option still deliberately closes live connections, which is the disconnection the requirement is trying to avoid; it is a useful complement to draining, not a replacement. D is incorrect because client reconnect with backoff is sound defensive engineering but accepts the drop and the resulting gap in a real-time stream rather than preventing it.

stem: A company needs to implement synthetic monitoring that verifies their e-commerce checkout flow works end-to-end. The synthetic test must simulate a user adding items to a cart, entering payment information, and completing a purchase. The test must run every 10 minutes from multiple regions. Which AWS service provides multi-step synthetic monitoring?

options.text: Deploy API Gateway health checks that call the checkout API endpoints in sequence: add-to-cart, create-order, process-payment. Each health check validates the HTTP response code and response body. Route 53 health checks aggregate the results from multiple geographic locations.

Deploy Lambda functions in multiple regions that call the e-commerce API endpoints to simulate the checkout flow. Each function runs the complete API call sequence every 10 minutes via EventBridge scheduled rules. Functions publish success/failure metrics to CloudWatch for alarming.

Configure CloudWatch RUM to capture real user checkout flows. RUM collects performance data from actual user sessions including page load times and JavaScript errors. Create CloudWatch alarms on the checkout completion rate to detect when the flow is broken for real users.

Configure CloudWatch Synthetics canaries with a blueprint that uses a headless Chromium browser to simulate the checkout flow. The canary script navigates through cart, payment, and confirmation pages, validating each step. Run the canary from multiple AWS regions on a 10-minute schedule.

explanation: D is correct: CloudWatch Synthetics canaries run a Puppeteer or Playwright script in headless Chromium, so one canary can add to cart, complete the payment form, submit and assert on the confirmation page as a genuine multi-step journey including client-side JavaScript. Canaries support rate and cron schedules for the 10-minute interval, are created per Region so the same canary deployed in several Regions gives geographic coverage, and capture screenshots, HAR files and per-step duration/success metrics on failure. A is incorrect because API Gateway has no health check feature and Route 53 health checks are independent single requests: they cannot carry a cart or order ID from one step to the next, so no flow is tested. B is incorrect because a hand-written Lambda prober can chain API calls but reimplements the canary runtime (retries, artifact capture, metric publication) and never exercises the browser layer where much of a checkout actually breaks. C is incorrect because RUM is passive real-user monitoring: it reports what customers already experienced, so it detects a broken checkout only after real users hit it and reports nothing during quiet periods.

stem: A company needs to implement an automated process that collects and preserves evidence when a security incident is detected. The evidence must include memory dumps, disk images, network captures, and running process lists from affected EC2 instances. Which AWS service facilitates automated forensic evidence collection?

options.text: Enable EC2 instance store snapshots that capture the complete machine state including memory contents. When a security incident is triggered, an automated Lambda function creates an instance store snapshot that preserves the running processes, network connections, and memory state for analysis.

Configure Amazon Inspector with deep inspection enabled. When Inspector detects a security finding, it automatically collects process lists, network connections, and installed software inventory from the affected instance. The collected data is stored as Inspector findings for forensic analysis.

Deploy AWS Elastic Disaster Recovery (DRS) with continuous replication for critical instances. When a security incident is detected, use DRS to create a point-in-time recovery instance in an isolated forensic VPC. Analyze the recovered instance without affecting the production environment or evidence.

Create an SSM Automation document that orchestrates evidence collection from affected instances. The document runs SSM Run Command to capture running processes and memory dumps, creates EBS snapshots for disk forensics, and stores all evidence in a dedicated forensic S3 bucket with Object Lock.

explanation: D is correct: forensic capture is an ordered multi-step workflow and SSM Automation is the orchestrator for it. One document can isolate the instance, invoke Run Command to capture volatile state (process list, network connections, loaded modules, and a memory image via a tool such as LiME or avml), call CreateSnapshot on each attached EBS volume for disk imaging, and copy every artifact into a dedicated forensic S3 bucket with Object Lock so the evidence is immutable and defensible. A is incorrect because there is no such thing as an instance store snapshot: instance store volumes cannot be snapshotted and their contents are lost on stop or terminate, and no AWS snapshot mechanism captures RAM. B is incorrect because Inspector produces vulnerability and software inventory findings (CVEs, package versions, network reachability); it is a posture assessment tool, cannot be aimed at an instance on demand for an incident, and collects no memory or disk image. C is incorrect because Elastic Disaster Recovery replicates disks for recovery, so a launched instance yields a disk copy but no memory or live process state, and DRS provides no chain-of-custody or immutable evidence store.

stem: A company needs to implement session management for their web application that uses ALB with Amazon Cognito authentication. Sessions must expire after 1 hour of inactivity and must be invalidated when the user's group membership changes in the Cognito user pool. Which session configuration enforces these requirements?

options.text: Configure the ALB authentication action with a session timeout of 3600 seconds and session cookie attributes that enforce the inactivity timeout. Implement a Cognito pre-token-generation Lambda trigger that checks group membership and denies token generation if the user's groups have changed.

Configure Cognito user pool token settings with an ID token expiration of 1 hour and a refresh token expiration of 1 hour. When group membership changes, use Cognito AdminUserGlobalSignOut to invalidate all tokens for the affected user, forcing re-authentication on the next request.

Configure the ALB authentication action to validate tokens on every request rather than using session cookies. Set the ID token expiration to 1 hour in Cognito. When group membership changes, revoke the user's tokens using the Cognito RevokeToken API to force immediate re-authentication.

Store session state in ElastiCache for Redis keyed by the ALB session cookie, with a 3600-second TTL that application middleware refreshes on every validated request so the session expires only after an hour of inactivity. An EventBridge rule on AdminAddUserToGroup and AdminRemoveUserFromGroup CloudTrail events invokes a Lambda function that deletes that user's Redis session entries immediately.

explanation: Option D is correct because it is the only design that satisfies both requirements. An inactivity timeout needs a sliding expiration, which the Redis session provides: middleware refreshes the 3600-second TTL on every validated request, so the session dies only after a full hour with no activity. Immediate invalidation on group change needs an out-of-band kill switch, which the EventBridge rule on the AdminAddUserToGroup and AdminRemoveUserFromGroup CloudTrail events supplies by deleting that user's session entries, so the very next request is rejected no matter what token the browser still holds. Option B fails on both counts: Cognito ID and refresh token validity are absolute lifetimes measured from issuance, not idle timers, so a session ends one hour after sign-in regardless of activity, and AdminUserGlobalSignOut revokes only refresh tokens - already-issued access and ID tokens, and the AWSELBAuthSessionCookie the ALB minted, stay usable until they expire. Option A fails because the ALB session timeout is likewise an absolute cookie lifetime, and a pre-token-generation trigger runs only when a token is minted, so it cannot affect a session already in flight. Option C fails because ALB authentication cannot be made to re-authenticate against the IdP on every request, and RevokeToken also invalidates only the refresh token.

stem: A company uses AWS CDK and needs to deploy a cross-region stack where an ACM certificate is created in us-east-1 (required for CloudFront) while the main application resources are deployed in eu-west-1. CDK stacks are deployed to a single region. Which CDK pattern handles cross-region resource deployment?

options.text: Create two separate CDK apps: one for the certificate in us-east-1 and one for the main application in eu-west-1. Deploy the certificate app first and manually copy the certificate ARN to the main app's configuration. Deploy the main app with the hardcoded certificate ARN.

Create a single CDK stack deployed to eu-west-1. Use a CloudFormation custom resource within the stack that creates the ACM certificate in us-east-1 by calling the ACM API with the region parameter set to us-east-1. The custom resource returns the certificate ARN for use in the stack.

Deploy the entire CDK application to us-east-1 and use cross-region resource references for the eu-west-1 resources. CloudFormation supports creating resources in different regions within a single stack by specifying the region property on each resource definition.

Create two CDK stacks: a CertificateStack deployed to us-east-1 and a MainStack deployed to eu-west-1. Use CDK's crossRegionReferences feature to automatically create SSM parameters that pass the certificate ARN from the us-east-1 stack to the eu-west-1 stack as a cross-region reference.

explanation: D is correct: a CDK app can contain stacks in different Regions, and setting crossRegionReferences: true on both stacks makes CDK do the plumbing automatically. Because native CloudFormation Export/ImportValue is Region-scoped, CDK writes the us-east-1 CertificateStack's exported value into an SSM parameter and synthesizes custom resources in the eu-west-1 MainStack that read it at deploy time, and cdk deploy orders the stacks by the inferred dependency. A is incorrect because manually copying the ARN breaks the dependency graph: nothing redeploys the consumer when the certificate is replaced, and a hardcoded ARN is an unversioned input to a supposedly reproducible deployment. B is incorrect because a custom resource calling ACM in us-east-1 can work, but you then own the Lambda, its IAM, the create/update/delete semantics and the DNS validation loop, which is needless complexity now that CDK supports cross-Region references natively. C is incorrect on the facts: a CloudFormation stack is created in exactly one Region and resources have no region property; multi-Region deployment requires StackSets or separate stacks.

stem: A company's CI/CD pipeline takes 45 minutes to complete, and developers complain about slow feedback. Analysis shows that the integration test stage takes 30 minutes because tests run sequentially. The test suite has 600 independent integration tests. Which approach reduces the integration test stage duration?

options.text: Move integration tests to a post-deployment stage that runs against the staging environment asynchronously. The pipeline deploys to staging immediately after unit tests pass and triggers integration tests in the background. Developers receive test results via email notification after deployment.

Upgrade the CodeBuild compute type to the largest available instance with more vCPUs and memory. Configure the test runner to execute tests in parallel threads using all available CPU cores. This reduces wall-clock time proportional to the number of available CPU cores on the build instance.

Implement test impact analysis that identifies which tests are affected by the code changes in the current commit. Run only the affected tests instead of the full 600-test suite. This reduces the number of tests executed per pipeline run, decreasing the total test duration.

Configure CodeBuild batch builds with fan-out mode to distribute the 600 tests across 10 parallel build tasks. Each task runs 60 tests independently. A fan-in task aggregates results from all 10 workers and reports the overall pass/fail status to the pipeline.

explanation: D is correct: CodeBuild batch builds in build-fan-out mode start multiple independent build containers from one buildspec, each with its own vCPU, memory and disk. Sharding 600 independent tests across 10 workers turns roughly 30 sequential minutes into about 3, and CodePipeline treats the batch as a single action whose result is the aggregate of all workers, so the quality gate semantics are unchanged. A is incorrect because moving tests after the deploy removes the gate entirely: broken code reaches staging and developers learn by email, which is later feedback and a weaker safety property, not a faster pipeline. B is incorrect because one build host is capped by its core count and shared I/O, and in-process parallelism contends for the same fixtures, ports and test database, so it cannot scale the way independent environments can. C is incorrect because test impact analysis is a genuine optimization but depends on accurate dependency mapping, which integration tests crossing service and data boundaries rarely provide; a wrong mapping silently skips the very test that would have caught the regression.

stem: A company needs to implement a multi-region active-active architecture for their DynamoDB-based API. Both us-east-1 and eu-west-1 must serve read and write requests. When a conflict occurs (simultaneous writes to the same item from both regions), the system must resolve it deterministically. Which DynamoDB feature handles multi-region write conflicts?

options.text: Configure DynamoDB Global Tables which provide active-active multi-region replication. Global Tables use last-writer-wins conflict resolution based on item timestamps. Writes from both regions are accepted and the most recent write (by timestamp) takes precedence for conflict resolution.

Configure DynamoDB Transactions across regions using the TransactWriteItems API. Transactions provide ACID guarantees across multiple items and regions, ensuring that conflicting writes are serialized and only one write succeeds while the other is rejected with a TransactionConflict error.

Deploy DynamoDB tables in both regions with DynamoDB Streams triggering Lambda functions for cross-region replication. Implement custom conflict resolution in the Lambda function that compares item versions and applies business logic to determine which write should win.

Deploy Amazon ElastiCache Global Datastore as a conflict resolution layer. All writes go through ElastiCache first, which serializes requests across regions. After conflict resolution in the cache layer, the resolved write is applied to DynamoDB tables in both regions.

explanation: A is correct: DynamoDB Global Tables provide managed active-active multi-Region replication in which every replica accepts reads and writes and changes propagate to peers typically within a second. Concurrent writes to the same item are resolved deterministically by last-writer-wins using the replication timestamp DynamoDB attaches to each write, so all Regions converge on the same version with no application logic. B is incorrect because TransactWriteItems is scoped to tables in a single Region and account: DynamoDB has no cross-Region transaction, so it cannot serialize a write issued in us-east-1 against one issued in eu-west-1. C is incorrect because Streams plus Lambda is the do-it-yourself version of Global Tables, leaving you to handle replication loops, ordering, retries and your own version comparison, while the Lambda round trip widens the window in which conflicts occur. D is incorrect because ElastiCache Global Datastore has a single active primary Region with read-only secondaries, so it cannot serialize writes originating in two Regions, and putting a cache in the write path adds a failure mode without durability or conflict semantics.

stem: A company needs to implement an observability strategy that provides correlated views of metrics, logs, and traces for troubleshooting. When an alarm fires, operators need to quickly navigate from the alarm to related traces showing which requests failed, then to the specific log entries for those failed requests. Which AWS observability service provides this correlated navigation?

options.text: Deploy Amazon CloudWatch with ServiceLens enabled. ServiceLens integrates CloudWatch metrics, X-Ray traces, and CloudWatch Logs into a unified view. Operators navigate from alarm to service map, drill into X-Ray traces showing failed requests, and click through to correlated CloudWatch Logs entries.

Deploy Amazon OpenSearch Service as a unified observability backend. Stream metrics, logs, and traces to OpenSearch. Use OpenSearch Dashboards to create correlated views that allow operators to pivot between metrics, traces, and logs within a single search and visualization interface.

Deploy a centralized observability dashboard using Amazon Managed Grafana with CloudWatch, X-Ray, and CloudWatch Logs data sources. Configure Grafana panels that link metrics, traces, and logs by correlation ID, enabling operators to navigate between the three signal types.

Configure CloudWatch dashboards with widgets for metrics, Logs Insights queries, and X-Ray trace summaries. Add dashboard annotations for alarm triggers. Operators use the dashboard to manually correlate the time period of the alarm with traces and logs within the same timeframe.

explanation: A is correct: ServiceLens is the CloudWatch feature that stitches the three signals together. Its service map is built from X-Ray traces and annotated with each node's CloudWatch metrics and alarm state; selecting a node opens its latency, error and fault charts, from there you drill into the individual traces behind the failing requests, and each trace segment links directly to the correlated CloudWatch Logs entries by trace ID and time, which is exactly the alarm-to-trace-to-log path required, with no integration to build. B is incorrect because streaming all three signal types into OpenSearch means operating a cluster and hand-building the correlation (index mappings, trace ID joins, dashboards) while duplicating data that already exists in CloudWatch and X-Ray. C is incorrect because Managed Grafana can query all three data sources and supports data links, but the correlation is only as good as the links you configure by hand, and it is an extra managed service and cost for what ServiceLens does natively. D is incorrect because putting widgets on one dashboard places the signals side by side without linking them: the operator still compares timestamps and copies request IDs between widgets, which is the manual correlation to be eliminated.

stem: A company needs to enforce that all CodePipeline pipelines in their organization include a security scanning stage. Pipelines created without a security stage must be detected and flagged. Which governance mechanism ensures pipeline compliance?

options.text: Create an EventBridge rule matching codepipeline:CreatePipeline CloudTrail events. The rule triggers a Lambda function that inspects the newly created pipeline for security scanning stages. If missing, the Lambda disables the pipeline and sends a notification to the DevOps team.

Deploy a CloudFormation Hook that validates CodePipeline resources before provisioning. The hook checks that every AWS::CodePipeline::Pipeline resource includes a stage with security scanning actions. Pipelines without the required stage are blocked from creation.

Create an SCP that denies codepipeline:CreatePipeline unless the pipeline definition includes an action with the category 'Test' or a specific action provider name matching the security scanning tool. The SCP condition evaluates the pipeline structure before creation is allowed.

Create an AWS Config custom rule that evaluates CodePipeline configurations. The rule's Lambda function inspects each pipeline definition for the presence of a security scanning stage (matching specific action names or categories). Non-compliant pipelines are flagged with corrective guidance.

explanation: D is correct: AWS Config records AWS::CodePipeline::Pipeline as a supported resource type, so a custom rule receives the full pipeline configuration item, including its stages and actions, and can assert that some stage contains an action of the expected category or provider. Because Config evaluates both on configuration change and periodically, it catches new pipelines and pipelines whose security stage is later removed, and a non-compliant evaluation is precisely the 'detected and flagged' outcome required, with optional SSM Automation remediation. A is incorrect because CreatePipeline is only one entry point: a pipeline later edited with UpdatePipeline to drop the stage never re-triggers the rule, and auto-disabling a team's pipeline is a disruptive response to a governance finding. B is incorrect because CloudFormation Hooks only see pipelines provisioned through CloudFormation or CDK; pipelines created via console, CLI or Terraform bypass them entirely. C is incorrect because SCP conditions can only test IAM condition keys present on the request, and CodePipeline exposes none describing stage or action structure, so an SCP cannot inspect the pipeline definition.

stem: A company deploys a customer-facing service to Amazon ECS on Fargate behind an Application Load Balancer and needs automated rollback for post-deployment failures. After a new task definition is released and the deployment has completed, if the service's healthy task count stays below the desired count for more than 5 minutes at any point during a 30-minute post-deployment observation window, traffic must automatically revert to the previous task definition. The previous version's tasks must still be running at that moment so the revert is an immediate traffic shift rather than a fresh launch, and the team wants the managed ECS deployment approach that requires the LEAST custom code. Which approach meets these requirements?

options.text: Enable the ECS deployment circuit breaker with rollback on the service. While a rolling deployment is in progress, the circuit breaker counts consecutive task launch and health check failures and, once the threshold of max(min(desiredCount x 0.5, 200), 3) is reached, it marks the deployment failed and rolls back to the last completed deployment.

Configure CloudWatch alarms on the ECS HealthyHostCount metric with a 5-minute evaluation period. The alarm triggers a Lambda function that calls UpdateService with the previous task definition ARN stored in SSM Parameter Store, reverting the service to the last known good version.

Configure an Auto Scaling step scaling policy on the ECS service that increases desired count when healthy task count drops. The scaling policy launches additional tasks with the new task definition. If all tasks are unhealthy, the scaling policy triggers continuous scaling attempts until successful.

Use CodeDeploy blue/green deployment for the ECS service with CloudWatch alarm-based rollback triggers. CodeDeploy maintains the original task set for rollback and automatically reverts traffic when the alarm detects unhealthy tasks during the deployment observation window.

explanation: Option D is correct. The CODE_DEPLOY deployment controller for ECS keeps the original task set running after traffic shifts to the replacement task set and monitors the CloudWatch alarms associated with the deployment group throughout the bake window. If the alarm on healthy task count enters ALARM during that window, CodeDeploy shifts the listener back to the original task set automatically - an immediate traffic revert to tasks that are already running, achieved with configuration rather than custom code. Option A fails because the deployment circuit breaker evaluates only while a deployment is in progress and triggers on a count of consecutive task launch or health check failures - max(min(desiredCount x 0.5, 200), 3) - so once the deployment reaches steady state it stops watching entirely and can never express a condition sustained for 5 minutes after the deployment completed. Option B would work functionally but is exactly the custom rollback machinery the stem excludes: an alarm, a Lambda function, an SSM parameter holding the previous ARN, and the code keeping them consistent; it also relaunches the old revision rather than shifting to running tasks. Option C fails because raising the desired count launches more copies of the faulty revision and never reverts anything.

stem: A company needs to implement a solution that automatically rotates IAM access keys for service accounts used by on-premises applications. The rotation must generate new keys, update the on-premises application configuration, and deactivate old keys without service disruption. Which approach automates service account key rotation?

options.text: Configure AWS IAM Identity Center with temporary credentials for on-premises applications. Identity Center issues short-lived credentials that automatically rotate without explicit key management. On-premises applications use the Identity Center SDK to obtain fresh credentials before each API call.

Implement a Step Functions workflow triggered monthly that orchestrates key rotation for all service accounts. The workflow creates new keys, tests them against a health check endpoint, pushes configuration updates to on-premises applications via AWS Direct Connect, and deactivates old keys after validation.

Deploy a Lambda function on a 90-day schedule that creates new access keys for each service account. The function stores new keys in Parameter Store, sends notification to the application team via SNS to update configurations, waits 7 days, then deactivates old keys to allow transition time.

Create a Secrets Manager secret for each service account's access keys with automatic rotation enabled. The rotation Lambda function creates new access keys via IAM API, stores them in Secrets Manager, updates the on-premises application via SSM Run Command, then deactivates the old keys after confirmation.

explanation: D is correct: Secrets Manager rotation is built for this lifecycle. A rotation Lambda implementing createSecret, setSecret, testSecret and finishSecret calls IAM CreateAccessKey for the new key and stores it as AWSPENDING, pushes it to the on-premises hosts (which are SSM hybrid-activated managed nodes, so Run Command reaches them), verifies the new key works, promotes it to AWSCURRENT and only then deactivates and deletes the old key. IAM's two-keys-per-user limit is what makes the overlap and therefore the zero-downtime cutover possible, and the schedule is managed by Secrets Manager. A is incorrect because IAM Identity Center issues credentials to workforce identities through a sign-in flow; the machine-to-machine equivalent for on-premises servers is IAM Roles Anywhere or SSM hybrid activations, and either way it is a re-architecture rather than rotation of the existing service account keys. B is incorrect because it hand-builds Secrets Manager's rotation state machine, and Direct Connect is a network link, not a configuration distribution mechanism. C is incorrect because it depends on humans updating configuration inside a 7-day window; if they miss it, deactivating the old key causes exactly the service disruption the requirement forbids.

stem: A company needs a blue/green deployment strategy for CloudFormation-managed infrastructure consisting of an ALB, an Auto Scaling group, and an RDS database. Both the blue and green environments must share the same RDS instance. In addition, blue and green must be independently deployable and independently rollback-able: each environment needs its own ALB and its own stack lifecycle, so green can be deployed, validated, or deleted without any stack operation that also touches blue's resources or the database. Which CloudFormation approach implements infrastructure blue/green deployment?

options.text: Create the RDS database in a shared infrastructure stack. Create separate blue and green stacks that reference the shared RDS endpoint via cross-stack references. The blue/green stacks each contain an ALB and ASG. Switch traffic by updating Route 53 weighted records to point to the green ALB.

Use CloudFormation nested stacks with a parent stack containing the ALB and RDS, and child stacks for blue and green ASGs. Deploy updates by replacing the child stack reference from blue to green in the parent. The parent stack routes ALB traffic to the active child stack.

Create a single CloudFormation stack with two ASG resources (blue and green) sharing the same ALB. Deploy the new version to the inactive ASG. After validation, update the ALB listener rule to forward traffic from the blue target group to the green target group for cutover.

Use CloudFormation stack policies that prevent updates to the RDS resource during deployment. Deploy the green environment as additional resources in the same stack. After validation, remove the blue resources using a stack update. The stack policy ensures the RDS is never modified.

explanation: Option A is correct. Placing RDS in its own long-lived stack that exports the endpoint, and giving blue and green their own stacks that each contain an ALB and an ASG and import that endpoint, is the only design that gives each environment a separate stack lifecycle: green can be created, updated, rolled back, or deleted as a stack operation that never touches blue's resources or the shared database, and Route 53 weighted records over the two ALBs provide the cutover and an instant weight-based revert. Option C fails the independence requirement even though the shared-ALB target-group swap it describes is a working blue/green technique in general: with both ASGs in one stack there is one lifecycle, so rolling green back is a stack update that also carries blue's state, and the two environments share a single ALB rather than each having their own. Option B fails because nested child stacks are only ever created, updated, or deleted through the parent, so they are not independently deployable, and any swap is a parent update that includes the shared ALB and RDS in its change set. Option D fails because a stack policy only guards a resource from modification; it supplies no traffic cutover, and blue and green still live in one stack, so removing blue is another update to the same stack.

stem: A company runs a containerized transaction API on ECS Fargate behind an ALB, backed by Aurora MySQL. The architecture must survive the loss of an entire AWS Region. Client traffic is a mix of GET reads and POST and PUT writes, and clients are third-party systems whose DNS caching behavior the company cannot control. Failover of both the request-routing tier and the database tier must be automatic on detected health failure, must complete in roughly 60 seconds, and must not require an operator to take any action. Which TWO components are essential for this multi-region high availability? (Choose two.)

options.text: Deploy Amazon CloudFront with origin groups pointing to ALBs in both regions. CloudFront automatically retries failed requests on the secondary origin when the primary returns errors. This provides application-layer failover without requiring Global Accelerator or Route 53 failover configuration.

Configure Aurora Global Database with the primary cluster in the main region and a secondary cluster in the DR region. Aurora Global Database provides storage-level replication with sub-second lag and supports managed cross-region failover by promoting the secondary cluster to primary.

Configure Route 53 Application Recovery Controller with routing controls for both regions. Recovery Controller provides data plane health checking and routing control that enables operators to manually or automatically fail over traffic between regions using high-availability routing controls.

Deploy ECS Fargate services in both regions behind AWS Global Accelerator with endpoint groups configured for each region. Global Accelerator health checks detect regional failures and automatically route traffic to the healthy region within seconds of detection for instant failover.

Enable Aurora cross-Region automated backup replication so snapshots and transaction logs are continuously copied to the second region. After a regional failure, restore a replacement Aurora cluster in the surviving region from the most recent copied backup and repoint the application.

explanation: Options B and D are correct. Option B, Aurora Global Database, is the only choice that gives the data tier a warm standby: storage-level replication with typically sub-second lag and a managed failover that promotes the secondary cluster, so the surviving Region has a writable database within the time budget. Option D puts the ECS Fargate tier behind AWS Global Accelerator, whose anycast IP addresses are advertised from the edge and whose health checks withdraw an unhealthy endpoint group within seconds; because the client-facing IP addresses never change, cutover does not depend on the third-party clients' DNS caches and needs no operator action. Option A fails because CloudFront origin groups fail over only for GET, HEAD, and OPTIONS requests, so the API's POST and PUT write traffic would keep erroring against the failed origin. Option C fails because Route 53 Application Recovery Controller routing controls are switches that an operator or external automation flips, and the resulting change is delivered as DNS answers subject to resolver caching - neither automatic on health detection nor independent of client DNS. Option E fails because restoring from a copied backup is a cold recovery measured in tens of minutes or longer, far outside the 60-second objective, and it is redundant once Aurora Global Database is in place.
